Agentforce/01-AI-Foundations/atlas-reaso.title: Atlas Reasoning Engine
Agentforce/01-AI-Foundations/atlas-reaso.content:
What It Is
The Atlas Reasoning Engine is the orchestration layer inside Agentforce that drives the agent’s decision loop. It determines which action to call, in what order, and when the task is complete.
Reasoning Loop
Observe (context + user input)
  → Plan (what action to take next?)
    → Act (invoke the action)
      → Observe (result of action)
        → repeat until goal met or max iterations reached


Multi-step: one user message can trigger multiple sequential action calls
Self-correcting: if an action returns an error or unexpected result, the engine can retry or choose an alternative action
Grounded: context window includes retrieved data (Data Cloud, Salesforce records) at each step

Key Behaviours to Know

























BehaviourDetailAction selectionEngine picks actions from the configured topic’s action list based on relevance to the current stateHallucination guardrailsConstrained to configured actions only; cannot invent API callsIteration capConfigurable max reasoning steps to prevent runaway loopsHandoffCan escalate to a human agent in Omni-Channel when confidence is low or user requests it
Grounding

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Knowledge Articles, Data Cloud Unified Profiles, Salesforce records injected into context
Grounding sources configured per topic or per action (e.g., Einstein Search grounding)



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

When asked how to ensure agent responses are accurate and up-to-date, answer: grounding via Data Cloud or Einstein Search + RAG, constrained action set, Einstein Trust Layer. Not fine-tuned models.




                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Atlas Reasoning Engine is not the same as a custom LLM. Customers do not train or fine-tune it. They configure topics, instructions, and actions.

Agentforce/01-AI-Foundations/data-fundam.title: Data Fundamentals for AI
Agentforce/01-AI-Foundations/data-fundam.content:
Trailhead: data-fundamentals-for-ai | +400 pts | ~35 min | Foundational | End User
Data is the foundation for AI. AI systems depend on relevant, accurate, complete, representative, and well-governed data to produce trustworthy outputs.
Units

Learn About Data and AI (~5 min)
Understand Data and Its Significance (~10 min)
Discover AI Techniques and Applications (~10 min)
Know Data Ethics, Privacy, and Practical Implementation (~10 min)

Skills Gained

Artificial Intelligence
Automation
AI Analytics
AI Ethics and Trust

Trails This Appears In

Become an Agentblazer Champion 2026
Learn Data for AI
Get Started with Artificial Intelligence
Gain The AI Skills You Need To Succeed


Why Data Matters

Data includes facts, figures, statistics, documents, images, videos, audio, observations, and other signals that provide insight.
Organizations use data to understand operations, customer behavior, market trends, risks, and opportunities.
Data-driven decision-making relies on analysis instead of intuition or personal experience.
Traditional decision-making can still be useful, but it is more vulnerable to bias and missed opportunities.

Key outcomes of data-driven decision-making:





















BenefitOutcomeBetter insightsFind patterns and correlations that are not obvious otherwiseImproved performanceReduce costs, improve efficiency, and optimize operationsCompetitivenessBuild products and services that better match customer needs
Data Classifications

























ClassificationMeaningExamplesStructuredOrganized in a defined format and easy to search or analyzeSpreadsheets, relational databasesUnstructuredNot organized in a fixed formatText, documents, images, audio, videos, reviews, Slack messagesSemi-structuredHas some structure but may include unstructured elementsXML, JSON
Data can also be grouped by format:

Tabular: rows and columns, such as spreadsheets
Text: emails, reports, documents, messages
Image: logos, charts, photos, infographics
Geospatial: coordinates and map shapes
Time-series: values tracked over time, such as daily stock prices

Data types can be quantitative or qualitative:

Quantitative: numerical data that can be measured and analyzed statistically
Qualitative: non-numerical data such as text, images, videos, reviews, and survey responses

Data Collection and Preparation
Data can come from internal, external, and public sources.

Internal sources: sales data, service data, customer data, operational data
External sources: market research, social media, partner data
Public datasets: open datasets used for analysis or research

Core preparation steps:

Data collection: gather data from relevant sources.
Data labeling: add tags or labels so data is searchable and analyzable.
Data cleaning: remove duplicates, correct errors, fill missing values, and fix inconsistencies.
Exploratory data analysis: inspect patterns, characteristics, and early insights before modeling.

Common collection methods include surveys, interviews, observation, and web scraping.
Data Quality in AI
Data quality directly affects AI model performance, accuracy, fairness, trust, and compliance.
Critical data quality dimensions:

Current
Accurate
Complete
Representative
Relevant
Diverse enough for the target population
Governed according to privacy, security, and legal requirements

Poor data can lead to inaccurate predictions, biased outcomes, weak generalization, low trust, and regulatory risk.


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

For Agentforce, weak data quality can show up as poor grounding, irrelevant answers, incorrect recommendations, or actions being taken from incomplete context.


AI Concepts
Artificial intelligence is a field where computer systems use data to draw inferences, perform tasks, and solve problems with human-like reasoning.
Important AI technologies:

Machine learning: algorithms learn from data to make predictions or decisions.
Deep learning: neural networks find associations between inputs and outputs, often improving with larger datasets.
Natural language processing: systems understand and generate human language.
Large language models: advanced models that understand and generate human-like text.
Computer vision: systems interpret visual information.
Robotics: systems perform physical tasks.

Machine Learning vs Traditional Programming

















ApproachHow It WorksTraditional programmingA programmer defines explicit rules for the system to followMachine learningThe system learns patterns from data and creates models that make predictions or decisions
Machine learning depends on high-quality training data. Common limitations include:

Overfitting: the model is too closely fitted to training data and performs poorly on new data.
Underfitting: the model is too simple and misses important patterns.
Bias: training data does not represent the real-world population or contains systematic errors.
Low transparency: complex models can be hard to explain.
Missing or flawed data: incomplete data weakens predictions and relevance.

Predictive vs Generative AI

























Predictive AIGenerative AIMakes predictions or decisions from existing dataCreates new content such as text, images, video, or audioCommon in fraud detection, medical diagnosis, churn prediction, forecastingCommon in writing, summarization, chat, creative generation, and content assistanceDepends heavily on labeled data qualityCan produce biased, inappropriate, or incoherent content if training data or context is flawedMay struggle outside the patterns it was trained onMay struggle with context, accuracy, and suitability for high-precision use cases
Data Lifecycle for AI
AI data work is iterative. Models should be updated and refined based on new data, feedback, evaluation, and changing business needs.
Stages of the data lifecycle:

Collection: gather data from sensors, systems, surveys, online sources, or business processes.
Storage: store data securely.
Processing: clean, transform, enrich, and prepare the data.
Analysis and use: extract insights or use the data for decisions, policies, or AI models.
Sharing: share data responsibly when needed.
Retention: define how long data should be kept.
Disposal: securely delete or destroy data when it is no longer needed.

Ethics, Privacy, and Fairness
AI and data analysis raise ethical concerns because they can affect people, privacy, and business decisions.
Common ethical issues:

Privacy violations from collecting or using personal data without consent
Data breaches and unauthorized access
Bias in data, algorithms, or decision processes
Unfair or discriminatory outcomes

Privacy and confidentiality strategies:

Encryption
Anonymization
Access controls
Purpose limitation
Consent and confidentiality practices

Bias and fairness strategies:

Diversify data sources.
Improve data quality and representativeness.
Conduct regular bias audits.
Add fairness metrics to decision processes.
Promote transparency and explainability.
Solicit stakeholder feedback.

Regulatory Context
Important legal and regulatory frameworks include:

CCPA: California privacy regulations for companies that collect personal data from California residents.
HIPAA: US healthcare privacy and protected health information rules.
GDPR: EU data protection regulation for personal data of EU residents.
EU AI Act: risk-based AI regulation that bans unacceptable-risk systems and places requirements on high-risk AI applications.

Data Lifecycle Best Practices

Implement data governance policies and procedures.
Conduct regular audits and assessments.
Ensure data is accurate, complete, and representative.
Store data securely and restrict access to authorized users.
Use data only for its intended purpose.
Share data responsibly and ethically.
Apply safeguards for sensitive data.
Define retention policies and securely dispose of data when no longer needed.

Einstein Trust Layer Connection
The Einstein Trust Layer is Salesforce’s secure AI architecture for generative AI and agents. It helps teams use AI while protecting data, privacy, and brand trust.
Relevant controls include:

Secure data grounding with Salesforce context
Sensitive data masking
Data and privacy controls
Trust-focused architecture for generative AI
Safer use of agents and generative features

Agentforce Architecture Lens
For Agentforce implementations, data fundamentals translate into practical architecture questions:

Which data sources ground the agent’s answers?
Is the data structured, unstructured, or semi-structured?
Is the data current, accurate, complete, representative, and governed?
Which permissions and sharing rules apply to grounded data?
What data must be masked, anonymized, encrypted, or excluded?
How will bias, inaccurate outputs, and unsafe recommendations be detected?
What audit trail is required for agent answers and actions?

Agentforce/02-Agentforce-Platform/agentf.title: Agentforce Overview
Agentforce/02-Agentforce-Platform/agentf.content:
What Is Agentforce
Agentforce is Salesforce’s platform for building and deploying autonomous AI agents that can reason, plan, and act across Salesforce data and external systems — without continuous human input.

Built on the Atlas Reasoning Engine (multi-step LLM reasoning loop)
Agents perceive context → decide actions → execute → observe results → repeat
Natively embedded in the Salesforce Platform; respects org data model, sharing rules, and permissions

Key Concepts

































ConceptDescriptionAgentA configured autonomous worker with a role, instructions, and a set of actionsTopicA cluster of related intents/tasks the agent can handle; maps to a system prompt segmentActionA discrete capability the agent can invoke (Flow, Apex, MuleSoft, Prompt Template, etc.)ChannelWhere the agent is deployed (Einstein Bots, Messaging, Experience Cloud, Slack, etc.)Atlas Reasoning EngineThe orchestration layer that decides which action to call and whenEinstein Trust LayerSecurity wrapper: data masking, toxicity filtering, zero-retention with LLM providers
Agent Types

Agentforce Service Agent — autonomous customer-facing support (replaces or augments Einstein Bots)
Agentforce Sales Development Representative (SDR) — outbound prospecting and lead nurturing via email
Agentforce Sales Coach — role-play, deal coaching, call debrief
Custom Agents — purpose-built with Agent Builder for any business process



                  
                  CTA angle 
                  
                

Know the distinction between Agentforce agents (autonomous, multi-step reasoning) and Einstein Bots (rule-based / intent-based dialog flows). The two can co-exist; Agentforce can hand off to or escalate through Omni-Channel.


How Agents Are Built

Define Role & Instructions (system prompt-level guidance)
Create Topics — group related tasks, add natural-language instructions per topic
Attach Actions — each action is an invokable unit (see Actions domain)
Configure Channel and test in Agent Builder preview
Activate and monitor via Agent Analytics

Relationship to Other Platform Capabilities

Uses Data Cloud for grounding when real-time or unified profile data is needed
Uses Prompt Builder for managed prompt templates (with merge fields)
Invokes Flows and Apex as actions — existing automation assets are reusable
Surfaces through Omni-Channel for routing and handoff to human agents
Governed by Einstein Trust Layer for all LLM calls

Agentforce/02-Agentforce-Platform/agentf.title: Agentforce vs Einstein Bots
Agentforce/02-Agentforce-Platform/agentf.content:
Quick Comparison























































DimensionEinstein BotsAgentforce Service AgentDecision modelRule-based dialog flows / NLU intent matchingLLM reasoning (Atlas Engine) — autonomous multi-stepConfigurationBot Builder: dialogs, rules, variablesAgent Builder: topics, instructions, actionsFlexibilityPredictable, scriptedDynamic, handles novel queriesFailure modeFalls back to defined fallback dialogMay produce unexpected responses if instructions are poorEscalationTransfers to Omni-Channel queueTransfers to Omni-Channel queue (same mechanism)Data accessSOQL via bot variables / FlowsActions (Flows, Apex, MuleSoft), grounded retrievalChannel supportMessaging, Chat, Experience CloudMessaging, Experience Cloud, Slack, email, voice (roadmap)Cost modelConversation creditsAgentforce conversations (separate SKU)CoexistenceCan coexist in same orgCan coexist; Agentforce can hand off to Einstein Bot or vice versa
When to Recommend Each
Einstein Bots — use when:

Interactions follow predictable, scripted flows (e.g., password reset, order status lookup with fixed steps)
Strict compliance requires fully deterministic responses
Budget is a constraint and conversation volumes are high

Agentforce Service Agent — use when:

Interactions are varied and require multi-step reasoning
Goal is to deflect more complex cases without scripting every path
Personalisation from unified customer data (Data Cloud) is needed

Both — use when:

Migrating incrementally: keep Einstein Bot for stable high-volume flows, add Agentforce for overflow or complex topics



                  
                  CTA angle 
                  
                

In a board scenario, justify the choice with: complexity of interactions, tolerance for non-determinism, cost, and existing automation investment. Always tie Agentforce back to Data Cloud grounding and Einstein Trust Layer for data security.


Migration Considerations

Existing Einstein Bot dialog flows can be exposed as Agentforce Actions via Flow
NLU intents do not automatically map to Agentforce Topics — need redesign
Test side-by-side with A/B routing before full cutover

Agentforce/03-Agentforce-Builder/agentfo.title: Agentforce Builder Preview — Gotchas & Known Issues
Agentforce/03-Agentforce-Builder/agentfo.content:
Source: PHP Capstone project — tenant-concierge-debug-log.md. Discovered during full restoration of PHP_Tenant_Concierge agent. Verified Spring ‘26 org farm environment.


1. @utils.escalate Is Not Supported in Builder Preview
Symptom: Agentforce Builder preview returns “Something went wrong. Refresh and try again.” with nothing in the Trace tab. Happens even if all other logic is correct.
Root cause: Salesforce explicitly does not support @utils.escalate in Agentforce Builder preview. Calling it crashes the preview session.
Official documentation states:

“You can’t test escalation in Agentforce Builder.”

Diagnosis method: Strip the agent back to a minimal baseline and re-add features one by one until the crash reproduces. The @utils.escalate call will be the last thing added before failure.
Resolution:

Remove @utils.escalate from the agent script entirely for preview purposes.
Replace with a static handoff message in the escalation subagent (e.g. “I’m connecting you to a team member — please hold.”).
The connection messaging block is separate from @utils.escalate and does not cause the crash — it can remain.
For scoring/rubric purposes: the decision logic (business hours check, severity routing, escalation message) is what judges evaluate, not the actual queue transfer. The static message demonstrates all of it.

Important: @utils.escalate may work fine in a live portal session (not preview). The limitation is preview-specific.

2. topic Keyword Is Deprecated — Use subagent
Symptom: Agent publishes without error but exhibits unexpected behavior — wrong routing, missed intents, or actions not triggering.
Root cause: The topic: keyword and @topic. references are deprecated in recent Agentforce versions. The Agent Script runtime silently degrades when deprecated keywords are used.
Resolution: Replace all occurrences:

















DeprecatedCurrenttopic:subagent:@topic.<name>@subagent.<name>
Search the .agent file for topic: and @topic. before debugging any routing or intent issue — this is a quick fix that eliminates a common source of confusion.

3. isExpSiteAuthMode in Experience Cloud Layout
Symptom (setting to true): The chat widget icon disappears entirely from the Experience Cloud site.
Symptom (setting to false): Chat button shows for all users who meet the site’s guest/auth policy. This is the safe default.
What the setting controls: isExpSiteAuthMode in the Experience Cloud site layout content.json (under scopedHeaderAndFooter) controls whether the logged-in user’s identity is automatically passed to the MIAW session.
Behavior matrix:




















ValueChat button visibleIdentity passed to MIAWfalse (default)Yes — for users meeting site policyNo (session is anonymous at MIAW level)trueOnly if org is correctly configured for auth modeYes — via MIAWIdentityTokenService
Practical guidance:

Setting isExpSiteAuthMode: true requires specific org configuration that may not be present in org farm / pc-rnd environments.
Enforce login at the site level instead (areGuestUsersAllowed: false in Network metadata) — the chat button then only shows for authenticated users regardless of isExpSiteAuthMode.
MIAWIdentityTokenService handles identity passing separately and does not depend on isExpSiteAuthMode.
Never change isExpSiteAuthMode without a rollback plan — reverting to false restores the chat button immediately.


4. Live Portal: Agent Joins Then Immediately Transfers (“Transfer Requested”)
Symptom: Authenticated user opens the portal. “PHP Tenant Concierge joined” appears immediately, followed within the same second by “Transfer requested” and “PHP Tenant Concierge left.” The agent never responds to any message.
Why same-second timing matters: LLM + Apex callouts take several seconds. A same-second transfer rules out any agent logic — this is infrastructure-level routing.
Root cause: An Escalation Flow was configured in Connections → Routing → Escalation Flow without an Inbound Routing Flow also configured. Without an Inbound Routing flow, new sessions may fall through to the Escalation Flow for all new sessions, immediately routing to the human queue.
Resolution options:

Configure an Inbound Routing Flow that handles new sessions before the Escalation Flow fires.
Remove the Escalation Flow from the Connections tab temporarily for demo purposes.
Remove @utils.escalate from the agent script (see Issue 1) — if the Escalation Flow still triggers, it will no longer crash the session, but the transfer may still happen if Inbound Routing is misconfigured.

Note for capstone demos: Judges evaluate via Agentforce Builder preview, not live portal transfer behavior. Portal transfer issues are not penalized if the agent logic is demonstrable in preview.

5. Debug Strategy: Binary Elimination Baseline
When Agentforce Builder preview returns a generic error with no trace:

Strip the agent to a minimal baseline (e.g. one subagent, no actions, no escalation).
Confirm baseline works in preview.
Re-add features one phase at a time, previewing after each addition.
The last addition before failure is the root cause.

This approach is significantly faster than reading logs or guessing — it isolates the problem in 3–5 preview cycles.
Phase order that worked for PHP_Tenant_Concierge:

Phase 1: tenant_gate + tenant_hub + basic subagents → stable
Phase 2: check_maintenance_history + off_limits + ambiguous_question → stable
Phase 3: classify_issue_severity (Prompt Template LLM callout) → stable
Phase 4: door_unlock (OTP + email callout) → stable
Phase 5: escalation with @utils.escalate → crashes (root cause found)
Phase 6: connection messaging block (without @utils.escalate) → stable

Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/ag.title: Agentforce and RAG: Best Practices for Better Agents
Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/ag.content:
Source: salesforce.com white paper — covers GA and open beta features. Roadmap items marked #Roadmap.

Comprehensive guide to using unstructured data and RAG on the Agentforce 360 Platform. Covers architecture, content curation, search index design, retriever configuration, prompt engineering, pro-code options, LLM selection, and troubleshooting.

RAG Overview
RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) grounds LLM prompts with accurate, up-to-date enterprise knowledge — files, emails, articles, call notes, object descriptions — retrieved by semantic similarity to a query.
Online runtime flow:

Retriever invoked with dynamic query from prompt template
Query vectorised → semantic search against the search index
Relevant chunks retrieved
Prompt augmented with retrieved content
Resolved prompt submitted to LLM → response generated

Offline preparation:

Connect unstructured data (DSO → DLO/UDLO → DMO/UDMO)
Create search index config → chunk + vectorise content
Store and manage index in Data Cloud

Key components: Search Index → Retriever → Prompt Template → Agent Action

Fastest Path: Agentforce Data Library (ADL)
ADL auto-creates all RAG pipeline components with default settings.

























ComponentDefaultSearch IndexFileUDMO_SI, hybrid search, 512-token chunks, E5 Large MultilingualRetrieverReturns 10 results; advanced retrieval offPrompt Template”Answer Questions with Knowledge” (dynamic retriever)Agent ActionAuto-created, same name as template
ADL supports: Files (Salesforce-managed storage) and Knowledge Articles only.
Use ADL when the use case fits exactly — fast to set up but limited configurability. Use manual setup for other object types or custom chunking/retrieval needs.


                  
                  Ensemble Retriever (ADL with both files + knowledge) 
                  
                

When an ADL has both data sources, an ensemble retriever is auto-created. It merges and dynamically reranks results from both sources, surfacing only the most relevant content. Reduces prompt bloat, latency, and cost. #Roadmap Manual bundling of arbitrary retrievers planned.



Designing RAG-Powered Agents
Approach 1 — One prompt template, multiple sources (ensemble)
Use when all data sources are relevant to most questions, or when it’s hard to distinguish which source to call per question type.
Approach 2 — Separate prompt template per data source
Use when agent instructions can clearly distinguish which action to call per question type, and a single source can fully answer the question.


                  
                  Avoid chaining RAG actions sequentially 
                  
                

Don’t instruct the reasoning engine to call multiple RAG actions in sequence. It may stop early, deeming intent fulfilled before all actions are called.


Both approaches can be combined in the same solution.

Curating Content for RAG
Content quality directly affects retrieval quality. Key guidelines:

Detailed and thorough — more context = better retrieval; include synonyms and abbreviations
Real-world examples — helps retrieval match user query patterns
Well-structured — logical paragraphs, H1–H6 headings (used as chunk delimiters)
Spread over fields — use Description, Resolution, Summary etc. separately in Knowledge Articles
Alt-text on media — images/video are ignored; their descriptions are indexed
Single-topic articles — avoid combining unrelated topics; semantic match degrades
Regular audits — stale/incorrect content leads to hallucinations

Intelligent Context (AI-powered curation workspace)

Interactive workspace in Data Cloud → Process Content → Intelligent Context
Upload sample files, use AI Smart Defaults or manual parsing, test in agent chat, then publish to UDMO
Supports prompt-based customisation (e.g. “Extract the drivetrain table as markdown”)
Supports multiple lenses on the same document (e.g. Sales lens vs Service lens)

Parsing Methods






























FeatureLLM-Based ParsingDocling ParsingApproachSemantic analysis + visual reasoningComputer vision + layout analysisBest forIrregular, messy, scanned docsStructured, born-digital PDFsTable handlingInterprets content meaningReconstructs structural layoutPerformanceSlower (inference heavy)Fast / optimised

Hybrid Search
Combines vector search (semantic similarity) and keyword search (lexical match) in a single call.

Use when: product names, brands, specific terminology, or jargon are critical to retrieval
Don’t use as a standalone keyword search engine for categories (micro-chunks degrade semantic results)
Tradeoff: ~2× Data Cloud credit consumption + increased latency
Popularity and recency ranking factors can be configured in the search index builder


Search Index: Field Selection, Chunking, Vectorisation
Four field roles






























RolePurposeIndex typeIndex fieldsChunked + vectorised; used for semantic searchDMO onlyPrepend fieldsValue prepended to every chunk for context enrichmentDMO onlyFilter fieldsAdded to index schema; used to filter search (not vectorised)DMO + UDMOReturn fieldsReturned with results; can come from index DMO or related DMODMO + UDMO


                  
                  Index field selection rules 
                  
                


Only long-form text fields with at least one semantically coherent sentence
Avoid categorical/picklist fields — micro-chunks break semantic search
Index as few fields as possible; for similar fields, pick the most detailed one
Use prepend fields to add title/summary context to every chunk



Chunking strategy

Max chunk size: 512 tokens (~400–500 words)
Platform uses semantic passage extraction markers, then merges up to configured size
Smaller chunks = better precision; larger chunks = more augmentation context

Enriched Indexing (#Roadmap / coming soon)
Generates three chunk types per original chunk:





















Chunk TypeContentsPLAINOriginal chunk textQUESTIONLLM-generated questions that the chunk answers (improves Q&A recall)METADATALLM-generated keywords, entities, topics, sentiment, title, summary
Prompt augmentation always uses PLAIN chunks; QUESTION/METADATA chunks only improve retrieval.
Embedding Models





















ModelUse whenE5 Large V2 (default)English-only contentE5 Large MultilingualMultilingual content; 100 languages; cross-language retrievalAda 002Used when enriched chunking is on (E5 models incompatible with enriched chunking)

Retriever Configuration
Default retriever
Auto-created for every search index. Returns 10 results. No advanced retrieval.
Custom retrievers (Einstein Studio)

Configure return fields (from index DMO or related DMO)
Configure static or dynamic prefilters
Dynamic prefilter: Account = $placeholder → mapped to a field value in Prompt Builder at runtime



                  
                  Prefilter limitation 
                  
                

Cannot add prefilter fields to an existing search index — must be defined at index creation.


Advanced Retrieval Mode #Roadmap
Iterative retrieval with LLM-based query rewriting:

First retrieval using original query
Summarise results
LLM rewrites query using original + summary
Second retrieval with rewritten query → augment prompt

Use when users enter imprecise or high-level queries.

Prompt Engineering for RAG
A minimal prompt (“answer this question using this information”) leads to hallucinations. The out-of-the-box “Answer Questions with Knowledge” template provides:

Instructions to understand the user question
Explicit grounding instructions (only use provided content)
Fallback when content is insufficient (“Sorry, I can’t find an answer…“)
Output formatting and language instructions



                  
                  Key prompt engineering principles 
                  
                


Explicitly instruct the LLM to use only the provided context
Specify what to do when context is insufficient
Include reasoning and output format instructions
More detailed instructions → less hallucination risk




Citations #Roadmap
Two approaches:

















ApproachDescriptionPlatform-managed (recommended)Auto-formats citations; “Sources” section at response end; inline citations for standard actions; available for agents created after May 26, 2025Instruction-basedCustom prompt instructions for citation format; more context window usage; requires rigorous testing
Setup: Enable citations in the retriever (Einstein Studio), then toggle “Turn on citations” in the Prompt Template’s retriever settings.
Image citations supported — uses image description from enriched processing; appears as external links in agent UI.

Pro-Code RAG (without Retrievers)
Use Apex + Data Cloud Connect API when:

Nested prefilter conditions needed
Post-retrieval filters required (user access checks etc.)
Operators unsupported by no-code retrievers

ConnectApi.CdpQueryInput input = new ConnectApi.CdpQueryInput();
input.sql = 'SELECT ... FROM vector_search(table(MyIndex__dlm), \'' + query + '\', \'\', 50) v ...';
ConnectApi.CdpQueryOutput output = ConnectApi.CdpQuery.queryANSISql(input);


                  
                  Automatic summarisation 
                  
                

If Apex/Flow returns content exceeding the context window, the platform auto-summarises it before passing to the LLM.



RAG in Flow
Flow as the orchestration layer instead of the prompt template.
Standard Flow actions for RAG:

Detect Language — for dynamic language prefilters
Transform Query for Case/Email/Conversation — LLM-based query optimisation (removes greetings, extracts intent)



                  
                  Retriever output in Flow 
                  
                

Retriever output is JSON (not a supported Flow type). Requires an Apex processor action to flatten it to a String before downstream use.



Selecting the Right LLM

















ConsiderationGuidanceContext windowMust accommodate full resolved prompt. GPT-4o/Turbo = 128K tokens; GPT-3.5 = 16K (often insufficient for RAG)Reasoning capabilityFor complex reasoning over retrieved context → stronger model (GPT-4); for simpler retrieval + generation → smaller model acceptable

Debugging and Troubleshooting
Stepwise chain to check:

Agent layer — is the right topic/action selected? Check in Agentforce Builder
ADL layer — is the right retriever/grounding source passed to the prompt template?
Search index layer — run SELECT * on Index DMO; compare record count vs source DMO count
Retriever layer — check result fields, retriever version in Prompt Builder
Prompt resolution — use ?c__debug=1 URL param in Prompt Builder for resolution-only mode (saves cost + time during debugging)

RAG Quality Metrics

























MetricMeasuresDiagnosesContext RelevanceRetrieved content vs queryRetrieval problemsFaithfulnessResponse grounded in context?LLM generation / prompt problemsAnswer RelevanceResponse vs queryOverall RAG quality
Common failure patterns:

Low context relevance + low faithfulness → retrieval problem (wrong content fetched)
High context relevance + low faithfulness → LLM/prompt problem (ignoring context)
High context + high faithfulness + low answer relevance → insufficient context retrieved (increase result count)


Non-Generative RAG Use Cases

Semantic similarity search — surface similar cases/articles to a service agent without generating a response; implement via Flow calling a retriever
Text classification — vectorise labelled training examples; classify new text by majority vote on top-50 similar results (requires Apex for COUNT-based SQL)


Summary: Key Decision Points

































DecisionGuidanceADL vs manual setupADL for files + knowledge only; manual for other objects or custom configOne vs multiple prompt templatesOne if all sources relevant to all queries; separate if agent can route by question typeHybrid vs vector searchHybrid when keywords/jargon matter; pure vector when natural language onlyChunk sizeSmaller = precision; larger = more augmentation context per resultEmbedding modelE5-V2 (English), E5-Multilingual (100 languages), Ada 002 (enriched chunking)Pro-code vs no-code retrievalNo-code for standard cases; Apex when post-filters or complex prefilters needed

Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/co.title: Context Variables: Topic Filtering and Prompt Grounding
Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/co.content:
Available Context Variables















































VariableTypeincludeInPromptNotes$Context.currentObjectApiNamelightning__sObjectInfoTypetrueAPI name of the Salesforce object for the current record. Skip if conversation already references a different object.$Context.currentAppNamelightning__textTypefalseSalesforce application name (e.g. standard__LightningSales). Topic filtering only.$Context.currentRecordIdlightning__recordIdTypetrueID of the record on screen. Only use if user says “this”, “current”, or “the record”.$Context.currentPageTypelightning__textTypefalsePage type (e.g. standard__recordPage). Topic filtering only.$System.LastCustomerInputlightning__textTypefalseLast user message. System variable; auto-populated.$System.isAuthenticatedbooleanfalseWhether the user is authenticated.
Variable Type Taxonomy
Two active types (PageContext and Custom Context Variable are now deprecated and merged in):




















TypePrefixDescriptionSystem Variable$SystemPredefined, auto-populated; cannot be customised. Includes action default values.Context Variable$ContextPredefined; tied to the messaging session (channel session / channel user). Covers former PageContext and Custom Context Variable types.


                  
                  Deprecated prefixes 
                  
                

$PageContext and the old Custom Context Variable category are both merged into $Context. Use $Context for all non-system variables going forward.


includeInPrompt — The Key Flag
Every context variable metadata record has an includeInPrompt boolean:

false → variable is available for topic filtering only; it is excluded from all planner prompts to avoid confusing the LLM.
true → variable is injected into planner prompts as additional context (e.g. page context, current record).

This flag is pre-defined in metadata (not set by the client at runtime), so end-users never need to configure it.
Metadata Shape
{
  "name": "currentRecordId",
  "description": "The Id of the record the user is currently viewing...",
  "type": "lightning__recordIdType",
  "includeInPrompt": true
}
Fields: name, description, type, includeInPrompt, defaultValues (null is valid for topic-filtering-only variables).
How Clients Set Context Variables
Clients (LEX, mobile, headless Copilot) call the setVariables API (Runtime V5.3) at session start or during a continue-session request:
{
  "variables": [
    {
      "name": "$Context",
      "type": "object",
      "value": [
        {
          "name": "currentRecordId",
          "type": "json",
          "value": {
            "name": "currentRecordId",
            "description": "...",
            "type": "lightning__recordIdType",
            "includeInPrompt": true,
            "value": "00D00000000062"
          }
        },
        {
          "name": "currentAppName",
          "type": "json",
          "value": {
            "name": "currentAppName",
            "description": "...",
            "type": "lightning__text",
            "includeInPrompt": false,
            "value": "standard__SalesApp"
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Runtime forwards all context variables to the planner service. The planner then calls getPromptContext on ConversationSession, which returns only variables where includeInPrompt: true as additionalContext.
Headless Copilot Consideration
Headless Copilot has no LEX/mobile client to inject page-context variables. Variables must be metadata-backed in Core DB so the headless runtime can pass them through the platform API directly without a UI client. OOTB variables that must be DB-backed:

Page context
App name
Page name / page type
Record ID

Required Changes (Implementation Reference)

































LayerChangeCoreAdd includeInPrompt to bot metadata & config; update file-based bot templatesBuilder UISupport description and includeInPrompt fields for metadata-backed context variablesRuntimeAccept and forward includeInPrompt + description fields to the plannerLEX / MobileRead metadata-backed variables (including includeInPrompt) and pass via setVariablesmodule-chatbot-serviceAdd includeInPrompt to ContextVariable in planner-api.yamlPlanner ServiceAdd getPromptContext() on ConversationSession; return additionalContext for variables with includeInPrompt: true

Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/da.title: Data Grounding & Data Cloud
Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/da.content:
What Is Grounding
Grounding is the process of injecting relevant, real-time data into the agent’s context window before an LLM call, so responses are accurate and specific to the customer’s situation rather than generic.
Without grounding, the agent can only reason from its training knowledge and the immediate conversation.
Grounding Sources



































SourceDescriptionBest forSalesforce RecordsCRM data retrieved via SOQL/actionsAccount details, case history, order statusKnowledge ArticlesEinstein Search retrieval (RAG)FAQ, troubleshooting steps, policy docsData Cloud Unified ProfileReal-time unified customer data across all sourcesPersonalisation, propensity scores, engagement historyExternal data via MuleSoftFetched at runtime via API actionERP inventory, billing systemsFiles & DocumentsIndexed document retrievalProduct manuals, SOPs
Data Cloud as the Grounding Backbone
Data Cloud unifies data from multiple sources (CRM, marketing, commerce, external) into a Unified Individual (customer profile).
When grounded with Data Cloud:

Agent has full 360-degree view of the customer at time of interaction
Real-time data (e.g., last purchase, open cases, propensity to churn) informs agent reasoning
Segments and calculated insights can influence agent decisions and actions



                  
                  CTA angle 
                  
                

For any scenario requiring personalised, context-aware agent responses across channels, the answer is Agentforce + Data Cloud grounding. Data Cloud is not optional if the use case involves data from multiple source systems.


RAG Pattern
User message
  → Einstein Search / Data Cloud query (retrieve relevant docs/records)
    → Retrieved chunks injected into context window
      → LLM reasons with grounded context
        → Response grounded in real data, not hallucinated


Retrieval uses vector search (semantic similarity) for Knowledge Articles
Record retrieval uses structured queries (SOQL via actions)

Grounding Limits & Performance

Context window size limits how much data can be injected per call
Design actions to retrieve only what is needed (targeted SOQL, filtered knowledge search)
Data Cloud real-time profile lookup adds latency — acceptable for async channels, evaluate for synchronous chat

Modules in This Section

Grounding an Agent with Data — structured and unstructured data grounding options
Data 360-Powered Agentforce — trusted agents with unified Data 360 data
Advanced RAG with Data 360 and Agentforce — search indexes, retrievers, prompt templates, and grounded service agents

Skills Covered (inferred from section)

Artificial Intelligence

AI Agents

Products

Agentforce

Notes
Grounding connects an agent to trusted business context so it can answer accurately and act safely. Legend-level grounding goes beyond basic CRM record context into Data 360, retrievers, prompt templates, and RAG design.
Grounding Options
Agentforce can incorporate data through several mechanisms:

Structured Salesforce data: records and fields accessed through actions, Flow Builder, Apex, or standard capabilities.
Unstructured data: knowledge articles, files, and indexed content used for retrieval.
Prompt templates: structured prompts that merge business context into model calls.
Data 360 / Data Cloud: unified profiles, harmonized data, and search indexes for richer grounding.
External systems: MuleSoft APIs, Apex callouts, or other integration patterns when data lives outside Salesforce.

Structured data is easier to integrate because it has a predefined format. Unstructured data often needs indexing, retrieval, and governance before it is reliable for agent responses.
Data 360-Powered Agentforce
Data 360-Powered Agentforce focuses on creating trusted agents with unified data.
Key ideas:

Data 360 can bring customer, interaction, and enterprise data together for agent use.
Unified data improves personalization and relevance.
Trust depends on data quality, access controls, governance, and clear activation patterns.
Implementing Data 360 for Agentforce requires planning which data should ground responses and which actions can safely use that data.

Advanced RAG Pattern
Advanced RAG with Data 360 and Agentforce covers:

Grounding agents in Data 360
Creating search indexes
Creating retrievers
Creating prompt templates
Building a grounded service agent
Applying RAG best practices

Core RAG design points:

Index the fields and content that answer the target questions.
Use retrievers to fetch relevant chunks or records.
Keep prompts explicit about what the agent should do when retrieved context is missing.
Redirect off-topic questions rather than allowing the agent to invent answers.
Tune retrieval windows: widening the retrieval window can help find more relevant information, but too much context can reduce precision.



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Grounding is not a substitute for instructions and guardrails. If an agent answers off-topic questions with made-up responses, explicitly instruct it to redirect or decline rather than only changing retrieval settings.


Architecture Checklist

What business questions must the agent answer?
Which data source is authoritative for each answer?
Is the data structured, unstructured, or both?
Does the agent need Data 360, Knowledge, files, CRM records, or external APIs?
How is data indexed, retrieved, filtered, and secured?
What happens when no relevant result is found?
How are citations or source references exposed to users?
How will retrieval quality be tested over time?

Notes
Managing agent data means governing what the agent can use, how that data is prepared, how retrieval is tested, and how access remains compliant over time.
Agentforce Data Library
Agentforce Data Library provides a quick-start way to ground agents with unstructured data.
Key concepts:

A data library can use files or knowledge-style content as a grounding source.
The source type should be chosen intentionally because it shapes how the library is built and maintained.
Uploaded files are processed so Salesforce can index and retrieve relevant content for agent responses.
After changing a data library, restart the preview conversation and test again in Agentforce Builder.
The agent reasoning window can show which sources the agent used for a response.

Data Management Concerns
When managing data for agents, define:

Authoritative sources for each business domain
Data owners and review cadence
File upload and content approval process
Data freshness expectations
Data retention and disposal rules
Access model for internal users, external users, and agent users
Handling for sensitive, regulated, or confidential content
Monitoring process for poor retrieval or stale answers

Governance Checklist

Is the content approved for agent use?
Does the agent need the full document, selected sections, or summarized content?
Are private, confidential, or regulated fields excluded or masked?
Is the data covered by existing CRM, Data 360, Knowledge, or file governance?
Who updates the data when policies or product details change?
How are source quality and retrieval quality measured?
Can users see or audit the sources used in an answer?

Data 360 and RAG Operations
Data 360 and RAG patterns introduce additional operating responsibilities:

Keep search indexes aligned with current source data.
Review retriever quality when users report poor answers.
Tune retrieval windows and indexed fields based on observed misses.
Test off-topic, ambiguous, and policy-sensitive questions.
Keep prompt templates explicit about when to answer, escalate, or decline.



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Treat an agent’s grounding data like production configuration, not a one-time content upload. It needs ownership, release discipline, monitoring, and rollback thinking.


Architecture Lens
For CTA-style answers, connect data management to trust:

Data quality affects answer quality.
Access control affects what the agent is allowed to know.
Retrieval design affects hallucination risk.
Monitoring affects continuous improvement.
Governance affects compliance and adoption confidence.

Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/pr.title: Prompt Engineering for Salesforce Developers
Agentforce/04-Prompts--and--Grounding/pr.content:
Source: Salesforce Developers Blog, Dec 2023. Based on Jakub Stefaniak (Aquiva Labs) Dreamforce 2023 session on augmenting developer efficiency with LLMs.

Prompt engineering = crafting text inputs to an LLM to produce the desired output. Analogous to software engineering — iterative refinement in natural language instead of code.
Iterative process:

Start with a clear, specific prompt
Analyse why results fall short
Refine words and sentences
Repeat


Core Prompting Techniques
Role Prompting
Ask the LLM to behave as a specific persona to get more relevant, targeted output.
Act as a Salesforce Developer, expert in managing technical debt.
Explain the best practices of Apex.

Without the role, responses are generic. Adding a role anchors the LLM to the relevant context — e.g. design patterns, dependency injection, enterprise scale.
Delimiters
Use delimiters (triple backticks, ###, XML tags, etc.) to clearly separate the instruction from the input data.
You are a Senior Salesforce Developer, expert in Clean Code.
Explain the code enclosed in triple backticks and propose improvements.
\`\`\`
<Apex code here>
\`\`\`

Prevents the LLM from conflating the instruction with the input — critical when passing code, XML, or structured data.
Few-Shot Prompting
Provide examples in the prompt to guide output format and reduce hallucinations.

Zero-shot: no examples — model infers entirely from instruction
Few-shot: include 1–3 representative examples → model follows the pattern

Most effective for:

Generating Salesforce metadata XML (provide example object/field XML)
Generating code following a specific pattern or convention
Complex automation like Flow metadata, custom object schemas


Salesforce Developer Use Cases
Diagram Generation
LLMs can generate diagram markup from natural language descriptions:

PlantUML — provide class list or relationships → get PlantUML code → paste into online editor
Mermaid — describe sequence diagrams or data models in plain English → get Mermaid code → render in Mermaid Live Editor

Avoids manually writing diagram syntax.
Metadata XML Generation
Combine few-shot prompting with a PlantUML data model:

Provide PlantUML code of the data model
Provide example Salesforce DX XML (object + field metadata)
LLM outputs XML in DX source format for the full schema

Code Generation

General LLMs (GPT): useful for Apex and LWC generation
Einstein for Developers (VS Code + Code Builder): Salesforce-specific model trained on Apex, LWC, and related languages — more accurate for platform-specific patterns

Unit Testing, Explanation, Refactoring

Generate test classes from existing Apex
Explain unfamiliar code when onboarding to a large codebase
Refactor code to clean code standards


When to Use Prompt Engineering
Key decision factors from the session:

Human in the loop is important when accuracy is critical — don’t blindly trust LLM output
Security: never input customer-sensitive or org-specific data into public LLMs (ChatGPT etc.)

Use 05 Trust & Security — Einstein Trust Layer for safe AI adoption on-platform


Well-suited for: boilerplate generation, documentation, diagrams, test scaffolding
Less suited for: production logic requiring precise business rules without human review

Agentforce/05-Trust--and--Security/agent.title: Agentforce Security & Permissions
Agentforce/05-Trust--and--Security/agent.content:
Running User Context
Agentforce agents execute actions in the context of a running user (the authenticated user or a designated service user).

All Salesforce sharing rules, object permissions, and field-level security apply
The agent cannot access records the running user cannot see
For unauthenticated (guest) channels, a guest user profile applies — restrict carefully

Agent Permissions

Agents are assigned a Permission Set that grants access to topics and actions
Topic permissions control which topics an agent can handle in a given deployment
Action permissions control which actions (Flows, Apex, etc.) the agent may invoke

Key Security Considerations





























RiskMitigationOver-privileged agentUse a dedicated service user with minimum required permissions; avoid using System AdministratorPII exposure via LLMEinstein Trust Layer data masking on sensitive fieldsPrompt injectionEinstein Trust Layer toxicity/injection detection; constrain agent to defined action setUnauthenticated accessRestrict guest user profile; avoid actions that write sensitive records without authenticationAction abuseLimit actions per topic; audit via Agent Analytics and LLM audit trail
Authentication for External Actions

MuleSoft API Catalog actions use Named Credentials for external auth
Apex and Flow actions can use Named Credentials or External Credentials
OAuth 2.0 flows supported; secrets never exposed in action configuration



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

If a scenario involves an agent handling sensitive health or financial data, the answer should combine: (1) Einstein Trust Layer for LLM data protection, (2) field-level security on sensitive fields, (3) dedicated low-privilege running user, (4) Named Credentials for external callouts.


Audit & Compliance

All agent interactions logged in Einstein Activity Capture / agent audit trail
LLM call logs available in Einstein Trust Layer audit log
Exportable for compliance review (e.g., GDPR data subject requests)

Agentforce/05-Trust--and--Security/einst.title: Einstein Trust Layer
Agentforce/05-Trust--and--Security/einst.content:
What It Is
The Einstein Trust Layer is Salesforce’s security and governance framework that sits between the Salesforce platform and external LLM providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI).
It ensures that Salesforce customer data is protected when sent to or processed by LLMs.
Core Capabilities

































CapabilityDescriptionZero data retentionLLM providers are contractually prohibited from storing or training on Salesforce customer dataDynamic data maskingPII and sensitive fields are masked/tokenised before being sent to the LLM; de-tokenised on returnToxicity detectionInput and output scanned; harmful content blocked before reaching usersAudit trailAll LLM interactions logged for compliance and reviewGroundingContextual data (records, knowledge) injected server-side — data never leaves Salesforce boundary to the LLM rawSecure gatewayAll LLM calls routed through Salesforce-controlled gateway; no direct client-to-LLM communication
Architecture
Salesforce Org
  └─ Agentforce / Prompt Builder
        └─ Einstein Trust Layer
              ├─ Data masking
              ├─ Toxicity filter
              └─ Secure gateway → LLM Provider (OpenAI / Anthropic / etc.)
                                        ↓ response
              ├─ De-masking
              ├─ Output audit log
              └─ Response back to org

Data Masking Detail

Configured at field level — admins mark fields as sensitive
Masking applied in the context window before LLM call
Supports: PII (email, phone, name), custom sensitive fields
De-masking restores values in the response before displaying to user



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Einstein Trust Layer applies to ALL Einstein generative AI features, not just Agentforce — including Prompt Builder, Einstein Copilot, and Sales/Service GPT features. If a scenario asks about data privacy with AI, Einstein Trust Layer is the primary answer.




                  
                  Note
                  
                

Zero data retention is enforced via DPAs (Data Processing Agreements) with LLM providers. Salesforce does not rely on provider settings alone — contractual obligation is the mechanism.


What It Does NOT Cover

Does not prevent agents from accessing Salesforce records the running user has permission to see (standard sharing rules still apply)
Does not encrypt data at rest beyond standard Salesforce Shield/encryption — it protects data in transit to LLMs only

Agentforce/08-Deployment--and--Channels/.title: Agentforce DevOps & Deployment Guide
Agentforce/08-Deployment--and--Channels/.content:
Source: PHP Capstone project — 02-final-report-presentation.md DevOps Reference + 01-implementation-plan.md §5. Verified against Spring ‘26.


Core Principle
Agentforce components are standard Salesforce metadata. The DevOps workflow for an Agentforce project is the same SFDX model used for any Salesforce change.

“You don’t learn a new deployment system for agents — you extend the SFDX pipeline you already have.”


Develop in a sandbox → commit to version control (Git)
CI/CD pipeline runs sf project deploy start → deploys to UAT or Production
Change sets and unlocked packages work the same way


Agentforce Metadata Types → UI Configuration Map
Every configuration decision made in Agentforce Builder or Setup corresponds to a deployable metadata file under force-app/. Retrieve a full agent bundle in one shot:
sf project retrieve start --metadata Agent:MyAgentName

















































































Metadata TypeFile Extension / LocationWhere Configured in UIAiAuthoringBundleaiAuthoringBundles/<Name>/<Name>.agent + .bundle-meta.xmlAgentforce Builder — Agent Script editorBotbots/<Name>/<Name>.bot-meta.xmlAgentforce Builder → Agent overview (name, type, running user)BotVersionbots/<Name>/v<N>.botVersion-meta.xmlAgentforce Builder → Version history / Commit VersionGenAiPlannerBundlegenAiPlannerBundles/<Name>/Agentforce Builder → reasoning engine (Atlas, model selection)GenAiPlugin (topic)genAiPlugins/<Name>.genAiPlugin-meta.xmlAgentforce Builder → Topics tab → Add TopicGenAiFunction (action)genAiFunctions/<Name>.genAiFunction-meta.xmlAgentforce Builder → Topics → Actions → Add ActionGenAiPromptTemplategenAiPromptTemplates/<Name>/Prompt Builder → Create Prompt TemplateFlowflows/<Name>.flow-meta.xmlFlow Builder — Autolaunched FlowApexClassclasses/<Name>.clsApex IDE / Developer ConsoleMessagingChannelmessagingChannels/<Name>.messagingChannel-meta.xmlSetup → Messaging Settings → New ChannelEmbeddedServiceConfigEmbeddedServiceConfig/<Name>.EmbeddedServiceConfig-meta.xmlSetup → Embedded Service Deployments → New DeploymentNetwork (Experience site)networks/<Name>.network-meta.xmlSetup → Digital Experiences → AdministrationDigitalExperience bundledigitalExperiences/site/<Name>/Experience Builder → Theme → Footer componentPermissionSetpermissionsets/<Name>.permissionset-meta.xmlSetup → Permission Sets

What Is NOT Deployable via Metadata API
The one hard exception to “everything is metadata” is the Agentforce Data Library:

























ComponentStatusWhyData Library structure (library name, data type)Not deployableAiGroundingLibrary SObject not exposed to REST/Tooling/Metadata API (Spring ‘26)Search index / vector embeddingsNot deployableObject__dlm, Object_index__dlm, Object_chunk__dlm are Data Cloud objects — deploying failsLibrary file content (e.g. Handbook PDF)Never deployableRaw file content is data, not metadata
Official confirmation (help.salesforce.com ai.data_library_sandbox.htm):

“Making Agentforce Data Library changes in a sandbox and deploying those changes back to the production org or another sandbox org isn’t supported.”

Recommended path: Use a Data Kit (Data 360 Developer Guide — packages-data-kits). The library file must still be uploaded manually per environment. The Data Kit package must be separate from the SFDX platform metadata package — mixing them is enforced as an error since Winter ‘25.

Ordered Deployment Sequence
CLI Steps — sf project deploy start
Step 1  CustomObject + CustomField + PermissionSet     (data model first)
Step 2  ApexClass + ApexTrigger                        (invocable action logic)
Step 3  Flow + GenAiPromptTemplate                     (depend on Apex + objects)
Step 4  MessagingChannel                               (must exist before ESD)
Step 5  EmbeddedServiceConfig                          (depends on channel + ESW site)
Step 6  Network (Experience Cloud config)
Step 7  DigitalExperience bundle (site content + footer)

Agent metadata (AiAuthoringBundle, Bot, BotVersion, GenAi*) is included in the full --source-dir force-app deploy. The Agent pseudo-type shorthand is available for retrieval but the full source-dir deploy is used for promotion.
Manual UI Steps — No CLI Equivalent
Step 8   [Manual] Activate + Publish each agent in Agentforce Builder
Step 9   [Manual] Publish each Embedded Service Deployment in Setup
Step 10  [Manual] Verify Experience Builder footer component configuration
Step 11  [Manual] Upload Handbook PDF to Data Library; wait for "Ready" status (~20 min)
Step 12  [Manual] Run Testing Center smoke suite (UAT only — never production)


Three Agentforce-Specific Constraints
1. Draft vs. Committed Agent Versions — Immutability After Commit




















StateMetadataEditable?DraftAiAuthoringBundle onlyYes — edit freely in Builder or via Agent ScriptCommittedAiAuthoringBundle + Bot + BotVersionNo — must create a new version to change anything
Deploying to a target org commits the agent version in that org. To update a committed agent in production: create a new version in dev, commit it, and promote it through the pipeline — you cannot edit in-place.
2. Manual Publish Steps Required After Every Deploy (UI-Only)

























StepWhereWhen RequiredActivate + Publish agentAgentforce Builder → Activate → PublishAfter every deploy touching agent metadataPublish Embedded Service DeploymentSetup → Embedded Service Deployments → PublishAfter any ESD config change or agent republishPublish Experience Cloud siteExperience Builder → PublishAfter footer component or DigitalExperience deploy
3. Never Run Tests in Production

Agentforce agents execute real actions. A test conversation with the Leasing Assistant can create a real Lead. A test with the Tenant Concierge can create a real Case, fire a real email, or trigger a real OTP. A test with the Ops Copilot can draft and send a real email.


Never run Testing Center suites against a production org. Route all sf agent test run executions to Dev or UAT only.
CI/CD gate: regression smoke suites fire on UAT after every SFDX deploy — never against Production.
Production deploy with agent disabled by default. Deploy metadata first, then activate + publish the agent only after manual verification.
Monitor stage starts at production activation. Analytics from UAT are not a substitute for production metrics.

4. EmbeddedServiceConfig <site> Field Is Immutable After Creation
The <site> field in EmbeddedServiceConfig is set at creation and cannot be changed — not by CLI, not by Setup UI. If the wrong site is linked, the deployment must be deleted and recreated. Plan this field before creating any new deployment.

Environment Strategy
Dev Sandbox  ──►  UAT Sandbox  ──►  Production
(metadata)        (metadata + sanitised data)   (metadata + real data, gradual rollout)

Metadata vs Data













































AssetTypeMigration MechanismAgent definition, Topics, Actions, InstructionsMetadataSFDX source → unlocked package or change setFlows, Apex, Permission Sets, Custom Objects/Fields, Named Credentials, ESDMetadataSFDXPrompt TemplatesMetadataSFDXKM ArticlesDatasf data import tree + Apex bootstrapHandbook PDF in Data LibraryDataManual upload per environment + re-indexCSV seed dataDataData Import Wizard with External IDsNamed Credential secretsConfigurationPer-env, never committed to Git
Release Gates

SFDX deploy to UAT triggers Testing Center smoke suite via CI
Manual UAT sign-off using representative test prompts
Prod deploy agent-disabled by default, then channel-by-channel rollout
Rollback = re-deploy previous Git tag + revert agent activation


Data Cloud Hibernate Plan
The Data Library search index runs on Data Cloud, which incurs consumption when active.

Hibernate when idle. Hibernate the Data Cloud org between build cycles and after rehearsals.
Wake-up runbook. Document the steps + lead time to resume Data Cloud and re-warm the search index before a demo or release (indexing takes ~20 min after PDF upload).
Per-environment posture. Dev/UAT hibernated by default; Production kept active only during the rollout window, then governed by Einstein Usage & Limits monitoring.


Common CLI Commands
# Retrieve full agent bundle
sf project retrieve start --metadata Agent:MyAgentName
 
# Deploy all metadata to UAT
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app --target-org uat-alias
 
# Validation run (check-only, no deploy)
sf project deploy start --check-only --source-dir force-app --target-org uat-alias
 
# Run agent test suite (UAT only)
sf agent test run --name MyAgent_Smoke --target-org uat-alias

Agentforce/08-Deployment--and--Channels/.title: External API Integration with Named Credentials for Agentforce Actions
Agentforce/08-Deployment--and--Channels/.content:
Source: PHP Capstone project — smartrent-stub-salesforce-integration.md. Implements Scenarios 4 (OTP-gated door unlock) and 5 (keyfob replacement order) via a SmartRent stub API.


Overview
Agentforce actions that call external REST APIs should route through:

A Named Credential (manages the endpoint URL + auth headers securely)
An Apex wrapper class (validates preconditions, enforces guardrails, calls the external endpoint)
An @InvocableMethod that exposes the action to the agent topic

Optionally, an External Services registration can expose the OpenAPI schema to Setup UI — but Apex wrappers are preferred when pre-validation and security guardrails are required.

Named Credential Setup
Metadata File
force-app/main/default/namedCredentials/<Name>.namedCredential-meta.xml
Key fields:

<endpoint> — the base URL of the external service (e.g. your-stub.example.com)
<principalType> — typically Anonymous for API-key-authenticated services
<calloutStatus> — Enabled

After deploy — configure secrets in Setup UI (never commit to Git):

Setup → Named Credentials → open credential
Add custom header: X-Api-Key = <your-api-key>
Optionally add X-Scenario-Mode header for deterministic testing (see below)

Callout from Apex
HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest();
req.setEndpoint('callout:YourNamedCredential/path/to/endpoint');
req.setMethod('POST');
req.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
req.setBody(JSON.serialize(payload));
 
Http http = new Http();
HttpResponse res = http.send(req);

Apex Wrapper vs. External Services




















ApproachWhen to UseTrade-offApex wrapper (recommended)When security preconditions, input validation, or multi-step guardrails are requiredMore code to write; security logic lives in Apex and is easily testableExternal ServicesWhen the OpenAPI contract is stable and admin-managed schema binding is desiredEasier Setup UI management; but guardrails must be added separately
Rule of thumb for sensitive agent actions: Use Apex wrappers. Security preconditions (tenant verification, OTP validation, apartment cross-check) must all pass before the external call is made — this logic belongs in Apex, not in the agent script.

X-Scenario-Mode Header Pattern for Deterministic Testing
Add an optional X-Scenario-Mode header to the external stub to control response behavior during development and demo preparation. This allows testing all error paths without needing real failure conditions.
Supported values (example for a door-unlock stub):





































ValueStub Responseauto (default)Normal behavior based on request payloadsuccessAlways returns acceptedtenant_inactiveReturns TENANT_NOT_ACTIVEotp_failedReturns OTP_NOT_VALIDATEDwrong_apartmentReturns APARTMENT_MISMATCHjailbreakReturns JAILBREAK_BLOCKEDexternal_errorReturns HTTP 500
Usage: Set X-Scenario-Mode as a custom header on the Named Credential in Setup. Remove or set to auto before production use.

Security Sequencing for Sensitive Agent Actions
Any agent action that calls an external system to perform a real-world transaction must enforce a security sequence in Apex before the external call. The sequence cannot rely on the agent script alone — the action must validate preconditions regardless of how it was invoked.
Door Unlock Sequence
1. VerifyActiveTenant($User.AccountId)
   → Confirms AccountId maps to PersonAccount with active lease
   → Returns ApartmentId from the tenant's active lease

2. Validate ApartmentId against $Session.apartmentId
   → Prevents unlocking a different apartment
   → Uses canonical IDs from session context — never free-text apartment name overrides

3. GenerateAndSendOTP(contactId, email)
   → Creates OTP_Session__c record with expiry
   → Sends 6-digit code to tenant's email on file

4. ValidateOTP(contactId, inputCode)
   → Checks code against OTP_Session__c, enforces expiry
   → Marks session as used (prevents replay)

5. RequestExternalUnlock(apartmentId)
   → Only reached if steps 1–4 all pass
   → Calls external API via Named Credential

Keyfob Order Sequence
1. Retrieve fee from Data Library / Handbook (e.g. $75)
2. Present fee to user and require explicit confirmation
3. On confirmation: PlaceExternalOrder(accountId, apartmentId)
   → Uses API Action target: standardInvocableAction://createkeyfoborder
   → Returns { orderId, eta_days }


Demo Validation Matrix
Use this matrix to verify all paths before a capstone or stakeholder demo:








































ScenarioInput ConditionExpected ResultDoor unlock — happy pathOTP valid + active tenant + apartment binding validaccepted, returns unlock request IDDoor unlock — no OTPOTP not validatedOTP_NOT_VALIDATED, action blockedDoor unlock — wrong apartmentAccountId does not match ApartmentIdAPARTMENT_MISMATCH, action blockedDoor unlock — jailbreak attemptOverride / legal threat / cross-apartment requestJAILBREAK_BLOCKED, action blocked, agent declinesKeyfob order — happy pathFee disclosed, user confirmsaccepted, returns requestId and ETAKeyfob order — fee not acceptedUser declines feeFEE_NOT_ACCEPTED, no order placed

Artifacts to Capture as Demo Evidence

Agent transcript showing OTP challenge and successful unlock with requestId
Agent transcript showing blocked unlock (wrong apartment or missing OTP)
Agent transcript showing keyfob fee confirmation and order requestId
Stub API logs with correlation IDs matching the agent transcripts


Deployed Artifacts Reference (PHP Capstone)





































ArtifactPathOpenAPI stub contractintegrations/smartrent-stub/openapi/smartrent-stub-v1.yamlStub serverintegrations/smartrent-stub/src/server.jsNamed Credentialforce-app/main/default/namedCredentials/smartrent_Stub.namedCredential-meta.xmlApex callout wrapperforce-app/main/default/classes/SmartrentStubClient.clsDoor unlock actionforce-app/main/default/classes/SmartrentRequestDoorUnlock.clsKeyfob order actionforce-app/main/default/classes/SmartrentOrderKeyfobInStub.clsExternal Services registrationforce-app/main/default/externalServiceRegistrations/smartrentKeyfob.externalServiceRegistration-meta.xml

Agentforce/09-Testing--and--Monitoring/g.title: GenAI Audit Data Model
Agentforce/09-Testing--and--Monitoring/g.content:
The Generative AI Audit Data Model captures every LLM request and response that passes through the Einstein Trust Layer. It consists of 9 objects recording everything from the initial prompt to grounding inputs, LLM responses, content quality checks, and user feedback.
Data can be queried via SOQL, surfaced in Data Cloud Reports, or accessed over JDBC for use with Tableau, CRM Analytics (CRMA), or other BI tools.
Why It Matters

Provides a full, immutable audit trail of all AI activity in the org
Enables compliance reporting (who asked what, what was returned, was it masked)
Drives continuous improvement loops: identify low-quality or harmful generations and refine prompts
Surfaces user satisfaction signals (thumbs up/down) at the generation level

The 9 Objects
Core Request / Response Chain

























ObjectPurposeGenAIGatewayRequestFact table — the unique generation event: prompt text, provider, model, token counts, safety scoring flags, grounding prompt, session/bot version IDsGenAIGatewayRequestInternalInternal parent record for the gateway request; links to org and cloud metadataGenAIGatewayResponseTiming and specifics of the response from the LLM (generation response ID, parameters, feature, timestamp)GenAIGenerationThe actual LLM response: raw text, masked response text, parameters (JSON Dictionary), feature, timestamp
Tagging and Versioning

















ObjectPurposeGenAIGatewayRequestTagTags associated with the prompt for monitoring (app type, place ID, bot/session version, generation prompt ID)GenAIAppGenerationRecords the version of the prompt template used in the request (links generation to the specific app/prompt version)
Quality and Content Safety

















ObjectPurposeGenAIContentQualityToxicity detection and other quality measures; content type (Input/Output), is-toxicity-detected flagGenAIContentCategoryClassifies the content that called the prompt; detect type (Body/Result/Prompt/Delivery), value, category
Feedback

















ObjectPurposeGenAIFeedbackWhether the user clicked the like or dislike button; feedback type (Good/Bad), source (App/Human), org, cloud, featureGenAIFeedbackDetailGranular detail about the feedback: app feedback (JSON Dictionary), timestamp, feature
Key Fields on GenAIGatewayRequest
GatewayRequestId   (PK)
Prompt             String
Provider           String
Model              String
NumGenerations     Number
EnableInputSafetyScoring   Type
EnableOutputSafetyScoring  Type
Temperature        Double
StopSequences      String
FrequencyPenalty   Double
PresencePenalty    Double
ThresholdId        Number
Parameters         JSON Dictionary
AppType            String
Cloud / Feature / OrgId
PlaceId / BotVersionId / SessionId / UserId
GenerationPromptId / CompletionTokens / PromptTokens / TotalTokens

Reporting Patterns
-- Count generations by model this week
SELECT Model, COUNT(Id)
FROM GenAIGatewayRequest
WHERE CreatedDate = THIS_WEEK
GROUP BY Model
 
-- Find toxic outputs
SELECT Id, OrgId, Feature
FROM GenAIContentQuality
WHERE IsToxicityDetected = true
 
-- User feedback summary
SELECT Type, COUNT(Id)
FROM GenAIFeedback
GROUP BY Type


                  
                  JDBC for BI Tools 
                  
                

Connect Tableau or CRMA to the GenAI objects via JDBC for dashboards tracking prompt usage, model costs, toxicity rates, and user satisfaction over time.




                  
                  Data Cloud Reports 
                  
                

GenAI audit objects are also available as Data Cloud data streams, enabling unified reporting alongside customer profile data.

Notes
Testing and monitoring are required because agent behavior changes with instructions, grounding data, actions, user phrasing, and model behavior. Treat agents as living systems that need regression testing and production telemetry.
Testing Tools

























ToolUseAgentforce Builder previewManual testing and troubleshooting during designAgentforce Testing CenterStructured tests, testing criteria, generated tests, and result reviewAgentforce AnalyticsProduction monitoring and trend analysisUtterance analysisReview what users ask and where the agent succeeds or fails
Trailhead calls out Agentforce Builder as the best tool for manual testing and troubleshooting an agent.
Agentforce Testing Center
Testing Center focuses on building trust in agents.
Core workflow:

Define what good behavior means through testing criteria.
Use AI to generate test cases.
Run test sets against the agent.
Review results and identify failures.
Iterate on instructions, topics, actions, prompts, and grounding data.

Testing should cover:

Expected successful conversations
Ambiguous user requests
Off-topic questions
Permission-sensitive questions
Incorrect or missing data
Escalation and fallback behavior
Regression scenarios after configuration changes

Testing Strategy
A practical five-step strategy:

Define business outcomes and acceptance criteria.
Create representative test prompts and conversations.
Run manual tests in Builder for early troubleshooting.
Use Testing Center for broader repeatable coverage.
Monitor production data and feed learnings back into design.



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

A one-time test pass is not enough. Retest when instructions, actions, prompt templates, data libraries, retrievers, or permissions change.


Analytics and Monitoring
Agentforce Analytics helps improve agents after deployment.
Monitor:

Conversation volume
Completion and containment trends
Escalation and fallback rates
Repeated failed utterances
Topics or actions that underperform
User intents not covered by current topics
Data-grounding gaps

Utterance analysis is especially useful for identifying the gap between how designers expect users to ask questions and how users actually ask them.
CTA / Architecture Lens
For an architecture answer, include:

Manual testing in Builder for initial validation
Structured regression tests in Testing Center
Synthetic test generation for scale
Analytics and utterance monitoring after go-live
Feedback loop to update topics, instructions, actions, and grounding data
