Agentforce/10-Developer-Tools/advanced-a.title: Create Advanced Agent Customizations
Agentforce/10-Developer-Tools/advanced-a.content:
Trailhead section (Legend trail): Create Advanced Agent Customizations | +10,100 pts | ~7 hrs 45 min | 8 steps

Largest section in the entire Agentblazer programme — covers the depth of platform customisation capability.

Modules in This Section

Service Agent Customization with Prompt Builder — craft, attach, and refine prompt templates for custom service agents
Agent Customization with Flows — make flows agent-ready, create agent-ready flows, and add flows as agent tools
Agent Customization with Apex — create Apex-based agent actions for custom deterministic logic
Agent Customization: Quick Look — compare common customization options and action patterns

Skills Covered (inferred from section)

AI Development
Artificial Intelligence
AI Agents
Automation
Configuration Management

Products

Agentforce
Agentforce Builder


Notes
Advanced customization is about deciding where an agent should rely on natural-language reasoning and where it needs deterministic business logic.
Customization Options






























OptionStrengthWhen to UsePrompt templatesFlexible natural-language generation, summarization, and response shapingWhen the output is generative and benefits from grounded contextFlow actionsDeclarative, deterministic business process automationWhen admins need low-code actions, record retrieval, or guided updatesApex actionsComplex logic, integrations, reusable code, and unit-testable behaviorWhen Flow is insufficient or behavior must be tightly controlledStandard actionsFast reuse of Salesforce-supported capabilitiesWhen the standard action meets the use case without customization
Prompt Builder Customization
Service Agent Customization with Prompt Builder covers:

Crafting effective prompt templates for service-agent replies
Bringing prompts into agent behavior through agent actions
Refining prompts so responses are accurate, grounded, and useful

Use prompt templates when the agent must produce a natural-language answer that combines instructions, data, and tone. Test prompt behavior with realistic service scenarios because small wording changes can affect output quality.
Flow-Based Agent Actions
Agent-ready flows need explicit input and output variables so Agentforce can pass context into the flow and use the response. Trailhead highlights that an agent action requires both input and output variables.
Design guidance:

Keep flow inputs narrow and intentional.
Return only fields the agent needs.
Prefer explicit field selection in Get Records instead of exposing broad record payloads.
Treat flow output as part of the agent contract.
Use flows for deterministic steps such as lookup, update, routing, or orchestration.



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Avoid sending unnecessary data to the agent. Over-broad flow outputs increase privacy risk and can dilute the context the model uses.


Apex-Based Agent Actions
Apex agent actions are appropriate when the agent needs custom logic that should be versioned, reviewed, and tested like application code.
Use Apex when:

Logic is too complex for Flow.
The action needs custom validation, transformation, or orchestration.
You need precise exception handling.
You need unit tests and deployment controls.
The action integrates with custom services or APIs.

For architecture review, justify Apex actions as deterministic extensions to an otherwise probabilistic agent experience.
CTA / Architecture Lens

Use prompt templates for generative response shaping.
Use Flow for admin-owned deterministic automation.
Use Apex for complex, testable, governed logic.
Keep each action small and named around a business capability.

Agentforce/10-Developer-Tools/agentforce.title: Agentforce Actions
Agentforce/10-Developer-Tools/agentforce.content:
What Is an Action
An Action is a discrete capability the Atlas Reasoning Engine can invoke. Actions are the “hands” of an agent — how it reads data, writes records, calls external systems, or generates content.
Action Types








































TypeMechanismNotesFlowAutolaunched FlowMost common; no-code, reusable, testableApex@InvocableMethodFull code flexibility; use when Flow can’tPrompt TemplateEinstein Prompt BuilderLLM-generated content (e.g., draft email, summarise case)MuleSoft API CatalogREST via MuleSoft AnypointExternal system calls, governed through API layerSalesforce APIsNative platform actionse.g., create/update records, send messagesCustom HTTPExternal API calloutAvailable via Flow HTTP callout or Apex
Design Principles

Granular actions — each action should do one thing; the reasoning engine composes them
Idempotency — actions that write data should be safe to retry
Error handling — return clear fault messages; engine uses them to self-correct
Input/output schema — well-defined parameters help the engine pick the right action
Reuse existing automation — existing Flows and Apex invocable methods work without rewrite

Action vs Topic

Topic = the category of tasks the agent can handle (e.g., “Order Management”)
Action = a specific tool available within (and across) topics
An action can belong to multiple topics



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

When asked how to extend an agent to interact with an external ERP: recommend a Flow with HTTP callout or MuleSoft API Catalog action. Justify MuleSoft when: the ERP is already integrated via Anypoint, governance/rate-limiting is needed, or reuse across multiple agents/channels is required.


Limits & Considerations

Actions are called synchronously within the reasoning loop — avoid long-running Apex
Callout limits apply to Apex actions (standard governor limits)
Flow actions support bulk-safe invocation but agents typically invoke one record at a time
Prompt Template actions count toward Einstein token consumption

Agentforce/10-Developer-Tools/mcp-for-ag.title: MCP for Agentforce
Agentforce/10-Developer-Tools/mcp-for-ag.content:
What Is MCP?
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for securely connecting AI agents to external systems — their tools, services, and data. It acts as a translator between systems, removing the need for custom API code, auth handling, and data-access wiring per integration.
Three components:

MCP Server — created by service providers (MuleSoft, Heroku, Snowflake, third parties); exposes server tools that agents can call
MCP Client — connects to one or more MCP servers to retrieve tools and data on behalf of an agent
MCP Host — the application coordinating servers and clients; in Agentforce, the platform itself acts as the host

Agentforce provides a native MCP client — no custom client code required.
Agentforce Registry
Used to register external and third-party MCP servers so agents can discover and use their tools.

Register via: Setup → Agentforce → MCP Servers → Agentforce Registry
After registration, select which server tools to expose
Add selected tools to an agent as agent tools in Agentforce Builder
Set reasoning instructions to control how the agent uses each tool

For MuleSoft MCP Servers and Salesforce Standard/Custom MCP Servers, registration is done through API Catalog instead of Agentforce Registry.


                  
                  Key distinction 
                  
                

Agentforce Registry = external/third-party servers
API Catalog = MuleSoft + Salesforce-hosted servers


Agentforce Gateway
The policy control layer for MCP usage. Lets admins define and enforce rules for how agents call MCP server tools.
What you can do:

Set rate limits — cap how many times an agent can call a server tool in a given period
Apply policies to specific agents or specific tools
Add or tune policies dynamically without redeploying
Use the same monitoring and observability as other Agentforce features

Policies can be applied manually or auto-triggered based on criteria.


                  
                  Exam angle 
                  
                

Gateway = governance and trust enforcement for MCP; Registry = registration and discovery


Trust and Security
MCP in Agentforce inherits the full Einstein Trust Layer:

Zero data retention policy applies
Salesforce data stays within Salesforce
Same security and compliance controls as all other Agentforce features

MCP for Development (Agentforce Vibes)
MCP also powers the Salesforce DX MCP Server for use with the Agentforce Vibes IDE extension:

Gives Vibes real-time access to org schema, metadata, Apex classes, profiles, and permission sets
Generates code aligned to your specific org config rather than generic training data
Set up via: enable Salesforce DX MCP server → connect additional servers → configure auth → chat with Vibes

See develop-with-agentforce-tools for broader Agentforce Vibes context.

Agentforce/12-AI-Strategy--and--Leadersh.title: AI Strategy
Agentforce/12-AI-Strategy--and--Leadersh.content:
AI strategy is the organization’s path to delivering business value with AI. It should connect AI work to business goals, establish governance and risk practices, and create a prioritized backlog of use cases that can be delivered and measured.
Trailhead source: AI Strategy
Why It Matters

AI programs lose momentum when they focus on technology without linking initiatives to measurable business objectives.
A strong AI strategy gives stakeholders a shared vision, clear governance, and a practical roadmap.
Data strategy is foundational: AI depends on data quality, data management, infrastructure, unification, governance, and scalability.
Strategy should be revisited after each AI project and on a regular cadence as technology, business goals, and regulatory expectations change.



                  
                  Note
                  
                

For Agentforce architecture, frame AI strategy around business outcomes first, then map those outcomes to data readiness, trust controls, agent capabilities, adoption, and measurable KPIs.


Strategic Stakeholders
An AI center of excellence, council, advisory board, or committee should bring together cross-functional leadership. Common participants include:

Business departments such as sales, marketing, service, and support
IT, engineering, security, and data science
Business intelligence, legal, finance, and operations
Executive sponsors who can secure funding, remove barriers, and drive adoption

The committee’s responsibilities typically include:

Defining the organization’s AI vision
Securing executive buy-in
Identifying strategic barriers
Establishing AI governance
Evaluating use cases and building an AI roadmap
Making decisions about core AI and data capabilities
Allocating resources and planning for scale
Championing adoption and reviewing outcomes

Top-Down and Bottom-Up Strategy
Trailhead recommends a two-pronged approach:

Bottom-up: Democratize access to AI so employees can experiment, learn, and surface use-case ideas.
Top-down: Set direction from leadership so experiments align with enterprise strategy, governance, and measurable value.

This avoids fragmented, department-only AI efforts while still encouraging practical innovation.
Define the AI Vision
Start with business goals, then determine where AI can create meaningful impact. Example Coral Cloud goals included improving guest satisfaction, increasing occupancy, reducing operating costs, raising cross-sell conversion, and growing revenue.
AI ambition can be phased:

Short-term: Start with internal pilots that boost productivity, improve employee satisfaction, and use out-of-the-box AI capabilities.
Mid-term: Implement turnkey and custom AI solutions for employees and customers, including personalization and AI agents.
Long-term: Build AI-powered products and services that can create competitive advantage or new business models.

Assess AI Readiness
AI readiness should cover people, process, technology, and maturity. Assess whether the organization has:

Clear business ownership and executive sponsorship
Data quality and governance practices
Security, privacy, and compliance processes
Skills for AI delivery, monitoring, and support
Change management capacity for user adoption
Technical architecture that can support scale

AI Governance
AI governance is the set of policies, processes, and best practices that helps organizations develop, use, and manage AI responsibly and at scale. Governance should maximize benefits while mitigating technical, ethical, operational, reputational, regulatory, and legal risks.
Governance work should include:

Responsible AI principles aligned to the organization’s mission and values
Awareness of the evolving regulatory landscape
AI inventory and ownership model
Risk assessment and risk prioritization
Risk mitigation strategies
Monitoring, documentation, and ongoing improvement

AI Inventory
An AI inventory helps the organization understand where AI is being used and where risk may exist. Inventory each AI tool, model, embedded third-party AI feature, and pilot.
Capture:

AI technologies currently in use
Business use cases and intended outcomes
Data flows into and out of each AI application
Owners and accountable teams
Review cadence and status



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Shadow AI creates governance risk because unapproved tools may use sensitive data, lack controls, or bypass legal and security review.


Risk Assessment
Evaluate risks by reviewing the AI inventory and engaging stakeholders across the organization.
Key steps:

Identify potential risks for each AI use case.
Categorize risks by type, such as technical, ethical, operational, reputational, regulatory, or legal.
Assess impact and likelihood for each risk.
Prioritize risks using a risk matrix.
Define mitigations and ownership.

This approach also prepares the organization for risk-based regulatory models such as the EU AI Act.
Risk Mitigation Strategies





























Risk TypeMitigation ExamplesTechnical and securitySecurity policies, anomaly detection, fallback options, secure infrastructure, red-teamingData and privacyAccess controls, anonymization, encryption, data audits, data quality standards, data cleaning and validationEthical and safetyResponsible AI principles, acceptable use policies, bias assessment, benchmarking, explainability, citations, feedback mechanisms, audit logsOperationalRisk assessments, incident response, change management, documentation, training, monitoring, internal ethics reviewCompliance and legalCompliance protocols, training, legal review, contracts, regulatory monitoring
Improve Governance Over Time
Governance is not a one-time setup activity. Mature practices through:

Training and education for employees and delivery teams
Ethical AI culture and responsible experimentation
Regular monitoring and review of risk mitigations
Documentation and reporting for audits, compliance, and stakeholder visibility
Metrics that show whether governance practices are effective

Identify AI Use Cases
Good AI use cases align to organizational goals and deliver actual business value. Trailhead highlights several ways to gather ideas:

Internal crowdsourcing, hackathons, surveys, idea exchanges, and Slack communities
Business process reviews to find inefficiency and automation opportunities
User research to ensure AI solves real problems
Data analysis to identify patterns and opportunities
Market research and competitive analysis

Example use-case areas include automated prospecting, forecasting guidance, sentiment analysis, AI service agents, streamlined check-in, product recommendations, dynamic pricing, and predictive maintenance.
Assess and Prioritize Use Cases
Evaluate each use case across business value and ease of implementation.
Business value should include:

Strategic alignment
Tangible financial or operational value
ROI, payback, net present value, or other relevant investment measures
Short-term and long-term gains
Ability to leverage existing platforms or investments
Clear KPIs to prove business outcomes

Ease of implementation should include:

Technical feasibility, timeline, scalability, integrations, and cybersecurity guardrails
Operational readiness and change management effort
Data readiness, including quality, unification, governance, and reuse potential
Risk profile
Executive buy-in

Prioritization Matrix
Use an impact-effort matrix to build a practical AI backlog.






























CategoryMeaningHow to TreatQuick winsHigh value, low effortStrong candidates for early pilotsLow-hanging fruitLow value, low effortDefer until higher-value work is completeBig betsHigh value, high effortConsider after maturity improves or when transformation is neededMoney pitsLow value, high effortAvoid or remove from the roadmap
Choose the First AI Project
Early AI pilots should be small enough to deliver quickly but meaningful enough to prove value.
Selection criteria:

Can be implemented in less than 6 months
Uses off-the-shelf AI where possible
Requires limited data cleanup or integration
Has low risk and high likelihood of success
Fits current organizational capabilities and resources
Is easy for users to adopt
Can scale to other business units or regions
Creates learning opportunities for later AI deployments

Agentforce Architecture Lens
For Agentforce planning, translate the AI strategy into architecture decisions:

Business outcome: What metric should the agent improve?
Users and channels: Who interacts with the agent, and where?
Data grounding: Which CRM, Data Cloud, knowledge, or external data is required?
Trust controls: What permissions, masking, audit, citations, or human handoff are needed?
Actions: Which flows, Apex actions, APIs, or standard actions can the agent invoke?
Lifecycle: How will the agent be tested, monitored, deployed, and improved?
Adoption: What enablement and change management are needed?

Agentforce/13-Licensing--and--Limits/age.title: Agentforce Action Metering & Cost Patterns
Agentforce Licensing
Agentforce/13-Licensing--and--Limits/age.content:
Pricing Model
Agentforce is priced per conversation, not per user seat.

















UnitDescriptionAgentforce ConversationOne end-to-end interaction between a user and an agent (from first message to resolution or handoff)OverageConversations beyond purchased volume are charged at a per-conversation rate


                  
                  Note
                  
                

As of 2025, Salesforce has publicised a target price of ~$2 per conversation. Enterprise contracts will vary. For CTA scenarios, the key point is consumption-based, not seat-based.


What Counts as a Conversation

Starts when a user first engages the agent on a channel
Ends when: issue resolved, user disengages, or handoff to human agent occurs
A single conversation can involve multiple reasoning steps and action calls — these do not multiply the conversation count

Included Entitlements

Some Agentforce features are included with certain Sales/Service Cloud SKUs (check current entitlement guide)
Einstein Bots conversations are a separate entitlement from Agentforce conversations — they do not share the same pool

Key Considerations for Solutioning

























QuestionGuidanceHigh volume, simple interactionsEvaluate Einstein Bots (lower cost, deterministic) vs AgentforceComplex, varied interactionsAgentforce value increases with interaction complexity — cost per deflected human caseData Cloud groundingData Cloud has its own licensing (credits model); factor in if adding unified profile groundingMuleSoft actionsMuleSoft Anypoint API calls may have their own consumption cost


                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

In a scenario with tight budget and predictable interaction patterns, recommend Einstein Bots. For high deflection value with complex interactions, justify Agentforce on cost-per-resolution vs cost-per-human-agent-handle-time.


Governance Recommendations

Monitor consumption via Einstein Usage & Limits in Setup
Set conversation caps per channel to prevent overage surprises
Build in escalation to human agents to avoid runaway reasoning loops driving up counts

Agentforce/agentforce-glossary.title: Agentforce Glossary
Agentforce/agentforce-glossary.content:
Alphabetical reference of key terms across the Agentforce domain. Each entry gives a concise definition and links to the dedicated note for deeper coverage.


                  
                  How to use 
                  
                

Use this as a quick-lookup companion during exam prep. Follow [[WikiLinks]] for the full treatment of any concept.



A
Action
A discrete capability the atlas-reasoning-engine can invoke on behalf of an agent — the “hands” of the agent. Actions read data, write records, call external systems, or generate content. Types include Flow, Apex, Prompt Template, MuleSoft API Catalog, and custom HTTP.
→ See agentforce-actions
Agent
A configured autonomous worker with a defined role, system-level instructions, a set of Topics, and associated Actions. The agent perceives context, decides which action to invoke, executes it, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met.
→ See agentforce-overview
Agent Builder
The declarative Salesforce UI (in Setup) used to configure an agent: define role/instructions, create Topics, attach Actions, and test the agent in a conversational preview panel before activation.
→ See introduction-to-agentforce-builder, customize-agentforce-and-deploy
AgentExchange
Salesforce’s marketplace for pre-built agent components (Topics, Actions, agent templates) from Salesforce and third-party partners. Equivalent of AppExchange for agent building blocks.
→ See agentexchange-quick-look
Agentforce
Salesforce’s platform for building and deploying autonomous AI agents that reason, plan, and act across Salesforce data and external systems. Built on the atlas-reasoning-engine, natively embedded in the Salesforce Platform, and governed by the einstein-trust-layer.
→ See agentforce-overview, introduction-to-agentforce
Agentforce Conversation
The licensing unit for Agentforce: one end-to-end interaction from first user message to resolution or handoff. A single conversation can span multiple reasoning steps and action calls; these do not multiply the conversation count.
→ See agentforce-licensing
Agentforce Sales Coach
A pre-built agent type that provides role-play simulations, deal coaching, and call debrief assistance for sales reps.
→ See agentforce-overview, sell-smarter-with-agentforce
Agentforce Sales Development Representative (SDR)
A pre-built agent type for outbound prospecting and lead nurturing via email, operating autonomously without a human sending each message.
→ See agentforce-for-sales-quick-look
Agentforce Service Agent
A pre-built agent type for autonomous customer-facing support. Replaces or augments einstein-bots and handles varied, multi-step service interactions.
→ See agentforce-for-service-module, agentforce-vs-einstein-bots
Atlas Reasoning Engine
The orchestration layer inside Agentforce that drives the agent’s decision loop: Observe → Plan → Act → Observe → repeat. Selects which action to call, in what order, and when the task is complete. Customers configure it via Topics and Actions — they do not train or fine-tune it.
→ See atlas-reasoning-engine
Audit Trail (LLM)
A log of all LLM interactions produced by the einstein-trust-layer, enabling compliance review of inputs, outputs, and data masking events. Separate from the standard Salesforce Setup Audit Trail.
→ See einstein-trust-layer

C
Channel
The surface through which users interact with an agent — for example: Messaging (SMS/WhatsApp), Experience Cloud chat, Slack, email, or voice. Configured during agent deployment.
→ See agentforce-overview, deploy-agent-to-slack, agentforce-on-mobile-quick-look
Context Window
The finite block of text passed to the LLM per call, containing the system prompt (role/instructions/topic), conversation history, and grounded data. Size limits constrain how much retrieved data can be injected per reasoning step.
→ See atlas-reasoning-engine, data-grounding-and-data-cloud
Conversation → See Agentforce Conversation
Custom Agent
A purpose-built agent configured from scratch in Agent Builder for any business process, as distinct from pre-built agent types (Service Agent, SDR, Sales Coach).
→ See agentforce-overview, customize-agentforce-and-deploy

D
Agentforce Data Library
A Salesforce feature that allows agents to search, retrieve, and reason over unstructured content (documents, PDFs, files) stored in Salesforce — without requiring a Data Cloud licence. Files are indexed and made searchable via vector embeddings, enabling RAG-style retrieval directly from native file storage (e.g., Salesforce Files, SharePoint via connector). Distinct from data-cloud-agentforce-context grounding: Data Library covers document/file retrieval; Data Cloud covers structured unified profiles and calculated insights.


                  
                  CTA angle 
                  
                

Use Data Library when the grounding requirement is document-based (manuals, SOPs, policy docs) and Data Cloud is not licensed or not warranted. Use Data Cloud when real-time unified customer profile data across source systems is the requirement.


→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud, manage-your-agents-data, ground-your-agent-with-data
Data Cloud (Agentforce context)
Salesforce’s real-time data platform, used as a grounding source to inject the unified-individual profile into the agent’s context window. Required when the use case demands personalised, 360-degree responses drawing on data from multiple source systems.
→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud, ground-your-agent-with-data
Data Processing Agreement (DPA)
The contractual instrument through which LLM providers commit to zero data retention of Salesforce customer data. Enforced by the einstein-trust-layer; not reliant on provider settings alone.
→ See einstein-trust-layer
Dynamic Data Masking
An einstein-trust-layer capability: PII and admin-designated sensitive fields are tokenised before being sent to the LLM, then de-tokenised on return — so raw sensitive data never leaves the Salesforce boundary.
→ See einstein-trust-layer

E
Einstein Bots
Salesforce’s rule-based / NLU-intent chatbot platform, predating Agentforce. Dialogs follow scripted flows; responses are deterministic. Priced on a separate conversation credit entitlement from Agentforce.
→ See agentforce-vs-einstein-bots
Einstein Search
Salesforce’s semantic search engine used to retrieve Knowledge Articles (and other content) as a grounding source via retrieval-augmented-generation.
→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud, atlas-reasoning-engine
Einstein Trust Layer
Salesforce’s security and governance framework that sits between the platform and external LLM providers. Core capabilities: zero data retention, dynamic data masking, toxicity detection, audit trail, and secure gateway routing. Applies to all Einstein generative AI features, not only Agentforce.
→ See einstein-trust-layer, agentforce-security-and-permissions

F
Flow Action
The most common Agentforce action type: an autolaunched Salesforce Flow exposed as an invocable action. No-code, reusable, testable, and bulk-safe. Preferred when Flow is capable of meeting the requirement.
→ See agentforce-actions

G
Grounding
The process of injecting relevant, real-time data into the agent’s context window before an LLM call, enabling accurate and context-specific responses. Sources include Salesforce records, Knowledge Articles, data-cloud-agentforce-context, and external data via MuleSoft.
→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud, atlas-reasoning-engine

H
Hallucination
A response generated by an LLM that is plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or invented. Mitigated in Agentforce by: grounding with real data (RAG), constraining the agent to a configured action set, and the atlas-reasoning-engine’s guardrails.
→ See atlas-reasoning-engine, data-grounding-and-data-cloud
Handoff
The mechanism by which an Agentforce agent transfers a conversation to a human agent in Omni-Channel when confidence is low, the user requests it, or escalation rules are met. Shares the same Omni-Channel routing infrastructure as einstein-bots.
→ See agentforce-overview, atlas-reasoning-engine

I
Instructions
Natural-language guidance written by admins/developers at two levels: (1) agent-level role instructions (system prompt); (2) topic-level instructions that constrain what the agent should and should not do within a topic. Instructions are the primary lever for shaping agent behaviour.
→ See agentforce-overview, programmatic-instructions-in-agentforce
@InvocableMethod
The Apex annotation that exposes an Apex class method as an invocable action, callable from Flows and Agentforce. Used when Flow cannot meet the requirement (e.g., complex logic, callouts with custom error handling).
→ See agentforce-actions
Iteration Cap
A configurable limit on the maximum number of reasoning steps the atlas-reasoning-engine can execute for a single user message, preventing runaway loops and uncontrolled cost.
→ See atlas-reasoning-engine, agentforce-licensing

L
Large Language Model (LLM)
A deep learning model trained on large text corpora, capable of natural language understanding and generation. Agentforce uses LLMs (via the einstein-trust-layer gateway) as the reasoning core. Salesforce partners with providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Azure OpenAI.
→ See large-language-models, einstein-trust-layer

M
MuleSoft API Catalog Action
An Agentforce action type that invokes a REST API governed and catalogued through MuleSoft Anypoint Platform. Preferred when the external system is already integrated via Anypoint, or when API governance, rate-limiting, and multi-agent reuse are required.
→ See agentforce-actions, MuleSoft & Middleware Positioning

N
Natural Language Understanding (NLU)
The intent-classification layer used by einstein-bots to map user input to scripted dialog flows. NLU intents do not automatically map to Agentforce Topics — topic design requires rethinking, not just migration.
→ See agentforce-vs-einstein-bots, natural-language-processing-basics

O
Omni-Channel
Salesforce’s routing and queue management framework. Used by Agentforce for escalation/handoff to human agents; shared infrastructure with Einstein Bots transfers. Not part of the reasoning loop itself.
→ See agentforce-overview, agentforce-vs-einstein-bots

P
Prompt Builder
The Salesforce declarative tool for creating and managing reusable prompt templates with dynamic merge fields. Templates are used as Agentforce actions (Prompt Template action type) for LLM-generated content such as case summaries, draft emails, or field generation.
→ See prompt-builder-basics, get-hands-on-with-prompt-builder
Prompt Template
A managed, versioned template created in Prompt Builder. Combines static instructions with merge fields (record data, related data) to form a well-structured LLM prompt. When used as an Agentforce action, token consumption counts toward Einstein quotas.
→ See prompt-builder-basics, prompt-fundamentals

R
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
The pattern of retrieving relevant documents or records at query time and injecting them into the LLM context window, so the model reasons from real data rather than training knowledge alone. Core grounding mechanism in Agentforce.
→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud, atlas-reasoning-engine
Role (Agent)
The agent-level definition of what persona and purpose the agent has — expressed as a system-level instruction. Sets the agent’s overall behaviour and constraints before any topic or action is considered.
→ See agentforce-overview, introduction-to-agentforce-builder

S
Secure Gateway
The einstein-trust-layer component that routes all LLM API calls through a Salesforce-controlled gateway, ensuring no direct client-to-LLM communication and enabling masking/audit on every call.
→ See einstein-trust-layer
System Prompt
The full instruction block passed to the LLM at the start of each reasoning step, composed of: agent role instructions + topic instructions + retrieved grounding data. Admins influence this via Instructions; they do not write raw system prompts.
→ See atlas-reasoning-engine, agentforce-overview

T
Token
The unit of text consumed by an LLM (roughly ¾ of a word). Prompt Template actions and grounding data contribute to token consumption, which is tracked against Einstein quota/limits.
→ See large-language-models, agentforce-licensing
Topic
A cluster of related intents or tasks the agent can handle, each with its own natural-language instructions and a set of associated Actions. Topics map to a segment of the system prompt. An Action can belong to multiple Topics.
→ See agentforce-overview, agentforce-actions
Toxicity Detection
An einstein-trust-layer capability that scans both user inputs and LLM outputs for harmful content, blocking toxic responses before they reach users.
→ See einstein-trust-layer

U
Unified Individual
Data Cloud’s merged, deduplicated customer profile that consolidates identity and behavioural data from all connected source systems. When used as an Agentforce grounding source, gives the agent a real-time 360-degree view of the customer.
→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud, data-fundamentals-for-ai

V
Vector Search
A semantic similarity search technique used by einstein-search to retrieve Knowledge Articles relevant to a user query. Complements structured SOQL retrieval for unstructured knowledge content.
→ See data-grounding-and-data-cloud

Z
Zero Data Retention
The contractual commitment (enforced via dpa) that LLM providers will not store or train on Salesforce customer data submitted through the einstein-trust-layer gateway.
→ See einstein-trust-layer

Agentforce/agentforce-setup-sequence.title: Agentforce Setup Sequence
Agentforce/agentforce-setup-sequence.content:
End-to-end journey from org enablement to production monitoring. Each phase should complete before the next is reliable; testing and iteration are continuous, not a single gate.
Mindmap Overview
mindmap
  root((Agentforce Setup))
    1 Foundation
      Enable Agentforce
      Trust Layer
      Permissions
    2 Planning
      Use Case
      Architecture
      Guardrails
      Prototype
    3 Configuration
      Agentforce Builder
      Agent Type
      Topics and Actions
      Instructions
    4 Grounding
      Data Library
      Data 360
      RAG
    5 Customisation
      Prompt Builder
      Apex Actions
      Flow Actions
      Prog Instructions
    6 Testing
      Conversation Preview
      Testing Centre
      5-Step Strategy
    7 Deployment
      Web Messaging
      Slack
      Mobile
    8 Monitoring
      Analytics
      Utterance Analysis
      Iterate


Phase 1: Foundation Enablement
Pre-requisites before any agent build can begin.



































StepFeatureWhat to configureTrailhead1.1Enable AgentforceSetup → Agents → Enable; understand agent types, conversation credits, and org limitsAgentforce Basics1.2Einstein Trust LayerReview data masking rules, zero data retention setting, secure gateway; verify org Trust Layer configThe Agentforce Trust Layer1.3Trusted Agentic AIUnderstand platform guardrail types, trust patterns, and ethical AI constraintsTrusted Agentic AI1.4Licenses & PermissionsAssign Einstein Copilot User permission set; configure Running User on the agent; confirm conversation credit entitlementArchitect the Right Solution


                  
                  Blocker 
                  
                

Agentforce Builder is unavailable until Agentforce is enabled and the current user has the Einstein Copilot User permission. Confirm both before starting any build.



Phase 2: Planning & Architecture
Define what the agent will do before touching the builder. This is the only structured methodology Salesforce provides for agent design — skipping it leads to rebuilds.









































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead2.1Use CaseDefine agent purpose, success metrics, target users, and channelsIdentify the Agent Use Case2.2Solution ArchitectureChoose agent type (Service, Sales, Custom), determine required data sources, actions, and integrationsArchitect the Right Solution2.3GuardrailsDefine scope limits, topics the agent must never handle, and escalation paths to human agentsDefine the Agent Guardrails2.4Agent Work OutlineMap out topics, sub-intents, required actions, and conversation flowsOutline the Agent’s Work2.5PrototypeBuild a minimal agent to validate the approach before the full buildPrototype the Agent

Phase 3: Agent Configuration
Core build in Agentforce Builder.















































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead3.1Agentforce BuilderSetup → Agents → New; understand the Builder UI — Conversation Preview panel, Topics panel, Actions panelIntroduction to Agentforce Builder3.2New Agentforce BuilderTour updated Builder features: inline testing, improved action management, topic editorNew Agentforce Builder: Quick Look3.3Agent Type & ChannelSelect agent type; assign the deployment channel (Messaging, Slack, Mobile, Experience Cloud)Agentforce Basics3.4System Prompt / InstructionsWrite agent persona, scope boundaries, tone, and escalation rules in the Instructions fieldIntroduction to Agentforce Builder3.5TopicsCreate topics representing conversation intents; each topic gets its own instructions and set of actionsProgrammatic Instructions in Agentforce3.6ActionsAdd standard actions (Flow, Apex, Prompt Template, Data Library) to each topicAgent Customization: Quick Look

Phase 4: Data Grounding
Give the agent access to real data so responses are accurate and current.



































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead4.1Data LibraryCreate a file-based Data Library; upload documents (PDFs, articles); expose as a Retrieval action on a topicAgentforce Data Library Basics4.2Grounding OptionsUnderstand all grounding methods: CRM record context, Data Library, Data Cloud, Prompt TemplatesGrounding an Agent with Data4.3Data 360 IntegrationConnect Data Cloud to Agentforce; enable unified customer profiles and semantic search on Data Cloud objectsData 360-Powered Agentforce4.4Advanced RAGBuild Search Index and Retriever in Data Cloud; create grounded Prompt Templates; tune retrieval for accuracyAdvanced RAG with Data 360 and Agentforce


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Data Library (file-based) requires no Data Cloud licence. Data 360 RAG requires Data Cloud and is needed for semantic search over large structured datasets.



Phase 5: Customisation
Extend the agent beyond standard configuration.









































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead5.1Prompt BuilderBuild Prompt Templates that inject CRM record context into LLM responses; attach templates as agent actionsCustom Service Agents with Prompt Builder5.2Prompt EngineeringApply few-shot, chain-of-thought, and role-prompting techniques to improve output qualityPrompt Engineering Techniques5.3Apex ActionsWrite @InvocableMethod classes; expose as agent actions for custom logic not available in standard FlowAgent Customization with Apex5.4Flow ActionsBuild agent-ready Flows (Autolaunched or Screen Flow); add to topics as actionsAgent Customization with Flows5.5Programmatic InstructionsAdd variables, conditional logic, and topic filters to Instructions to enforce business rulesProgrammatic Instructions in Agentforce

Phase 6: Testing
Validate agent behaviour before deployment.



































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead6.1Conversation PreviewUse Builder’s Conversation Preview panel for interactive ad-hoc testing during the build cycleIntroduction to Agentforce Builder6.2Testing CentreCreate a Test Suite; define test cases with expected outcomes; use AI to auto-generate tests from agent configAgentforce Testing Center6.3Testing Tools & StrategiesApply the 5-Step testing strategy; run tests in a sandbox; review action-level pass/fail resultsAgentforce Testing Tools and Strategies6.4Results & IterationDiagnose action failures; refine Instructions, topics, or actions; re-run until stableView Test Results


                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Run Testing Centre after every significant change to Instructions, topics, or actions — not just as a final gate before deployment.



Phase 7: Deployment
Activate the agent on the target channel(s).



































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead7.1Deployment OverviewUnderstand channel options; activate the agent in Builder; publish to the selected channelAgentforce Deployment: Quick Look7.2Web / Embedded ServiceConfigure Embedded Service Deployment; assign agent to a Messaging Channel for web or in-app chatAgentforce Deployment: Quick Look7.3SlackConnect Salesforce org to Slack; configure the Slack agent; publish to a Slack channel or DMAgentforce Configuration for Slack7.4MobileEnable Agentforce on the Salesforce Mobile App; configure mobile-specific agent and channel settingsAgentforce on Mobile: Quick Look

Phase 8: Monitoring & Iteration
Post-launch visibility and continuous improvement loop.



































StepFeatureWhat to doTrailhead8.1Agentforce AnalyticsMonitor conversation volume, resolution rate, handoff rate, and topic distribution in the Analytics dashboardAgentforce Analytics and Monitoring8.2Utterance AnalysisIdentify unhandled utterances and conversation gaps; map them to missing topics or actionsMonitor Agent Conversations with Utterance Analysis8.3Conversation ReviewDive into individual transcripts to find prompt failures, wrong action selections, or low-confidence responsesDive into Agentforce Analytics8.4Continuous ImprovementUse analytics data to prioritise new actions, refine Instructions, and expand topic coverageUse Your Data to Make Better Agents

Pre-Built Agent Specialist Paths
These agents follow the same 8-phase sequence but ship with Salesforce-managed configuration and have their own dedicated setup modules.
