CTA-Notes/Communication/the-exam-diagram.title: The Exam Diagrams
CTA-Notes/Communication/the-exam-diagram.content:
The Important Diagrams
When presenting your solution to the CTA Board there are ABSOLUTELY NO DIAGRAMS REQUIRED! It is not something that is a mandatory graded part of your presentation. Your are ultimately graded on your ability to solve for the requirements written in the scenario and for your dispersal of that information when you present and do the Q&A session with your judges. With that said, I ALSO DO NOT BELIEVE IT IS POSSIBLE TO PASS WITHOUT CREATING THE 4 DIAGRAMS LISTED BELOW.
Make sure however that you only use your diagrams as supporting documents to help easily visualize your solution. DO NOT just open your diagrams and start speaking to your diagrams out of context of the requirements. Instead, open your diagrams on the right side of your screen/monitor and your solution/google doc on the left side of your monitor. When you get to a solution within your word doc that can be visually assisted by your diagrams, pull the diagram up and explain (with the assistance of your diagram) how you are solving that solution.
I have also added two optional diagrams at the bottom of this page to consider creating and presenting should you have the time, but again, they are not required and I wouldn’t draw them unless you had a ton of extra time at the end of your scenario somehow. I personally used very minimal diagramming compared to most recommendations in the ecosystem. I only presented the four “required” diagrams listed below and nothing else. REMEMBER all of these required diagrams are just what I believe should be created to help tell a story easily to the judges, but if you listen to Suzanne’s AMA that I listed on the home page of this site, she states that no diagrams are required, so they are not TRULY required, they are just what I think is gonna assist in your story telling the most.
Additionally, I would make 100% of your diagrams in lucid chart, and present them via lucid chart. There is no reason to utilize google slides unless you are just a glutton for punishment or something.
Here is a link to my suggested approach/template for creating diagrams via lucidchart to present for your CTA Review Board: CTA Review Board Lucidchart Template.

1) Company Overview and Org Strategy (REQUIRED)
This is not so much a diagram as it is just a lucid chart tab where you will type up a quick overview about the company, what it is trying to achieve with this project you are solutioning for, what org strategy you are choosing to solve the client’s needs (single or multi-org) and why, what mobile strategy you are choosing to solve the client’s needs and why, any major risks you have identified while solving your CTA scenario (for example a really short timeline for a huge project) and how you plan to address then, and any assumptions you are making that are important to understanding your solutioning for a scenario (for instance, assuming that their ERP system already has a payment gateway you can leverage).
Example Company Overview and Org Strategy Tab:



2) Actors (User Personas) and Licenses Diagram (REQUIRED)
This diagram is used to communicate the required Salesforce licenses for each user persona (for example a sales rep), why you are suggesting those licenses (maybe a sales rep needs a sales cloud license because they need access to the Quote object or to Opportunity Forecasting), and the amount of licenses you will need to purchase for that persona (this is important because the amount of licenses has impacts on other parts of your solution, for instance how much data and file storage are available in your org).
The purpose of this diagram is the following:

This allows for an easy understanding of what each user persona will be doing in the system and to easily justify their licenses.
I would suggest including all user personas mentioned in the scenario, even if they will not actually be users in the Salesforce system so the judges know that you at least considered them and what your plan for them is, and to include all required license types for each user persona (including Salesforce feature licenses).

IMPORTANT NOTE: For your CTA scenario you should not try to cut costs with the basic licenses (Sales, Service, Platform, and Experience Cloud licenses), you should just assume you have infinite money and use the license that will enable you to build the solution in its simplest form. For instance, if your Sales Reps only need a Sales Cloud license because they need access to the Opportunity object and not for anything else ABSOLUTELY DO NOT suggest a lower cost setup where you would replace the Opportunity object with a custom object so that you could give Sales Reps platform licenses instead… That is a recipe for disaster.
Example Actors and Licenses Diagram:


3) The Data Model Diagram (ERD) (REQUIRED)
This Diagram is the MOST CRITICAL diagram to get right on the exam. Basically everything hinges on on your database/object setup. The data model (if you are unfamiliar with it) is basically the same as an ERD (entity relationship diagram).
Your Data Model Diagram Should Ideally Include the Following:

Every object you are proposing for your solution, and the relationships between them.
An easy way to identify the custom versus standard objects used in your solution and your planned usage of each of them (making the outline of a custom object a different color for example).
An easy way to identify a master-detail relationship you are proposing for your solution (coloring the relationships in lucid chart a different color for instance)
An easy way to identify Large Data Volume Objects (LDV). You should ideally make sure to label objects that are slated to house millions of records on your diagram and their volume (something simple, for example, put the acronym LDV and then the quantity of records next to it like this: “LDV:4mil”).
A simple way of showing your OWD setting for each object (unless it’s controlled by parent). You should ideally label an objects OWD settings (Private, Read, Read/Write) on the object in your data model diagram (for example you could do the following on your object in the diagram: “OWD:P” to represent an OWD of private).
An easy way to visualize which user personas will be the owners of the records for each object. Knowing who the owners of each records are is important to understanding whether your proposed security architecture will work. You could denote this on your objects in the following way “O: Sales Rep” as a shorthand for “Owner: Sales Rep”.

Example Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD):


4) The System Landscape Diagram (REQUIRED)
The system landscape diagram will help you illustrate the different systems included within your solution and their relationships with one another (For instance, how does an ERP in your landscape integrate with your Salesforce org).
Your System Landscape Diagram should ideally include the following things:


Every system mentioned within your scenario, even if it is being retired or is not at all connected to your Salesforce org.


An easy way to identify a retired system in your landscape (I would suggested just making the retired systems outline red or some other obvious color).


Your Salesforce org as well as all of the clouds, add-on products, and managed packages you are suggesting to solve your scenario.


Your mobile solution and how it authenticates to your Salesforce org (it’s gonna use PKCE auth).


Your IAM (identity and access management) systems (like okta and active directory).


An ETL and ESB and how systems connect to your Salesforce instance through them, if your solution requires one (I’ve never seen one that didn’t).


A data warehouse if your solution has large data volumes and the use of a data warehouse is justified.


A way to easily identify each authorization flow you are using for each system integration you are proposing. For instance, are you using JWT or OAuth to connect to your ERP system (if your scenario has one). You can easily show this by putting the flow name next to the line that indicates an integration between two systems.


Example System Landscape Diagram:


5) The Role Hierarchy Diagram (OPTIONAL)
The role hierarchy diagram will help you to explain the roles your users will have in the system and how it will impact your sharing and visibility model.
The purpose of this diagram is the following:

To help explain your approach to data sharing and visibility in your CTA scenario

This Diagram should ideally include the following if you decide to create it:

This should include a full role hierarchy that shows how each role relates to one another. However in the case where you have multiple identical roles (ex: One role for every country an org does business in) you can just identify the first couple of roles and just indicate that more similar roles would be made for the other countries to save on time.
Do not forget your community/experience cloud site roles for cc+ and partner users (even the auto-generated ones)
Indicate any license type limitation of users assigned to the roles.

A reminder that I would not waste time on this diagram unless you have solved every requirement and have the time to come back and make this to support your solution.
Example Role Hierarchy Diagram:


6) The Environment Diagram (OPTIONAL)
The environment diagram will help to illustrate your approach to the different SF environments (orgs and org types) you intend to use and why you intend to use them. Again this is an optional diagram, only draw this if you have a ton of left over time.
The purpose of this diagram is the following:

This diagram is used to show how you intend to setup your various environments (dev sandboxes, integration, QA, UAT, Prod, etc) and to help explain why you would setup your environments that way.

This Diagram Should ideally Include the Following:

What environment types are being used at each stage of development/deployment
Justification as to what sandbox type you select for each environment (dev, partial, full)
What will take place in each environment and what kinda testing will be involved (does development take place in the sandbox or is it a training sandbox. Are we doing Apex and Jest tests only in the sandbox or are we also doing regression and user testing?).
What will be deployed to each environment and when that would take place in the software development lifecycle (SDLC)
Include any external applications you are planning to use to get your environment pipeline up and running (ex: github, jenkins, flosum, copado, etc)

Example Environment Diagram:

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Migration.title: Data Migration
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Migration.content:
Moving data from legacy systems (or another Salesforce org) into Salesforce. In a CTA scenario this shows up as: “the customer has N million records in system X — how do you get them in, without breaking sharing, automation, or the cutover window?”


                  
                  Exam framing 
                  
                

A good answer names four things: (1) the approach (big bang / phased / rolling), (2) the tooling (ETL + Bulk API), (3) how you protect the platform during the load (automation + sharing), and (4) how you prove the data is right afterwards (reconciliation + rollback).


Topics

Migration Lifecycle
Migration Approach
Load Design
Protecting the Platform During Load
Tooling
Validation, Cutover & Rollback
What Not to Migrate
Design Checklist for Migration Scenarios


Migration Lifecycle






























StageActivitiesKey outputs1. Extract & cleanseConnect legacy source to the ETL tool; profile data; deduplicate, standardise, enrichClean staging dataset; data-quality report (data-quality-and-mdm)2. Transform & mapMap legacy schema → Salesforce schema; define External IDs; convert picklists, dates, currencies, ownersMapping spec; transformation rules3. LoadLoad in dependency order; group children by parent; suspend automation and defer sharingLoaded records; error/success logs4. Post-loadRe-enable automation; resume sharing calculation; run reconciliationSigned-off migration; rollback decision
(CTA toolkit — Data Migration, adapted)


                  
                  Rehearse 
                  
                

Run at least one full trial migration in a Full sandbox before the production cutover to time the load and surface mapping errors. See environment-strategy.



Migration Approach





























OptionProsConsWhen to useBig bangSimple to plan; short transition; no dual-runningHigh risk; long downtime window; hard to recover if it failsSmall/medium data volume; single business unit; legacy can be switched off at a weekend cutoverPhased (incremental)Lower risk; easier to manage; less downtime per phaseMore complex planning; data consistency risk between old and new systems during overlapMultiple business units, regions, or clouds going live in wavesRollingMinimal downtime; flexibility to adjust mid-flightResource-intensive; overlapping operations need integration/syncContinuous operation required; segments migrate in succession
(CTA toolkit — Migration Approach)

Phased/rolling means legacy and Salesforce run side by side — you need a system-of-record decision per object and usually a sync integration (see Integration Patterns).
Plan a delta load (changes made in legacy after the initial extract) for every approach, including big bang.


Load Design
Dependency order
Parents before children, so lookups resolve:

Users, roles, profiles/permission sets (owners must exist first)
Accounts → Contacts → Opportunities / Cases / custom parents
Child and junction records
Files, notes, attachments (ContentVersion → ContentDocumentLink)

External IDs

Create an External ID field on each migrated object holding the legacy primary key.
Use upsert keyed on the External ID so reruns are idempotent (no duplicates when a load is retried).
Populate relationships by referencing the parent’s External ID in the child CSV instead of looking up Salesforce IDs first.
Keep the External ID after go-live — it supports delta loads, reconciliation, and ongoing integrations.

Preserving history and ownership

Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation (permission) lets the load set CreatedDate, CreatedById, etc. to the legacy values.
Update Records with Inactive Owners lets you keep ownership by users who have since been deactivated — load them as users, then deactivate.
Field history, feed history, and system-generated audit data can’t be loaded as-is — see What Not to Migrate.

Avoiding record-lock failures

Group child records by parent ID within the load file so parallel batches don’t contend for the same parent lock.
Loading millions of children under a single parent (or a single owner) creates data skew and lock contention — see Data Skew.
Prefer Bulk API 2.0 for volume, but it runs parallel only; when lock contention can’t be avoided by sorting, use Bulk API 1.0 in serial mode — see Bulk API 1.0 vs 2.0 Comparison.


Protecting the Platform During Load





























Before the loadAfter the loadDisable Flows, triggers, process automation (use a bypass flag — custom permission or hierarchy custom setting — rather than deactivating metadata in production)Re-enable automationSuspend / defer sharing calculationsResume sharing calculation → full recalculation runsDisable or relax duplicate rules for the loading user (API can set the duplicate-rule header to allow saves)Re-enable duplicate rules; run a duplicate-detection passRelax validation rules that legacy data wouldn’t satisfy (via bypass), or clean data firstRe-enable validationDisable email notifications / outbound messages / platform-event publishersRe-enable


                  
                  Deferred sharing is not free 
                  
                

Deferring sharing only postpones the cost — a full recalculation is required after resuming, and implicit sharing is not deferred. Benchmark it in the trial migration. See 26-deferred-sharing-maintenance, 22-sharing-recalculation, and Sharing & LDV.




                  
                  Why order matters 
                  
                

Loading with the final sharing model (OWD Private, deep role hierarchy, criteria-based rules) in place makes every insert pay the sharing-calculation cost. Common LDV-migration pattern: load → recalculate once.



Tooling



































ToolScaleUse forData Import WizardSmall (tens of thousands of records)Business-user imports of common objectsData Loader (Bulk API option)LargeAdmin/developer one-offs, scripted loadsETL / iPaaS (MuleSoft, Informatica, Talend, etc.)Large, repeatableCleansing + transformation + load in one pipeline; scheduled delta loads; recommended in CTA scenariosBulk API 2.0 directMillions of recordsCustom-built pipelines; see bulk-api-and-cursorsOrg-to-org tools / Salesforce ConnectVariesSalesforce-to-Salesforce consolidations; leave data in place and virtualise — see 32-salesforce-connect

In a board answer, name the ETL tool as the transformation + orchestration layer and Bulk API as the load transport.
If the same ETL tool is also used for ongoing integration, say so — it reduces the tool count (see 50-mulesoft).


Validation, Cutover & Rollback
Reconciliation (prove it’s right)

Record counts per object: source vs. Salesforce (include rejects).
Field-level checks: sample comparison or checksums on key fields (amounts, dates, status).
Relationship integrity: orphan checks (children with no parent), owner checks.
Business sign-off: users validate representative records and reports in UAT.

Cutover plan

Freeze changes in legacy (or start capturing deltas).
Final extract → transform → load.
Delta load for changes during the window.
Reconcile; go/no-go decision.
Switch integrations and users to Salesforce.
Keep legacy read-only for an agreed period, then decommission.

Rollback

Define the go/no-go criteria and rollback trigger up front.
Because of the External ID, a failed load can be deleted by External ID / load batch tag and rerun. Add a Migration_Batch__c text field if you need to identify records from a particular run.
Legacy stays authoritative until sign-off — rollback is “don’t cut over”, not “restore Salesforce”.


What Not to Migrate

Old inactive data nobody uses — archive it outside Salesforce and expose it on demand. This reduces storage cost and keeps the org fast. See data-archiving-and-backup.
Field history / audit trails — can’t be reloaded as history; keep in the archive or load key values into a custom history object only if there’s a real requirement.
Derived data that Salesforce recalculates (roll-ups, formulas).
Duplicates and junk — fix in the staging area, not after load (data-quality-and-mdm).



                  
                  Archive during migration 
                  
                

The preferred exam pattern is to archive old data while migrating (straight from legacy to the archive store, surfaced via OData / Salesforce Connect) rather than loading everything into Salesforce first and archiving later.



Design Checklist for Migration Scenarios

 Volume per object; which objects are LDV? (ldv)
 Approach chosen and justified (big bang / phased / rolling)
 ETL tool + Bulk API version named
 External ID on every migrated object; upsert for idempotency
 Load order and parent grouping to avoid locks / skew
 Automation bypass and deferred sharing plan
 Duplicate and data-quality handling before load
 History / ownership / audit-field preservation addressed
 Files and attachments strategy
 Trial migration in Full sandbox; timing measured
 Reconciliation, cutover, delta, and rollback plan
 Legacy decommission plan


Related Notes

data-quality-and-mdm — cleansing, deduplication, system of record
data-archiving-and-backup — what stays out of Salesforce
ldv — volume, skew, sharing impact
bulk-api-and-cursors — Bulk API 1.0 vs 2.0
26-deferred-sharing-maintenance — defer sharing calculations
environment-strategy — sandbox types for trial migrations
data-model — target schema decisions

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Model/dat.title: Data Model Constraints & Limits
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Model/dat.content:
Exceptions and hard limits in the Salesforce data model that change a solution decision — things that look possible on a whiteboard but aren’t (e.g. “route Assets through a queue”). Complements standard-object-oddities (standard-object quirks) and data-model (ERDs and design guidance).


                  
                  Exam framing 
                  
                

When you pick an object or relationship, check it against this list before you commit. If a constraint bites, say so in the board answer and name the workaround — it shows you know the platform’s edges.


Topics

Ownership & Queues
Relationship Limits
Converting & Changing Relationships
Delete Behaviour
Reporting Impact
External Object Relationships
Deployment Gotchas
What Still Needs Verifying

Sources are cited inline. Help articles were retrieved 2026-11-14; the Object Reference is v63.0 (Spring ‘25) from the vault’s SF Docs library, so re-check object lists against the current release before quoting them.

Ownership & Queues
Ownership drives sharing, queues, assignment rules, and Omni-Channel routing, so “can this object be queue-owned?” is a frequent make-or-break question.
Who can own what
The Object Reference shows each object’s OwnerId target type. If it refers to User only, the record cannot be owned by a queue.






























Owner can be…Standard objects (Object Reference v63.0)Solution impactUser onlyAccount, Contact, Campaign, Contract, Asset, Solution, Individual; also Note, ContentDocument, ContentVersionNo queue ownership → no queue-based work distribution, no assignment-rule-to-queue, no queue-based Omni-Channel routing for these recordsUser or Group (queue)Case, Lead, Order, Task, Work Order, Service Appointment, Contact Request, Incident, Problem, Swarm, Messaging Session, Voice Call, Return Order, Fulfillment Order, Location, and othersQueue ownership is possible — confirm the object is enabled for the queue in SetupUser or CalendarEventEvents can’t be queue-owned; the owner can be a calendarCustom objectsQueueSobject supports custom objects (Object Reference — QueueSobject)A custom object is the usual escape hatch when you need queue ownership


                  
                  "Refers To: Group" ≠ queue-enabled 
                  
                

The Object Reference tells you the owner field can point at a Group. Whether you can actually add the object to a queue is set up per queue (Setup → Queues → Supported Objects). The earlier, shorter queue-ownable list in standard-object-oddities is a subset of what the Object Reference shows — verify in the org before relying on either. This note did not verify Opportunity, Quote, Product, Entitlement, or Service Contract.


Master-detail children have no owner

On the detail side of a master-detail relationship the Owner field isn’t available; the record takes the master’s owner.
Custom objects on the detail side can’t have sharing rules, manual sharing, or queues, because those require the Owner field.
Detail records inherit security from the master and you can’t set permissions on the detail independently.
(Object Relationships Overview)

Queue behaviours that affect design













































BehaviourImpactSourceQueue members can be users, roles, public groups, territories, connections, or partner usersGroup-based membership keeps queue admin lowCreate QueuesGuest users can’t be queue membersSite/guest flows can’t “own” work through a queueCreate QueuesWork can be routed to queue members only, not their managersEscalation to a manager needs a separate rule or queueCreate QueuesGrant Access Using Hierarchies on the queue is overridden if the object’s sharing setting disables hierarchy accessRole-hierarchy visibility into queue records can silently not applyCreate QueuesFor Task queues, email/notification/reminders are sent only after the task is reassigned to a specific userDon’t rely on task notifications for queue-owned tasksCreate QueuesA queue holding multiple object types (e.g. Cases + Messaging Sessions) can cause Omni-Channel routing priority problems — one type can block anotherUse separate queues per channel, or make sure reps are online for all channels in the queueCreate QueuesBulk API can’t insert/update more than 18 queues at onceChunk queue data loads in a migrationObject Reference — QueueSobject
Workarounds when the object can’t be queue-owned



































OptionProsConsWhen to useAdd a queue-ownable work item (Case, or a custom “Request” object) pointing at the Asset/AccountFull queue, assignment rule, and Omni-Channel supportExtra object and relationship; work item and record can driftWork distribution is the real requirement (e.g. asset inspection requests)Custom object for the entityQueue-ownable; full controlLose standard-object features and integrationsEntity doesn’t need Account/Asset-specific featuresPublic group + sharing (+ Flow round-robin assignment to users)Stays on the standard objectNo queue UI/semantics; assignment logic is customFew users; no queue SLA neededField-based assignment (owner assigned by Flow/territory)Simple; transparentNo claim-from-queue; user must be pre-chosenAccount/territory-driven ownership


                  
                  Board takeaway 
                  
                

For Asset, Account, Contact, Campaign, and Contract: “queues aren’t supported on the object, so work distribution runs through a queue-ownable record (Case/Work Order/custom) that references it.”



Relationship Limits
(Considerations for Object Relationships, Object Relationships Overview)





























































ConstraintSolution impactEach custom object can have up to 2 master-detail relationships and up to 40 total relationships; each relationship also counts toward the custom-field limitJunction objects use both M-D slots; a hub object can run out of relationship slotsMultilevel master-detail: up to 3 custom detail levelsDeep hierarchies (master → detail → subdetail → sub-subdetail) cap out at 3 custom levelsStandard objects can’t be on the detail side of a custom masterModel the standard object as the master or use a lookupAn object can appear only once in multilevel master-detail relationshipsA subdetail can’t also be the master of another multilevel chainCustom junction objects can’t have their own detail objects, and can’t be on the master side of another M-DDon’t hang children off a junction; add a separate child object with a lookupRoll-up summaries: a master can’t roll up subdetail directly — the detail needs its own roll-up field firstMulti-level totals need intermediate roll-upsSelf-relationships must be lookups (not master-detail), and a record can’t link to itselfParent/child on the same object (account hierarchy, bill of materials) is lookup-basedNo many-to-many self-relationship — the junction’s two masters can’t be the same object”Contact ↔ Contact” style links need a different designHierarchical relationship is available for the User object onlyManager chains use hierarchical; everything else uses a self-lookupCan’t create a master-detail on a custom object that already has dataCreate as lookup, populate every record, then convertBy default records can’t be reparented in master-detail; admins can allow reparenting on custom objectsPlan for reparenting on migration/merge scenariosBest practice: don’t exceed 10,000 child records per master in a master-detailRoll-up and sharing recalculation cost — see ldv, 23-data-skewMultilevel master-detail doesn’t support division transfersRules out multilevel M-D if the org uses divisions

Converting & Changing Relationships






























ChangeRuleSide effectMaster-detail → lookupOnly if no roll-up summary fields exist on the masterFor a custom detail object the OWD becomes public read/writeLookup → master-detailOnly if the lookup is populated on every recordOWD becomes Controlled by Parent; sharing model updated to public read/writeLookup → master-detail when child OWD is already Controlled by ParentNot allowed—Change the “Related To” object after saveNot allowedChoose the parent carefully


                  
                  Silent security change 
                  
                

Converting M-D ↔ lookup changes the child’s OWD. Re-check sharing and external access before and after.



Delete Behaviour









































ConstraintSolution impactDeleting a master deletes its detail and subdetail records (cascade)Intentional for line items; dangerous for records you must retainCan’t undelete a detail record if its master was deleted separately afterwardsRecycle Bin recovery has dependenciesCan’t delete a custom object that is the master in a master-detailRemove the relationship firstLookup: can’t delete an object or record when the combined records of the two linked objects exceed 100,000Deleting parents in high-volume lookup models needs child cleanup first — relevant to ldv and archiving (data-archiving-and-backup)“Delete this record also” (cascade delete on lookup) is only for a custom lookup field on a custom object, disabled by default, and must be enabled by contacting SalesforceNot available for lookups to standard objectsCascade delete bypasses security and sharingUsers can delete records they can’t seeMany-to-many: a user can’t delete a parent with more than 200 junction records if the junction has a roll-up summary to the other parentBulk-delete junction rows first in migration/cleanupJunction records are deleted when either master is deleted; deleted permanently when both areAccount for reverse-direction deletes

Reporting Impact





















RelationshipStandard report typesLookupTwo objects joined in one reportMaster-detailMaster + detail + one other lookup (three objects)Many-to-manyTwo report types joining the primary/secondary master and junction; master order matters (the first master defines the record scope)

Multilevel master-detail uses custom report types; they count toward the org’s custom report type limit, and no reports generate if the limit is exceeded.
Cross-object reporting beyond these joins needs custom report types or analytics — see reporting.


External Object Relationships
(Considerations for Object Relationships)

Only lookup, external lookup, and indirect lookup relationships are available for external objects.
No cascade delete on external object relationships.
Lookup search isn’t available for external lookup or indirect lookup fields — users type the External ID / target field value manually (not applicable for the cross-org adapter on external lookup).
Lookup filters aren’t available for external lookup fields.
Indirect lookup fields can be created on external objects only, and the parent needs a custom field that is External ID + Unique (case-sensitive match if the source is case-sensitive).
Related lists of child external objects can load slowly when the external system is slow or unavailable.
Creating a child record from the parent detail page doesn’t auto-populate the relationship field.
Relationship fields can be overwritten when you sync the external object.
Salesforce Connect external objects are an extra-cost add-on for Enterprise, Performance, and Unlimited editions.

See 32-salesforce-connect for the adapter side.

Deployment Gotchas
Relevant to environment-strategy and data-migration:

A Metadata API deployment that adds or converts to a master-detail field permanently deletes detail records in the Recycle Bin — soft-delete or populate parents first, or the deployment fails.
A profile/permission set with a master-detail child entity can have a broken permission dependency (e.g. child View All requires parent View All); Salesforce fixes the parent on the first save.


What Still Needs Verifying
Not confirmed from official docs while writing this note — check before quoting numbers in a board answer:

Per-edition limits on custom objects, custom fields, and record types per object (Limits Quick Reference); the guide’s old URL no longer resolves and I could not retrieve the current page.
Roll-up summary field count per object and supported aggregate fields.
Formula field size/complexity limits and cross-object formula depth.
Queue enablement for Opportunity, Quote, Product, Entitlement, Service Contract and Knowledge article versions.
Person Account compatibility restrictions — see Person Accounts.
Whether any exception on this list changed after Spring ‘25 (v63.0).


Related Notes

standard-object-oddities — no-CRUD, no-quick-action, no-lookup, and zero-storage objects
data-model — ERDs and relationship design
ldv — skew and volume constraints
04-sharing-rules, 09-implicit-sharing — sharing behaviour that ownership and master-detail affect
data-migration — load order, parent grouping, ownership preservation

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Model/dat.title: Data Model
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Model/dat.content:
Hub for data-model design. In a CTA scenario you draw a data model diagram (key objects, relationships, cardinality, volumes) and justify each choice against sharing, volume (LDV), reporting, and licensing. The fastest way to get fluent is to know Salesforce’s official ERDs for the core clouds — this note walks through each one and pulls out what matters for a board answer.


                  
                  Exam framing 
                  
                

Every relationship and record-type decision has a side effect on security or performance. State the decision, then the consequence: “Master-detail → child inherits sharing from parent”, or “Lookup → child needs its own OWD.”


Topics

Reading the Official ERDs
Sales Cloud
Service Cloud
Activities (Tasks & Events)
Knowledge
Field Service & Work Orders
Sharing & Team Selling
Notes, Attachments & Documents
Consent & Privacy
Design Decisions
External Data
Design Checklist


Reading the Official ERDs
Salesforce publishes product ERDs with a common notation. Each diagram’s legend points to the full notation guide at sfdc.co/erdnotation.









































Legend elementMeaningCloud entity (tinted box, API name in italics)An object owned by that product’s data modelRelated entity (white/black border)Object from another area shown for context (e.g. Account, Contact on the Service ERD)Extended related entityRelated object with additional attributes shownExternal entityObject outside SalesforceRecord type entity (dashed border)A record type of an object, not a separate objectConceptual entity (dotted)A grouping idea, not a real objectSupertype / subtypeAbstract group with concrete members (e.g. Activity → Task, Event)Relationship linesParent-child, required, optional, many-to-many, extension, mutually exclusive (“OR”)
Official ERDs are published in the Data Model Gallery; the notation is explained in Salesforce Data Model Notation.


                  
                  ERDs are dated 
                  
                

The ERDs below carry “subject to change without notice” and last-modified stamps of 2021–2022. Use them to learn structure; confirm object and field names in the Object Reference before putting them on a board diagram.



Sales Cloud

Source: Sales Overview Data Model (Salesforce Data Model Gallery).
What to take from it:

Account is the hub. Contacts, Opportunities, Cases, Assets, Contracts, Quotes, and Orders all hang off it.
Account hierarchy: Account has a self-relationship (parent / child) — use for corporate hierarchies; watch hierarchy depth and account skew.
Contact ↔ Account many-to-many: Account Contact Relation (AccountContactRelation) lets one Contact relate to several Accounts, in addition to the Contact’s primary Account.
Contact roles are junction objects: Opportunity Contact Role, Contract Contact Role — and Campaign Member, which targets a Contact or a Lead (mutually exclusive).
Lead conversion: a Lead is promoted to Account, Contact, and Opportunity — it’s not a long-lived parent.
Opportunity detail: Opportunity → Opportunity Product (OpportunityLineItem) → Price Book Entry → Product (Product2). Quote and Order are priced from the same price book entries.
Teams: Account Team Member and Opportunity Team Member link the record to Users (see Sharing & Team Selling).
Territory management: Territory2 with ObjectTerritory2Association (Account ↔ Territory) and UserTerritory2Association (User ↔ Territory).
Partners: Partner and Partner Role relate Accounts to Opportunities.
Forecasting: Forecast Item / Opportunity Forecast Item hang off Opportunity.

Deeper diagrams for pricing, forecasting, and territories are embedded in sales-cloud:

Product & price book
Opportunity forecasting
Territory management



                  
                  Board takeaway 
                  
                

If a scenario needs many-to-many between customers and contacts (e.g. shared contacts across subsidiaries), name Account Contact Relation rather than a custom junction. Pair with standard-object-oddities: Account Contact Relation cannot be used in a lookup field and is part of community sharing-set design.



Service Cloud

Source: Support Overview Data Model (Salesforce Data Model Gallery).
What to take from it:

Case is the hub. It is reported by a Contact (and the Account via the Contact), and is the subject of many child objects.
Child objects of Case: Case Comment, Email Message, Case History, Case Milestone, Case Team Member (with Case Team Role), Case Article, Case Solution, Case Related Issue, Swarm / Swarm Member, Contact Request.
Entitlements and SLAs: Service Contract → Contract Line Item → Entitlement → (Entitlement Contact) → Case. Entitlements belong to an Account; Milestones attach to Cases through Case Milestone.
Incident / Problem: a Case relates to an Incident or a Problem through Case Related Issue (mutually exclusive in the diagram).
Knowledge links: Case Article joins a Case to a Knowledge Article; Case Solution links to the legacy Solution object. Both Solution and Knowledge use Category Data / Category Node (data categories).
Account Contact Relation appears here too — it’s the same junction as on the Sales ERD.

Design consequences:

























ObservationConsequenceCase has many high-volume children (Email Message, Case Comment, Case History)Plan for storage and LDV — Email Messages count toward data storage (calculating-data-storage)Case Team Member / Case Team RoleTeam-based sharing for Cases — see 04-sharing-rulesEntitlement → CaseEntitlement objects don’t support quick actions (standard-object-oddities)Cases can be queue-ownedStandard queue-ownable object (standard-object-oddities)
Capability context: service-cloud.

Activities (Tasks & Events)

Source: Tasks & Events Data Model (Salesforce Data Model Gallery).
What to take from it:

Activity is an abstract supertype with two concrete members: Task and Event.
Activities use polymorphic relationships:

“Who” (Activity Participant): Contact or Lead.
“What” (Activity Object): Account, Campaign, Case, Asset, Contract, Opportunity, Product, Solution, Order, or any custom object with the activity flag enabled.


Shared Activities: TaskRelation and EventRelation (many “Who” per activity, invitees). The diagram notes TaskRelation is only available with Shared Activities enabled.
Events can be invited to Users and Leads, and relate to Public or Resource Calendars.
Activities have a recurrence self-relationship (recurring series).

Design consequences:

Polymorphic WhoId / WhatId make reporting and SOQL harder — joins need type filters.
Activities are the classic LDV table (Task/Event volume grows fast) and a frequent skew source: millions of tasks under one Account.
Controlled-by-parent behaviour for Activity: see standard-object-oddities.


Knowledge

What to take from it:

Abstract vs concrete objects: KnowledgeArticle / KnowledgeArticleVersion are the abstract objects; the org’s actual objects are Knowledge__ka (article) and Knowledge__kav (version), derived from them. The same pattern applies to ViewStat, VoteStat, and VersionHistory.
Article types in Lightning Knowledge are record types — Knowledge__kav carries RecordTypeId “for article type”.
Data categories: Knowledge__DataCategorySelection links versions to category group/name (drives visibility).
Linking to work: CaseArticle links a Case to an article; LinkedArticle links Work Orders / Work Order Line Items to an article (plus LinkedArticleFeed / History).
Engagement: Knowledge__ViewStat, Knowledge__VoteStat, Vote, and Knowledge__Feed / FeedComment.

Capability context: knowledge-articles.

Field Service & Work Orders

Current official version: Field Service Core Data Model (Salesforce Data Model Gallery); the image above is an older diagram.
The diagram groups objects by colour: standard sales/service objects, workforce objects, territory & scheduling objects, and Service Appointment (the central object).
What to take from it:

Work Order relates to Case, Account, Entitlement, Contact, Asset, Work Type, and Price Book. It has a self-relationship (parent work order).
Work Order Line Item is a child of Work Order (also self-related), carrying Asset, Work Type, and price book entry details.
Service Appointment is the central scheduling object. Its parent record can be a Work Order, Work Order Line Item, Account, Asset, Lead, or Opportunity.
Service Territory (with parent territory) groups resources; Service Territory Member joins Territory ↔ Service Resource and carries Operating Hours.
Service Resource ↔ User; resources have Skills (Service Resource Skill ↔ Skill), Capacity, Absences, and Preferences.
Skill Requirement can be set on Work Type, Work Order, or Work Order Line Item — scheduling matches requirements to resource skills.
Assigned Resource is the junction between Service Appointment and Service Resource (or Service Crew); Service Crew / Crew Member model teams.
Operating Hours → Time Slots; Shift ties resources to territories.

Design consequences:

Work Orders and Line Items are on the standard-object CRUD exception list (standard-object-oddities).
A scenario asking for dispatch/scheduling is a justification point for Field Service vs custom — see work-orders-without-fsl.


Sharing & Team Selling

What to take from it:

Every sharing-enabled object has a <Object>Share table (CaseShare, LeadShare, ContactShare, AccountShare, CampaignShare, OpportunityShare). Each share row grants access to a UserOrGroupId — either a User or a Group.
Group has RelatedId pointing to UserRole — this is how role and role-and-subordinates groups exist as groups.
GroupMember joins Groups to Users or other Groups (nested groups).
Team tables: AccountTeamMember, OpportunityTeamMember, and UserTeamMember (default team: OwnerId has UserId members).

Design consequences:

Share tables grow with sharing complexity — a large driver of sharing-recalculation cost and LDV problems (Sharing & LDV, 22-sharing-recalculation).
Objects without a share table (e.g. Price Book, Product) can’t use sharing rules — see standard-object-oddities.
Implicit and team sharing behaviours: 09-implicit-sharing, 04-sharing-rules.



                  
                  About this diagram 
                  
                

It is a simplified, plain-notation ERD (not the standard Salesforce ERD style). Treat it as a mental model of the sharing tables, not a complete schema.



Notes, Attachments & Documents

What to take from it:

Note and Attachment both use a polymorphic ParentId to point at Account, Contact, Opportunity, Case, Campaign, Solution, Product, and others.
Document sits in a Folder and has an AuthId to a User (legacy Documents tab).



                  
                  Legacy objects 
                  
                

This ERD shows the legacy Notes/Attachments/Documents objects. New designs use Files (ContentDocument / ContentVersion / ContentDocumentLink) and Enhanced Notes. File storage and external storage options: document-management-systems, file-solution. Migrating legacy attachments to Files: see data-migration.



Consent & Privacy

Current official version: Privacy Consent Data Model (Salesforce Data Model Gallery); it is broader than the simplified diagram above.
What to take from it:

Individual is the hub. Lead, User, Person Account, and Contact each relate to an Individual record (the privacy profile for that person).
Contact Point Consent and Contact Point Type Consent record consent by channel/type, linked to the Individual and a Contact Point.
Data Use Purpose and Data Use Legal Basis capture why data is processed and the legal basis.
Brand relates to the consent objects so consent can be tracked per brand. The diagram numbers five objects (Individual, Contact Point Type Consent, Contact Point Consent, Data Use Purpose, Brand) 1–5.
Privacy and consent objects take zero storage — see standard-object-oddities.

Capability context: privacy-and-consent-management.

Design Decisions
Relationship Types









































OptionProsConsWhen to useLookupLoose coupling; child keeps its own owner, OWD, and sharing; parent optionalNo native roll-ups; no cascade delete by defaultIndependent entities that reference each otherMaster-detailChild inherits sharing and owner from parent; cascade delete; native roll-up summaryChild has no owner or own OWD; parent required; max 2 per objectTight parent-child (line items); when you need roll-upsJunction object (two master-details)Many-to-many; roll-ups on both parentsInherits sharing from both parents; junction skew at volumeMany-to-many (see Campaign Member, Opportunity Contact Role in the Sales ERD)Self-lookup / hierarchyParent-child within one objectDepth and reporting limitsAccount hierarchy, Service Territory hierarchyPolymorphic lookupOne field → several object types (WhoId, WhatId, ParentId)Harder to report and queryActivities, notes, attachments

Lookup → master-detail requires every child to already have a parent; master-detail → lookup requires removing roll-up summary fields first.
Standard objects can’t be the detail side of a custom parent; custom objects can be the detail side of a standard parent.
Hard limits that change designs — max 2 master-detail / 40 relationships per custom object, 3 custom detail levels, no master-detail on a populated custom object, cascade delete bypassing sharing, the 100,000-record lookup delete restriction, report-join limits: see data-model-constraints-and-limits.
Junctions and huge fan-out are data skew candidates — Junction Object Skew, account skew.



                  
                  Rule of thumb 
                  
                

Start with lookup. Choose master-detail only for sharing inheritance, cascade delete, or roll-ups when the child never exists without the parent.


Record Types

Control which page layouts, picklist values, and business processes (Opportunity sales process, Case support process, Lead process) a user sees; assigned via profiles / permission sets.
They do not affect record access.
On the Knowledge ERD they also define article types (Knowledge__kav.RecordTypeId).






























OptionProsConsWhen to useRecord types on one objectOne object, shared reporting and sharing modelAdmin overhead per type; same OWD and field set for allVariations of one entity (B2B vs B2C Account)Separate objectsDifferent fields, sharing, lifecycle; clean security boundaryDuplicate config; cross-object reporting is harderGenuinely different entities or very different volumes/sharingDynamic FormsShow/hide fields without extra record typesNot available on every object (standard-object-oddities)Layout variation only
Ownership & OWD

Every record has one owner (except master-detail children); only certain standard objects can be queue-owned — Asset, Account, Contact, Campaign, and Contract can’t; Case, Lead, Order, Task, and Work Order can (Ownership & Queues, standard-object-oddities).
OWD is set per object; special cases and “Controlled by Parent” are in Sharing Model Fields.
Many records under one owner or parent → skew and 23-data-skew. Design so sharing is expressible with roles + OWD, not thousands of criteria-based rules (Sharing & LDV).

Standard vs Custom Objects

Prefer standard objects when they fit — features, reporting, and integrations come free.
Standard-object quirks (no quick actions, no CRUD toggles, zero storage, no lookups, special team sharing): standard-object-oddities.
Storage: calculating-data-storage. Licensing: licenses-guide.

Person Accounts

Combine Account and Contact into one record for B2C.
Enabling is permanent — decide deliberately.
Affects storage (a person account is both an Account and a Contact record), sharing, and Experience Cloud design; check ISV package compatibility first.
The Consent ERD shows Person Account as an Individual-linked entity. Related: customer-identity-and-headless-identity.

Packages & Industry Solutions to Consider
Justify each choice in the Q&A, even if you don’t pick it:

CPQ — products, quotes, pricing rules
Lightning Scheduler — appointment scheduling
Field Service (formerly Field Service Lightning) — dispatch, work orders, mobile (see ERD above)
Financial Services Cloud (optional)


External Data
When data shouldn’t be copied into Salesforce (volume, cost, system of record elsewhere), use external objects via Salesforce Connect.

























TopicSummaryExternal objects (__x)Map external tables to Salesforce objects; no Salesforce storageExternal lookupChild standard/custom → parent external objectIndirect lookupChild external → parent standard/custom, matched via External IDOData adapter / Custom Apex adapterOData when the source exposes it; Apex adapter otherwise
Detail: 32-salesforce-connect. For archived data exposed this way: data-archiving-and-backup.

Design Checklist

 Key objects, relationships, and cardinalities on one diagram (start from the relevant official ERD)
 Master-detail vs lookup justified per relationship (sharing, roll-ups, deletion)
 Polymorphic and junction objects flagged for reporting and skew risk
 Record types vs separate objects decided
 OWD and ownership model per object
 Record volumes per object; LDV and skew risks flagged
 External data / archive objects marked
 System of record identified for shared entities (data-quality-and-mdm)
 Person Accounts decision explicit


Related Notes

standard-object-oddities — standard-object exceptions

                  Org-validated build

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Model/dat.title: Data Quality & Master Data Management
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/Data-Model/dat.content:
Covers keeping Salesforce data clean, unique, and trustworthy — both at migration time and in steady state — and deciding which system owns which data when several systems hold the same entity (customer, product, etc.).


                  
                  Exam framing 
                  
                

Most multi-system scenarios imply a master-data question even if the word “MDM” never appears. State the system of record per entity, how duplicates are prevented/resolved, and who owns data quality (governance).


Topics

Dimensions of Data Quality
Prevention vs Detection vs Cure
Duplicate Management in Salesforce
Enrichment & Validation
Master Data Management
Data Governance
Design Checklist


Dimensions of Data Quality



































DimensionQuestionTypical Salesforce controlCompletenessAre required values present?Required fields, validation rules, page-layout/record-type rulesValidityDoes the value conform to format/domain?Restricted picklists / global value sets, validation rules, field typesUniquenessIs the entity stored once?Duplicate/matching rules, unique External ID fieldsConsistencyDo systems agree?System-of-record decision, integration, MDMAccuracy / TimelinessIs it correct and current?Enrichment, review cadences, integration sync

Prevention vs Detection vs Cure

























StageApproachExamplesPrevent (best)Stop bad data enteringValidation rules, restricted picklists, duplicate rules set to Block, address/email validation at entry, integration contractsDetectFind problems that got inReports/dashboards on completeness, duplicate jobs, data-quality scorecardsCureFix existing dataMerge duplicates, mass update, enrichment batch runs, cleansing in the ETL (data-migration)


                  
                  Rule of thumb 
                  
                

Cleaning data once is cheap; keeping it clean needs prevention and an owner. Pair every cleansing exercise with a prevention control and a governance role.



Duplicate Management in Salesforce
Native Duplicate Management uses two building blocks:

















ComponentRoleMatching ruleDefines how two records are considered a match (fields, exact/fuzzy logic). Standard rules are provided for Account, Contact, Lead; custom rules can be created.Duplicate ruleDefines what happens when a match is found: Block or Allow with alert, and whether to Report the match. Can run on create and/or edit.

Supports Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Person Accounts, and custom objects; rules can match across objects (e.g. a new Lead against existing Contacts).
Detected duplicates are stored as Duplicate Record Sets / Items and can be surfaced in reports.
Records are merged via the standard merge flow (up to three records at a time for Accounts, Contacts, Leads).
Duplicate rules can be bypassed for API loads by the caller (useful in migration — then run a separate detection pass afterwards).



                  
                  Limits of native duplicate management 
                  
                

It is a detect-and-resolve-in-Salesforce tool. It does not make Salesforce the master for a customer that is mastered elsewhere, and it does not reconcile conflicting attribute values across systems (survivorship). For that you need an MDM approach (below).




                  
                  Verify before quoting limits 
                  
                

Per-object rule counts, batch duplicate-job availability by edition, and cross-object matching scope vary by release/edition — confirm in Salesforce Help (“Duplicate Management”) before citing numbers in a board answer.



Enrichment & Validation
Third-party AppExchange / external services typically cover:

Address / email / phone validation at entry or in batch
Firmographic enrichment (company size, industry, hierarchies) from commercial data providers
Fuzzy dedup and merge beyond native matching (specialised dedup tools)

The CTA study guide lists Data Enrichment & Validation among the AppExchange categories to know at a high level: how it works, when to use it, and how it integrates (callout/real-time at entry vs. scheduled batch). See cta-study-guide-overview.


                  
                  Data.com Clean 
                  
                

The legacy native Data.com / Data.com Clean offering is retired — don’t propose it as a solution. Name a current provider category rather than a retired product.



Master Data Management
MDM = a governed way to produce a single trusted view (the golden record) of key entities across systems.
Key terms

System of record (SoR): the authoritative system for an entity or attribute.
Golden record: the consolidated, best-version record.
Survivorship rules: which source wins per attribute when values conflict (most recent, most trusted source, most complete).
Match & merge: identifying that records across systems are the same entity.
Cross-reference (xref) key: mapping of each system’s ID to the master ID — often implemented with Salesforce External IDs.

MDM implementation styles








































StyleHow it worksProsConsWhen to useRegistryHub holds only match keys / cross-references; data stays in sources, read through on demandMinimal intrusion; quick to stand upCross-system reads can be slow; no cleansed golden copy written backMany sources, low appetite to change them; read-mostly useConsolidationHub copies data from sources, cleanses and matches it, and serves a golden record (read-only to sources)Good analytics/reporting view; sources unchangedGolden record is not pushed back; latency vs. sourcesReporting/BI-driven masteringCoexistenceGolden record is created in the hub and synchronised back to sources, which still allow editsConsistent across systems; sources remain usableComplex bidirectional sync and conflict handlingSeveral systems must stay live and alignedCentralised (transaction)Hub is the sole place records are created/edited; sources consumeStrongest consistencyLarge change to existing systems and processesGreenfield or when sources can be re-pointed
Where Salesforce fits

























RoleNotesSalesforce as customer SoRCommon for Sales/Service-led companies: Account/Contact is mastered in Salesforce and published to ERP/billing via integration (Integration Patterns)Salesforce as consumer of a hubAn external MDM (or ERP) is the SoR; Salesforce receives the golden record and holds an External ID xrefData Cloud identity resolutionUnifies profiles across sources using match and reconciliation rules for activation/analytics — a unified profile, not a replacement for transactional MDMMuleSoft / iPaaSOrchestration layer that routes and transforms between SoR and consumers; not an MDM by itself (50-mulesoft)


                  
                  Say it explicitly in a scenario 
                  
                

For each shared entity: “X is mastered in system A; Salesforce holds a read/replicated copy keyed on External ID; conflicts resolved by rule R; sync via pattern P.”



Data Governance
Data quality fails without owners. Typical roles to name on the governance board:

























RoleResponsibilityData ownerAccountable executive for an entity/domain; sets policyData steward / custodianDay-to-day quality, dedup decisions, retention scheduleData architectModel, standards, integration contractsAdmin / DevOpsImplements controls (validation, rules, jobs)
Governance outputs worth mentioning: data dictionary, quality KPIs (duplicate rate, completeness %), review cadence, retention and archiving policy (data-archiving-and-backup), and privacy handling (privacy-and-consent-management).

Design Checklist

 System of record identified per shared entity
 MDM style chosen (or explicitly “not needed” with reason)
 Duplicate prevention at entry + detection job + merge process
 Cleansing done before load; prevention controls active after
 External IDs / xref keys for cross-system matching
 Enrichment/validation approach (real-time vs batch) named
 Governance owners and KPIs defined


Related Notes

data-migration — cleansing happens in the migration pipeline
data-model — relationships, record types, Person Accounts
data-archiving-and-backup — retention schedule owned by stewards
Integration Patterns — sync patterns for mastered data
privacy-and-consent-management — consent as data to govern

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/calculatin.title: Calculating Data Storage
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/calculatin.content:
Data Storage Per Object Record


                  
                  Per-record KB table not found in current official docs 
                  
                

The classic “2KB per record, 4KB for Person Accounts/Knowledge Articles, 8KB for Campaigns, 0KB for Assets/Products/Pricebooks/Privacy objects” table (as originally written in this note, sourced from a community study-guide gist) does not appear anywhere in the current live Data and File Storage Allocations article as of 2026-09-29. The current article only lists which objects count toward data storage (Accounts, Contacts, Opportunities, Cases, Campaigns, Custom objects, etc.) — it does not publish a per-record byte cost. Likely a legacy figure from an older version of Salesforce’s storage documentation that has since been dropped, similar to other retired Help articles found elsewhere in this vault (e.g. skinny tables). Treat any specific KB-per-record claim as unverified until a live source is found.



Data Allocated to a Salesforce Org
Storage is split into data storage and file storage, allocated per edition, not per internal-vs-community role. (Data and File Storage Allocations)









































EditionData storage minimum per orgData storage per user licenseFile storage per orgContact Manager, Group, Professional, Enterprise10 GB20 MB10 GBPerformance, Unlimited10 GB120 MB (20 MB for Lightning Platform Starter user licenses)10 GBEssentials, Starter10 GBN/A (flat allocation, no per-user increment)1 GBDeveloper5 MBN/A20 MBPersonal20 MB (~10,000 records)N/A20 MB


                  
                  "Internal user = 120MB" is edition-dependent, not universal 
                  
                

This note previously stated a flat 120MB per internal user. That figure only holds for Performance/Unlimited editions — Contact Manager, Group, Professional, and Enterprise editions get 20MB per user license instead. Always check the org’s edition before applying a per-user figure.




                  
                  Community/Partner-specific MB figures not in current docs 
                  
                

This note previously listed per-license figures for Customer Community (0MB), Customer Community Plus (2MB), Partner (5MB), and Partner Login (1MB). None of these appear in the current official article — it states only: “The minimum values apply to Salesforce and Salesforce Platform user licenses. If your org uses custom user licenses, contact Salesforce to determine your exact storage amount.” These figures may be outdated (Experience Cloud/community licensing has changed significantly since older editions of this documentation) or may require a direct Support/AE conversation to confirm for a specific org. Do not quote them as current exam facts.


Other storage categories (not previously in this note):

Order Management: 50 MB for managed orders + 50 MB for unmanaged orders, counted separately from general data storage
Big Objects: 1 million records per org (Contact Manager, Group, Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, Developer, Personal editions); contact Salesforce to increase
File and data storage are calculated asynchronously — large imports/uploads won’t reflect in usage immediately


Example Calculations


                  
                  Example below needs an edition assumption 
                  
                

The original example (“600 internal users × 120MB”) only holds for a Performance/Unlimited edition org. For Professional/Enterprise/Group/Contact Manager editions, substitute 20MB per user instead.


If you had 2 million Opportunity records, storage depends on the (currently unverified) per-record KB cost — see caution above. Using the commonly-cited but unverified 2KB/record figure as a rough estimate: 2,000,000 × 2KB = 4,000,000KB ≈ 4GB.
For a Performance/Unlimited edition org with 600 internal (Salesforce/Salesforce Platform) users:

600 users × 120MB = 72,000MB = 72GB
Plus the 10GB org minimum = 82GB total data storage allocation before any community/partner user or custom-license storage is added



                  
                  Community/partner user math removed 
                  
                

The original example added 10,000 CC+ users × 2MB = 20GB. Since the current official article doesn’t confirm a CC+-specific per-user figure (see caution above), this portion of the calculation can’t be reproduced from a verified source — confirm the actual increment with Salesforce Support/AE for community/partner licenses before using it in a real sizing exercise or quoting it on the exam.

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/data-archi.title: Data Archiving, Retention & Backup
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/data-archi.content:
Three related but different jobs — keep them separate in a scenario:

























ConcernQuestion it answersTypical mechanismRetentionHow long must we keep this data, and when must we delete it?Policy from the governance board (legal, compliance, privacy)ArchivingWhere does old, rarely-used data live so Salesforce stays fast and cheap?Off-platform store, Big Objects, external objectsBackup & restoreHow do we recover from loss or corruption?Backup service, data export, recycle bin


                  
                  Exam framing 
                  
                

Volume growth is the trigger. If a scenario has unbounded growth (e.g. millions of cases/events per year), say explicitly: active working set stays in Salesforce; records older than X move to an archive on a schedule; archived data is still viewable on demand.


Topics

Retention
Archiving Options
Making Archived Data Visible
Recommended Patterns for the Exam
Big Objects Key Facts
Backup & Restore
Design Checklist


Retention

Retention schedules are owned by data stewards / custodians on the governance board, not by the architect — align with them and with legal (see Data Governance).
Drivers: regulation (financial, healthcare), contracts, litigation hold, and privacy deletion obligations (GDPR right to erasure) — see privacy-and-consent-management.
Archiving is not deletion. If a privacy request requires erasure, it must reach the archive and backups too.
Records you can delete outright should be deleted — cheapest option. Deleting at volume: see ldv-best-practices (Deleting Data) and Bulk API hard delete in bulk-api-and-cursors.


Archiving Options



































OptionProsConsWhen to useBig ObjectsNative; queryable via SOQL (__b); no impact on standard object limitsRead-only after write; no triggers, workflows, or sharing; limited query on index fields only; no standard UIAudit logs, historical snapshots, event historyExternal objects (Salesforce Connect)Live view of external data; no Salesforce storage costLatency; no Salesforce sharing model; external system must be availableData already in, or moved to, an external system — see 32-salesforce-connectCustom archive objectFull platform features, can have sharingStill costs storage; still in the orgOnly when archived data needs sharing/workflow — rarely the right answer for true LDVOff-platform archive / data lake / warehouse (e.g. S3, Snowflake, Postgres on Heroku)Effectively unlimited scale; cheap; analytics-friendlyNeeds integration to view in SalesforceCompliance-only retention; continuous high ingest; the default CTA answer


                  
                  Big Objects in the exam 
                  
                

The CTA toolkit advises avoiding Big Objects as the primary CTA archive answer because they are hard to justify (index design is fixed, limited querying, no sharing) and have caveats with Shield. Use them when you can defend the access pattern; otherwise prefer an external store. (CTA toolkit — Archiving)



Making Archived Data Visible
Archived data usually must still be reachable by users and reports. Options:






























Access methodHowNotesSalesforce Connect (OData)Middleware/warehouse exposes OData → external objectReal-time, no copy; user sees related listCustom LWC + REST APIComponent calls the archive’s API on demandFull control over UX; need auth via 40-named-credentialsHeroku Connect external objectPostgres on Heroku synced with SalesforceStructured data only; files need S3CRM Analytics connectorLoad archive into analytics for reportingReporting only, not record-level UI

Files: structured stores (Postgres) don’t hold files; use object storage (S3) or a content system — see document-management-systems.
Cross-links: Integration Patterns (data virtualization).


Recommended Patterns for the Exam
The toolkit describes three defensible architectures. All use an ETL to move data and provide access via OData or REST:





























PatternComponentsFiles?NotesPostgreSQL on HerokuHeroku Connect external objects; REST API + LWCNo — pair with S3Seamless Salesforce sync; structured data; connector for CRM AnalyticsAWS S3 bucketMiddleware with OData connector; REST API + LWCYesScalable, cost-effective; structured + unstructuredSnowflake (on S3)Middleware with OData connector; REST API + LWCYesStrong analytics and warehousing
(CTA toolkit — Archiving)


                  
                  Archive during migration 
                  
                

A pattern easier to defend than “load everything, then archive”: archive older data during the migration itself, exposing it via OData, with a scheduled archive job for ongoing growth. See What Not to Migrate.


AppExchange archiving products exist (e.g. data-archive tools that store in S3 and expose Lightning components), but some require the data to be loaded into Salesforce before archiving — hard to defend for LDV migrations. There is no single native Salesforce archiving product in the toolkit’s view; verify the current Salesforce portfolio before asserting this in a board answer.
Data Warehouse Pattern
For objects with continuous high ingest that must keep historical data: archive records irrelevant to day-to-day work to a warehouse/off-platform store on a defined schedule (with governance approval), keeping the active working set in Salesforce. Call this out explicitly when volume growth is unbounded. Also see Archiving & Data Retention.

Big Objects Key Facts
(Big Objects Developer Guide)

Use the __b suffix.
Indexed fields are defined at object creation — cannot change without recreating the object.
Query with SOQL, but only on index fields (leftmost-first order); no WHERE on non-index fields.
No standard UI; access via Apex, APIs, or Data Pipelines.
Async SOQL for bulk extraction: the standalone Async SOQL guide could not be relocated as of 2026-09-23 — likely retired/superseded by Bulk API 2.0 query. Verify support before citing it in a board answer.
Storage allocation: see calculating-data-storage.


Backup & Restore
Backup is not archiving — it protects against loss, corruption, and bad deployments.

































OptionNotesRecycle BinShort-term safety net only for deleted recordsData Export Service (weekly/monthly)Native; manual restore; coarseSalesforce Backup and RestoreNative managed backup/restore; toolkit (Nov 2023) notes daily-only backups and no file support at that time — re-verify current capabilitiesThird-party backup (e.g. Own Backup)Scheduled backups to external storage; typically richer restoreCustom-builtETL/Bulk API extracts to S3 or a warehouse; only if bespoke needsSandbox refreshNot a backup — it’s a copy for testing

Define RPO (how much data loss is acceptable) and RTO (how fast to restore) before choosing — see environment-strategy.
A good backup also supports sandbox seeding and migration rollback (Validation, Cutover & Rollback).

(CTA toolkit — Archiving, Backup section)

Design Checklist

 Retention schedule agreed with data stewards / legal
 Growth rate estimated; archive trigger (age/status) defined
 Archive store chosen with justification (not just “Big Objects”)
 Access path for archived data (OData / LWC / analytics)
 Files strategy (S3 / content system)
 Privacy deletion reaches archive and backups
 Backup tool, RPO/RTO, and restore process
 Archive job scheduled and monitored


Related Notes

calculating-data-storage — what counts against storage
data-migration — archive instead of migrating old data
data-quality-and-mdm — governance roles
