document-management-systems — files

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/ldv-best-p.title: LDV Best Practices
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/ldv-best-p.content:
Condensed from the Best Practices for Deployments with Large Data Volumes guide. This note covers the Best Practices and Case Studies chapters; the mechanics (query optimizer, indexes, skinny tables, skew, sharing, archiving) live in ldv.
Topics

Two Guiding Principles
Reporting
Loading Data from the API
Extracting Data from the API
Searching
SOQL & SOSL
Deleting Data
General & Sandboxes
Case Studies
Related Notes


Two Guiding Principles
Almost every LDV best practice reduces to one of two levers (Best Practices):

Make it selective — write narrow queries/reports/list views that reference indexed fields so the optimizer scans fewer rows. A report by one city in one state beats a report by all cities in a state.
Reduce active data — archive or discard at the same rate data arrives, so the working set stays small (see Archiving & Data Retention).



                  
                  CTA framing 
                  
                

If asked “how do we keep this performant at scale?”, anchor your answer on these two levers, then cite the specific technique (selective filters + indexing, skinny tables, defer sharing, Bulk API, archiving to Big Objects).



Reporting

























GoalBest practiceMaximize report performanceSegment on a data value (e.g. one state, not all states); partition data to match usage; minimize records per objectReduce joinsMinimize objects and relationships in the report; de-normalize by rolling summary values onto the parent record rather than summarizing children at run time (don’t over-de-normalize)Reduce data returnedQuery only required fields in reports, list views, and SOQLReduce records to queryArchive unused records to a custom object; filter on indexed fields wherever possible

Loading Data from the API





































GoalBest practiceImprove throughput> 2,000 records → Bulk API 2.0 (async). Fewer than 2,000 → bulkified synchronous REST (Composite) or SOAPMost efficient opinsert() > update() > upsert(). If possible split upsert into create + update. Clean data first — batch errors trigger slow single-row processingReduce data movedSend only changed fields (delta-only updates)Reduce transmission costAuthenticate once per load (not per record); use GZIP + HTTP keep-aliveAvoid sharing computationUse Public Read/Write during the initial load to skip sharing calcOrder sharing setupLoad users into roles → record data (owners) → groups/queues → sharing rules one at a time, letting each finishDefer computationDisable triggers, workflow/flows, and validation rules during load; reprocess with batch Apex afterward


                  
                  Ownership skew during load 
                  
                

Combine with ownership-skew avoidance: don’t let one user own > 10,000 records, or sharing recalculation on load becomes a bottleneck.



Extracting Data from the API

































GoalBest practiceBatch size vs timeoutsSOAP: use as many batches as possible (up to 200) that still avoid network timeouts when records are large or processing is heavyJava clientsUse the WSC (Web Service Connector) rather than AxisAvoid lock conflictsGroup child records by ParentId in the same batchDefer sharingUse the Defer Sharing Calculation permission until after all data is loadedAvoid loading at allUse mashups for coupled integrations (leave data in the source system)Efficient syncgetUpdated() / getDeleted() for syncs at intervals > 5 min; outbound messaging for more frequent syncs; Bulk API 2.0 Query for results > 1M rows

Searching





















GoalBest practiceFewer records returnedKeep searches specific; avoid wildcards (Michael, not Mi*)Fewer joinsPrefer single-object searches for speed and accuracyEfficiencyEnable language optimizations; turn on enhanced lookups and auto-complete for lookup fields

SOQL & SOSL
SOQL

Use selective filters on indexed fields with a wide value range — non-selective filters bypass the index.
Filter on Name instead of FirstName + LastName.
Avoid negative filters (status != 'failed', field != NULL).
Use IN instead of a long chain of ORs.
Avoid cross-object reference formula fields — they aren’t indexable.
If two indexed fields are joined by OR and the result can exceed the index threshold, decompose into two queries and merge results in code.
Avoid querying/filtering on non-deterministic formula fields (see Custom Indexes — 10% tier (stricter)).
Replace nulls with a sentinel like NA for picklist/foreign-key filters (nulls can’t use the index).

SOSL

Selective filters cut irrelevant results; > 2,000 matches risks search crowding.
Don’t index custom objects you don’t want searched; filter out unwanted objects.
Use specific terms and targeted search groups (NAME, EMAIL, PHONE), e.g. FIND 'Avery Smith' IN NAME FIELDS RETURNING Account(Id,Name), Lead(Id,Name).



                  
                  Avoiding SOQL timeouts 
                  
                

Tune scope + selective filters first. Then consider Bulk API 2.0 Query, or add a LIMIT (start at 100,000). In batch Apex, use chaining with LIMIT or push filter logic into the execute method.



Deleting Data





















GoalBest practiceDelete ≥ 1M recordsUse Bulk API hard delete (skips the Recycle Bin)Records with many childrenDelete children firstKeep queries fastEmpty the Recycle Bin — soft-deleted rows still affect query performance

General & Sandboxes

























GoalBest practiceAvoid sharing computationNo user should own > 10,000 recordsImprove performanceData-tiering — spread data across objects, bring in on demand from another object or external storeFaster full sandbox copiesExclude field history if not needed; don’t mass-change data until the copy completesEfficient deploymentsDistribute child records so no parent has > 10,000 children (e.g. dummy accounts to spread orphan contacts)

Case Studies
Real customer problems from the guide, written as Situation → Solution → Takeaway so they double as ready-made board answers. (Case Studies)
Sort Optimization on a Query — ORDER BY + LIMIT to force index use

Situation: A “records from the last 3 days” query performed poorly because the object had grown past the standard-index threshold (30% of the first 1M rows), so the optimizer skipped the CreatedDate index and table-scanned.

SELECT Id, Product_Code__c
FROM Customer_Product__c
WHERE CreatedDate = LAST_N_DAYS:3

Solution: Add ORDER BY on the indexed field plus a LIMIT under 100,000. Threshold checks are skipped and the CreatedDate index drives the query.

SELECT Id, Product_Code__c
FROM Customer_Product__c
WHERE CreatedDate = LAST_N_DAYS:3
ORDER BY CreatedDate
LIMIT 99999


                  
                  Exam-gold pattern — ORDER BY index trick
                  
                

When querying data added over the LAST_N_DAYS and the filter alone isn’t selective enough, an ORDER BY on an indexed field with LIMIT < 100,000 lets the optimizer use that index and bypass threshold evaluation. Returns up to 99,999 rows in created order. (Sort Optimization case study)


Indexing with Nulls — sentinel value or formula index

Situation: The customer needed to allow nulls in a field and query for them. Single-column indexes for picklists and foreign keys exclude null rows, so no index could serve WHERE Status__c = ''.
Solution (preferred): Don’t store nulls — use a sentinel like N/A so the value is indexable.
Solution (if nulls already exist): Index a formula field that maps blanks to text, then filter on the formula.

-- Bad: index cannot be used
SELECT Name FROM Object__c WHERE Status__c = ''
 
-- Good: index a deterministic formula, then filter on it
-- Status_Value__c = IF(ISBLANK(Status__c), "blank", Status__c)
SELECT Name FROM Object__c WHERE Status_Value__c = 'blank'

Takeaway: Extends to multiple fields (WHERE Status_Value__c = '' OR Email = ''). See Index tables & null rows.

Data Aggregation — pre-compute with batch Apex

Situation: Monthly (4M) and yearly (9M) metrics stored in custom objects; standard reports aggregated across millions of rows and were slow.
Solution: Create an aggregation custom object that stores the summarized values in report-ready form, populated by batch Apex; run reports off the summary object.
Takeaway: Trade real-time aggregation for pre-computed roll-ups when the source volume is large.

Custom Search Functionality — restrict fields, de-normalize, pick SOQL vs SOSL

Situation: A Visualforce search let users enter 1–20 arbitrary fields with wildcards across multiple objects — impossible to tune, and wildcards/multi-object joins were slow.
Solution: Limit to essential search fields (so Salesforce can tune indexes); de-normalize the multiple objects into one custom object to avoid multi-query calls; dynamically choose SOQL or SOSL — specific (no-wildcard) values → SOQL to leverage indexes.

Rendering Related Lists — data skew + separate loading

Situation: Hundreds of thousands of accounts with 15M invoices (master-detail); some parents had thousands of children, so account pages rendered slowly.
Solution: Root cause was lookup/parent data skew — reduce children per parent and keep skew minimal; enable Separate Loading of Related Lists so account detail renders while the related-list query completes.
Takeaway: Cross-link lookup skew.

API Performance — don’t filter with sharing

Situation: A custom integration used a sharing-scoped API user to limit records; queries over several-million-row objects took minutes.
Solution: Give the query access to all data (e.g. an admin API user) and use selective filters instead of sharing as the filter; add a delta extraction to reduce volume.
Takeaway: Sharing is great for UI visibility, poor as a high-volume query filter.

Multi-Join Report Performance — filter, trim, clean

Situation: A report joined 4 related objects (Accounts 314k, Sales Orders 769k, Sales Details 2.3M, Account Ownership 1.2M) with very little filtering.
Solution: Add selective, indexable filters; reduce data per object; empty the Recycle Bin (soft-deleted rows slow queries); remove complex sharing rules on the joined objects.

CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/ldv.title: Large Data Volumes (LDV)
CTA-Notes/Data-Management/LDV/ldv.content:
Topics

What Counts as LDV
Why LDV Causes Problems
Data Skew — Ownership · Lookup/Account · Junction
Indexes — Selectivity · Index-bypass cases
Skinny Tables
Sharing & LDV
Archiving & Data Retention — details in data-archiving-and-backup
Batch Processing & LDV
Reporting on LDV
Design Checklist for LDV Scenarios
Related Notes


What Counts as LDV
No hard threshold — context-dependent.


                  
                  Not an official citation 
                  
                

The LDV Best Practices Guide — Introduction only defines LDV loosely (“tens of thousands of users, tens of millions of records, or hundreds of GB of storage”); it does not state the per-object-type thresholds below. Those are practitioner/community guidelines (unverified against an official Salesforce source as of 2026-09-23) — treat them as rules of thumb, not exam-quotable facts.



























Object typeIndicative thresholdStandard/custom objects> 1 million recordsChatter / Feed items> 5 million recordsContentDocument / Files> 500k recordsSharing table (e.g. AccountShare)> 10 million rows
Salesforce recommends staying well under ~50 million records per object. At or near that scale, you must plan offload/archive.


                  
                  CTA framing 
                  
                

Examiners expect you to proactively raise LDV concerns whenever a scenario involves high-volume transactional data, migrations, or sharing rule proliferation — not just when explicitly stated. Call out any object likely to hit 1M+ records; at 50M+, archiving/offload is mandatory in the design.




                  
                  Experience Cloud + Account/Contact LDV 
                  
                

If LDV is on Account and/or Contact records tied to Experience Cloud users, do not casually archive them. Prefer monitoring for account/ownership skew and performance issues, and use custom indexes and skinny tables if slowdowns appear. Archiving contacts linked to community users is risky unless absolutely required.



Why LDV Causes Problems


                  
                  Verification status 
                  
                

The intro page cited below only defines LDV loosely — it does not itemize these problems. Each bullet’s verification status is noted; treat “not verified”/“inference” items as things to double-check before quoting on the exam, not as confirmed facts.



Full table scans when indexes are absent or not selective (plausible — well-established platform behavior, but not confirmed against a specific quoted source)
Sharing recalculation becomes long-running → lock contention (not verified — source page renders client-side only; couldn’t confirm exact claim)
Report timeouts (10-minute limit) (not verified — no specific limits source located)
Batch Apex chunking inefficiency (plausible — batch size/scope trade-offs are real, but “chunking inefficiency” is paraphrased, not a quoted claim)
SOQL governor limits hit faster on unindexed queries (inference — reasonable derived consequence, not something the guide states directly)
Search index lag (confirmed — Search Architecture: “it could take about 15 minutes or more for the updated text to become searchable”)


Data Skew
Skew is the #1 LDV interview topic. Three types (the “Data Skew” article this cited — sf.performance_data_skew.htm — no longer appears in Salesforce’s current Help sitemap; no live replacement found as of 2026-09-23, likely retired/folded into the LDV Best Practices Guide):
Ownership Skew
One user/queue owns a disproportionate number of records (e.g. integration user owns 500k Accounts). Practical risk often starts around > ~10k records owned by a single user.
Impact: A skewed-ownership user moving roles or being added to/removed from a public group used by a sharing rule triggers a long-running recalculation of access rights across that user’s owned records. (Avoid Ownership Skew / Group Membership Skew)
Fix:

Use multiple integration/owner users to distribute ownership (no single user crosses the ~10k-record danger zone, so no one user’s role/group change triggers a large recalculation)
Use a dedicated “data owner” user per business unit (isolates skew to a stable, rarely-moved account rather than a real user who might change roles or teams)
Avoid assigning a role to a skewed-ownership user at all, if possible (no role membership means no role-hierarchy-implied sharing to recalculate in the first place)
If a role is unavoidable, place that user in a separate role at the top of the role hierarchy, never move them out of it, and keep them out of public groups used as sharing-rule sources (a top-level role has no parent to cascade into, and never moving the user or changing their groups means the recalculation trigger never fires)
If private OWD is required, prefer criteria-based sharing rules over role-hierarchy-implied access — criteria-based rules don’t recalculate when a skewed-ownership user’s role/group membership changes, avoiding that specific trigger (not a general claim that private OWD beats public — Public Read/Write still avoids sharing computation entirely and is the stronger fix when recalculation cost itself, not just the role-move trigger, is the problem; see W during load)

Lookup Skew (Parent Skew) / Account Skew
Many child records point to the same parent (e.g. 100k Cases linked to one Account). Account skew is the common CTA case: > ~10k child records under a single Account can cause record locking and sharing issues. (Avoid Account Data Skew)
Root cause: This is a general lookup-relationship behavior, not specific to Account as parent or to master-detail relationships. On every insert/update, Salesforce must lock the target record(s) each lookup field points to, on any object, to maintain referential integrity — so whichever record has many children looked-up to it becomes a lock bottleneck under heavy concurrent insert/update activity. Account is the common example (and the CTA exam case) simply because it’s the most frequently over-referenced parent object in practice. (Managing Lookup Skew to Avoid Record Lock Exceptions)
Impact: Lock contention on the parent during concurrent child insert/update → “unable to lock row”; sharing recalculation pain.
Fix: Four mitigation categories, per Managing Lookup Skew to Avoid Record Lock Exceptions:

Reducing record save time — shorten how long the lock is held:

Avoid locking the parent in triggers on the child (don’t update parent aggregate fields synchronously)
Use Platform Events or async processing to defer parent updates (Platform Events Developer Guide)
Redesign aggregation; use roll-up summaries carefully
Consolidate to a single trigger per object and move non-critical logic off the synchronous path (source: Managing Lookup Skew blog)


Distributing the skew — reduce concentration on any one target record:

For Account skew: distribute children across multiple parent accounts where the data model allows
Add more distinct lookup values instead of concentrating records on one target, and prefer leaving a lookup blank over pointing everything at a generic “catch-all” record (source: same blog)


Using a picklist field — if the field has a small, fixed set of lookup values, use a picklist instead of a lookup; picklists don’t require record locks (source: same blog)
Reducing the load — run high-volume automated processes serially, in off-peak windows, or with smaller batch sizes to reduce lock duration and contention with end users (source: same blog)

Junction Object Skew
One record on either side of an M:M junction has too many junction records.
Impact: Same lock contention as lookup skew; cascading deletes become extremely slow.
Fix: Limit relationship depth; consider soft-delete pattern instead of cascading.


                  
                  Not independently verified 
                  
                

No official Salesforce source could be confirmed for this section specifically — checked the DRAES ownership-skew doc, the Managing Lookup Skew blog, and both current LDV developer guides (Introduction, Best Practices) — none name “junction object skew” directly, and web search via available tooling did not surface a usable source as of 2026-09-24. Content here is an inference: a junction object’s two lookup/master-detail fields are subject to the same general lookup-locking mechanism described in Lookup Skew — so this section is likely a specific case of that mechanism rather than a separate one, but that framing itself is unconfirmed.




                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

Ownership skew and lookup/account skew have different root causes and different fixes. Don’t conflate them.



Indexes
(Indexes for SOQL Query Performance · LDV — Standard and Custom Indexes)
Standard Indexes (auto-created) — 30% tier
Platform-maintained indexes on most objects:

Primary key: the unique Salesforce record Id; plus Name, OwnerId
Foreign keys: lookup & master-detail relationships (also CreatedById, LastModifiedById)
Audit / system: CreatedDate, SystemModstamp (LastModifiedDate), RecordTypeId, Division
Email (on Contact and Lead)

Divisions
A Setup feature (Company Settings → Divisions) that adds a standard Division picklist field to major objects (Account, Contact, Opportunity, Lead, Case, and enabled custom objects), letting users work within one active division at a time and scope list views, reports, and search to it.
How it helps LDV performance: Division is part of the platform’s standard, auto-created index set (same tier as Id, Name, OwnerId, CreatedDate — see Standard Indexes (auto-created) — 30% tier). Filtering or reporting by division is therefore a selective, indexed lookup rather than a full scan, so on a very large object split across business units by division, division-scoped queries/reports avoid touching the full row count.


                  
                  Not independently verified 
                  
                

Division’s standard-index status is sourced from the LDV Best Practices developer guide (cited above). The description of what Divisions does and its performance rationale could not be confirmed against a live official article as of 2026-09-24 — Salesforce Help (help.salesforce.com) renders client-side only and returns no fetchable content for any article ID, and the current LDV Best Practices / Introduction developer guides don’t mention Divisions at all (it’s a legacy Setup feature, not part of the current LDV guide). Treat this section as a reasonable inference from the indexed-field fact, not a directly quoted source. Also note: Divisions only scopes queries/UI to an active division — it does not reduce actual data storage or change sharing computation, so it isn’t a substitute for archiving, skinny tables, or sharing-cost reduction.


Custom Indexes — 10% tier (stricter)

Auto-created on custom fields marked External ID or Unique. External IDs are allowed only on Auto Number, Email, Number, Text field types
Created on request — via Salesforce Customer Support, or by deploying a custom index XML file through the Metadata API. For other/standard field types, go through Support
Support-created custom indexes in production are copied to all sandboxes made from that org (contrast with skinny tables, which only Full sandboxes get automatically)
These use the stricter 10% threshold — being “auto-created” does not make External ID / Unique fields standard indexes



                  
                  Fields that can't be custom-indexed
                  
                

Long text areas, rich text areas, encrypted text, multi-select picklists, and non-deterministic formula fields. Deterministic formulas can be indexed; a formula is non-deterministic if it references other entities / cross-object fields, uses dynamic date-time (TODAY, NOW), or references owner / autonumber / division / audit fields (except CreatedDate & CreatedById), currency fields in a multi-currency org, etc. Some special standard fields are also non-indexable (e.g. Opportunity Amount / ExpectedRevenue / IsClosed / IsWon; Case ClosedDate / IsClosed; Product IsActive / IsArchived).




                  
                  Index tables & null rows 
                  
                

Because the multitenant custom-field storage isn’t directly indexable, Salesforce builds a separate index table (a copy of the field data + type info) and indexes that. By default the index table excludes null rows — which is why WHERE Field__c = null typically can’t use the index. You can ask Support to create a custom index that includes nulls, but you must explicitly enable and rebuild it.


Selectivity Thresholds
Salesforce’s query optimizer only uses an index when the query is selective — i.e. the filter is expected to return few enough records that an index scan beats a full table scan. The threshold is tiered and cumulative (percentages apply to record bands), with exactly two tiers: standard and custom. (LDV — Standard and Custom Indexes)























Index tierFieldsSelective when matched rows are belowHard capStandardId, Name, OwnerId, lookup/master-detail FKs, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, RecordType, Division30% of first 1M + 15% of rows beyond 1M1,000,000CustomExternal ID, Unique, Support-created custom indexes10% of first 1M + 5% of rows beyond 1M333,333
Worked example (custom index, 2M-row object): threshold = (10% × 1,000,000) + (5% × 1,000,000) = 150,000. Match < 150k ⇒ index; ≥ 150k ⇒ table scan. Exceeding the first-million tier alone disqualifies the index, regardless of the rows-beyond-1M band.


                  
                  Two tiers only — common myths 
                  
                

There are only two threshold tiers: standard = 30% / 15%, custom = 10% / 5%. Beware incorrect claims that “the primary-key/Id index has a 10% threshold” (it’s a standard index → 30%) or that “custom indexes are 15%” (15% is the standard index’s rate for rows beyond the first million). External ID / Unique fields are custom indexes (10%), even though auto-created.




                  
                  AND (composite) queries — double-threshold rule 
                  
                

For filters combined with AND, the optimizer treats the overall condition as selective if either: (a) each individual filter targets < 2× its own threshold — the “2×” is fixed and does not scale with the number of conditions — or (b) the intersection of all the AND’d filters targets < 1× the threshold. Salesforce calls this a Composite Index Join.




                  
                  LDV guide phrasing — AND / OR / LIKE 
                  
                

The LDV Best Practices guide summarises the multi-filter rules as:

AND — indexes are used unless one filter returns > 20% of the object’s records.
OR — indexes are used unless all filters return > 10%, and every field in the OR must be indexed for any index to be used.
LIKE — the optimizer ignores its statistics table and instead samples up to 100,000 actual records to decide whether to use the custom index.

If one indexed field’s criteria aren’t met, only that index is dropped — other qualifying indexes in the WHERE clause may still be used.




                  
                  When indexes are NOT used 
                  
                


CONTAINS operator: requires full index scan; only used if rows to scan < 333,333
Negative operators: !=, NOT IN, NOT CONTAINS, NOT STARTS WITH
Empty value comparisons: Name != ''
Filter returns > threshold records regardless of index





                  
                  CTA application 
                  
                

When designing for LDV, always identify which fields appear in WHERE clauses and verify they are index-eligible and selective. A custom index on a low-cardinality field (e.g. Status with 3 values) will rarely be selective enough to be used. The commonly cited rule of thumb is < 200k records on objects with > 2M records total.


Additional Index-Bypass Cases
(LDV — Standard and Custom Indexes — unverified against current page text as of 2026-09-23; recheck before quoting)

LIKE '%value' (leading wildcard)
Functions on indexed fields: WHERE UPPER(Name) = ...
Null comparisons: WHERE Field__c = null (use = '' for text or handle in code)
OR conditions spanning multiple non-indexed fields



                  
                  Design principle 
                  
                

Always design your data model so that the fields used in WHERE and ORDER BY clauses are index-eligible. Flag this explicitly in the CTA presentation.



Skinny Tables
(Skinny Tables Help article — sf.performance_skinny_table.htm — no longer appears in Salesforce’s current Help sitemap; no live replacement found as of 2026-09-23 · LDV Skinny Tables · LDV Best Practices PDF)
Skinny tables speed up read-only operations (reports, list views, SOQL) on tables with millions of records by avoiding joins between standard/custom field storage and omitting soft-deleted rows.
flowchart LR
    Q1["Query"] --> J["Standard + custom<br/>field tables · JOIN"] --> SLOW["Slow"]
    Q2["Query"] --> SKN["Skinny table"] --> FAST["Fast"]

ASCII Fallback
Without a skinny table:
  Report/List View/SOQL
        |
        +--> [Standard-field table] --+
        |                              |--> JOIN --> slow at scale
        +--> [Custom-field table]  ----+
        (soft-deleted rows still scanned)
 
With a skinny table:
  Report/List View/SOQL
        |
        +--> [Skinny table: subset of columns, single object, no soft-deletes]
                    |
                    +--> no join, fewer rows scanned --> fast
Notes


Skinny tables collapse the standard/custom-field split and the join between them into one narrow, denormalized table for a known query pattern.


Soft-deleted rows are excluded, so scans touch only live data.


This is a generated illustration of the mechanism described in the cited docs, not a diagram taken from Salesforce’s own documentation (no such diagram could be found on the live pages).


Must be requested via Salesforce Support (not self-service)


Creates a narrow copy with only needed columns for a query pattern


Kept in sync when source data changes


Not a substitute for good index design — use when indexes alone aren’t enough


Max columns: up to 200 (current LDV guidance)


Can’t contain fields from other objects — single base object only (no cross-object/related fields)


Adding a field used by reports/list views does not auto-update the skinny table — contact Support to rebuild/add fields


Skinny tables (and skinny indexes) can also contain encrypted data


Full sandboxes: skinny tables are copied automatically


Other sandbox types: skinny tables are not copied — contact Salesforce Customer Support to activate production skinny tables for non-Full sandboxes


Supported objects: Account, Contact, Opportunity, Lead, Case, and custom objects.
Supported field types: Checkbox, Date, Date/Time, Email, Number, Percent, Phone, Picklist (multi-select), Text, Text Area, Text Area (Long), URL.


                  
                  Pre-computed field pattern (avoid repeated computation) 
                  
                

Instead of filtering on an expensive date range like CloseDate >= 01/01/11 AND CloseDate <= 12/31/11 — a repeated computation for annual or year-to-date reports — add a Year field to the skinny table and filter on Year = '2011'. Materializing the derived value into a stored, skinny-table-backed field turns a range scan into a cheap equality lookup.



Sharing & LDV
Sharing recalculation is the most expensive operation at scale. (Sharing Recalculation and LDV)
Per-object sharing rule caps (and Support increase maxes): Sharing rule limits.
Strategies to Reduce Sharing Cost





























StrategyWhen to useFewer sharing rulesSimplify role hierarchy; avoid complex criteria-based sharingDefer sharing recalculationDuring bulk data loads — re-enable after load completesParallel sharing recalculationAvailable for Accounts; request via Salesforce SupportPrivate OWD + Apex managed sharingFull control; avoid rule proliferationTerritory ManagementFor Account-heavy orgs needing complex geo/product-based access


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Criteria-based sharing rules with LDV are dangerous — each rule evaluation touches every record during recalculation. Prefer owner-based sharing rules or Apex sharing for LDV objects. (Sharing Model Fields)



Archiving & Data Retention
When records can’t be kept in the active working set, move them out on a governed schedule (aligned with data stewards on the governance board) rather than letting volume grow unbounded.

Default CTA answer: off-platform archive (data lake / warehouse) with on-demand access via OData / Salesforce Connect or an LWC — keep the active working set in Salesforce.
Big Objects (__b) are native but read-only, index-fixed, and no sharing — use only when the access pattern is defensible.
External objects give a live view without storage cost, at the price of latency and no sharing model.
Archive during migration where possible instead of loading old data in and archiving later.



                  
                  Full detail 
                  
                

Options table, access patterns, Big Objects facts, the Data Warehouse pattern, and backup/restore are in data-archiving-and-backup.



Batch Processing & LDV
(Batch Apex Developer Guide)

Use Database.QueryLocator (up to 50M records) vs Iterable (50k limit) for large datasets
Set batch size conservatively (200 default; lower if each record triggers complex logic)
Avoid SOQL inside loops — all queries must be bulkified
Chain batches for multi-step processing; use AsyncApexJob to monitor
Platform Events + triggered flows/batches preferred for near-real-time at scale (Platform Events Developer Guide)



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

For migrations, use Bulk API 2.0 (parallel jobs). Avoid REST/SOAP for LDV loads. (Bulk API 2.0 Developer Guide) See also bulk-api-and-cursors.



Reporting on LDV

Reports timeout at 10 minutes
Dashboards refresh async — less of a concern but data can be stale
Mitigations:

Add indexed filters to all LDV reports (Indexes for SOQL Query Performance)
Use report filters on RecordType, OwnerId, CreatedDate (all indexed)
Consider CRM Analytics (Tableau CRM) for large-scale reporting — extracts data out of the transactional store
Async SOQL / Data Pipelines for scheduled aggregation into summary objects




Design Checklist for LDV Scenarios

 Identify which objects will exceed 1M records (flag 50M+ for mandatory archive/offload)
 If Account/Contact + Experience Cloud users → avoid casual archive; plan monitoring + indexes/skinny tables
 Confirm OWD and sharing model — flag recalculation risk
 Check for ownership skew (integration users, queues; ~10k+ owned by one user)
 Check for lookup/account skew (~10k+ children on one parent)
 Identify query patterns → ensure indexed fields in WHERE/ORDER BY
 Define archiving strategy (Big Objects, warehouse/EDW, external, off-platform) with governance owners
 Plan bulk load approach (Bulk API 2.0, parallel jobs)
 Address reporting needs (indexed filters, CRM Analytics)
 Consider skinny tables for critical read-only query paths (Support-managed)

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
Salesforce Customisation Hierarchy
The CTA exam expects you to justify where on this hierarchy your solution sits and why.
1. Declarative (no-code)        → Flows, Validation Rules, Formula Fields, Record Types
2. Low-code                     → Flow + Apex actions, OmniStudio
3. Programmatic (Apex)          → Custom logic not possible declaratively
4. Programmatic (LWC/Aura)      → Custom UI not possible with standard components
5. External / Off-platform      → Heroku, MuleSoft, custom middleware



                  
                  CTA principle 
                  
                

Always justify going down the hierarchy. Using Apex where a Flow works is a maintenance burden. Using an external system where Apex works adds integration complexity. Examiners probe: “Could this have been done declaratively?”



Development Approach
Agile Delivery

2-week sprints; Definition of Done includes: unit tests passing, code review approved, SIT sign-off
Feature flags / custom metadata for in-progress features to avoid blocking releases
Technical debt backlog maintained alongside feature backlog; reviewed with COE

Team Structure

































RoleResponsibilityEnterprise Architect (EA)Solution design, cross-stream architecture decisions, ARBTech LeadStream-level technical design; code review; standards enforcementSenior DeveloperComplex Apex/LWC build; integration codeDeveloperStandard feature development; unit testsAdmin / Declarative SpecialistFlow, configuration, page layouts, reportsRelease EngineerCI/CD pipeline; deployment; environment management

Apex Development Standards

Trigger framework: one trigger per object; handler class per object; no business logic in trigger body
Bulkification: all DML and SOQL outside loops; use Map/Set patterns for relationship traversal
Governor limit awareness: query for all needed data upfront; batch long-running processes
Error handling: use Database.insert(records, false) for partial success in bulk; log errors to a custom object or Platform Event
Test class naming: <ClassName>Test — separate class, never in the same file

Naming Conventions

Classes: PascalCase (AccountService, OpportunityTriggerHandler)
Variables / methods: camelCase
Custom objects/fields: snake_case API name with __c suffix
Test classes: AccountServiceTest


LWC Development Standards

Components follow single-responsibility principle — one component, one concern
Data access via @wire adapters where available (prefer over imperative Apex calls for read)
Use lightning-record-form / lightning-record-edit-form before custom Apex for standard CRUD
ESLint configured with @salesforce/eslint-config-lwc; run in CI pipeline
Avoid innerHTML (XSS risk); never hardcode org IDs or URLs


Integration with Development Lifecycle

Each feature branch in Git = one story/feature; branch from develop
Pull Request: minimum 1 reviewer; CI pipeline must pass (static analysis, unit tests, validation deploy)
Merge to develop triggers deployment to Integration sandbox
Release branch cut weekly or per sprint; deployed to SIT after merge gate


Communication Plan









































AudienceChannelCadenceContentSteering CommitteeSteering deckMonthlyProgress, risks, decisions neededBusiness stakeholdersStatus report / sprint demoBi-weeklyFeatures delivered, upcomingDevelopment teamSprint ceremoniesDaily/weeklyStand-up, planning, retroEnd usersTraining, release notesPer releaseWhat’s changing, how to use itIT OperationsChange request, runbookPer releaseDeployment steps, rollback plan

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.title: DevOps Strategy
CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
Package Types Comparison













































TypeNamespaceUpgradableIP ProtectedSubscriber can modifyUse caseUnmanagedNoneNoNoYes (full source visible)Internal reuse, starter templatesUnlockedOptionalYes (versioned)NoNoModular internal apps; source-driven devManaged (1GP)RequiredYes (push)Yes (code obfuscated)NoAppExchange ISV productsManaged (2GP)RequiredYesYesNoModern ISV; supports unlocked dependencies
Unlocked Packages in Practice

Define package in sfdx-project.json; metadata assigned to package directory
Version commands: sf package version create → generates a version ID
Install in org: sf package install --package <versionId> --target-org <alias>
Dependencies between unlocked packages are supported but must be versioned
Best for: large internal implementations wanting modular, independently-deployable metadata



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Unlocked packages do not protect IP (source is visible to admins in the subscriber org). If IP protection is needed (AppExchange listing), use managed packages.



Source-Driven vs Org-Driven Development








































Org-drivenSource-drivenSource of truthThe orgVersion control (Git)Deployment mechanismChange setsMetadata API / sf CLI / packagesSuitable forSmall teams, admin-led, simple orgsDeveloper teams, complex orgs, CI/CDRollbackManual re-deploy prior change setgit revert + re-deployMerge conflictsNot applicableProfiles, permission sets, flows are common conflict sourcesRecommendedTransitional onlyYes — target state for all enterprise orgs
Migrating from Org-Driven to Source-Driven

Retrieve all metadata from production using sf project retrieve start
Commit to a Git repository (initial baseline)
Define .forceignore — exclude generated files (debug logs, session data, API versions)
Train developers to pull before making changes; commit frequently
Move to CI validation deployments before full CI/CD pipeline


Version Control Strategy

.forceignore: analogous to .gitignore — exclude: *.meta.xml for certain system objects, user-specific data, debug artifacts
Profile handling: profiles are the most problematic metadata — they contain FLS for every field; partial profile deployments often cause conflicts

Best practice: use permission sets instead of profiles for all custom access; deploy minimal profiles
Some teams exclude profiles from source control and manage them separately


Flow versioning: each saved flow version creates a new file; only activate the latest; clean up old versions to reduce noise


Salesforce DX CLI Reference
# Authenticate
sf org login web --alias myOrg
 
# Retrieve metadata
sf project retrieve start --metadata "ApexClass,CustomObject"
 
# Deploy metadata
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app --test-level RunLocalTests
 
# Check-only (validate without deploy)
sf project deploy start --dry-run --source-dir force-app
 
# Create scratch org
sf org create scratch --definition-file config/project-scratch-def.json --alias featureScratch --duration-days 7
 
# Run Apex tests
sf apex run test --test-level RunLocalTests --output-dir test-results --result-format tap
 
# Create unlocked package version
sf package version create --package "My Package" --installation-key "" --wait 10

Third-Party DevOps Tools



































ToolStrengthsConsider whenCopadoNative Salesforce UI; pipeline management in SF; Copado Robotic Testing for UI automationTeam needs everything in Salesforce; non-developer-heavy teamsGearsetDelta deployment (only changed components); conflict detection; easy migration from change setsTeams moving from change sets; need delta deploy to avoid overwrite issuesAutoRABITCompliance, full audit trail, data backup, rollbackRegulated industries (FSC, Health Cloud); complex multi-orgFlosum100% native SalesforceTeams wanting no external tool; smaller budgetsGitHub Actions + sf CLIFree (if on GitHub); full control; YAML pipelinesEngineering-led teams comfortable with CLI

CTA Decision Guide





































RequirementRecommendationSmall team, mostly admins, simple orgChange sets; plan migration to source-drivenDeveloper team, version control neededsf CLI + Git; Metadata API; source-drivenLarge programme, modular independent teamsUnlocked packages + sf CLIAppExchange productManaged package (2GP)Enterprise with non-developer-heavy teamCopado or Gearset wrapping sf CLIRegulated industry needing audit trailAutoRABITIsolated feature developmentScratch orgs per feature branch

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.title: Environment Strategy
CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
Sandbox Types













































TypeDataMetadataStorageRefresh IntervalUseDeveloperNone (or manual load)Full copy200 MB data / 200 MB file1 dayIndividual developer feature workDeveloper ProNoneFull copy1 GB data / 1 GB file1 daySmall teams, complex features, data loadingPartial CopySample (up to 5 GB, configurable)Full copy5 GB data5 daysQA, SIT; representative data without full volumeFullAll production dataFull copySame as production29 daysUAT, performance testing, regression; most expensive


                  
                  CTA exam trap 
                  
                

Partial Copy does not copy all records — it copies a configurable sample set. Never recommend Partial Copy for performance or LDV testing; use Full sandbox. Examiners test this distinction.


Scratch Orgs

Ephemeral, source-driven orgs — spun up from a scratch org definition JSON
Day limit: 30 days max; typically used for hours or days then deleted
Allocation: Enterprise/Unlimited — 40 active, 80/day; Developer Edition — 3 active, 6/day
Best for: feature development in SFDX/package-based projects; CI pipeline validation
Cannot contain production data; must be scripted with data via SFDX or seeding scripts


Environment Tier Model
A typical enterprise environment strategy uses 4–6 tiers:
[Scratch Orgs / Dev Sandboxes]  ← individual feature work
         ↓
  [Integration Sandbox]         ← merge of all feature branches; integration testing
         ↓
  [SIT / QA Sandbox]            ← test team validation; Partial Copy data
         ↓
  [UAT Sandbox]                 ← business sign-off; Full sandbox preferred
         ↓
  [Staging / Pre-Prod]          ← final deployment rehearsal; Full sandbox
         ↓
  [Production]



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

You don’t need all tiers for every scenario. Size the environment strategy to the team and project complexity. A 2-stream team might use Dev → SIT → UAT → Prod; a large programme might need an Integration sandbox to manage concurrent stream merges.



Sandbox Refresh Strategy

Refresh = reset sandbox to production snapshot — all customisations made in the sandbox are lost
Plan refresh cadence around major milestones (e.g. refresh UAT at start of each UAT cycle)
After refresh: re-apply sandbox-specific config (endpoint URLs, test user passwords, Connected App settings)
Automate post-refresh steps with a sandbox post-copy Apex class implementing SandboxPostCopy interface

global class PostCopyScript implements SandboxPostCopy {
    global void runApexClass(SandboxContext context) {
        // re-assign test users, update endpoints, etc.
    }
}

Org Migration Strategy
Moving from one Salesforce org to another (e.g. consolidating two orgs, upgrading edition):

























ApproachWhenMetadata migration (sf CLI / Metadata API)Migrate configuration and code; no dataData migration (ETL tools)Migrate records; External IDs required for relationshipsPhased migrationMigrate business units or clouds progressively; dual-running periodBig-bang cutoverAll users move on a single cutover date; highest risk, fastest

Key dependencies: resolve namespace differences, custom object ID references, hardcoded org IDs in code, Connected App reconfiguration
Always run a trial migration in a Full sandbox before production cutover


CTA Decision Guide

































RequirementRecommendationDeveloper needs isolated feature workDeveloper or Developer Pro sandboxQA team needs representative dataPartial Copy sandboxUAT with business users on real dataFull sandboxCI pipeline build validationScratch org (ephemeral, disposable)Performance/LDV testingFull sandbox with production data volumeReproducing a production issueFull sandbox (most accurate replica)

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.title: Governance & Centre of Excellence
CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
Why Governance Matters on the CTA Exam
Every CTA scenario includes a delivery component. Examiners expect a concrete governance model — not just “we’ll have a COE.” You must name roles, describe how decisions are made, and show how quality gates are enforced across environments.

Organisational Structure
Executive Sponsor / Steering Committee
        │
   Program Manager
        │
  ┌─────┴──────┐
 PMO          COE / ARB
        │
  ┌─────┴──────────────┐
Stream Leads     Release Manager
(Dev, QA, BA)






































RoleResponsibilitySteering CommitteeStrategic direction, funding, escalation; approve major milestonesProgram ManagerCross-stream coordination, risk, interdependenciesPMOStandards, project methodology, governance complianceCOESalesforce best practices, architectural guidance, reuseARB (Architecture Review Board)Review and approve architectural decisions; enforce standardsRelease ManagerOwns the release calendar, deployment gates, change requestsTech Lead (per stream)Day-to-day technical decisions within stream

Centre of Excellence (COE)
The COE drives consistency and quality across all Salesforce workstreams.
COE Models





















ModelWhen to useCentralisedSingle product / single team; small org; consistent standards needed fastDecentralisedMultiple business units with independent Salesforce orgs; BU autonomy is priorityHybrid (most common)Central standards + patterns; BU teams own delivery; COE does architecture review
COE Functions

Define and maintain coding standards, configuration patterns, naming conventions
Manage Salesforce platform releases (3× per year) — assess impact, approve enablement
Own the governance backlog (tech debt, security posture, org health metrics)
Run Architecture Review Board sessions for significant changes


Architecture Review Board (ARB)

Reviews proposed solutions before build begins
Checks: scalability, security, adherence to patterns, governor limit exposure, integration approach
Outputs: approved, approved with conditions, or rejected (must redesign)
In practice: weekly or bi-weekly; chaired by Enterprise Architect or COE lead



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

The examiner may ask: “A team wants to bypass the ARB to hit a deadline. What do you do?” → Escalate to Steering Committee; technical debt and risk are documented; short-term bypass requires sign-off and remediation plan.



Change Management Process

Change Request (CR) raised — describes what, why, impact, rollback plan
ARB / Tech Lead review — approve or reject
Deployment to non-prod — SIT / UAT validation
Release Manager sign-off — confirms test evidence, business sign-off
Production deployment — scheduled maintenance window or CI/CD promotion
Post-deployment verification — smoke tests, monitoring

Change Freeze Periods

Salesforce seasonal releases (Spring/Summer/Winter) → freeze 1–2 weeks either side
Business blackout periods (year-end close, peak trading) → no non-critical changes
Communicated via release calendar; enforced by Release Manager


Project Management Frameworks





















FrameworkWhen to useAgile / ScrumRequirements evolve; client collaboration needed; iterative deliveryWaterfallFixed-scope, well-understood requirements; compliance-heavy deliveryHybridPhased programme — early discovery waterfall, delivery sprints agile


                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Most enterprise Salesforce programmes use hybrid: a structured discovery/design phase (Waterfall gates for architecture sign-off) followed by Agile sprints for build. State this and justify it rather than saying “pure Agile.”



Adoption and KPIs
A governance model without measurement is incomplete on the CTA exam.

























KPI CategoryExamplesDeliverySprint velocity, defect escape rate, deployment frequencyQualityTest coverage %, critical defect count in productionAdoptionDAU/MAU, feature usage (Lightning Usage App), training completionOperationsMTTR, incident frequency, org storage utilisation

Communication Plan: stakeholder map → message per audience → channel and cadence
Change Management: end-user training, champions network, feedback loops

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.title: Project Governance CoE
CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
What is Governance?
The goal of project governance, and the creation of a COE is to establish, maintain and enforce enterprise standards across all projects. It’s also in place to ensure that every project stays on track and conforms to the businesses ideal vision for the it.

What is a COE?
A COE is essentially a body of individuals who manage the governance and operations for a Salesforce Org (or IT initiatives company wide). At a larger business you will likely have multiple COE’s, but there will be two major types of COE’s:


Global COE - This is the enterprise wide COE that tries to maintain a vision for the entire business/suite of technology the business uses. This sets the baseline architecture, security, data standards, etc for all IT groups within a business


Local COE - This is a COE local to your project. It ensures that all project teams working in your Salesforce Org (or tech stack) follow the same rules, and align to the businesses vision for what needs to be delivered to customers.



Common Governance Acronyms/Matrixes
COE - Center of Excellence
ROAM - Resolve, Own, Accept, Mitigate. This is a risk management acronym/matric. When a risk is identified it is placed into one of those four categories by the COE.
RACI - Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed. This is a responsibilities matrix whose goal is to bring structure and clarity to the roles that each stakeholder plays in a project.
Common COE Roles
When sitting for the CTA Board you need to make a decision on who to add to your COE based on the criteria in your scenario. You SHOULD NOT just produce a generic COE structure. You need to link your COE actors back to requirements in the scenario.
Executive Sponsor - Responsible for getting executive support throughout the business, and making sure the projects goals are aligned to the goals of the business.
Steering Committee - Keep project goals, timeline, and budget in check. Also responsible for resolving any conflict between project teams.
Architect Review Board - Ensure all architecture domain standards/guides are in place and that all projects are adhering to those standards. It approves and denies any new architecture/development efforts.
Change Control Board - This group is the final group of decision makers as to whether or not a new initiative can take place. They make sure that new initiatives are following the rules and staying within budget.
QA Team - Ensures high quality testing and quality control standards are in place.
PMO (Project Management Office) - This group sets and maintains all project standards.
Compliance Team - This team ensures that all regional government mandated legalities/rules are upheld by the project team.
Security Team - This team ensures that projects abide by both the businesses and the local governments security standards for the data in their systems.
Release Management Team - This team ensures that all apps/projects follow the same release management cadence and have the right suite of tools in place to make releases as smooth as possible.
Translations Team - Team is in charge of ensuring any/all translation work required follows the same quality control guidelines.
Data Steward -
Data Custodian -

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
Branching Model (Git Flow)
main ──────────────────────────────────────────► (production)
  │                                        ▲
  └─ release/v1.2 ──────────────────────► merge + tag
          │                         ▲
          └─ develop ───────────────┤
                │          ▲        │
                ├─ feature/ABC ─────┘
                ├─ feature/DEF ─────┘
                └─ feature/GHI ─────┘

hotfix/fix-123 ──────────────────────────► main + develop






























BranchPurposemainProduction state; every commit is deployabledevelopIntegration branch; all features merged herefeature/<ticket>One branch per story/feature; short-livedrelease/<version>Stabilisation branch cut from develop; only bug fixeshotfix/<ticket>Emergency fix cut from main; merged back to both main and develop


                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Examiners ask: “A critical bug is found in production the day after a major release. How do you handle it?” → Create a hotfix branch from main, fix and test in a hotfix sandbox, merge back to main and develop to prevent regression.



Deployment Tooling Comparison















































ToolWhat it deploysBest forLimitationsChange SetsMetadata onlySmall teams, admin-led, no CI/CDNo version control, no rollback, no dependency check, UI-onlyMetadata API / sf CLIMetadata onlyDeveloper-led, source control, CI/CDComplex package.xml, profiles/perm sets are brittleSalesforce DX (sf CLI)Metadata + scratch orgsSource-driven dev, package-based projectsSteeper learning curveUnlocked PackagesVersioned metadata bundlesModular apps, reuse, ISV-liteNamespace required if sharing outside orgManaged PackagesVersioned, IP-protected bundlesAppExchange ISV, OEMCannot modify after release, upgrade is pushThird-party DevOps (Copado, Gearset, AutoRABIT)Metadata + delta deploymentEnterprise teams needing GUI, conflict detectionCost; vendor lock-in


                  
                  What change sets cannot deploy 
                  
                

Some metadata types are not deployable via change sets: flows in certain states, some setup pages, Einstein features, Salesforce CMS content. Use Metadata API / sf CLI for these.



CI/CD Pipeline Design
A typical Salesforce CI pipeline stage:
PR raised
  → Static analysis (PMD / ESLint / Checkmarx)
  → Unit test execution (minimum 75% coverage; 85% target)
  → Deployment to Integration sandbox (validation only: checkOnly flag)
  → Automated regression tests (UTAM / Selenium)
  → Code review approval
  → Merge to develop

Release promotion:
develop → release branch → UAT sandbox → approved → main → production

CI/CD Tools





























ToolNotesGitHub Actions / GitLab CINative CI; Salesforce CLI commands in YAML pipelineCopadoSalesforce-native DevOps; pipeline UI in SF; Copado Robotic TestingGearsetDelta deployment, conflict detection; good for change-set teams migrating to CIAutoRABITEnterprise-grade; compliance-focused; complex configurationFlosumSalesforce-native alternative to Copado

Release Governance

Release Calendar: published quarterly; includes Salesforce seasonal release dates + freeze windows
Release sign-off checklist:

 All unit tests passing, coverage ≥ 75% (target ≥ 85%)
 SIT sign-off from QA lead
 UAT sign-off from business owner
 Security review (if applicable)
 Rollback plan documented
 Post-deployment smoke test script ready


Deployment window: scheduled maintenance window (off-peak hours); communicated to users in advance
Rollback: metadata rollback via sf CLI (deploy prior version); data changes require separate rollback plan


Salesforce Seasonal Releases

3 releases/year: Spring (Jan/Feb), Summer (May/Jun), Winter (Oct/Nov)
Sandboxes get the release ~1 week before production — use this window to regression test
Release freeze: avoid non-critical deployments 1–2 weeks around a seasonal release



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Examiners test whether you know to test new Salesforce features in sandbox before they hit production. A governance calendar that ignores seasonal releases is incomplete.

CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.title: Testing Strategy
CTA-Notes/Deployment--and--Dev-Lifecycle.content:
Testing Phases



























































PhaseOwnerObjectiveSandboxUnit TestingDeveloperValidate individual Apex/LWC components in isolationDev sandbox / scratch orgStatic Code AnalysisDeveloper / CI pipelineEnforce coding standards; catch common bugsCI (no sandbox needed)System Integration Testing (SIT)QA TeamValidate end-to-end flows; integration points workingPartial Copy / Developer ProRegression Testing (RT)QA Team + automationEnsure new changes haven’t broken existing functionalityPartial Copy / SIT sandboxUser Acceptance Testing (UAT)Business usersValidate solution meets business requirementsFull sandboxPerformance TestingTech TeamValidate system under expected and peak loadFull sandboxSecurity TestingSecurity / Tech TeamPenetration testing, OWASP top 10, Salesforce Shield configDedicated security sandboxStaging / Pre-ProdRelease ManagerFinal deployment rehearsal; validate release packageFull sandbox

Salesforce Unit Testing

Minimum requirement: 75% overall code coverage to deploy to production
Best practice target: 85%+ per class; test meaningful behaviour, not just coverage
Use @isTest annotation; Test.startTest() / Test.stopTest() for governor limit reset
Test data: use @TestSetup method or TestFactory class — never rely on org data (SeeAllData=false default is correct)
Test classes must assert outcomes — empty test methods that hit 75% give false confidence

Static Code Analysis Tools






























ToolLanguageWhat it checksPMDApexUnused variables, empty catch blocks, SOQL in loops, complexityESLintJavaScript (LWC)Style, accessibility, security (no innerHTML, etc.)Checkmarx / CodeScanApex + JSSecurity vulnerabilities (SOQL injection, XSS)Graph Engine (Salesforce)ApexFlow analysis, false-positive reduction

Automated Testing
UTAM (Unified Testing Automation Model)

Salesforce-native framework for UI testing of LWC and Aura components
Page Object Model in JSON; test scripts in JavaScript using WDIO
Best for: regression testing of standard Salesforce UI flows
Runs against a full org (not scratch org); requires data setup

Selenium / WebDriver

Browser-based UI automation; language-agnostic (Java, Python, JS)
Use for complex custom UI scenarios not covered by UTAM
Maintain alongside releases — UI changes break locators

Apex Test execution via sf CLI (CI integration)
sf apex run test --test-level RunAllTestsInOrg --result-format json --output-dir test-results

Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)

Maps each requirement → test case → test result
Ensures full coverage of requirements before UAT sign-off
CTA exam: mention RTM as evidence of test completeness when asked about quality governance


Performance Testing Considerations

Target: validate against expected peak load (not just average)
Salesforce governor limits make performance testing different from traditional apps:

SOQL query limits per transaction
Apex CPU time (10s synchronous, 60s async)
API call limits per day


Tools: JMeter, LoadRunner against the REST/SOAP API layer
Test LDV scenarios in Full sandbox — indexing and sharing recalculation behaviour differs at scale



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Performance testing must use a Full sandbox with production-equivalent data volume. A Partial Copy sandbox will not surface SOQL timeout or sharing recalculation issues that appear in production.



CTA Decision Guide





































RequirementTesting approach75% code coverage gateApex unit tests; @isTest; Test.startTest/stopTestEnforce no SOQL-in-loopsPMD in CI pipelineRegression after each sprintAutomated UTAM suite on SIT sandboxBusiness sign-offUAT in Full sandbox with real usersComplex integration end-to-endSIT with test stubs or integration sandbox pointing at test endpointsLDV / performance validationFull sandbox with data load + JMeter API testsSecurity postureCheckmarx scan + manual pen test prior to go-live

CTA-Notes/Experience-Cloud/exp-cloud-rel.content:
User Types & Licenses



































LicenseAudienceSharing ModelCustomer CommunityB2C customersHigh-volume (HVCP); sharing setsCustomer Community PlusB2C customers needing role hierarchyRole-based; Account/ContactShare NOT availablePartner CommunityPartners / PRMRole hierarchy per partner account; teams supportedExternal AppsCustom apps, broad accessHigh-volumeAuthenticated WebsiteBroad public-facingHigh-volume

Up to 100 Experience Cloud sites per org (active, inactive, and preview)
Customer Community Plus and Partner Community require roles associated with an account → role proliferation degrades performance
Default org portal role limit: 50,000 (increasable via Salesforce support)
Guest users do not consume external licenses; page view limits apply by Salesforce edition (e.g. Enterprise: 6M page views/year, overages calculated annually)

Login-Based vs Member-Based Licenses

Member-based — user has a named seat
Login-based — purchase a number of monthly logins; one login consumed per day regardless of number of logins that day; switching between sites after login does not consume extra logins
Login overages calculated over a 12-month period from contract start date; entitlements roll over month to month
Monitor login consumption: LoginHistory table; Usage-based Entitlements list in Setup → Company Information


Sharing for Experience Cloud Users
High-Volume (HVCP / Customer Community / Authenticated Website)

Do NOT use the standard sharing model (no roles, no ownership-based sharing rules)
Sharing works by foreign key match between portal user and record

The portal user’s Account and Contact IDs must match a lookup on the record


Sharing rules and manual sharing are NOT available to high-volume users as sources or targets (since they have no roles / can’t be in public groups)
HVCP license is ONLY for Customer Portal — not Partner Portal

Customer Community Plus — Apex Sharing Limitation

AccountShare and ContactShare objects are not available to Customer Community Plus users
Workaround: use a trigger running without sharing (or an inner utility class with without sharing) to execute the DML operation
After enabling digital experiences: records accessible via “Roles and Subordinates” Apex managed sharing are automatically updated — change code to use “Role and Internal Subordinates” group instead

Partner Community — Role Hierarchy

When the first external user is enabled on a partner account, a 3-level role hierarchy is created rolling up to the account owner:

Partner User
Partner Manager
Partner Executive


To transfer a Partner account: must have Manage Users or Manage External Users permission
Partner accounts can only be transferred to users with Manage External Users permission
Partner users can’t be associated with person accounts
Partner and Channel Account users can’t see emails in the case feed


Sharing Sets
A sharing set grants site users access to any record associated with an account or contact that matches the user’s account or contact.

Uses indirect lookups: e.g. user’s Contact → Account → Account lookup on the target record
One sharing set per profile
Access granted via sharing sets does not roll up the role hierarchy
Access is available to all high-volume users in the sharing set’s access group

Available Objects for Sharing Sets
Account, Asset, Campaign, Case, Contact, Custom Objects (with account or contact lookup), Individual, Knowledge, Lead, Opportunity, Order, Service Appointment, and others.
Excluded from Sharing Sets

Objects with OWD of Public Read/Write
Custom objects without an account or contact lookup field

Contact on Multiple Accounts

If a contact has multiple account relationships, use the “Related Account” condition in the sharing set to include records reachable through any of the associated accounts


Share Groups

Allow records owned by high-volume site users to be shared with authenticated internal and external users
Cannot share records owned by high-volume users with guest users via share groups — use guest user sharing rules instead
High-volume users have no roles → eliminates role hierarchy calculation overhead
Share groups apply across all Experience Cloud sites (not site-specific)
Associated with a sharing set (activated from the sharing set settings page)
Deactivating a share group removes all other users’ access to records owned by high-volume community users — an email notification is sent on deactivation



                  
                  Note
                  
                

Share Groups functionality is NOT available to Customer Community Plus or Partner Community license users.



Guest User Sharing

Guest users access Experience Cloud sites without logging in
Not counted against external licenses; page view quotas apply
“Let guest users see other members of this site” site preference controls user sharing for guest users
Use guest user sharing rules (criteria-based) to control what records are visible to guests
Release updates have increasingly restricted guest user access to prevent accidental data exposure


Super User Access

“Partner Super User Access” (Setup → Communities Settings) grants partners access to data owned by other users in the same partner account
Useful for Partner Managers / Partner Executives who need visibility into all reps’ pipeline


Control User Visibility

























SettingLocationEffectPortal User VisibilityOWD for user recordsPortal users in same customer/partner account can see each otherSite User VisibilityExperience Builder → Administration → Preferences”See other members of this site” — controlled per siteGuest User VisibilityAdministration → Preferences”Let guest users see other members of this site”

Mobile Architecture





















ApproachDescriptionNativePlatform-specific (iOS/Android); best UX; requires separate codebasesWeb (Mobile Web)Responsive HTML; single codebase; limited device accessHybridNative wrapper around web content (e.g. Salesforce Mobile SDK); access to device features
Mobile Publisher

Packages an Experience Cloud site as a branded native app
Distribution channels: App Store / Google Play (self-managed) or via Salesforce Mobile Publisher


External Sharing Methods Summary





























MethodUse CaseSharing SetsGrant high-volume users access to records via account/contact relationshipShare GroupsShare records owned by high-volume users with internal/external authenticated usersGuest User Sharing RulesCriteria-based rules to expose records to unauthenticated guestsApex Managed SharingComplex access requirements not met declaratively; custom row causesExternal Account HierarchyAllow parent-account portal users to see child-account records

Key Numbers





























ItemValueMax Experience Cloud sites per org100Default portal role limit50,000Partner roles per partner account3 (User, Manager, Executive)Sharing sets per profile1Channel licenses: users per partner accountup to 40 (expandable)

CTA-Notes/Experience-Cloud/experience-cl.title: Experience Cloud Features
CTA-Notes/Experience-Cloud/experience-cl.content:
What is Experience Cloud

Experience Cloud Licensing
There are 6 license types for exp cloud users. There is more info on each one in the Licenses section of this wiki:

Customer Community - If your users login a ton, they don’t need access to reports, and sharing sets are sufficient for their needs, this is the choice to go with. It’s also the cheapest option.
Customer Community Login - Same as above, but should be used when users infrequently login (like maybe 5-10 times a year or less).
Customer Community Plus - If users login a ton and they either need access to reports & dashboards, or more advanced sharing mechanisms, this is the license to choose.
Customer Community Plus Login - Same as above, but should be used when users infrequently login (like maybe 5-10 times a year or less).
Partner User License - If users need to collaborate on the following OOTB objects: Leads, Opportunities, Campaigns, Quotes and/or Market Development Funds, they have to have a Partner User License. Make sure to think long and hard about this as these are very expensive licenses compared to the two above.
Partner User Login License - Same as above, but should be used when users infrequently login (like maybe 5-10 times a year or less).


Guest User Sharing

Sharing Sets
Sharing Sets are THE ONLY sharing option available for Customer Community (CC) licenses users. They give you the ability to share records that a CC user doesn’t own with them via a record related to their user (Account, Contact, Related Account (ACR), Manager Account & Manager Contact). You can only setup ONE sharing set per object! You can also use this for CC+ & Partner users.

Sharing Groups
Sharing Groups are a mechanism to share records owned by Customer Community (CC) members with internal users and CC+ & Partner users. One each sharing set you can add a sharing group where you can share the records in the sharing set with any internal user as well as any external user with the same parent account.
NOTE: These cannot be used with guest users

Exp Site User Roles
CC+ & Partners can have up to 3 roles available to them (roles are not used for CC licensed users). You can set up how many roles are available to CC+ and/or Partner in Digital Experiences by specifying whether they will have 1, 2, or 3 roles. The three roles made available by default are the following: Partner Executive → Partner Manager → Partner User (for CC+ replace Partner with Customer). You can alter, on a site by site basis, the name of the first part of the role. For instance you can change the name “Partner” to “Taco” for a particular site, and then your roles would be: Taco Executive → Taco Manager → Taco User.
When you convert a Contact record into an experience cloud site user, you will need to manually select one of the roles for your user.
It’s important to note that for each Account a new group of roles gets created, so for instance if you had a group of exp site users that were all tied to the “Taco Bell” account they would fall under the role “Taco Bell Partner User”, and if you had another group of users tied to the “Burger King” account they would fall under the “Burger King Partner User” role.
CC+ & Partner users account specific roles fall beneath the role of the first internal user that converted the first contact for that account into an experience site user. So for instance if an internal user that had the role of “Sales Associate” was the first user to convert a contact that was associated to the account “Taco Bell” into an exp site user, the “Taco Bell Executive”, “Taco Bell Manager”, and “Taco Bell User” roles would all be created underneath the “Sales Associate” role in the role hierarchy.
NOTE: Be wary of the number of roles you would be creating when suggesting roles. More than 2 million roles will cause performance issues at which point Account Role Optimization may be considered, as well as alternative licensing/setup options for your users.

Account Role Optimization (ARO)
If you have multiple roles enabled for your CC+ or Partner users, when a new contact is enabled for the first time for an account, up to 3 new roles are automatically created for those users. If you are anticipating you will likely have many CC+ or Partner users and are concerned that you might meet the 50k role limit (which can be pushed to an absolute maximum of 500k roles), you should consider using ARO. ARO only creates a single role for an account until multiple users are activated for that account. Meaning you can cut back on unnecessary roles until they actually become necessary.

Exp Site Translations

Super Users
Super User Access is available to CC+ & Partner licensed users in an experience cloud site. When this feature is enabled it allows users to view and edit (based on object permissions) all cases, leads, opps, and custom object records of all users in the same role as them, as well as any roles beneath them.

Topics In Exp Sites

CMS in Exp Sites

Account Relationships
Account Relationships allow you to share object records from one accounts users to another accounts users. This feature only is available to Partner & CC+ licensed users. You can share the following objects records that are associated with the accounts:

Order
Contact
Account
Campaign
Case
Lead
Opportunity
Partner Fund Allocation
Custom Objects

To set this up you’ll do the following:

Go to Settings → Digital Experience Settings → Check the “Enable Account Relationships” checkbox.
You’ll then go to your account rec, place the account relationships related list on the page and create a relationship.
Finally in Setup you’ll go to “Account Relationship Data Sharing Rule Settings” and create the sharing rules for you account relationship records on an object by object basis.


Delegated Account Management
This feature allows you to give external users (CC+ & Partner) the ability to manage their account members and their account brand information. Basically they get the following capabilities:

Create and Edit Users/Members
Reset a Users Password
Activate or Deactivate a User
Upload Brand Logos
Create Co-Branded Emails
Create Marketing Campaigns

You allow users this functionality by assigning the permission “Delegated External User Administrator” via a profile or perm set.

External Managed Accounts
This allows you to designate a user (CC+ or Partner) the ability to manage users on an account that is not directly tied to them. Maybe someone is the owner of one business and a co-owner of another, they might wanna manage the users for both businesses despite only being linked to one of them directly on their contact. This is an OOTB way to do just that.
To enable this feature do the following:

Go to a profile or perm set and enable the “Manage External Users” Permission.
On that same permission set or prof enable read access to the “External Managed Accounts” Object
Add the External Managed Account object to the related lists on Account page layouts.
Give the user the “Account Switcher User” permission on their user record.
Put the Account Switcher component in a community.

More info here

Approval Processes in Exp Sites
CC+ & Partner users can be assigned as approvers in an approval process or part of a queue that is assigned as an approver. Everything else works exactly the same as any other standard approval process setup.

Content Moderation

Experience Cloud Gamification

Experience Cloud on Mobile

Self-Registration & Login Pages

Login Discovery Handlers

Features not available in Exp Sites
Below is a list of internal SF features that cannot be leveraged in exp sites.

Dynamic Forms
