CTA-Notes/Integration/00-integration-ove.title: Integration Overview
CTA-Notes/Integration/00-integration-ove.content:
Integration Framework
(Salesforce Integration Patterns and Practices)
Every integration decision should be framed along five dimensions:





























DimensionQuestions to answerNatureReal-time vs near-real-time vs batch?DirectionSalesforce → External, External → Salesforce, or bidirectional?TimingSynchronous (caller waits) or asynchronous (fire and forget)?PatternWhich canonical pattern fits? (see Integration Patterns)SecurityOAuth, mTLS, IP allowlist, named credentials?


                  
                  CTA framing 
                  
                

State these five dimensions upfront when presenting an integration solution. Examiners look for structured thinking, not just technology choices.



Sync vs Async
Synchronous
Caller blocks until response is received. Use when the result is needed immediately.



































TechnologyDirectionNotesREST APIBothMost common; JSON; statelessSOAP APIBothXML; legacy; enterprise systemsComposite APIBothBatch multiple REST calls in one round-tripUI APIInboundMobile/web apps; respects metadataApex calloutOutboundFrom Salesforce; 120s timeout
Asynchronous
Caller fires and moves on. Use when decoupling, high volume, or long-running processing is needed.



































TechnologyDirectionNotesPlatform EventsBothEvent-driven; durable; at-least-once deliveryChange Data Capture (CDC)OutboundTriggers on record changes; no custom payloadPub/Sub APIBothgRPC; high-throughput event streamingBulk API 2.0BothLarge data loads/extractsOutbound MessagingOutboundSOAP-based; triggered by workflow; legacy

CDC vs Platform Events vs Batch (SystemModstamp)
A common CTA decision point:





















ApproachUse whenCDCYou need to react to any field change on a standard/custom object; no custom payload neededPlatform EventsYou need a custom payload, or the trigger is business-logic-driven (not just a record save)Batch on SystemModstampNear-real-time not required; external system polls on a schedule; simpler integration contract


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

CDC is not listed in the Remote Process Invocation — Async pattern because CDC is outbound-only and change-driven; it is not used to invoke a remote process. PE is the correct tool for that pattern.



Salesforce-to-Salesforce (S2S) Integration
Options in order of preference for new work:

Platform Events — loosely coupled; both orgs subscribe/publish; no direct org dependency
REST/SOAP API — direct callout; simpler for small volumes; tight coupling
Salesforce Connect (External Objects) — real-time data virtualisation; no data copy
Native S2S (legacy) — deprecated path; avoid for new designs



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

For CTA, prefer Platform Events for S2S when the orgs should remain decoupled (e.g. subsidiaries, partner orgs). Use REST API when one org is clearly the system of record and volumes are low.



Apex Callouts

Callouts from Apex must be made from a non-trigger context (use @future(callout=true), Queueable, or async)
Exception: synchronous callout is allowed from a trigger only if no DML has occurred in the same transaction
Max 120s timeout per callout; 100 callouts per transaction
Use Named Credentials to avoid storing endpoint URLs and credentials in code


mTLS (Mutual TLS)
(Mutual Authentication / mTLS)

Both client and server present X.509 certificates — stronger than OAuth alone
Inbound mTLS: External system presents cert to Salesforce → configure via Connected App + cert validation
Outbound mTLS: Salesforce presents cert to external system → configure via Named Credential + client cert
Pub/Sub API does not support mTLS — use OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer for Pub/Sub
Plan for cert rotation and revocation in the integration design


Outbound Messaging (Legacy)
(Outbound Messaging)

Triggered by Workflow Rule (not Flow) — legacy mechanism, still present in older orgs
Sends SOAP XML notification to an external endpoint
At-least-once delivery; retries for up to 24 hours
Max 100 notifications per call; 2M notifications/day org limit
Superseded by Platform Events + Flows for new work


ESB / Middleware Role
Use an ESB or integration platform (e.g. MuleSoft) when:

Protocol conversion is needed (SOAP ↔ REST, FTP ↔ API, etc.)
Orchestration across 3+ systems is required
ETL transformation is needed before data enters Salesforce
DMZ placement is required for security/compliance
Retry, routing, or canonical data model mapping is complex



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

For CTA, position middleware as the integration hub when there are 3+ external systems. Point-to-point is acceptable for 2-system, simple-contract scenarios.



Key Governor Limits

































LimitValueSynchronous Apex callout timeout120 secondsCallouts per transaction100Outbound messages per day2 millionPlatform Event publishes per hour (high-vol)250,000 (expandable)Bulk API 2.0 records per 24h150 millionAPI requests per dayOrg edition + user-based (check limits UI)

Study Sequence
Notes are numbered in reading order — framing first, then patterns, then the technologies that implement them.
1. Framework & patterns

Integration Patterns — canonical patterns with decision guide
Integration Patterns (Official Reference) — Salesforce Architects reference
Integration Solution Template — structure for presenting an integration solution

2. Request/response APIs (synchronous)

REST API — the default; JSON, stateless
Composite API — batching REST calls in one round-trip
GraphQL API — query exactly the fields needed
SOAP API — Enterprise vs Partner WSDL
UI API — mobile/web UIs that respect metadata
Bulk API 1.0 vs 2.0 — large data loads/extracts (in Data Management → LDV)
Metadata API — deploy/retrieve; CI/CD backbone
Tooling API — code coverage, execute anonymous, IDE features

3. Event-driven (asynchronous)

Platform Events & Change Data Capture — custom events vs record-change events
Sub API — high-throughput streaming via gRPC
Streaming API (PushTopic) — legacy; know for migration scenarios

4. Declarative & data virtualization

External Services — declarative REST integration via OpenAPI spec
External Services Setup Guide — setup steps
Salesforce Connect & External Objects — data virtualization; OData adapter

5. Security & connectivity

Named Credentials — secure credential storage for callouts
OAuth 2.0 Flows — Web Server, JWT Bearer, Client Credentials, Device
Mutual TLS (2-Way SSL) — certificate-based mutual authentication
Networking Basics — firewalls, DMZ, reverse proxies

6. Middleware & use cases

MuleSoft & Middleware Positioning — API-led connectivity; when to use middleware
MuleSoft Notes
Payment Gateway Integration — worked example

7. Tools

Postman — Testing Salesforce APIs

CTA-Notes/Integration/01-patterns.title: Integration Patterns
CTA-Notes/Integration/01-patterns.content:
(Salesforce Integration Patterns and Practices)
The Six Canonical Patterns
1. Remote Process Invocation — Request and Reply
Salesforce invokes an external process synchronously and waits for the result before continuing.





























DimensionDetailDirectionSalesforce → ExternalTimingSynchronousTechnologiesApex callout (REST/SOAP), External Services + Named CredentialsWhen to useResult is needed immediately to complete the Salesforce transaction (e.g. credit check, address validation, real-time pricing)Key constraint120s callout timeout; avoid in triggers without async wrapper


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Never make a synchronous callout from a trigger directly — wrap in @future(callout=true) or Queueable if the result is not needed before the DML commits.



2. Remote Process Invocation — Fire and Forget
Salesforce triggers an external process asynchronously and does not wait for the result.





























DimensionDetailDirectionSalesforce → ExternalTimingAsynchronousTechnologiesPlatform Events, Outbound Messaging (legacy), @future(callout=true), QueueableWhen to useExternal process doesn’t need to return data to Salesforce immediately (e.g. trigger a workflow in an external system, send a notification)Key constraintAt-least-once delivery with Platform Events; retry logic needed for callout-based approaches

3. Batch Data Synchronization
Large volumes of data are moved between Salesforce and an external system on a scheduled basis.





























DimensionDetailDirectionBothTimingAsynchronous / scheduledTechnologiesBulk API 2.0, MuleSoft/ESB, Scheduled Apex + SOQL, CDC with batch catch-upWhen to useNightly syncs, data migrations, periodic reporting extractsKey constraintHandle duplicates and conflict resolution; define the system of record

4. Remote Call-In
An external system calls Salesforce to query or modify data.





























DimensionDetailDirectionExternal → SalesforceTimingSynchronousTechnologiesREST API, SOAP API, Bulk API 2.0, GraphQL, UI APIWhen to useExternal system needs to read or write Salesforce data on demand (e.g. ERP pushing orders, mobile app reading records)Key constraintAuthentication (OAuth 2.0), API limits, FLS enforcement

5. UI Update Based on Data Changes
The Salesforce UI or an external UI updates in real time when data changes.





























DimensionDetailDirectionSalesforce → Client (browser/app)TimingNear-real-time / event-drivenTechnologiesPlatform Events + LWC empApi, CDC + CometD/Pub/Sub API, Streaming APIWhen to useLive dashboards, real-time notifications, collaborative editing indicatorsKey constraintCometD/empApi is browser-only; Pub/Sub API for external systems


                  
                  Note
                  
                

CDC is applicable here for data-change-driven UI updates. PE is applicable when the trigger is a business event, not necessarily a record save.



6. Data Virtualization
Salesforce displays data from an external system without storing it locally.





























DimensionDetailDirectionExternal → Salesforce (on demand)TimingSynchronous (at read time)TechnologiesSalesforce Connect (External Objects), OData adapter, Custom Apex adapterWhen to useData lives in an external system and must not be duplicated; real-time accuracy required; data is too large to copyKey constraintNo sharing model on external objects; no triggers; latency depends on external system; OData or Apex adapter required

Salesforce → External System Technologies



























































TechnologyPatternSync/AsyncNotesApex callout (REST)RPI Request-ReplySync120s timeout; Named CredentialsApex callout (SOAP)RPI Request-ReplySyncLegacy; WSDL-based@future calloutRPI Fire-and-ForgetAsyncCannot be called from batchQueueable calloutRPI Fire-and-ForgetAsyncChainable; better than @futurePlatform EventsRPI F&F, UI UpdateAsyncPreferred for decoupled asyncOutbound MessagingRPI Fire-and-ForgetAsyncLegacy; workflow-triggered; SOAPBulk API 2.0 (outbound)Batch SyncAsyncFor large data extractsCDCUI Update, Batch SyncAsyncRecord-change-driven
External System → Salesforce Technologies















































TechnologyPatternSync/AsyncNotesREST APIRemote Call-InSyncMost commonSOAP APIRemote Call-InSyncLegacy; XMLBulk API 2.0Batch SyncAsyncLarge volume ingestGraphQLRemote Call-InSyncFlexible queriesUI APIRemote Call-InSyncMobile apps; layout-awarePlatform Events (publish)RPI F&FAsyncExternal publishes; Salesforce subscribes

Integration Solution Template
When documenting an integration in a CTA scenario:

















































FieldValueIntegration nameDirectionSalesforce → External / External → Salesforce / BothNatureReal-time / Near-real-time / BatchTimingSynchronous / AsynchronousPattern(one of the 6 above)TechnologyAuthenticationVolumeRecords per call / per dayError handlingRetry strategy, dead letter, alertingSecurityOAuth, mTLS, IP allowlist, encryption

CTA-Notes/Integration/02-integration-pat.content:

current Salesforce Architects guide. This is the vocabulary the board expects — use these
exact pattern names when presenting, and be ready to defend the fit ranking (Best /
Good / Suboptimal) of the mechanism you picked.

Security/networking layer: integration-security-considerations
What’s being retired: legacy-integration-retirements



                  
                  How the official doc is structured 
                  
                

Every pattern follows the same template: Name → Context → Problem → Forces →
Solution → Sketch → Results → Sidebars → Example. In a board, the Forces are your
clarifying questions and the Solution fit table is your justification. Reciting
Context and Sketch wins no points; naming the force that drove your choice does.



1. Three integration categories
Classify before you choose a mechanism. Examiners probe whether you understand why
the data is moving, not just how.

























CategoryThe requirementPatternsProcess IntegrationA business process spans two or more applications. Usually long-running, stateful, needs orchestration and compensating/rollback logic on failure.Remote Process Invocation (Request & Reply, Fire & Forget), Remote Call-InData IntegrationTwo or more systems must hold timely, meaningful, consistent data. No business logic invoked — this is synchronisation.Batch Data Synchronisation, Remote Call-In, UI Update Based on Data ChangesVirtual IntegrationA user must view, search, or modify data that stays in the external system. No copy, no reconciliation.Data Virtualisation


                  
                  The most common mis-classification 
                  
                

“Sync the ERP order into Salesforce so reps can see it” is often not Data
Integration — if reps only read it and it must be real-time, it’s Virtual
Integration and you should not be storing it at all. Ask about reporting,
sharing, and offline needs to decide: those three requirements are what push you
from Data Virtualisation back to replication.



2. Pattern selection matrices
Salesforce → another system



































TypeTimingPatternProcessSynchronousRemote Process Invocation — Request and ReplyProcessAsynchronousRemote Process Invocation — Fire and ForgetDataSynchronousRemote Process Invocation — Request and ReplyDataAsynchronousUI Update Based on Data Changes / Batch Data SynchronisationVirtualSynchronousData Virtualisation
Another system → Salesforce






























TypeTimingPatternProcessSynchronousRemote Call-InProcessAsynchronousRemote Call-In (publish a platform event, then discard the response)DataSynchronousRemote Call-InDataAsynchronousBatch Data Synchronisation


                  
                  Key CTA exam point 
                  
                

Inbound calls to Salesforce are always synchronous request-reply at the transport
level. There is no inbound async API. “Asynchronous inbound” is simulated either by
the caller discarding the response, or by the caller publishing a platform event
so Salesforce-side processing is decoupled. Bulk API 2.0 is the exception in spirit:
the job is processed asynchronously, but the submission call itself is synchronous.



3. Remote Process Invocation — Request and Reply

























Type / TimingProcess (or Data) / SynchronousDirectionSalesforce → remoteProblemAn event in Salesforce must start a remote process, pass data, receive a response, and track state from it — all in one transaction.Volume profileSmall, real-time, single-record (a few hundred at most).
Forces to ask about: Must Salesforce wait before continuing? Must the response be
processed in the same transaction? Message size? Is the trigger a UI action or a DML
event? Can the endpoint respond with low latency, and how many users will do this at
peak?
Solution fit



































SolutionFitWhyExternal Services invokes a REST API declarativelyBestNo code. Requires an OpenAPI 2.0/3.0 (or YAML) schema; primitive types plus nested objects and header params supported. Invocable from Flow. See External Services.LWC/Aura/page → Apex REST or SOAP callout (use a Continuation if latency risk)BestFull control; WSDL2Apex generates a proxy class for SOAP. Continuations avoid burning synchronous Apex governor limits on slow endpoints.HTTP Callout action in FlowGoodDeclarative sync REST from Flow with no Apex and no OpenAPI spec required. The pragmatic middle ground when External Services doesn’t fit.Trigger → async Apex calloutSuboptimalAll callouts from trigger context must be async, so you can’t reply into the same transaction. This is really the Fire-and-Forget pattern.Batch Apex → sync calloutSuboptimalWorks, but callout limits apply per execution context (~200-record chunks). Not a real-time pattern.
Sidebars that get challenged

Timeliness: Apex callout timeout is configurable up to 120 seconds; the doc
recommends setting it to 5 seconds. Mitigate the org limit of 50 concurrent
long-running (>5s) synchronous transactions — blow through it and unrelated users
start failing. This is the number to quote when someone proposes a chatty sync callout
on a high-traffic page.
Error handling: the caller owns it. Show the user an actionable message.
Recovery: nothing commits in Salesforce until a successful response is received,
so the retry is naturally safe on the Salesforce side.
Idempotency: the remote procedure must be idempotent. Standard mechanism —
the consumer sends a unique message/correlation ID and the receiver tracks
duplicates. Creates in the remote system must check for duplicates first, keyed on
a unique Salesforce ID. If the call originates from the UI, handle idempotency at the
integration layer (middleware), not in the browser.
State management: either Salesforce stores the remote surrogate key (use an
External ID field — available in the same transaction because this is synchronous),
or the remote system stores the Salesforce record ID.
Security: one-way SSL by default; two-way SSL/mTLS supported with self-signed
or CA-signed certs (Mutual TLS (2-Way SSL)); use Named Credentials
(Named Credentials) and OAuth 2.0 (OAuth 2.0 Flows); Apex Crypto for hashes
and digital signatures (cryptography).
WS-Security is not natively supported — inject headers via a security/XML gateway
(preferred) or hand-code them via WSDL2Apex (not recommended).

Official example: a utility company creates a billing account in an external system
during ordering. Consume the billing HTTP API via External Services or Flow HTTP
Callout (use an Apex proxy only for SOAP), store the returned account number on the
Salesforce account to track state.

4. Remote Process Invocation — Fire and Forget





















Type / TimingProcess / AsynchronousDirectionSalesforce → remoteProblemStart a remote process and pass data without waiting; the remote side acknowledges receipt and hands control straight back.
Forces to ask about: Is guaranteed delivery required? Is the message small? Can
the remote system participate in contract-first integration where Salesforce owns the
contract? Does the endpoint/ESB support long polling (CometD) or gRPC (Pub/Sub)?
Are declarative methods preferred over Apex?
Solution fit























































SolutionFitWhyFlow-driven platform eventsBestDeclarative publish on insert/update. Many subscribers, zero coupling. Platform Event-Triggered Flows let you build the listener declaratively too. See Platform Events & Change Data Capture.Pub/Sub APIBestThe recommended way for external consumers to subscribe (and publish). gRPC + HTTP/2, OAuth/JWT/session auth. See Sub API.Change Data CaptureBestFully declarative, publishes create/update/delete/undelete change events. Right choice when the trigger really is “any record change”.Event RelayBest (AWS)Serverless, low-code streaming of platform events and CDC straight to Amazon EventBridge — no integration app to write, and events can flow back.OmniStudio Integration ProceduresGoodDeclarative server-side orchestration: multiple actions in one server call, transformations, caching. No user interaction.Apex-driven platform eventsGoodSame bus, but published from Apex when you need logic the Flow can’t express.Flow-driven outbound messagingSuboptimalLegacy. SOAP, contract-first, retries until positive ack (a form of guaranteed delivery). New builds must use Flow + platform events.LWC → async Apex calloutSuboptimalCustomisation, and you must code guaranteed delivery.Apex trigger / batch → async calloutSuboptimalWorks, but limits per execution context and no built-in durability.
Sidebars that get challenged

Publishing behaviour — the classic gotcha.





















SettingBehaviourChoose whenPublish After CommitEvent published only if the transaction commitsSubscribers will read records the publishing transaction created/changedPublish ImmediatelyPublished when the publish call runs, ignoring rollbackYou want the event regardless of outcome (e.g. logging, audit, error signalling)

Idempotency / reliable messaging: platform events are published to the bus
once — Salesforce does not retry. It is the subscriber/ESB’s job to request replay
via Replay ID. Messages are retained for 72 hours. Design the subscriber to be
an idempotent receiver (dedupe on a correlation ID).
CDC gap events: when Salesforce cannot generate a change event it sends a gap
event instead (header carries the change type, e.g. GAP_CREATE). Overflow events
signal that more than the allowed number of changes happened in one transaction. A
robust subscriber must handle both — this is a favourite QA question.
Error handling: with events, the subscriber owns error handling — the event is
handed off. Failed flows email the admin (and Flow_Interviews / paused interviews);
events are not retried by the platform on the publish side.
State management: because the process is async, storing the remote key requires a
callback into Salesforce (that callback is the Remote Call-In pattern).
Limits: 100,000 events/hour standard-volume, 250,000/hour high-volume
(usage-based), 1 MB max message size. See governor-limits-and-best-practices.

Official example: telco converts a Close-Won opportunity to an order. Flow publishes
a platform event; the ESB subscribes via Pub/Sub API, forwards to the ERP, then
calls back with OAuth 2.0 + a connected app to write the order number onto the
opportunity. Demonstrates async invocation, end-to-end guaranteed delivery, and a
callback for state.

5. Batch Data Synchronisation





















Type / TimingData / Asynchronous, scheduledDirectionBothProblemImport into and export out of Salesforce in bulk without interfering with end users.
Forces to ask about: Should the data even be stored in Salesforce (if not →
Data Virtualisation)? Event-driven refresh or scheduled? Does it support a primary
business process? Are there reporting requirements that depend on it being local?
Solution fit



























































SolutionFitData masterWhyThird-party ETL (MuleSoft, Informatica) with CDC on the sourceBestRemoteTool detects source changes, transforms, calls Bulk API 2.0. Use REST if volumes are small.Third-party ETL driving off Salesforce timestampsGoodSalesforceQuery by SystemModstamp/status to filter the target set; extract via Bulk API 2.0 or REST.Data 360 actions & activationsBestData 360Sync between orgs after ingestion — especially strong for Marketing Cloud.Data 360 + Data Graphs + Connect APIBestData 360MuleSoft Anypoint extracts via Connect/Data Graph API and moves to another org.Composite Graph APIBestSalesforceUp to 75 graphs per payload, 500 nodes per graph (REST v50+). Great for related multi-object writes. See Composite API.Data Import Wizard / Data LoaderFitEitherFine for stewardship and one-offs; not an integration strategy.Remote call-in as the syncSuboptimalRemoteContinuous chatter, heavy error handling and locking, user-facing performance risk.Remote process invocation as the syncSuboptimalSalesforceSame objection in reverse.
The ETL control-table (watermark) design — say this out loud in a board
The official pattern is explicit, and it is what separates a real answer from “we’ll use
MuleSoft”:

Implement change data capture on the source data set.
Keep control tables in an intermediate database the ETL tool owns.
Each run: read the control table for the last successful run timestamp, use it as
the extract filter, apply validation/enrichment, write to Salesforce, then update
the watermark on success — or write restart values and exit on failure.



                  
                  Salesforce is the spoke, not the hub 
                  
                

Put the control tables somewhere the ETL tool can reach even when Salesforce is
unavailable. The ETL infrastructure is the hub.


Other must-mention practices: chain/sequence jobs; match on primary keys from both
systems (External IDs); extract only changed data; group child records by parent
key before loading to avoid UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW; make post-import triggers process
selectively; and for volume, follow ldv-best-practices and
calculating-data-storage.
Sidebars that get challenged

Timeliness: design to a batch window. Loading during business hours causes
contention — a user update fails, or worse a partial batch fails. For 24/7 global
orgs a window may not exist: use data segmentation (record types, filter criteria)
to avoid contention.
State management: surrogate keys both ways. If you need transactional integrity
across objects, don’t use batch — use Remote Call-In with Apex.
Optimistic locking: Salesforce holds no edit state. It records the read time; on
save it checks whether someone else updated the row and forces the user to re-read.
Middleware must support Bulk API and must persist the last successfully processed
timestamp (watermarking) internally or externally.
Error handling: on read, retry non-infrastructure errors and log/terminate/notify
via control+error tables. On write, use the per-record result set (record ID,
success/failure, error collection) to drive selective retries.

Official example: a mainframe nightly job assigns prospects to reps; an ETL tool
detects the source changes and loads them into Salesforce via the REST API.

6. Remote Call-In





















Type / TimingProcess or Data / Synchronous (always, at transport level)DirectionRemote → SalesforceProblemHow does a remote system connect, authenticate, notify Salesforce of external events, and create/update records?
Forces to ask about: Is this an event notification (EDA — publisher decoupled from
consumer) or CRUD on specific records? One object per transaction or several related
ones? SOAP or REST? Message size? Can the remote system do contract-first (Salesforce
supplies the WSDL)? Is transaction processing required? How much customisation in
Salesforce are you willing to tolerate?
Solution fit




























































SolutionFitWhyComposite APIBestUp to 25 subrequests in one call, referencing each other’s results. Cuts round trips and API consumption.Composite Graph APIBest75 graphs / 500 nodes; each graph succeeds or fails as a unit.REST APIBestPublish events, query (incl. Named Query), CRUD, describe metadata. See REST API.Bulk API 2.0Best for bulkREST-based async insert/upsert/query/delete. Anything > 2,000 records belongs here.GraphQL APIBestSuperior to REST for complex multi-object reads with selective fields. See GraphQL API.Pub/Sub APIBestThe recommended way for external systems to publish onto the event bus (gRPC, OAuth/JWT/session).Platform Events via APIBestPublishing is just POST /services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Event__e/. Decouples the remote caller from Salesforce-side logic.SOAP APISuboptimalOnly when the client can’t do REST, or contract-first is mandated. See SOAP API.Apex web services (webservice / SOAP)SuboptimalChoose only for full transactional support across objects or custom logic on the way in. Each service has its own WSDL — code-first, so the contract only exists after you build it.Apex REST services (@RestResource)SuboptimalSame reasoning without WSDL/stub generation. Composite resources can give you multi-update in one transaction.


                  
                  Why "Best" APIs beat "Suboptimal" custom Apex services 
                  
                

Custom Apex services are ranked lower not because they’re bad, but because they put
transformation, orchestration and error handling inside Salesforce where they cost
maintenance and governor limits. The doc’s line: those concerns belong in
middleware. Only reach for Apex REST/SOAP services when you need multi-object
transactional atomicity or custom pre/post logic the standard APIs can’t express.


Sidebars that get challenged

Data volumes: SOAP/REST create/update/delete handle 200 records per call
(call repeatedly for more). > 2,000 records → Bulk API 2.0. Queries return up to
2,000 rows before queryMore.
Governor limits: API request caps are per 24 hours, by edition × licence count
(e.g. Unlimited Edition allows 5,000 requests per Platform licence per 24h). Platform
events: 100k/hr standard, 250k/hr high-volume, 1 MB max message.
Timeliness: session timeout per org setting; SOQL query timeout is 120 seconds.
Security: the platform enforces the logged-in (integration) user’s profile,
sharing and permission sets — so design that user deliberately, with API-only
access. Add profile IP restrictions. TLS 1.2+ with ≥128-bit ciphers. Establish an
OAuth trust, and cache and reuse the access token rather than re-authenticating
per call. See oauth-saml-flows-and-iam and data-security.
Idempotency: the remote system (or middleware) must manage duplicate calls on
timeout/retry — otherwise you get duplicate inserts and duplicate downstream automation.
Reliable messaging: REST/SOAP are synchronous with no WS-ReliableMessaging. The
remote system must implement retry. With platform events, subscribers can use
Replay ID within the 72-hour window.
Complex scenarios: aggregation, orchestration, transformation cannot be done by
SOAP/REST API — middleware, preferably.

Official example: an on-premises Printer Management System pushes ink/paper levels.
Salesforce defines a platform event; the PMS authenticates (OAuth web-server or
bearer) and publishes the event via SOAP/REST API; a Flow subscriber updates the
asset and creates an order. Platform events were chosen because the number of
subscribers is variable and non-finite — for simple updates to a known set of
records, plain SOAP/REST would do.

7. UI Update Based on Data Changes





















Type / TimingData / Asynchronous (near real time)DirectionSalesforce → Salesforce UIProblemNotify the user in the Salesforce UI without a refresh and without losing their work.
Forces to ask about: Does the data need to be stored in Salesforce? Can a custom UI
layer be built? Will the user have access to invoke it?
Solution
Platform events are the recommended solution — structured payload independent of any
object, durable topic with a 72-hour replay window so a consumer that comes online
late still gets the message. Moving parts:

an Apex trigger or Flow that publishes the event,
the topic/channel,
Pub/Sub API (gRPC + HTTP/2) for efficient consumption by external clients,
a Lightning web component subscribing via lightning/empApi,
a JavaScript library as a static resource (for CometD-era implementations).

Limits you must volunteer





















BenefitUnsupported requirementNo custom polling mechanism neededDelivery is not guaranteedNo user-initiated refresh loopOrder is not guaranteedBulk API record changes do not generate notifications


                  
                  The Bulk API blind spot 
                  
                

If the upstream process loads data with Bulk API, the UI will not light up. This
single line has sunk otherwise-good board answers where a nightly bulk load was
expected to drive a live agent console.


Official example: telco managers want to know when a rep closes a case successfully.
Apex trigger publishes an event on Status = Closed + Resolution = Successful; a
custom UI subscribes (Pub/Sub API / empApi) and shows alerts filtered to that manager’s
reps.

8. Data Virtualisation





















Type / TimingVirtual / SynchronousDirectionRemote → Salesforce, on demandProblemView, search and modify external data without moving it into Salesforce.
Forces to ask about: Do you want declarative/point-and-click or a UI mashup? Is the
data set too large to copy? Do you only need small amounts at a time? Is real-time
accuracy required? Are there data residency constraints?
Solution fit






























SolutionFitWhySalesforce Connect (external objects)BestMaps external tables to external objects (__x). Adapters: OData 2.0/4.0, cross-org, custom Apex (Apex Connector Framework). No storage consumed, no sync. See Salesforce Connect & External Objects.Data 360 + Zero CopyBestSync via connectors/APIs/MuleSoft, or reference data with zero copy, then use the OOTB integrations from Data 360.Data 360 + Data Cloud OneBestHarmonise via the Customer 360 Data Model, identity resolution and data federation into one customer view.Request & Reply (custom page/button → Apex callout, or a mashup/Canvas app)SuboptimalWorks for narrow read-only views; you own the UI, error handling and caching. Justify it on cost when Salesforce Connect can’t be licensed.
External object relationships — memorise this table





























RelationshipAllowed childAllowed parentMatched onLookupStandard, Custom, ExternalStandard, Custom18-character Salesforce record IDExternal lookupStandard, Custom, ExternalExternalThe External ID standard fieldIndirect lookupExternal onlyStandard, CustomA custom field marked External ID and Unique
Sidebars that get challenged

No record-level sharing on external objects. Access to the object means access to
every row. If row-level security is a requirement, Data Virtualisation via external
objects is out — say so before the examiner does.
Timeliness: configurable 120-second max wait for the external system. Users are
waiting, so this pattern is small-volume real-time only — never batch payloads.
Rate limits: OData adapters have hourly callout caps. If you hit them, enable
High Data Volume on the external data source to bypass most rate limits (accepting
its own behaviours/limitations). Reports over external objects are the usual culprit.
Paging: choose server-driven or client-driven paging via the Server Driven
Pagination field on the external data source.
CSRF: OData 2.0/4.0 external data sources have specific CSRF behaviours to review.
Validation: the Salesforce Connect Validator is a free tool for shaking out
common query failures.
Compatibility: external objects behave like custom objects but a long list of
features doesn’t apply (and report performance suffers) — cite the considerations docs.

Official example: manufacturer’s service agents need live ERP order data. Configure
an OData external data source (directly or through middleware — Boomi, Informatica,
Jitterbit, MuleSoft and Progress all ship adapters), sync tables to external objects, and
Salesforce Connect makes the real-time callout when the page loads.

9. Cross-pattern decision cheatsheet




























































If the requirement says…PatternFirst-choice mechanism”must show the result to the user immediately”Request & ReplyExternal Services / Flow HTTP Callout / Apex + Continuation”notify the downstream system when X happens”Fire & ForgetFlow → platform event; Pub/Sub API subscriber”any change to the record must flow out”Fire & ForgetCDC (declarative, no payload design)“stream events to AWS”Fire & ForgetEvent Relay → EventBridge”nightly / weekly load of millions of rows”Batch Data SyncETL + Bulk API 2.0 + watermark control tables”ERP pushes order status into Salesforce”Remote Call-InREST/Composite API, or publish a platform event”external system needs 25 related writes atomically”Remote Call-InComposite Graph API (or Apex REST for true cross-object transactions)“agent’s screen must update live”UI UpdatePlatform event + LWC empApi”don’t copy the data — show it live”Data VirtualisationSalesforce Connect (OData / cross-org / Apex adapter)“unified profile across many sources”VirtualData 360 (+ Zero Copy / Data Cloud One)


                  
                  Board discipline 
                  
                

Name the pattern, name the mechanism, then immediately give volume, timing,
authentication, error handling and idempotency. Every pattern above has an
error-handling and an idempotency sidebar for a reason — those are the two topics QA
reliably returns to.

CTA-Notes/Integration/10-rest-api.title: REST API
CTA-Notes/Integration/10-rest-api.content:
(REST API Developer Guide)
Overview

Stateless, resource-based API using standard HTTP methods
Supports JSON and XML (JSON default)
Authentication: OAuth 2.0 Bearer token in Authorization header
Base URL: https://<instance>.salesforce.com/services/data/vXX.X/


Core Operations
(REST API Resources)
Query
GET /services/data/vXX.X/query?q=SELECT+Id,Name+FROM+Account
Authorization: Bearer <token>


Returns up to 2,000 records per page
If done: false, use nextRecordsUrl to fetch subsequent pages (Query More)
Cursor expires after 10 minutes of inactivity — not suitable for very large result sets (use Bulk API 2.0 instead)

Insert
POST /services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Account/
Content-Type: application/json
{ "Name": "Acme" }


Returns id and success in response body
Use Sforce-Auto-Assign: FALSE header to suppress assignment rules if needed

Update
PATCH /services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Account/<Id>
{ "Name": "Acme Updated" }


Returns HTTP 204 No Content on success

Upsert (External ID)
PATCH /services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Account/<ExternalIdField__c>/<value>


Creates if not found, updates if found
Field must be marked as External ID

Delete
DELETE /services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Account/<Id>


Moves to recycle bin (use Bulk API hardDelete for permanent deletion)


Query Pagination
(SOQL Query Results)
{
  "totalSize": 5000,
  "done": false,
  "nextRecordsUrl": "/services/data/vXX.X/query/01gxx000000..."
}

Follow nextRecordsUrl with GET until done: true
Cursor is server-side; valid for 10 minutes
For > 50k records or offline processing, use Bulk API 2.0 Query instead


Useful Endpoints





































EndpointPurpose/sobjects/List all objects and metadata/sobjects/<Object>/describeField/relationship metadata for an object/limits/Current org API limit usage/query/SOQL query/queryAll/SOQL including soft-deleted records/search/SOSL search/composite/Batch multiple requests (see Composite API)

Authentication Flows

























FlowUse caseOAuth 2.0 Web Server (Authorization Code)User-context web appsOAuth 2.0 JWT BearerServer-to-server; no user interactionOAuth 2.0 Client CredentialsMachine-to-machine; no user contextOAuth 2.0 Username-PasswordLegacy; avoid in new designs


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Username-Password flow sends credentials directly and does not support MFA enforcement. Do not use for new integrations.



Key Limits

























LimitValueRecords per query page2,000Apex synchronous callout timeout120 secondsDaily API request limitOrg edition + user-basedMax response size50 MB

CTA-Notes/Integration/11-composite-api.title: Composite API
CTA-Notes/Integration/11-composite-api.content:
(Composite API Developer Guide)
Why Composite?
Reduces round-trips between client and Salesforce by bundling multiple REST operations into a single HTTP request. Critical for mobile apps and integrations where latency or API call limits are a concern.

Four Resources Compared





















































ResourceMax records/requestsDependenciesallOrNoneFormatBest forComposite25 subrequestsYes — reference outputsConfigurableJSONOrdered, dependent operationsComposite Batch25 subrequestsNoNo (partial success)JSON, XMLIndependent parallel operationssObject Collections200 recordsNoConfigurableJSONBulk CRUD on one or many object typessObject Tree200 records total, 5 levels deepParent-child onlyYesJSON, XMLInserting a record hierarchyComposite Graph500 recordsYes — reference outputsAlways trueJSONComplex, multi-object graphs

Composite Resource
(Composite Resource)

POST /services/data/vXX.X/composite
Executes up to 25 subrequests in order
Output of one subrequest can be referenced as input to a later one using @{referenceId.field}
Single call counts as 1 against API limits
allOrNone: true rolls back all on any failure

{
  "allOrNone": true,
  "compositeRequest": [
    {
      "method": "POST",
      "url": "/services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Account/",
      "referenceId": "NewAccount",
      "body": { "Name": "Acme" }
    },
    {
      "method": "POST",
      "url": "/services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/Contact/",
      "referenceId": "NewContact",
      "body": {
        "LastName": "Smith",
        "AccountId": "@{NewAccount.id}"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Composite Batch
(Composite Batch)

POST /services/data/vXX.X/composite/batch
Up to 25 subrequests, executed serially but independently
Each subrequest counts against API rate limits individually
Partial success allowed — check hasErrors in response
Supports JSON and XML
Use when subrequests are independent and partial success is acceptable


sObject Collections
(sObject Collections)

GET | POST | PATCH | DELETE /services/data/vXX.X/composite/sobjects
Up to 200 records per request
Records can be of different object types (on POST/PATCH)
On GET/DELETE, all records must be the same object type
allOrNone configurable
Upsert: PATCH /composite/sobjects/<ExternalIdField__c> — up to 200 records



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

sObject Collections is the right tool for bulk DML from an integration (e.g. syncing 200 records at a time). More efficient than 200 individual REST calls.



sObject Tree
(sObject Tree)

POST /services/data/vXX.X/composite/tree/<SObjectName>
Inserts a tree of parent-child records in a single call
Up to 200 records total across all trees; up to 5 levels deep
Insert only — no upsert or update
allOrNone is always true
Ideal for creating an Account + related Contacts + Opportunities in one shot


Composite Graph
(Composite Graph)

POST /services/data/vXX.X/composite/graph
Most powerful composite resource — handles complex, multi-object dependency graphs
Up to 500 records across multiple graphs in one request
Supports cross-object references (not just parent-child)
allOrNone is always true — all or nothing
Useful for complex data setup where many records depend on each other


Limits and Gotchas

Not all composite resources support all CRUD operations — check docs per resource
Inbound API call limit applies differently: Composite counts as 1; Batch counts per subrequest
Duplicate reference ID in the same transaction causes an error
Same external ID on the same object type cannot appear twice in one Composite transaction
referenceId is not returned in Composite Batch or sObject Collections responses — only in Composite and Graph


Decision Guide





























ScenarioUseCreate Account then related Contact using new Account IdComposite (ordered, dependent)Update 200 records from external syncsObject CollectionsInsert Account + 5 Contacts + 3 Opps in one shotsObject Tree10 independent reads/updates in one round-tripComposite BatchComplex multi-object insert with cross-referencesComposite Graph

Related Notes

REST API — core REST API operations and pagination
Integration Overview — sync vs async and pattern selection

CTA-Notes/Integration/13-soap-api.title: SOAP API
CTA-Notes/Integration/13-soap-api.content:
(SOAP API Developer Guide)
What It Is

XML-based web services API — the original Salesforce integration API (predates REST)
Strongly typed via WSDL; most enterprise ESBs and ERP systems (SAP, Oracle) integrate via SOAP
Still fully supported and widely used in enterprise integrations


Two WSDLs

















WSDLUse caseEnterprise WSDLStrongly typed to your specific org’s schema; generated per org; must regenerate after metadata changesPartner WSDLGeneric, org-agnostic; works across any org; used by ISVs and middleware


                  
                  CTA positioning 
                  
                

Use Partner WSDL for ISV apps and middleware (MuleSoft, Informatica) — it doesn’t break when org schema changes. Use Enterprise WSDL when you control both ends of the integration and want compile-time type safety.



Core Operations






































































OperationEquivalent RESTPurposequery()GET /querySOQL query; returns 2000 records + queryLocatorqueryMore()follow nextRecordsUrlPage through large result setsqueryAll()GET /queryAllInclude soft-deleted recordscreate()POST /sobjectsInsert recordsupdate()PATCH /sobjectsUpdate by Idupsert()PATCH /sobjects/<ExtId>Insert or update by external IDdelete()DELETE /sobjectsMove to recycle binmerge()N/A in RESTMerge duplicate records (3 at a time)convertLead()N/A in RESTConvert a Lead to Account/Contact/OpportunitygetUpdated()N/A directlyGet IDs of records modified in a time rangegetDeleted()N/A directlyGet IDs of records deleted in a time rangedescribeSObject()GET /sobjects/<obj>/describeObject metadata


                  
                  Note
                  
                

merge(), convertLead(), getUpdated(), and getDeleted() are SOAP-only — no direct REST equivalent. These come up in legacy integration scenarios.



SOAP vs REST


















































SOAP APIREST APIFormatXMLJSON (default) or XMLProtocolSOAP over HTTPHTTPTypingStrongly typed via WSDLLoosely typedToolingGenerate client from WSDLGeneric HTTP clientsEnterprise ESB supportNativeRequires adaptermerge() / convertLead()YesNoLearning curveHigherLowerNew integrationsAvoid unless forcedPreferred

Authentication

Username-Password SOAP login: login() call returns sessionId and serverUrl
OAuth 2.0 Bearer token also accepted in SOAP header (preferred over username-password)
Session expires after inactivity timeout (org-configurable)


When SOAP API Still Makes Sense

External system only speaks SOAP (legacy ERP, mainframe middleware)
merge() or convertLead() operations required without custom Apex
Enterprise WSDL needed for strongly typed client generation in Java/.NET
Existing integration using SOAP with no migration budget



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

For all new integrations, use REST API. Only recommend SOAP when the external system mandates it or one of the SOAP-only operations is required.



Key Limits





















LimitValueRecords per query() call2,000 + queryLocatorRecords per create()/update() batch200Concurrent API requestsOrg edition dependent

Related Notes

REST API — REST API (preferred for new work)
Integration Overview — sync/async framework
Integration Patterns — Remote Call-In and RPI patterns

CTA-Notes/Integration/14-uiapi.title: UI API
CTA-Notes/Integration/14-uiapi.content:
(UI API Developer Guide)
What It Is

REST API that exposes Salesforce data and metadata together in a single response
Returns not just field values but also labels, picklist options, page layout sections, actions, and object metadata
Powers the Salesforce mobile app and Lightning web components (@wire service uses it under the hood)
Respects user permissions, field-level security, and record type configuration automatically



                  
                  Note
                  
                

UI API is the right choice when you are building a custom UI that should behave like the Salesforce native app — respecting metadata, layout, picklists, and FLS — without having to make separate describe calls.



Why UI API





























NeedUI API advantageBuild a custom mobile appReturns layout + data + picklists in one callRespect field-level securityFLS enforced automatically in the responseDisplay picklist valuesReturns dependent picklist options per record typeShow actions (Quick Actions, buttons)Returns available actions for the record and layoutNo separate describe callsMetadata and data are bundled

Core Resources
(Record Resource)
Get Record
GET /ui-api/records/<recordId>
GET /ui-api/records/<recordId>?fields=Account.Name,Account.Phone
GET /ui-api/records/<recordId>?layoutTypes=Full&modes=View

Returns field values + field metadata (label, data type, editable, required).
Get Record UI
GET /ui-api/record-ui/<recordId>

Returns record data, layout sections, object metadata, and actions in a single response. Used to render a full record page in a custom UI.
Create / Update Record
POST /ui-api/records
PATCH /ui-api/records/<recordId>

Accepts and returns the same rich metadata format; enforces FLS and required field validation.
Get Object Info
GET /ui-api/object-info/<objectApiName>

Returns field metadata, record types, child relationships, and supported actions for the object.
Get Picklist Values
GET /ui-api/object-info/<objectApiName>/picklist-values/<recordTypeId>/<fieldApiName>

Returns dependent picklist options for a given record type.
Get Actions
GET /ui-api/actions/record/<recordId>

Returns available actions (Quick Actions, standard buttons, custom buttons) for a record.

UI API vs REST API



































REST APIUI APIResponse contentData onlyData + metadata (labels, layout, picklists, actions)FLS enforcementManual — you query what you requestAutomaticDescribe calls needed?Often yesNo — bundled in responseBest forServer-to-server integrationsCustom mobile apps, custom UIsLWC wire serviceNoYes (getRecord, getObjectInfo, etc.)

LWC Wire Adapters (UI API under the hood)
Common @wire adapters that call UI API:

























AdapterUI API endpointgetRecord/ui-api/records/<id>getObjectInfo/ui-api/object-info/<object>getPicklistValues/ui-api/object-info/.../picklist-values/...getRelatedListRecords/ui-api/related-list-records/...

When to Use UI API

Building a custom mobile app (iOS/Android) that mirrors Salesforce UX
Building a custom Lightning component that needs layout-aware rendering
Need to display picklists, actions, or layouts without hardcoding metadata
Replacing a screen scraping or metadata-describe-heavy integration



                  
                  CTA positioning 
                  
                

In scenarios involving custom mobile apps or partner-facing portals, UI API is the correct answer when the requirement mentions “respecting Salesforce configuration” or “no hardcoded field lists”.



Key Limits

















LimitValueRecords per batch get800API request limitsShared with REST API daily limit

Related Notes

REST API — REST API for non-UI data access
GraphQL API — alternative for flexible, relationship-traversal queries
Integration Overview — integration overview

CTA-Notes/Integration/15-metadata-api.title: Metadata API
CTA-Notes/Integration/15-metadata-api.content:
(Metadata API Developer Guide)
What It Is

SOAP-based API for deploying and retrieving org metadata (configuration and code)
The backbone of all CI/CD tooling: Salesforce CLI (sf deploy), ANT Migration Tool, IDEs, and change sets all use it under the hood
Operates on metadata types (CustomObject, ApexClass, Flow, Profile, PermissionSet, etc.)


Two Deployment Formats
File-Based (ZIP) Deployment
(File-Based Metadata)

Package components into a ZIP with package.xml manifest
Call deploy() → poll checkDeployStatus() until complete
Use for: CI/CD pipelines, full org deployments, change sets equivalent
package.xml defines exactly what is included

CRUD-Based

Direct create/read/update/delete of individual metadata types via API calls
Less common; useful for programmatic metadata manipulation (e.g. creating a custom field via Apex)


Key Operations

































OperationPurposedeploy()Deploy a ZIP package to target orgcheckDeployStatus()Poll async deployment for resultretrieve()Extract metadata from an org into a ZIPcheckRetrieveStatus()Poll async retrievelistMetadata()List all components of a given metadata typedescribeMetadata()List all supported metadata types


                  
                  Note
                  
                

All deployments are asynchronous — deploy() returns a job ID; you must poll checkDeployStatus().



Metadata API vs Tooling API vs Source Deploy









































Metadata APITooling APISF CLI Source DeployProtocolSOAPRESTCLI wrapper over Metadata APIFormatZIP + package.xmlJSONSource format (unpacked)Use caseFull deployments, CI/CDCode coverage, dynamic metadata, IDEDeveloper workflow, scratch orgsAsyncYesMostly syncYesSupports all metadata typesYesSubsetYes

Deployment Options and Their Tools



































ToolUnder the hoodWhen to useSalesforce CLI sf deploy metadataMetadata APICI/CD pipelinesChange SetsMetadata APIAdmin-friendly; no CLIWorkbenchMetadata APIManual deployments, debugANT Migration Tool (legacy)Metadata APIOlder pipelines; still worksVS Code / SFDXMetadata APIDeveloper daily workflow

Deployment Flags Worth Knowing

































FlagEffectrunAllTestsRun all tests in target org on deployrunSpecifiedTestsRun named test classes onlycheckOnlyValidate without committing (dry run)ignoreWarningsWarnings don’t fail the deploymentallowMissingFilesDon’t fail if a file is missing from packagerollbackOnErrorDefault true — entire deployment rolls back on failure


                  
                  CTA DevOps angle 
                  
                

checkOnly + CI gate on every PR is the recommended pattern for validating metadata changes before merge. Pair with runSpecifiedTests for speed, runAllTests for release validation.



Package.xml Structure
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<Package xmlns="soap.sforce.com/2006/04/metadata">
  <types>
    <members>MyClass</members>
    <name>ApexClass</name>
  </types>
  <types>
    <members>*</members>
    <name>CustomObject</name>
  </types>
  <version>59.0</version>
</Package>

* wildcard retrieves all components of that type
Wildcard not supported for all types (e.g. Profiles require explicit names)


Key Limits

























LimitValueMax ZIP file size (deploy)39 MB (compressed) / 400 MB (uncompressed)Max components per deployment10,000Deployment timeout0–240 minutes (configurable)Concurrent deployments1 active deploy per org (others queue)

Related Notes

CTA-Notes/Integration/16-tooling-api.title: Tooling API
CTA-Notes/Integration/16-tooling-api.content:
(Tooling API Developer Guide)
What It Is

REST and SOAP API for building developer tooling — IDEs, CI inspection, dynamic code management
Provides fine-grained access to Apex, Visualforce, and metadata at the component level
Powers VS Code Salesforce Extension, Developer Console, and code coverage queries
Not intended for production data access or large-scale deployments (use Metadata API for that)


Key Use Cases









































Use caseTooling API resourceQuery Apex code coverageApexCodeCoverageAggregate, ApexCodeCoverageExecute anonymous ApexexecuteAnonymousRun specific test classesRunTestsRequestQuery deployment statusDeployRequestInspect Apex class metadataApexClass, ApexTriggerAccess Flow metadataFlowDefinition, FlowVersionViewCreate/modify custom fields dynamicallyCustomField (CRUD-based)Symbol table / code structureSymbolTable on ApexClass

Tooling API vs Metadata API








































Tooling APIMetadata APIProtocolREST (primary) + SOAPSOAPGranularityIndividual componentsPackage-level (ZIP)Code coverage queriesYesNoExecute Anonymous ApexYesNoFull org deploymentNoYesBest forIDE features, CI inspection, coverage reportingCI/CD deployments

Common Queries
Code Coverage (Aggregate by Class)
GET /services/data/vXX.X/tooling/query
  ?q=SELECT+ApexClassOrTriggerId,ApexClassOrTrigger.Name,
     NumLinesCovered,NumLinesUncovered
     FROM+ApexCodeCoverageAggregate

Execute Anonymous Apex
GET /services/data/vXX.X/tooling/executeAnonymous
  ?anonymousBody=System.debug('hello');

  ?q=SELECT+Id,Name,Status,ApiVersion+FROM+ApexClass

Query Flow Versions
GET /services/data/vXX.X/tooling/query
  ?q=SELECT+Id,MasterLabel,VersionNumber,Status+FROM+Flow


Authentication

Same OAuth 2.0 Bearer token as REST API
Base URL: /services/data/vXX.X/tooling/


CTA Relevance
Tooling API comes up in DevOps and governance discussions:

Code coverage reporting in CI pipelines — query ApexCodeCoverageAggregate after test runs
Dynamic metadata management — create fields or update picklist values programmatically (rare but asked)
IDE integration architecture — knowing that VS Code uses Tooling API explains why it can show inline coverage



                  
                  CTA framing 
                  
                

You won’t be asked to implement Tooling API calls, but knowing it exists and what it’s for distinguishes a thorough answer on DevOps pipeline architecture.



Related Notes

Metadata API — deployment and retrieve operations
Integration Overview — integration overview

CTA-Notes/Integration/20-platform-event.title: Platform Events & Change Data Capture
CTA-Notes/Integration/20-platform-event.content:
Platform Events
(Platform Events Developer Guide)
What They Are

Custom event messages published and consumed on the Salesforce event bus
Decouples publishers and subscribers — neither knows about the other
At-least-once delivery with durable storage (replay from any point in the last 3 days)
__e suffix on the API name

Event Types




















TypeVolume limitUse caseStandard Platform EventsLower throughputBusiness process events (e.g. Order Placed, Case Escalated)High Volume Platform Events250k/hour (expandable)High-throughput integrations, IoT, telemetry


                  
                  Note
                  
                

For CTA, always specify High Volume Platform Events when volume is a concern. Standard PE are rarely the right choice for integration scenarios.


Publishing
(Publishing Platform Events from Apex)

Apex: EventBus.publish(new MyEvent__e(...)) — publishes after transaction commits
Flow: Publish Platform Event action — same commit-time behaviour
REST API: POST /services/data/vXX.X/sobjects/MyEvent__e/
Bulk API 2.0: Supported for high-volume publishing

Subscribing

Apex Trigger (on platform event object) — runs asynchronously; has its own governor limits
Flow: Platform Event–Triggered Flow
CometD / EMP Connector — external subscriber via long polling
Pub/Sub API — gRPC-based; preferred for high-throughput external subscribers (see Sub API)

Replay and Durability

Events stored for 3 days on the event bus
Subscribers can replay from a specific replayId or from -2 (all retained) / -1 (new only)
If a subscriber is down, it can catch up on missed events within the 3-day window

Parallel Subscriptions

Multiple subscribers (triggers, flows, external) can all subscribe to the same event simultaneously
Each subscriber processes events independently — no ordering guarantee across subscribers


Change Data Capture (CDC)
(Change Data Capture Developer Guide)
What It Is

Automatically published events when Salesforce records are created, updated, deleted, or undeleted
No custom payload — event body reflects the changed fields only
ChangeEventHeader contains: changeType, changedFields, recordIds, entityName

Supported Objects
(CDC Supported Objects)

Most standard objects (Account, Contact, Opportunity, Case, etc.) and all custom objects
Must be enabled per object in Setup → Change Data Capture

CDC vs Platform Events








































CDCPlatform EventsTriggerAny record saveExplicit publish callPayloadChanged fields only; automaticCustom fields; designer-definedDirectionOutbound onlyBoth (publish + subscribe)Use caseSync external system with Salesforce data changesCustom business events, RPI async patternReplay3 days3 daysCustom logic requiredNo (automatic)Yes (must publish explicitly)


                  
                  CTA decision point 
                  
                

Use CDC when an external system needs to mirror Salesforce record changes without custom code. Use Platform Events when the integration event is business-logic-driven or requires a custom payload.


CDC vs Batch on SystemModstamp



































CDCBatch on SystemModstampLatencyNear-real-time (seconds)Scheduled (minutes/hours)Missed changesReplay buffer (3 days)Depends on poll frequencyDeleted recordsYes (changeType = DELETE)No (deleted records not queryable)Implementation complexitySubscriber setup requiredSimple SOQL + Bulk APIBest forReal-time sync, event-driven architecturePeriodic ETL, simpler integrations

Key Limits





























LimitValueStandard PE publishes per hourOrg edition dependentHigh Volume PE publishes per hour250,000 (expandable)Event retention (replay window)3 daysMax subscribers per channelVaries; check limits docsApex trigger max retries on failure3 (then goes to dead letter queue)

Related Notes

Sub API — gRPC-based high-throughput subscriber for PE and CDC
Integration Overview — sync vs async framework
Integration Patterns — RPI async, UI Update Based on Data Changes patterns

CTA-Notes/Integration/21-pubsub-api.title: Pub/Sub API
CTA-Notes/Integration/21-pubsub-api.content:
(Pub/Sub API Developer Guide) (Pub/Sub API Overview)
What It Is

gRPC-based API for publishing and subscribing to Salesforce event bus channels at high throughput
Replaces the CometD / EMP Connector approach for external subscribers
Works with Platform Events (standard and high-volume) and Change Data Capture events
Uses Apache Avro binary format for event payloads — more efficient than JSON over CometD


Why Pub/Sub API over CometD








































CometD / EMP ConnectorPub/Sub APIProtocolHTTP long-pollinggRPC (HTTP/2)Payload formatJSONApache Avro (binary)ThroughputLower; polling overheadHigh-throughput streamingBidirectional streamingNoYesPreferred for new workNo (legacy)YesmTLS supportNoNo (OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer)

Core Concepts
Channels

Each event type has a channel: /event/MyEvent__e for Platform Events, /data/ChangeEvents for all CDC, /data/AccountChangeEvent for a specific object’s CDC
Subscribe to a channel to receive all events published to it

Subscribe Flow

Authenticate with OAuth 2.0 (JWT Bearer recommended for server-to-server)
Call GetTopic to get the schema ID for the channel
Call GetSchema to retrieve the Avro schema
Call Subscribe (server-streaming RPC) — send FetchRequest to request events
Receive ConsumerEvent messages; decode with Avro schema
Manage replayId — persist it to resume from the correct position after reconnect

Publish Flow

Authenticate
Call GetTopic to get schema ID
Call Publish (unary RPC) — send Avro-encoded events


Replay

Same 3-day replay window as CometD
On Subscribe, set replay_preset:

LATEST — only new events
EARLIEST — all retained events (up to 3 days)
CUSTOM — resume from a specific replayId


Always persist the last processed replayId — if your subscriber crashes without persisting, you will miss events



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Pub/Sub API does not guarantee exactly-once delivery. Design your subscriber to be idempotent — processing the same event twice should produce the same result.



Authentication

OAuth 2.0 JWT Bearer — recommended for server-to-server (no user interaction)
OAuth 2.0 Username-Password — supported but avoid in production (no MFA enforcement)
mTLS is not supported for Pub/Sub API — if mTLS is a requirement, use REST API with Named Credentials instead


When to Use Pub/Sub API

External system needs to consume Platform Events or CDC at high throughput
Replacing a legacy CometD subscriber
Building a real-time data pipeline (e.g. Salesforce → Kafka → Data Warehouse)
Bidirectional streaming is required



                  
                  CTA positioning 
                  
                

Position Pub/Sub API as the preferred mechanism for external systems consuming Salesforce events. For internal Salesforce-to-Salesforce or Flow-based consumption, use Apex triggers or Flow subscriptions instead.



Key Limits

























LimitValueEvent retention (replay)3 daysMax events per Subscribe request batch100Concurrent subscriptions per orgCheck limits docsHigh Volume PE publish rate250,000/hour (expandable)

Related Notes

Platform Events & Change Data Capture — Platform Events and CDC fundamentals
Integration Overview — integration framework overview
Integration Patterns — event-driven patterns

CTA-Notes/Integration/22-streaming-api.title: Streaming API (PushTopic)
CTA-Notes/Integration/22-streaming-api.content:
(Streaming API Developer Guide)
What It Is

Server-push mechanism based on CometD (Bayeux protocol over HTTP long-polling)
Delivers near-real-time notifications to subscribed clients when Salesforce data changes
Legacy — largely superseded by Platform Events and Change Data Capture for new work


PushTopic

A SOQL query registered as a PushTopic object defines what changes trigger notifications
When a record matching the SOQL query is created/updated/deleted, a notification is pushed to subscribers
Subscribers connect via CometD and listen on /topic/<PushTopicName>

PushTopic pt = new PushTopic();
pt.Name = 'AccountUpdates';
pt.Query = 'SELECT Id, Name, Phone FROM Account';
pt.ApiVersion = 59.0;
pt.NotifyForOperationCreate = true;
pt.NotifyForOperationUpdate = true;
pt.NotifyForFields = 'Referenced';
insert pt;

Streaming API vs Platform Events vs CDC















































Streaming API (PushTopic)Platform EventsChange Data CaptureData sourceRecord changes (SOQL-defined)Custom published eventsAny record changeCustom payloadNo — fixed SOQL fieldsYesNo — changed fields onlyDurability / replayNo replay; events lost if disconnected3-day replay3-day replayProtocolCometD (long-polling)CometD or Pub/Sub API (gRPC)CometD or Pub/Sub APIStatusLegacyCurrent — preferredCurrent — preferredMax concurrent clients1,000 per orgHigher (High-Volume PE)Higher


                  
                  Legacy 
                  
                

PushTopic / Streaming API is deprecated for new development. Use Platform Events for custom event notifications and CDC for record-change-driven integrations. Only mention Streaming API in CTA when the scenario involves a legacy system already using it.



Generic Streaming (StreamingChannel)

A variant of Streaming API without a SOQL query — channel-based, arbitrary payload
Used for custom push notifications (e.g. push a message to a specific browser session)
Also legacy; Platform Events are the modern replacement


When It Still Comes Up in CTA

Legacy integrations (pre-PE/CDC) using CometD clients that haven’t been migrated
Customer has existing Streaming API implementation and migration is out of scope
Question about “how did this work before Platform Events?” — know the history


Migration Path

























FromToPushTopic (record changes)Change Data CapturePushTopic (business events)Platform EventsGeneric StreamingPlatform EventsCometD subscriberPub/Sub API (gRPC)

Related Notes

Platform Events & Change Data Capture — Platform Events and CDC (current approach)
Sub API — gRPC-based replacement for CometD
Integration Overview — integration overview

CTA-Notes/Integration/30-external-servic.title: External Services
CTA-Notes/Integration/30-external-servic.content:
(External Services) (External Services Key Concepts)
What It Is

Declarative integration feature — register an external REST API via its OpenAPI (Swagger) spec
Salesforce auto-generates invocable actions from the API spec
Those actions become available in Flow and Einstein Bots without writing any Apex
Enables admins and non-developers to call external APIs from automation



                  
                  CTA framing 
                  
                

External Services is the answer when the requirement says “no custom code” or “admin-maintained integration”. It trades flexibility for declarative simplicity.



How It Works

Obtain the external system’s OpenAPI 2.0 or 3.0 spec (JSON or YAML)
Register it in Setup → External Services → Add an External Service
Salesforce validates the spec and generates typed invocable actions (one per API operation)
Use those actions in Flow Builder as Action elements
Responses are available as Flow variables for subsequent steps


Requirements

External API must have a valid OpenAPI 2.0 or 3.0 specification
API must be accessible from Salesforce (HTTPS; add to Named Credentials)
Authentication handled via Named Credential linked to the External Service registration
Only REST APIs — no SOAP support


External Services vs Apex Callout








































External ServicesApex CalloutWho can build itAdmin (no code)DeveloperAPI spec requiredYes (OpenAPI)NoUsed in FlowYes (native action)Via @InvocableMethodFlexibilityLimited to spec operationsFull controlError handlingBasic (success/failure)Full custom logicBest forSimple, well-documented APIs; admin-drivenComplex transformations, error handling, high volume

Limitations

OpenAPI spec must be well-formed — Salesforce is strict about spec compliance
Complex request/response schemas (deeply nested, polymorphic types) may not import cleanly
No support for streaming or async responses
Not suitable for high-volume or LDV scenarios — each Flow invocation = one API call
External Services actions inherit all Flow governor limits



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Don’t recommend External Services for integrations with complex error handling, retry logic, or high call volumes. Use Apex callout + Named Credentials instead.



When to Use External Services

Admin needs to call a simple external API from a Flow (e.g. address validation, credit check)
The external API has a published OpenAPI spec
No custom transformation logic needed
Part of a “low-code first” architecture strategy


Related Notes

Named Credentials — authentication for External Services registrations
Integration Overview — integration framework
Integration Patterns — RPI Request-Reply (declarative variant)

CTA-Notes/Integration/31-external-servic.title: External Services Guide
CTA-Notes/Integration/31-external-servic.content:
What are External Services
They are a declarative way to integrate with a REST API using OpenAPI standards (no apex involved), but your endpoint must be able to output a schema in JSON format (swagger schema for instance). If your endpoint cannot output a schema in a JSON format and is not a REST endpoint, this will not work.
After setting up an external service you can use them within flows to integrate with external systems declaratively.

How to Setup External Services
You need to do the following:


Makes sure you have an accessible OpenAPI definition (schema file) available for your REST API.


Configure a named credential to authenticate to the REST endpoint resource server.


Register/Create an external service for your REST endpoint.


Setup a flow with an Apex Action that leverages your external service.


Run your flow.


NOTE: If you put this in a record triggered flow or a scheduled action this will not work, as callouts via external services abide by the same limitations as callouts via apex. You can add an async path in your record triggered flow to do the external service call after the transaction has ended however. You can also setup an Apex class with an invocable action that calls an async method, that async method can access your registered external service to simplify its integration still.

When to use External Services
You should use them when you have a simple operation that can be done via a flow, and a REST endpoint that can generate JSON formatted OpenAPI definition file.

CTA-Notes/Integration/32-salesforce-conn.title: Salesforce Connect & External Objects
CTA-Notes/Integration/32-salesforce-conn.content:
(Salesforce Connect) (External Objects)
What It Is

Platform feature that maps external system data to External Objects in Salesforce — without copying the data
Data is fetched in real time from the external system on demand
External Objects appear in the UI like standard/custom objects (related lists, page layouts, SOQL)
Implements the Data Virtualization integration pattern


Adapters






























AdapterProtocolWhen to useOData 4.0OData REST protocolExternal system exposes an OData endpoint (SAP, SharePoint, Azure SQL via gateway)OData 2.0OData REST protocol (legacy)Older OData implementationsCustom Apex AdapterAnyExternal system doesn’t support OData; full control over request/responseCross-orgSalesforce REST APIConnect two Salesforce orgs; data stays in source org
(OData 4.0 Adapter) (Custom Apex Adapter)

External Object Characteristics













































FeatureBehaviourSuffix__x (e.g. Order__x)StorageNo Salesforce storage — data stays in external systemSOQLSupported but limited (no JOINs across external + standard objects in one query)TriggersNot supportedWorkflow / FlowNot supported on the external object itselfSharingNo sharing model — all users with object access see all recordsReportsNot supported nativelySearchSupported (global search) if adapter supports itRelated ListsSupported — external object can appear as a child on a standard object

Relationship Types





















RelationshipDescriptionExternal LookupChild standard/custom object → Parent external object (foreign key on child)Indirect LookupChild external object → Parent standard/custom object (matched via External ID field)Standard LookupExternal object → External object


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Indirect lookup is required when the external system uses its own ID (not Salesforce Id) as the foreign key back to a Salesforce record.



Salesforce Connect vs Data Copy








































Salesforce Connect (External Objects)ETL / Data CopyData locationStays in external systemCopied into SalesforceReal-time accuracyYesDepends on sync frequencySalesforce storage costNoneYesFull Salesforce featuresNo (no triggers, sharing, reports)YesExternal system availabilityRequired at read timeNot required at read timeBest forReal-time read-only access; data too large to copyFull integration; write-back; reporting; offline access

Custom Apex Adapter

Implement DataSource.Provider and DataSource.Connection Apex classes
Override query(), search(), upsertRow(), deleteRows() methods
Full control over how Salesforce translates SOQL/SOSL into external API calls
Supports read and write operations (if implemented)
Required when external system has no OData endpoint


When to Use Salesforce Connect

Data volume is too large to store in Salesforce (classic LDV avoidance)
External system is the system of record and data must not be duplicated
Real-time read access is needed but write-back is not (or minimal)
External system can expose an OData endpoint or tolerate per-record API calls



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Salesforce Connect makes one external API call per record access. For list views or related lists with many records, this can generate significant load on the external system. Always discuss pagination, caching, and rate limits in a CTA scenario.




                  
                  Warning
                  
                

No sharing model on external objects — all authenticated users with object-level access see all records. This is a common CTA gotcha when security requirements involve row-level access control.



Row Limits (Winter ‘26 Update)

Previously, all adapters were capped at 100,000 new rows retrieved or created per hour
No hourly row limit now for: OData 4.01, GraphQL, and SQL adapters for Amazon Athena and Snowflake
Other adapters (OData 2.0/4.0, Custom Apex, etc.) are unchanged
API callout limits are not affected by this change
Available in Lightning Experience and Classic for Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, and Developer editions on Hyperforce; rolling availability began in Spring ‘25
Useful for LDV scenarios — real-time access to large external datasets without row throttling

(Discover What’s New with Data for Winter ‘26)


                  
                  Tip
                  
                

In a CTA LDV scenario, prefer OData 4.01 / GraphQL / Athena / Snowflake adapters when hourly row caps would be a concern. The 100k/hour cap still applies to older adapters.



CTA Decision: Connect vs Copy vs Virtualize





























RequirementRecommendationReal-time accuracy; read-only; data too large to copySalesforce ConnectWrite-back required; full Salesforce features neededETL/copy into SalesforceData must never leave external system (compliance)Salesforce ConnectReporting and analytics on external data in SalesforceETL/copy (Connect doesn’t support reports)Occasional lookups into external systemSalesforce Connect or Apex callout
