CTA-Notes/Integration/40-named-credentia.title: Named Credentials
CTA-Notes/Integration/40-named-credentia.content:
(Named Credentials) (Named Credentials Protocol Settings)
Quick Mental Model





























Object=AnswersCoversNamed CredentialWHERE to callURL / endpoint / callout aliasendpoint URL, callout labelExternal CredentialHOW to authenticateauth protocol, identity type, principals, headers, tokensOAuth flows, Basic, API key, AWS Sig V4, mTLSExternal Auth Identity ProviderWHO issues the OAuth tokenauthorization URL, token URL, client/app settings, custom auth paramsIdP config for OAuth 2.0 flows

What They Are

A secure store for external endpoint URLs and authentication credentials in Salesforce Setup
Apex callouts reference a named credential by label instead of a hardcoded URL + token
Salesforce manages token refresh, credential storage, and merges auth headers automatically
Keeps secrets out of code — no credentials in Apex, no credentials in version control



                  
                  CTA best practice 
                  
                

Any architecture with outbound Apex callouts must use Named Credentials. Hardcoded endpoints and credentials in Apex is an automatic flag in a CTA presentation.



Two Components (New Model — API v53+)
The current model separates credentials from endpoints:
External Credential
Defines the authentication protocol and credentials:

OAuth 2.0 (Client Credentials, JWT Bearer, Web Server flow, etc.)
Basic authentication (username + password)
Custom headers / API keys
AWS Signature V4
Certificate (mTLS)

Named Credential
Defines the endpoint URL and links to an External Credential:

callout:MyNamedCredential/path syntax in Apex
One Named Credential can point to one External Credential
Supports per-user authentication (each user has their own OAuth token) or org-wide


Legacy vs New Model






























Legacy Named CredentialNew Model (API v53+)StructureSingle object (URL + auth combined)External Credential + Named CredentialPer-user authLimitedFirst-class (Principal: Per User)OAuth flows supportedBasic + OAuthAll flows + customReusabilityURL + auth always pairedOne External Credential → multiple Named Credentials

Per-User vs Org-Wide Authentication

















Principal typeUse whenNamed Principal (org-wide)All callouts use the same service account credentialsPer UserEach Salesforce user authenticates independently to the external system (e.g. Google Drive, SharePoint)


                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Use Per User when the external system enforces user-level access control and you need to honour it from Salesforce. Use Named Principal for server-to-server integrations with a service account.



Using in Apex
// Reference named credential — no URL or token in code
HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest();
req.setEndpoint('callout:My_Named_Credential/api/v1/resource');
req.setMethod('GET');
Http http = new Http();
HttpResponse res = http.send(req);

callout: prefix tells Salesforce to resolve the named credential
Path after the credential name is appended to the stored endpoint URL
Auth headers injected automatically by the platform


Remote Site Settings vs Named Credentials






























Remote Site SettingsNamed CredentialsPurposeAllowlist outbound endpointsStore endpoint + credentialsAuth handlingNone — just URL allowlistingFull auth managementRequired for Apex calloutsYes (if not using Named Credentials)Named Credentials bypass Remote Site Settings requirementBest practiceUse Named Credentials insteadYes


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Named Credentials automatically bypass the need for a Remote Site Settings entry. Don’t add both — it’s redundant and signals unfamiliarity with the platform.



mTLS with Named Credentials

Upload client certificate to Salesforce (Setup → Certificate and Key Management)
Create External Credential with protocol: Certificate
Salesforce presents the certificate on outbound callouts automatically
See Integration Overview for inbound mTLS setup


CTA Checklist

 All Apex callouts use Named Credentials (no hardcoded URLs)
 Service account credentials stored as Named Principal
 Per-User auth used when external system enforces user-level access
 mTLS configured via certificate-based External Credential where required
 Remote Site Settings not duplicating Named Credential entries

OAuth 2.0 Flows — OAuth flow types used in External Credentials
REST API — REST API callouts that use Named Credentials

CTA-Notes/Integration/41-oauth-flows.title: OAuth 2.0 Flows
CTA-Notes/Integration/41-oauth-flows.content:
(OAuth Authorization Flows)
Overview
Salesforce supports multiple OAuth 2.0 flows. Choosing the right one depends on: who is authenticating (user vs server), whether a browser is available, and the security requirements.

Flow Comparison



























































FlowUser involvedBrowser requiredBest forWeb Server (Authorization Code)YesYesWeb apps with server backendUser-Agent (Implicit)YesYesClient-side SPA (legacy; avoid)JWT BearerNoNoServer-to-server; service accountsClient CredentialsNoNoMachine-to-machine; no user contextDeviceYesNo (on device)CLI tools; IoT; headless devicesUsername-PasswordYesNoLegacy; development onlySAML BearerNoNoWhen SAML assertion already existsRefresh TokenN/ANoExtend existing session

Web Server Flow (Authorization Code)
(Web Server Flow)
1. App redirects user → Salesforce authorization endpoint
2. User logs in and approves
3. Salesforce returns authorization code to redirect URI
4. App exchanges code for access_token + refresh_token
5. App uses access_token for API calls


Most secure for user-context apps — code never exposed to browser
Supports MFA enforcement
Refresh token allows long-lived sessions without re-login
Use for: Web apps, Experience Cloud integrations, partner apps


JWT Bearer Flow
(JWT Bearer Flow)
1. App creates JWT signed with private key (client cert)
2. POST to token endpoint with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
3. Salesforce validates JWT signature against registered certificate
4. Returns access_token (no refresh token)


No user interaction — fully automated
Certificate-based — private key never leaves the app server
No refresh token — must re-request access token when expired (short-lived: ~1–2 hours)
Use for: Server-to-server integrations, CI/CD pipelines, Named Credentials, Pub/Sub API



                  
                  CTA default for server-to-server 
                  
                

JWT Bearer is the recommended flow for any server-to-server integration. It’s secure (no client secret in URL), supports automation, and is compatible with Named Credentials External Credentials.



Client Credentials Flow
(Client Credentials Flow)
1. App POSTs client_id + client_secret to token endpoint
2. Salesforce returns access_token


No user context — runs as a connected app (or designated user)
Simpler than JWT Bearer but uses a shared secret (less secure than certificate)
Must enable in Connected App settings; assign a “Run As” user
Use for: M2M integrations where certificate management is not feasible



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Client secret must be stored securely (e.g. Named Credentials, secrets manager). Never hardcode in application code.



Device Flow
(Device Flow)
1. Device requests a device_code and user_code from Salesforce
2. User visits a URL on a separate device and enters user_code
3. Device polls Salesforce until user approves
4. Salesforce returns access_token + refresh_token


For devices with no browser or limited input (CLI, IoT, TV apps)
Salesforce CLI uses this flow for sf org login device
Use for: CLI tools, kiosk apps, headless servers where a human needs to authenticate once


Username-Password Flow

App POSTs username + password + security token directly to token endpoint
Returns access_token immediately
Avoid in production:

Bypasses MFA enforcement
Credentials sent in plaintext over HTTPS (no browser redirect)
Salesforce may block if IP restriction policies are active


Acceptable for: Development, Postman testing, sandbox automation where MFA is not enforced


Implicit (User-Agent) Flow

Returns access_token directly in URL fragment after browser redirect
Token exposed in browser history and logs
No refresh token
Deprecated for most uses — use Web Server flow for SPAs instead
Only kept for specific legacy use cases


Connected App Configuration
(Connected App Setup)
Every OAuth integration requires a Connected App:

Define allowed OAuth scopes (api, refresh_token, web, etc.)
Set callback URL for Web Server flow
Upload certificate for JWT Bearer flow
Enable Client Credentials flow (opt-in)
Configure IP relaxation and refresh token policy


Scope Reference









































ScopeAccess grantedapiAccess all APIs (REST, SOAP, Bulk)webWeb-based access; required for Web Server flowrefresh_tokenIssue refresh tokensfullFull access (superset of api + web)openidOpenID Connect identity claimsprofileUser profile datachatter_apiChatter API onlycustom_permissionsAccess custom permissions on the Connected App

CTA Decision Guide

































ScenarioRecommended flowWeb app where users log in with SalesforceWeb Server (Authorization Code)Server-to-server nightly syncJWT BearerMuleSoft → Salesforce with no user contextJWT Bearer or Client CredentialsCLI tool used by an adminDevice flowPostman testing in dev sandboxUsername-Password (dev only)External system already has a SAML assertionSAML Bearer

CTA-Notes/Integration/42-mutual-tls-2way.title: Mutual TLS 2-Way SSL
CTA-Notes/Integration/42-mutual-tls-2way.content:
mTLS in relevance to the CTA Board
I don’t believe this is ever something that you absolutely must call out in your system diagram, however it won’t hurt, and you should be prepared for the potential for a judge to ask you about mTLS possibly, so it’s good to know what it is and when to use it.
What is mTLS?
mTLS is a mechanism that allows both the client application AND the server to verify they both know each other and are supposed to be communicating with each other instead of just the client verifying that they know the server.
Below is a flow of how this works:

This video goes over mTLS in greater detail
When to use mTLS?
mTLS should be suggested/used when you are doing a server to server integration (non-browser based integration) and with IoT device. You’d want to consider setting up mTLS between your ESB (and ETL) and Salesforce to ensure that no malicious actors were trying to impersonate your ESB and call into your SF org to make updates.
It’s important to note that platform events (and CDC) don’t support mutual authentication. This is by design and will not be altered. You can view that here.
If encryption in transit is specifically called out (for both server and client) you should consider suggesting this.
What does mTLS prevent?
mTLS prevents the following (typically):


On-Path attacks that attempt to intercept packets/traffic between systems. Because both systems communication is encrypted due to mTLS, the attacker could not decrypt the information even if they retrieved it.


Spoofing Attacks that try to imitate a client application because the fake application couldn’t fake who it was because it would not be able to verify itself with the sever.


Credential stuffing (trying to use a username and password to auth to the server) won’t work because the attacker couldn’t prove (via a certificate) that it is who it is.


How to enable mTLS in Salesforce
You must send in a help ticket request to enable mTLS in your org. Once you do you can setup mutual authentication in Certificate and Key management within setup. Clients will need to connect to Salesforce on port 8443. It is also suggested to setup IP restrictions in SF for that client app as well.
How to enable mTLS in SF Guide here
How to setup mTLS in SF Guide here

CTA-Notes/Integration/43-networking-basi.title: Networking Basics
CTA-Notes/Integration/43-networking-basi.content:
What is a LAN?
A LAN is a local area network, a network that can talk to each other within a limited range. A good example is your home network (devices in your actual house) or a school.

What is a WAN?
WAN (wide area network) is essentially the internet

What is an IP Address?
It’s a 32bit numeric identifier for a computer or a device on a network (ex: 192.168.1.4). Part of the IP indicate the network the device is on, and part of the ip indicates the host device. Which numbers in the ip are network or host related are determined by the subnet mask. If a subnet mask is 255.255.255.0 and an IP address is 192.168.1.4 then the numbers 192, 168, and 1 indicate the network address, the number 4 indicates the host address of the ip. There is a network portion and a host portion to an IP address so that you can break large networks of computers (say at an office) into smaller networks of computers (subnets) and utilize routers to intelligently communicate between each subnet.

What is a Subnet
Subnets are divisions of your LAN, which are separated by a router on your LAN. It helps manage traffic for large organizations.

What is a Firewall?
Firewalls are a set of rules defined to set communications between your internal network and an external network. It’s a safety barrier between a private network and the public internet.
There are two types of firewalls, software firewalls that protect ONLY the computer the software is on, and a network based firewall which is a combination of hardware and software that sits in front of a router (or within the router for smaller organizations) to prevent malicious connections to machines on your company network.

What is a DMZ?
DMZ’s (Demilitarized Zones) are subnetworks that expose devices to untrusted networks. If you want to expose a specific device/server/resource to the internet, without exposing your entire LAN, you would setup a DMZ and designate that device to be accessible via the DMZ.
Typically when you setup a DMZ you setup 2 firewalls, an external firewall in front of your DMZ and an internal one behind your DMZ.

What is a Forward Proxy Server?
This is a server that retrieves data on the internet on behalf of a user. Proxy servers have several benefits listed below:

It hides your machines IP address because the proxy is making the request to the webpage so the webpage only sees the proxy servers IP address.
Can improve webpage retrieval as the proxy server will cache webpages meaning subsequent requests are very fast.
Proxy servers can also log company employee activity/web page history.
It can block you from visiting certain webpages.

Proxy Servers typically live within the DMZ, in front of the internal LAN firewall and behind the external firewall.

What is a Reverse Proxy Server
This is a server that retrieves data on your LAN for users on the internet. It typically sits in your DMZ and listens for legitimate requests to access data on your servers that likely also reside in your DMZ.
This provides the following security:

It hides your resource servers (the resources people on the internet are requesting info from) IP addresses and only exposes the IP of your reverse proxy. Making DDoS attacks challenging to accomplish.
Reverse proxies can handle load balancing when you have a huge amount of users.
It caches static content so it can quickly return data.

Proxy Servers typically live within the DMZ, in front of the internal LAN firewall and behind the external firewall.

Example Networking Setup


Additional Notes
Great Networking Tutorials can be found here: Power Cert Animated Videos
A great video on reverse proxies can be found here: Byte Byte Go Proxy Servers

CTA-Notes/Integration/50-mulesoft.title: MuleSoft & Middleware Positioning
CTA-Notes/Integration/50-mulesoft.content:
MuleSoft Overview

Salesforce’s integration platform (acquired 2018) — Anypoint Platform
Full-lifecycle API management: design, build, deploy, manage, monitor
Positions as the integration hub between Salesforce and other enterprise systems
Core product: Anypoint Platform — includes API Designer, Exchange, Studio, Runtime Manager


API-Led Connectivity
MuleSoft’s canonical architecture pattern — three tiers of APIs:
System APIs       → Unlock backend systems (SAP, ERP, DB, legacy)
Process APIs      → Orchestrate and transform data across systems
Experience APIs   → Tailored for each consumer (mobile, Salesforce, portal)


























LayerPurposeExampleSystem APIThin wrapper around a backend systemSAP Orders API, Salesforce Accounts APIProcess APIBusiness logic, orchestration, transformationOrder fulfilment API (SAP + Salesforce + WMS)Experience APIConsumer-specific interfaceMobile app API, Salesforce integration API


                  
                  CTA framing 
                  
                

When a scenario has 3+ systems with complex data transformation or orchestration needs, API-led connectivity is the model to propose. It avoids point-to-point integrations that become unmaintainable at scale.



When to Use MuleSoft (vs Direct Integration)





































Use MuleSoftUse Direct Integration3+ systems to connect2 systems, simple contractProtocol conversion needed (SOAP ↔ REST, FTP ↔ API)Both systems speak RESTCanonical data model / transformation requiredMinimal transformationAPI governance and lifecycle management requiredInternal integration, no governance needReuse of integration logic across multiple consumersSingle consumerLegacy system with no modern APIExternal system has REST/OpenAPICentral monitoring, alerting, and SLA enforcementSimple logging sufficient

MuleSoft in the Salesforce Context
Salesforce → External via MuleSoft

Salesforce publishes a Platform Event → MuleSoft subscribes via Pub/Sub API or CometD
MuleSoft transforms and routes to target systems
Decouples Salesforce from external system contracts

External → Salesforce via MuleSoft

MuleSoft acts as the inbound gateway — validates, transforms, rate-limits
Calls Salesforce REST/Bulk API to write data
Canonical data model maintained in MuleSoft, not Salesforce

MuleSoft Salesforce Connector

Native connector in Anypoint Studio for Salesforce REST, Bulk, Streaming, Metadata APIs
Handles OAuth, pagination, and error handling automatically


Anypoint Platform Key Components

































ComponentPurposeAPI DesignerDesign APIs with RAML or OAS (OpenAPI)ExchangeAPI marketplace — publish and discover APIsAnypoint StudioIDE for building Mule applicationsRuntime ManagerDeploy and monitor Mule runtimes (cloud, hybrid, on-prem)API ManagerApply policies (rate limiting, OAuth, SLA tiers) to published APIsVisualizerVisual map of all integrations and dependencies

Deployment Models

























ModelDescriptionWhen to useCloudHubMuleSoft-managed cloud runtime (SaaS)Fastest to deploy; no infra managementRuntime FabricCustomer-managed containers (Kubernetes)Data residency requirements; private cloudHybridRuntime on-prem, managed by Anypoint PlatformLegacy on-prem systems that can’t be exposed externally

MuleSoft vs Other Options for CTA









































ScenarioMuleSoftPlatform EventsDirect Apex CalloutMany systems, complex orchestration✓ Best fitToo simpleToo brittleSingle external API callOverkillN/A✓ Best fitEvent-driven async integrationPossible✓ Best fitN/ACustomer already has MuleSoft licence✓ Use itComplementaryAvoid duplicationAdmin-maintainable integrationPossibleVia FlowExternal Services


                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Don’t recommend MuleSoft for simple 2-system integrations — examiners will challenge over-engineering. Always justify middleware with complexity, reuse, or governance requirements.



Salesforce + MuleSoft Licensing Note
MuleSoft is licensed separately from Salesforce. In CTA scenarios, confirm whether the customer has (or is willing to procure) MuleSoft before proposing it as the solution.

CTA-Notes/Integration/52-payment-gateway.title: Payment Gateway Integration
CTA-Notes/Integration/52-payment-gateway.content:
(Salesforce Payments Overview) (Payment Center Overview)
Integration Approaches
There are two main ways to integrate a payment gateway with Salesforce:
1. Salesforce Payments (Native)

Built-in payment processing via Stripe (for Commerce Cloud / Experience Cloud orgs)
No custom integration code required
Supports card payments, refunds, and payment method management natively
Tied to Salesforce Commerce Cloud / B2B Commerce

2. Custom Gateway Integration (Apex callout)

Salesforce calls the payment gateway’s REST/SOAP API via Apex callout
Use Named Credentials to store endpoint + auth credentials securely
Payment result returned synchronously (RPI Request-Reply pattern)
Store transaction result on a custom object or Order/Payment record


Architecture Considerations
Never process card data through Salesforce

Salesforce is not PCI-DSS certified as a card data environment
Card number, CVV, expiry must go directly from the browser to the gateway (client-side tokenisation)
Salesforce only receives and stores the payment token (non-sensitive)

Tokenisation Flow
Browser → Payment Gateway JS SDK → Gateway returns token
Browser → Salesforce (token only, no card data)
Salesforce Apex → Gateway API (charge token) → Result stored in Salesforce

Recommended Pattern

RPI Request-Reply for synchronous payment authorisation
RPI Fire-and-Forget for async notifications (e.g. webhook from gateway → Platform Event → Salesforce order update)


Webhook Handling (Gateway → Salesforce)
Most gateways send webhook notifications for async events (payment captured, refund processed, dispute raised):

Gateway POSTs to a Salesforce endpoint
Use a Site (Experience Cloud guest user endpoint) or Connected App to receive the webhook without requiring OAuth user auth
Validate the webhook signature in Apex before processing
Publish a Platform Event or call a Flow to process the notification asynchronously



                  
                  Warning
                  
                

Validate webhook signatures (e.g. Stripe uses Stripe-Signature HMAC). Never process a webhook payload without verifying it came from the legitimate gateway.



Security Requirements





























RequirementImplementationNo card data in SalesforceClient-side tokenisation via gateway JS SDKSecure credential storageNamed Credentials (no hardcoded keys)Webhook authenticityHMAC signature validation in ApexEncryption in transitHTTPS/TLS enforced by Salesforce platformPCI scope reductionTokenisation keeps Salesforce out of PCI scope

Key Objects for Storing Payment Data

Order + OrderPaymentSummary (Order Management)
Custom Payment_Transaction__c object if not using Order Management
Store: gateway token, transaction ID, amount, status, timestamp — never card number or CVV

Integration Patterns — RPI Request-Reply and RPI Fire-and-Forget patterns
Integration Overview — integration framework overview

Setup: CORS for Postman

https://*.postman.com

Videos #3 (Generic Adventuring Tours) and #9 (Roads for Everyone) hit YouTube’s caption-server rate limit (HTTP 429) repeatedly during download. Raw .vtt/.txt not yet captured — retry later and append their sections below using the same format.



Greens and Veg
Scenario: Global vegetable wholesaler acting as middleman between farms/suppliers and restaurant customers, operating in 200+ countries. Core problem: consolidating multiple legacy systems (Marketplace app, Evergreen, NetSuite, Genesis CTI) into a single-org Salesforce design, covering multilingual/multi-currency data, recurring order schedules, LDV archival, complex visibility across internal/supplier/customer personas, and identity/integration architecture (Okta, ESB/ETL, external services).
Key architecture topics:

Single-org strategy, licensing (Service/Community licenses), role hierarchy vs. territory management
Data model: Order/Order Product/Order Schedule (recurring orders), Contract, Entitlements
LDV mitigation: custom indexes, archival to data warehouse, hard delete after ETL
Integration: fire-and-forget, request-reply, platform events, external services, JWT/OAuth
Sharing: OWD private, criteria-based sharing, Apex managed sharing, Tableau CRM security predicates
Identity: Okta vs. Salesforce as IdP for external users
DevOps/governance: branching, CI/CD, design authority, release cadence

Question patterns observed:

“You replaced Evergreen in the marketplace at the same time — what’s the impact/risk of that decision?”
Push on why a system was decommissioned vs. incrementally replaced
“Did you see any requirement that asks to control the security of contract different than account?”
Normalization trade-off probing: “Why do you have it as a separate object rather than denormalizing it on the order?”
Edge case/scale test: “You said the agent services Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg — what’s the simplest way to solve that?”
“Why not X” alternatives: “Why can’t you create a lead directly from LWC and use lead assignment + omnichannel out of the box?”
“How does IDV work when the customer calls in rather than logging in?”
Enforcement-mechanics drill-down on stated patterns (predicate design, ESB/REST governance)

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Be ready to defend/adjust data model choices live, not just defend them.
Anticipate “why not the declarative alternative” for every custom build.
Have a concrete story for edge-case scale beyond owner-based sharing.
Know limits of named tools (sharing rule limits, predicate thresholds) for follow-ups.


Greenhouse Recycling (No Q&A)
Scenario: US/Canada industrial/medical waste disposal provider needing a unified Salesforce architecture to close gaps in automation and integration. Single-org, multi-license model with an LDV-heavy data model (accounts, waste profiles, locations, pickups/routes) and a heavy integration layer tying together two ERPs, four logistics systems, a lead database, and a desktop tool, plus SSO/identity federation and governance.
Key architecture topics:

Org strategy, licensing, role hierarchy design
Data model with master-detail/junction objects, LDV handling (skinny tables, archiving)
Sharing/visibility (Apex sharing, criteria-based sharing, external account hierarchy)
Integration (ETL vs ESB, JWT bearer, 2-way SSL, Bulk API, CometD, fire-and-forget/request-reply/remote call-in)
Identity/SSO (ADFS SAML, social sign-on, Kerberos/IWA)
Data migration (staging, dedup, sequencing, sandbox-phased loads)
Reporting (standard reports vs. Tableau CRM)
Governance/ALM (CoE, ARB, CI/CD, branching, phased promotion)

Question patterns observed:
This recording is presentation-only, with no judge Q&A. Structural traits worth noting instead:

Strict sequential walkthrough: assumptions → licensing → landscape → data model → requirements → migration → sharing → reporting → governance → identity deep-dive
Proactively states assumptions aloud when ambiguous (e.g., “videos are very short, maybe 10 megs”)
Justifies each design choice inline as introduced
Closes with a dedicated technical deep-dive on SAML SSO and JWT bearer flows

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Narrate justifications/assumptions continuously — preempts many challenge questions a real board would ask.
Tie license/pattern choices to explicit business justification.
Exhaustive checklist structure signals board-review-style completeness.
Ending with an identity-flow deep dive suggests panels value explicit IAM detail even unprompted.


Flowers Racing
Scenario: International adventure-race organizer expanding from North America/Europe into Asia/South America, presenting a single-org solution for the NA rollout. Core problems: unifying disparate systems, managing a complex person-account/racer data model at scale (500K+ registrations, 5M pledges/year), and orchestrating integrations (identity matching, payments, shipping/GPS) via ETL/ESB middleware.
Key architecture topics:

Role hierarchy and licensing mix (Sales/Platform/Service Cloud, Customer Community Plus, Guest)
Data model with OWDs, LDV handling (pledge summary object, skinny tables)
Six+ integration patterns via ETL/ESB
Identity: Okta IdP, SAML SSO, JWT bearer, social login
Sharing model (sharing sets, Apex sharing, criteria-based rules, FLS)
Data migration (staging, transform, de-dupe, external IDs)
ALM/branching and environment pipeline
Governance (steering committee, CoE, ARB, PMO)

Question patterns observed:

Why weren’t standard objects (Lead/Opportunity) reused: candidate explains it doesn’t convert to account/contact cleanly.
“We need two-way SSL… cannot be done with External Services” — probing integration tool choice.
Judges challenge a security shortcut, prompting candidate self-correction (“we’re not sending credentials over email”).
Push on fire-and-forget vs. request-reply justification each time used.
Likely probing on LDV/archival assumptions (Tableau CRM vs. on-platform).
Case-assignment design probe: “considered case assignment rules but they’re not dynamic enough.”

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Always justify “why not” the obvious standard-object/OOTB approach.
State assumptions proactively to preempt challenges.
Tie every integration pattern choice back to a business requirement.
Self-correcting security/compliance gaps live signals maturity.


Universal Safety (session A)
Scenario: Security device design/installation/monitoring/maintenance provider with ~150 offices and 15 regions across US/Canada, needing a unified Salesforce solution to replace fragmented systems. Single-org data model spanning sales, field service, contractor/customer community access, ERP/external design-system integration, and a 4-month delivery timeline creating governance risk.
Key architecture topics:

Single-org decision, licensing (Sales/Service Cloud, Customer Community Plus)
Data model: mostly standard objects plus custom Location and Maintenance Schedule
Service Cloud Voice vs. Lightning Dialer/Open CTI
Mobile (Salesforce Mobile + Mobile Publisher), AppExchange add-ons
Integration patterns: ETL/ESB, remote call-in, platform events, real-time External Services to ERP/SAP
Sharing model for contractors (sharing sets)
Governance, hybrid waterfall/agile, environment/branching strategy (Copado)

Question patterns observed:

“Have you delivered or seen anyone deliver a project with this scope and complexity in four months?”
“What if there are multiple projects running on a particular location… what will be changing your solution?”
Panel reveals timeline late, forcing candidate to abandon Service Cloud Voice for Open CTI
“Can you explain how do you set up skill based omni channel?”
“You stated you don’t want big bang, but now you want to switch CTI on day one?” (consistency check)
“Would it commercially be justifiable… vs enterprise edition + separate full sandbox?”
“What are your deliverables as part of a blueprint?”

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Panels stack constraints incrementally to test consistency of revisions.
Be ready to reverse a design decision gracefully under a new late constraint.
Have concrete “how” answers ready for standard features, not just naming them.
Justify platform/edition choices with cost comparisons.


Universal Safety (session B)
Scenario: Universal Safety Technologies, a US/Canada provider of safety/security design, installation, monitoring, and maintenance (150 offices, 100k commercial customers, 10%/yr growth), replacing a legacy CRM and two regional ERPs with a unified single-org platform. Spans data model design at LDV scale, heavy ERP/monitoring integration via MuleSoft, multi-region licensing/sharing, and archival strategy. Longer, more detailed session than “session A” above on the same fictional company.
Key architecture topics:

Single-org justification, licensing model, partner/contractor access
Data model: standard objects plus custom Installation, Location, Financial Data
LDV/archival: virtualizing Assets/Cases to Heroku via Heroku Connect + external objects (OData)
Integration via MuleSoft ESB: platform events, remote call-in, request-reply, batch/bulk ETL
Identity: OpenID Connect, SP-initiated SAML, Identity Connect for AD-based SSO
Sharing: sharing sets, criteria-based rules, financial data restriction
Data migration with fuzzy matching against ERP
Environment/release strategy and governance (CoE, ARB)

Question patterns observed:

“Any other master details that you are missing or not highlighted?”
Ownership challenge: “Who’s gonna be the owner of this object?” then catches a self-contradiction.
“You said you’re enabling FSL but you’re not using FSL… clarify.”
“Can you explain how we’re sending order line items?” / “How do you make sure the cases are not duplicated?”
Scale realism check: “we have 10 office managers inside Canada… do you think your role hierarchy is right?”
“How would you virtualize the asset data… only want to show specific users?” (external-object security)
Requirement-scale stress test on file-size assumptions (4K video uploads)
“How can we compare using ESB versus ETL here?” / “Why not just use MuleSoft for ETL as well?”

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Judges heavily test internal consistency between diagram, data model, and stated requirements.
Security of external/virtualized objects (search visibility, sharing) gets probed hard.
Role hierarchy/sharing must reflect the scenario’s actual operational structure, not a generic template.
Be ready to justify tool/pattern choices with rationale tied to real-time/error-handling needs.


Untitled Scenario (Greenhouse Recycling variant)
Scenario: A greenhouse recycling/waste disposal company serving industrial and medical customers (200K customers, 5%/yr growth, US/Canada, 150 offices/300 facilities) replacing a paper-based, siloed system with Salesforce, unifying lead-to-cash, customer waste-profile/scheduling, field logistics integration, and multi-channel notifications while decommissioning legacy tools.
Key architecture topics:

Data model: Location, Waste Profile (junction), Schedule, external object for pickup data (~52M records/year)
Sharing/security: private OWD, role hierarchy, sharing sets, account teams, FLS for ERP fields
Integration: MuleSoft ESB, request-reply and remote-call-in, platform events, external objects
Identity: existing IdP SSO, OAuth/OIDC social sign-on, registration handlers
Data migration: Informatica ETL, dedupe/cleansing, phased load sequencing
Case management: entitlements, milestones, escalation
DevOps/governance: CoE, branching, 4-month discovery timeline

Question patterns observed:

“Could you just talk through the process… in relation to the contracts?”
“The actual drop-offs… how does that fit into your data model?”
“You chose Informatica, can you walk me through your decision process?” / “Are you saying MuleSoft cannot do this ETL process?”
Malicious-actor security drill-down repeated until candidate concedes and revises the solution
“Is there anything we need to be concerned about in terms of those numbers?” (volume)
“Is it possible to solve this without creation of entitlements and milestones?”
“Explain the standard methods implemented in the registration handler interface… how does Salesforce decide which to call?”
“You have MuleSoft outside your firewall… walk me through your thought process.”

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Be ready to defend security holes end-to-end; judges escalate with “malicious user” framing until a concrete mitigation is proposed.
Product-choice questions expect trade-off reasoning, not a stated preference.
It’s acceptable to pass on a deep platform mechanic rather than guess incorrectly.
Judges repeatedly anchor multiple unrelated challenges back to the data model slide.


Global Adventure Tours
Scenario: Adventure tourism booking platform matching 300,000+ adventurers with 500 boutique tour operators worldwide, consolidating multiple regional Salesforce orgs into a single global org, adding Service Cloud, retiring a legacy tour management system, and integrating with a payment gateway and field-dispatch system via ESB/ETL, using a phased MVP rollout starting with the US.
Key architecture topics:

Single-org vs. multi-org strategy and org consolidation
Data model for tours/schedules/bookings (LDV on Order object), person accounts
Security/sharing (criteria-based sharing, sharing sets, role hierarchy, high-risk record visibility)
Multi-currency, multi-language, SSO/identity (Okta IdP chaining)
Integration: fire-and-forget platform events, remote call-in, request-reply via ESB
Data migration/archival (staging, dedup, AWS data warehouse/S3)
DevOps/CI-CD and hybrid “Wagile” governance
Registration scoring logic (custom metadata vs. Einstein Lead Scoring)

Question patterns observed:

“Did you consider anything else?” (round-robin via AppExchange vs. custom build) → candidate reverses solution under pressure
“How about some standard object for this one?” (Lead vs. custom Application object)
Edge-case probes: documents can’t be uploaded at registration, reapplication after a year
“Why do you think near-real-time is a valid assumption?” then “is there a retry mechanism… how will it recover?”
“At which point would you consider data scalability at risk?”
Repeated drilling on governance/political mechanism: “what’s the mechanism to ensure the US doesn’t just build for itself” under single-org strategy
Build-vs-buy justification: products/price books vs. custom metadata; entitlements/milestones vs. field-based SLA

Exam-relevant takeaways:

Judges force candidates to defend or reverse decisions when a simpler OOTB alternative exists — be ready to pivot, not just defend.
Expect deep drill-downs on error handling/recovery (platform event replay/retries), not just the happy path.
Governance/political trade-offs are tested as rigorously as technical design.


Cross-Video Question Pattern Analysis


                  
                  Recurring judge question archetypes across all sessions 
                  
                


“Why not X instead?” — tests whether the candidate evaluated the standard/declarative/OOTB alternative before building custom (Lead vs. custom object, sharing rules vs. Apex sharing, ETL vs. ESB).
Consistency/contradiction check — judges cross-reference an earlier claim against a later statement (e.g., “you said no big bang, but now…”) and expect the candidate to reconcile or revise live.
Edge-case/scale stress test — introduces a volume, geography, or timeline constraint not in the original brief (“what if it’s 10x volume”, “four months”, “10 office managers in Canada”) to see if the design still holds.
Security drill-down via “malicious user” framing — repeated escalation until the candidate proposes a concrete mitigation, not just a stated control.
“How does X actually work” mechanics check — moves from naming a feature/pattern to demanding the underlying mechanism (registration handler interface, predicate design, retry/replay behavior).
Build-vs-buy / trade-off justification — requires explicit reasoning for any tool or pattern choice, not just a preference statement.
Late-breaking constraint injection — judges withhold a key constraint (e.g., timeline) until after a design choice is made, forcing a graceful pivot.



See also: cta-exam-structure, cta-study-guide-overview

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/AppExchange-(Bu.title: Payment Gateways Chargent
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/AppExchange-(Bu.content:
What are Payment Gateways
Payment gateways are services that determine whether a card used for a payment is legit or fraudulent and it determines whether or not it will be approved or declined for a transaction (a user has enough funds).

What are Payment Processors
These are services that actually move the money from a payee’s account to the merchants account. Most companies that provide payment processing services also provide payment gateway services (for example stripe), so you typically only need one platform to do both things.

When should you suggest the use of Payment Gateways
If there is a need for a user/customer to pay for something, you will likely need to leverage a payment gateway to make that happen, unless it is explicitly stated this is already setup on another platform.

What functionality do payment gateways have?
Most payment gateways have the following functionality (and unless it is otherwise stated you should assume they have it and put it in your assumptions slide):

REST & SOAP API Services (would only suggest API use if a perfect fluid UI is explicitly stated and I would suggest using chargent to make that ultra simple)
The ability to store payment options/preferences
The ability to manage recurring billing
**Hosted Checkout/Payment Pages (I would always pick this over the API unless a perfect fluid UI is explicitly stated)  **

It’s important to remember that each of these features exist. There is no need to build this functionality within Salesforce and risk PCI compliance when your payment gateways can manage all of that.

Paypal Example of Hosted Checkout Page
Information on how to setup a hosted checkout page and both send and receive information from it: PayPal Configure Hosted Checkout Page
Information on how Gateway Secure Token’s work and Transparent Redirects: Gateway Secure Tokens and Transparent Redirects
NOTE: Transparent redirects allow you to post to your payment gateway without actually traversing to a separate page.

Populate Examples of Payment Gateways that are also Payment Processors
All of the platforms below offer both payment gateway and payment processing services

Stripe
Paypal
Square
Helcim


What is Chargent
Chargent is a managed package that allows you to easily integrate with you payment gateway of choice to allow for easy payments, recurring billing and more. If you have a need in your scenario to connect to a payment gateway, and no other mechanism to connect exists (via your ERP or other systems) Chargent is a simple way to make that integration happen easily while being PCI compliant.
NOTE: I would typically only suggest this if one of the following is true:

You need an extremely fluid UI in your exp site to take payments
The scenario explicitly states that you need to manage recurring payments and you cannot infer (or it’s completely ruled out) that your ERP is able to provide this functionality.


How does Chargent store payment options
Chargent does not store your payment options for you, the payment gateway should be the one storing those payment options. For example, if your payment gateway is PayPal, PayPal has the ability to store all of that information for someone. I would not suggest hosting that within Salesforce unless it explicitly states a need to do so.

Chargent Anywhere
This product just allows you to make payments tied to any object in Salesforce, so chargent pay can be hosted on any object page, and chargent transactions can be linked to any object.

Chargent Recurring Payments
Chargent has the ability to setup recurring payments within its product. In many cases you also need to have this feature enabled with your payment gateway as well. You then have the ability to setup a batch job within SF (provided by Chargent) that can reach manage all the recurring payments in your system.

Chargent Pay Flow Component
Chargent has an easy to configure and use flow component that you can place into any flow to allow a customer to easily pay using chargent.

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.title: CPQ Objects
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.content:
CPQ Key Features

Favoriting Products - Mark a product as a favorite to allow you to quickly add them to future quotes
Quote Line Groups - Allows you to group products together and apply parameters to just that group of products instead of the whole quote
Twin Fields - This allows you to do automatic data mapping between two fields on two different objects
Product Rules - Rules you can setup that prevent invalid product combinations
Price Rules - Rules you can setup to automatically adjust the price of an product (for instance a discount price rule)
Guided Selling - A configurable interface that allows you to show sales reps the best product to sell a customer based on their inputs.
Summary Variables - Similar to rollups, but only present themselves in the quote line editor and do not contribute to roll up summary limits (25 per obj - 40 max).
Contract Amendments and Renewals - Automated functionality to allow you to create amendments to contracts, as well as auto-renew a contract.
Contracted Pricing - Allows you to setup contracted price discounts for products on an account by account basis.
Multi-Dimensional Quoting - Allows you to allow for discount/price to vary for a product over the lifespan of a contract. Allows you to mix subscription based products with non-subscription based products in a quote.

CPQ Objects
This Section houses all data on the OOTB CPQ objects.

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.title: Field Service Lightning
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.content:
Setting up a User for Field Service Lightning
After purchasing Field Service Lightning and enabling it in Salesforce (via Setup → Field Service Settings), you only need to check the “Service Cloud User” and “Knowledge User” checkboxes on most users that will be accessing your Field Service System. However, there are some exceptions here:


Field Service Dispatcher - If a user needs access to the FSL Dispatcher console, they will need to have this permission set license given to them to grant them access.


Field Service Scheduling - This allows a user to be shown on the dispatcher console Gantt chart. So if you need a field tech (or someone similar) to show up there, then they will need this license.


Field Service Mobile - Any resource that needs access to the special Salesforce Field Service Mobile app will need this license applied to them.



Field Service Objects
Service Resource - This represents a user or an asset that someone can schedule time with.
Operating Hours - This is kind of a shell/parent object that represents the different operating hours for every region your business operates in around the world. The “Time Slot” object records and “Operating Hours Holiday” records associated with your operating hours record actually represent the hours your business is available.
Time Slots - This is a child record of the operating hours object that represents the times your business is open each day.
Operating Hours Holiday - This is a child record of the operating hours object that represents times and days that your business is not available due to holidays.
Service Territories - These records represent a region/territory, you will associate your operating hours, and each service resource in a territory, to that territory. This ensures that each territory you do business in can only be serviced by service resources in that area, and during time frames appropriate for that area. You can create service territory hierarchies to break larger regions into smaller sub regions.
Service Territory Resource - This object is a junction object between service territory and service resource. It exists because a service resource can work in multiple service territories at once in some instances.
Service Appointment - This represents an appointment scheduled with a service resource to complete a job.
Work Type - This object is used to define a work type which can then be assigned to work orders and work order line items to ensure that we match the right service resource to the work order. Work Types have Skill records associated to them to define the skills needed to get a work order done right. These essentially act as a template for common jobs.
Skill - This represents a skill that a service resource has or that is required for a work order to be completed. Note: You can only create skills in the Field Service Admin Guided Setup, or via SF Classic and you cannot delete skills after you have created them!
Skill Setup Documentation
Product Required - This object is a junction between work type and product (the OOTB Product Object) to determine what products are needed to complete a work type
Timesheets - This represents a timesheet for a specific period of time for a service resource (note you can only setup timesheets for “technician” service resources).
Timesheet Entry - These are daily timesheet entries that service resources will fill out to log the hours their worked each day against their timesheet.
Work Order - Work Orders represent a customer request to for a service or product to be delivered to them.
Work Order Line Items - This object represents the individual tasks that need to be completed in order to fulfill the parent work order records request.
Product Consumed - This object is a junction between a product item and a work order. When you create one of these Product Consumed records Salesforce will automatically decrement the “Quantity on Hand” field on the product item record based on how much product you denoted as consumed on your Product Consumed record.

The Field Service Managed Package
Field Service has an optional manage package installation that will give you the following improvements to the Field Service Lightning Experience:


Guided Setup: This tool walks you through key setup tasks, including assigning permission sets, creating service resources, and customizing appointment booking settings.


Scheduling and optimization: Optimize your team’s schedule in a way that enforces your business objectives. Assign appointments according to your rules and priorities, such as worker skills, location, and availability.


Dispatcher console: Give dispatchers and supervisors a view of your field service operations. The dispatcher console includes a customizable appointment list, easy-to-reach scheduling actions, dynamic Gantt chart, and interactive map. Dispatchers can check that jobs are routed to the right people, receive alerts, and monitor appointments in real time.


Administration app: Manage optimization, customize the dispatcher console, and update your managed package settings in one place.


Crew Management - After you install the managed package, you will be able to grant your users access to do crew management via the crew management tab. To grant your users access to the crew management tab you need to do the following:

Give them either the “FSL Admin Permissions”, or “FSL Dispatcher Permissions” permission set
Setup a custom Lightning Page and drop the custom Lightning component onto the page.
Create a new permission set that grants users access to all of the following:



The Crew Management tab you made in step 2 



FSL.CrewManagement Visualforce page  



FSL.CrewsResourceLightbox Visualforce page  



FSL.CrewsSaLightbox Visualforce page  



FSL.CrewsWorkorderLightbox Visualforce page  



FSL.CrewsWorkorderLineItemLightbox Visualforce page  



FSL.CrewManagement Apex class

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.title: Knowledge Articles
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.content:
What are Knowledge Articles
Knowledge articles are used to help customers, partners, and internal Salesforce users self-service their own problems. Maybe a customer needs to know how to reset the tv they purchased from your company? You could have them call a rep, but why not make an easily searchable knowledge article for them to find them information themselves? Case deflection at its finest! Or make knowledge articles for your internal users to help them navigate your org!

Knowledge Features
Scheduled Publish - When publishing a knowledge article you have the option to schedule a future date in which it will be published. Don’t forget this OOTB feature exists!
Public Knowledge Sharing -
Knowledge Article Versioning & Version Comparison -
Voting -

Knowledge Translations
If you go to Setup → Knowledge Article Settings you can check a box that allows you to turn on multi-language support for Knowledge. You will also be able to select the languages you’d like to support, determine the user or queue assigned for a language translation, and the default user or queue to review the translation.
Then when on a knowledge article there will be a button that allows you to submit for translation.

Knowledge Case Suggestions
In Setup → Knowledge Settings you will see an option that allows you to turn on knowledge article suggestions for cases and determine which fields on a case are used to find suggested articles in the OOTB case suggested articles component you can place on a case record page.

Knowledge Licenses & Security
Knowledge Licenses - You do have to purchase additional licenses for those users who are creating and publishing knowledge articles within Salesforce, this is an additional license and additional cost. This is a feature licenses though and doesn’t need to be called out on a CTA Board, but doesn’t hurt to know. People that are just viewing knowledge don’t need this additional license.
You assign this additional license by checking the “Knowledge User” checkbox on a users user record.
Knowledge Article Record Security - When creating a knowledge article you have the option (via checkboxes) to determine who it is accessible to via 3 checkboxes. You can make it available to customers, partners, and/or internal users. Make sure to check the boxes for the users you want to access the articles
Data Categories

Knowledge Article Topics

Knowledge Classic Only Features
There are unfortunately a ton of these, honestly if they aren’t in this article above, you shouldn’t learn them or suggest them imo. You don’t wanna suggest classic only features on the board. It’s a shame there are so many good ones they have still yet to port to lightning.
Knowledge ERD

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.title: Partner Relationship Management
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.content:
What is PRM
PRM is a mechanism that Salesforce gives you to better manage your relationships with Partners you work with. It allows you to forecast their sales, allocate marketing funds to them for campaigns, and collaborate with them better on leads, campaigns, quotes and opportunities.
(Only licenses that are needed for this are partner and/or partner login licenses, you also need experience cloud sites enabled)

Market Development Funds
If you have partner licenses and experience cloud enabled in your org you will find a bunch of objects centered around market development funds. They are the following:
Partner Marketing Budgets - This object represents a budget that provides funds to channel partners for selling and marketing products and services. You’ll typically start here and setup budgets for everyone to use.
Partner Fund Allocations -  Represents allocated funds from a partner marketing budget for channel partners.
Partner Fund Claims -  Represents a claim of funds from the partner marketing budget by a channel partner.
Partner Fund Requests -  Represents a request for funds from the partner marketing budget by a channel partner.
You will find that these are most commonly used for distributing funds for Campaigns (product marketing campaigns, emailing campaigns, etc). However, these could technically be used to fund anything and be tied to any object.

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.title: Sales Cloud
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.content:
What is Sales Cloud
Sales Cloud is really Salesforce’s core product, and it will absolutely be included in your CTA scenarios, so you MUST know its functionality inside and out. Its primary focus is streamlining the sales process for Sales reps as well as some functionality via the campaign object that is commonly utilized by marketing teams to track marketing events and campaigns. We will go over each object, what it’s used for as well as the major OOTB config features for marketing cloud (like lead conversion, enterprise territory management and sales forecasting) below.
Note: Unless otherwise stated, all objects have the ability to have sharing rules, sharing sets, sharing groups and OWD access set for record visibility.
Additionally, unless otherwise noted, all objects are Full objects, meaning they can have profiles and/or perm sets setup for users to restrict object and field visibilities.

Core Sales Cloud Objects ERD (Entity Relationship Diagram)

Core Sales Cloud Object Guide
Below is a list of every object related to sales cloud functionality, why and when it should be used, what its OOTB relationships are, how much data is stored per record, OOTB ways to share records for the object, and the licenses required to use it without significant custom builds.

Account Object
The account object records represent an organization or an individual that your company is involved with in some way. It is not really a Sales Cloud specific object as it is utilized in the vast majority of Salesforce implementations. It is also the most critical object to understand as it has many unique OOTB features (especially sharing features).
Record Storage:  Accounts take up the typical 2kb of storage.
License Requirements: Accounts can be used by every license type
Required Fields:

Name
LastName (If it is a person account)

OOTB Lookups:

ParentId - Used for account hierarchies (for instance if you had an account that represented Coca-Cola and you wanted to tie their child company Dasani to it).
MasterRecordId - Used only if account was merged by the OOTB merge tool into another account.
Operating Hours - Represents the operating hours/business hours for the account.

OOTB Objects That Have Lookups To Account:

Assets
Territories (ObjectTerritory2Association)

Campaign Object
Campaigns are built for and represent marketing campaigns, shows, promotions, webinars, events, etc. It allows you to track the cost of the event, the opportunities generated from that event, the people who went to that marketing event, leads generated from that event, etc. You can also use the parent campaign functionality for large campaigns that have multiple events attached to them (for instance a tradeshow that has 10 webinars and 20 promotional emails and 5 shows) to get visibility into the profitability of the entire marketing campaign.
Record Storage: Campaign is an object that is unique in that it uses 8kb of storage per record instead of the typical 2kb that most object records take up.
License Requirements: Campaigns are accessible to the Sales, Service and Partner Licensed Salesforce users.
Required Fields:

Name

OOTB Lookups:

ParentId - This lookup allows you to link a campaign to a parent campaign.
TentantId (Only relevant if you use pardot) - Gives you the ability to associate a campaign to a pardot business unit.

OOTB Objects That Have Lookups To Campaign:

Campaign Member
Opportunities

Sharing Options/Considerations:

For a user to be able to do ANYTHING OOTB (create, edit, delete, transfer) aside from view a campaign, they must have the “Marketing User” checkbox checked on their user record.
If you use Campaign Hierarchies, anyone with access to the parent record can see all statistical campaign data for campaigns lower in the hierarchy.
Campaigns have a unique OWD options where you can give all users in your org FULL ACCESS, as in they can all view, edit, transfer, delete and report on every record. This is uncommon and not typically suggested, but good to know it exists. It also can be private, public read, and public read/write.

Asset Object
An asset represents an item of commercial value that a customer (account or a contact with an associated account) has purchased. Basically anything on of your consumers now actually owns and is relevant for you to track should be housed in this table.
Record Storage: The Asset object is sometimes referred to as a magic object because it DOES NOT COUNT AGAINST STORAGE AT ALL! That’s right, it takes up 0kb of storage to store asset records… wyld. There is no documentation over this, I was informed by Johann Furmann, could only find this idea post discussing it and tested it myself. Turns out, it’s true lol.
License Requirements: Asset is an object that is accessible via both Sales, Service, CC, CC+, and Partner license types. It is NOT available for SF Platform licenses.
Required Fields:

Name
AccountId OR ContactId (but the contact must have an associated account record)

OOTB Lookups:

ParentId - Used if there is a parent asset (for instance you have a headset that came with a computer).
Product2Id - Used optionally if a product is associated with the asset.
AccountId (required if ContactId not filled out) - used to determine the account the asset is owned by.
ContactId (required if AccountId not filled out) - Used to determine the contact the asset is owned by.
RootAssetId - Used to determine the absolute parent of an asset (for instance if the asset is 3 levels deep in the asset parent chain it shows the top level asset).

OOTB Objects That Have Lookups To Asset:

Case
Work Order
Work Order Line Items
Contract Line Items (requires engagement management being enabled)
Entitlements (requires engagement management being enabled)

Sharing Options:

Asset has the ability in the OWD to be controlled by parent (contact or account id) or be public read, public read/write, or private, but ONLY if Asset Sharing is enabled in Asset settings in setup! If it’s not enabled than access can only be determined by parent object records.
Assets are now what’s referred to as a full object (can control its object and field level access in profiles).


Quote Object
Quote Overview
The Quote object allows your sales reps a mechanism to haggle with the customer. If you need a way to provide a variety of pricing options for a customer, quotes are the way to go.
Quote Unique Features
Quotes have a couple unique features that are worth mentioning:


You can sync a quote with its parent opportunity by clicking the “Sync Quote” button on the Quotes record page. Quote syncing keeps products (QLI’s & OLI’s) sync’d between the two records. You can only have one quote on an opportunity sync’d at a time. More on Quote Syncing here.


There is an OOTB feature/button that allows you to generate a PDF for a Quote. This is unique to the quote object. You can also setup multiple Quote templates for that PDF generation. More about Quote Templates here.


Quote Oddities:
The weirdest thing about quotes are that the following:


Quote syncing, Quote PDFs, and Quote PDF generation are not available on SF Mobile. Also QLI addition and deletion must be one by one on mobile instead of multiple QLI updates at a time.


Quotes have a master detail relationship to Opportunity (in Fall 2023 I believe this will cease to be true/be optional).

CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.title: Service Cloud Voice CCaaS
CTA-Notes/SF-Solutioning/Choosing-the-Ri.content:
What It Is
Partner Contact Center (formerly Service Cloud Voice / Salesforce Voice) is Salesforce’s native CCaaS (Contact Center as a Service) capability — it brings telephony into the Service Console as just another Omni-Channel work item, alongside case, chat, email, and messaging.


                  
                  Naming history 
                  
                

Service Cloud Voice → Salesforce Voice → Partner Contact Center. Expect exam/vendor material to use any of these names interchangeably. “Partner” refers to the telephony partner model (bring-your-own-telephony or Amazon Connect), not a Partner Community concept.


Core Value Proposition

Telephony, digital channels, and CRM data unified on one platform (Agentforce Service / Service Console) instead of a CTI screen-pop bolted onto a separate phone system
Real-time voice transcription → feeds Einstein for next-best-action and knowledge article recommendations mid-call
Supervisors get real-time Omni-Channel visibility into calls, analytics, and rep performance (Omni Supervisor)
No-code phone channel setup, plus choice of telephony provider

Telephony Models (Choose the Right Capability)



































OptionProsConsWhen to usePartner Contact Center (bring your own telephony)Keep existing telephony investment/contract; choose any supported partner via AgentExchangeSome features (e.g. real-time transcription) depend on what the partner supports; still need a managed package integrationOrg has an existing telephony contract/investment it doesn’t want to abandonPartner Contact Center with Amazon ConnectFully native, pre-integrated; single Salesforce bill for Salesforce + AWS; real-time transcription, call recording, AI baked inLocked into AWS infrastructure; must manage AWS service quotas (concurrent calls, transcription jobs, outbound country list)Greenfield contact center, no existing telephony investment, want fastest path to full feature setPartner Contact Center with telephony from Amazon ConnectLeverage an existing Amazon Connect instance, integrate it with VoiceStill requires AWS-side setup/ownershipOrg already runs Amazon Connect and wants to add Salesforce on topLegacy CTI (Open CTI / call-center packages)Familiar, incremental, doesn’t require a platform switchScreen-pop model only; call control lives in console footer, separate from digital channels; AI can’t leverage full record/knowledge context the way Voice doesOrg not ready to re-platform; short-term bridge only — CTA should treat as a capability being displaced, not a long-term recommendation
Partner Contact Center vs. CTI (Exam Angle)






























DimensionPartner Contact CenterCTIIntegration modelNative to platform; Amazon Connect out-of-box or AgentExchange partnerThird-party telephony package installed per computerData captureAutomatic transcription populates records; AI-driven next actionsManual note-taking; limited automationConsole experienceOne Omni-Channel widget for all channelsSeparate call-control tool in console footerSupervisor visibilityOmni Supervisor sees all channels + live call transcriptsLimited to call-specific analytics
When architecting: CTI still shows up in the field, but for new implementations the default recommendation should be Partner Contact Center — flag CTI only when there’s a hard constraint (unsupported region/provider, existing multi-year telephony contract, or M&A carve-out timeline).
Prerequisites & Constraints (worth memorizing for boards)

Lightning Experience only (no Classic)
Add-on license on top of Service Cloud or Sales Cloud
Browser support limited to Chrome and Firefox; cookies required for SSO
Requires a custom domain + SSO URL, and Omni-Channel enabled before Voice is turned on
If using Amazon Connect telephony: review/increase AWS service quotas — max concurrent calls, max transcription jobs, outbound-callable country list
Sequencing: set up case management (fields, assignment rules, routing) before adding Voice — adding a phone channel on top of an immature case model just moves the chaos into real time

Implementation Planning Checklist

Baseline current state: phone system, number of call centers, phone number inventory, license/seat count, who needs Omni Supervisor access
Decide telephony model (table above) — this is a purchasing decision, not just a technical one; needs someone authorized to buy
Number porting — start early; regulated, provider-dependent, cannot be rushed against a go-live date
Environment/testing strategy — sandbox count, Amazon Connect test instances, prod↔test data migration plan
AWS networking review if using Amazon Connect (don’t block required ports)
Routing design — map existing case assignment/skills-based/queue routing onto Omni-Channel routing; decide how much of the current IVR logic carries over
Reporting/analytics — Voice ships a contact center dashboard (call volume, AHT, average speed to answer, resolution %); decide what custom reports are still needed beyond it
Rep enablement — training on Omni-Channel widget vs. old softphone, call scripts, brand voice/tone (not just tooling: this is a change-management stream)

Trade-off Considered: Voice vs. Staying on CTI

CTI: lower short-term disruption, but caps the org’s ability to use AI (next best action, transcription-driven knowledge surfacing) because CTI call data isn’t native to the platform
Partner Contact Center: higher setup cost (porting, AWS quotas, retraining) but unlocks Omni-Channel-native routing, AI, and unified supervisor tooling — the CTA case for switching hinges on whether AI-driven service and unified reporting are strategic priorities, not just “can reps make calls”

Related

service-cloud
Related to Agentforce voice-enabled agents (Agentforce/03 Agentforce Builder) — Partner Contact Center is the human-agent telephony layer; Agentforce Voice sits on top for AI-agent-handled calls and can share the same telephony partner connection

Sources

(Explore the Benefits and Features of Voice Integration) — Trailhead
(Prepare Your Team for Effective Voice Implementation) — Trailhead
(Optimize Voice Implementation Strategy) — Trailhead
Salesforce Help: Connect to a Partner Contact Center, Choose a Telephony Model, Voice Limitations, Voice Prerequisites
Developer Guide: Partner Contact Center
