CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: Customer Identity (CIAM) and Headless Identity
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
Identity for customers and partners (“external users”) differs from employee IAM: much higher volume, self-service registration, social login, brand control, and cost-sensitive licensing. Terms: iam-concepts-and-terminology.
Authentication options for Experience Cloud sites
By default external users log in with a Salesforce-assigned username and password; employees use their normal login. Beyond that you can extend the site with (Authenticate Experience Cloud Site Users):

SAML SSO — extend the org’s SAML to the site (use the site login URL, /login in the assertion) → saml-sso
Authentication providers — Google, Apple, Facebook, OIDC → openid-connect-and-auth-providers
SAML between orgs / sites — hub-and-spoke
OAuth — API access for apps and headless clients
Login Discovery and passwordless login for simpler flows



                  
                  Note
                  
                

Session cookies are set at the domain level. Logging in as a different user in the same browser replaces the existing session cookies for that domain, logging out the first user.


External licence choices
Licence choice drives cost, object access, and sharing options. “External Identity” is named in Salesforce Help alongside Community, Customer Portal and partner licences.



































Licence familyTypical audienceStrengthsLimitsExternal IdentityLarge-scale B2C / identity-only use (login, profile, consent, light custom objects)Lowest cost per user; designed for high volumeLimited standard-object access; not for CRM-heavy portalsCustomer Community (+ Login variants)B2C/B2B customers who log in often/rarelyCheap; sharing sets; Cases, Contacts, AccountsNo reports/dashboards; limited sharingCustomer Community Plus (+ Login)Customers needing reports, role hierarchy and sharing rulesRicher sharingCostPartner Community (+ Login)Partners needing Leads, Opportunities, Campaigns, QuotesFull partner object setMost expensive
Login variants suit infrequent users (a few logins per month/year) and are billed per login. See experience-cloud-features for the full licence decision.


                  
                  Board point 
                  
                

Match licence to what the user must do, then to login frequency. A pure identity or consent use case with millions of consumers → External Identity. Add Customer Community Plus only when reports or richer sharing are required.


Self-registration

Standard self-registration page, or Apex handler Auth.ConfigurableSelfRegHandler to control how the User, Contact and Account are created and which profile/permission sets apply.
Each external user needs a Contact (and usually an Account). Design the account model deliberately: shared “bucket/household” accounts, person accounts or per-customer accounts all have sharing and scale consequences.
Add email/phone verification to prevent junk accounts; consider CAPTCHA and rate limiting at the edge.
Social sign-on creates users through the registration handler (openid-connect-and-auth-providers).

Passwordless and verification methods

Passwordless login by email or phone: user receives a one-time code instead of a password. Registering with an email address or phone number makes the identifier the login.
Users can register/deregister methods: email, SMS, TOTP, security key (U2F/WebAuthn), Salesforce Authenticator, and use them to log in.
For high-risk actions add step-up via mfa-and-step-up-authentication.
Login Discovery asks for an identifier first and routes to the right method.

Branding and login experience

Experience Builder login/registration pages, Apex login controllers, custom login pages, dynamic branding per site/URL.
Login flows collect progressive-profile data and consent after authentication.
Custom domain gives a branded URL while still running on Salesforce infrastructure.

Headless Identity
Headless Identity lets an off-platform app (mobile app, SPA, partner portal) own the entire login and registration UI while Salesforce acts as the identity back end. It is available only for external users (customers and partners) (OAuth Authorization Flows).
Building blocks:





































CapabilityPurposeHeadless Registration APICreate external users from your UI (email/phone verification)Headless Login API / passwordlessAuthenticate with password or OTP, then issue tokensHeadless Forgot Password APIPassword reset from the custom UIAuthorization Code and Credentials flowOAuth flow for headless login; can be blocked org-wide if not usedAuthorization Code + PKCERedirect-based fallback when a hosted login page is acceptableNative SSO parameter on web-server / user-agent flowsLooks like native app SSO to an external IdP while the app keeps UX control; works with My Domain and Experience Cloud sitesSocial login in headlessVia the SSO parameter and an auth provider
Considerations:

The custom app is a public client — no secret in the app; use PKCE, short-lived access tokens, secure token storage (Keychain/Keystore).
You own security UX: rate limiting, bot protection, error messages that don’t leak account existence, password reset hardening.
Salesforce API limits and licence limits still apply; model the login volume.
Use Headless when the Salesforce-hosted login page UX is unacceptable; otherwise a branded Experience Cloud site with Login Discovery is far less work.



                  
                  Don't reach for the user-agent/implicit flow 
                  
                

Older “headless” guidance used the OAuth user-agent flow with a username and password sent from the client. That flow is discouraged and can be blocked (oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps). Use the Headless Identity APIs or Authorization Code + PKCE.


Design checklist for the board

Who are the users, how many, how often do they log in? → licence.
Self-registration or invite? → handler, Contact/Account model.
Social or enterprise IdP login? → auth provider vs SAML.
Passwordless / MFA expectations?
Branded hosted pages vs fully custom (headless)?
Consent, privacy regulations → privacy-and-consent-management.
Guest user and sharing implications → Permissions & Sharing overview.

Related

iam-solution-design-and-scenarios
user-provisioning-and-lifecycle

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: IAM Concepts and Terminology
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
The vocabulary the board expects you to use precisely. Everything else in this domain (saml-sso, openid-connect-and-auth-providers, oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps) builds on these terms.
What IAM covers
IAM = the tools, processes, monitoring and governance used to grant internal and external users the right access to systems. For external users (customers, partners) it is often called CIAM — see customer-identity-and-headless-identity.
A complete IAM solution has four parts:






























ElementPurposeTypical productIdentity repositoryHolds user details and credentialsActive Directory, LDAP directory, databaseManagement toolboxCreate / edit / disable identitiesOkta, Entra ID, Ping, Salesforce IdentityMonitoringLog and audit user activityShield Event Monitoring, Login History, IdP logsPolicy enforcerEnforce who can do whatProfiles / permission sets, login policies, MFA policy
Core terms





















































































TermMeaningSalesforce angleIdentityThe unique identifier for a user (employee ID, username, email)Username, FederationIdentifier on UserAuthentication (AuthN)Proving who you arePassword, MFA, SSO assertionAuthorization (AuthZ)What you may do once authenticatedProfiles, permission sets, sharing — see Permissions & Sharing overview. Design to least privilegeIdentity storeSystem of record for identity data + credentialsActive Directory, LDAPIdentity Provider (IdP)Authenticates users and asserts identity to other apps; a layer on top of the identity storeOkta, Entra ID, ADFS, Ping — or Salesforce itselfService Provider (SP)The app the user wants to reach; trusts the IdPSalesforce (usually)Relying partyOIDC/OAuth term for an SP that relies on an external IdPSalesforce with an Auth ProviderSSOAuthenticate once, access many appsSAML, OIDCFederation IDStable unique key linking an IdP identity to the SP userUser.FederationIdentifier (case-sensitive)MFA / 2FAVerify with two or more categories: know / have / areSee mfa-and-step-up-authenticationProvisioning / deprovisioningCreate / update / disable user records in the SPSee user-provisioning-and-lifecycleRBACAccess granted via roles/groups mapped to SP permissionsIdP group → Permission Set (Group)IDaaSIdentity delivered as SaaSOkta, Auth0, Entra IDLDAPProtocol for querying hierarchical directoriesDirectory behind AD / OpenLDAPKerberosTicket-based SSO inside a corporate network (KDC issues TGT → service ticket)Usually fronted by the IdP / ADFS (Integrated Windows Auth)


                  
                  Note
                  
                

The IdP vs identity store distinction is a common board probe. The IdP standardises the authentication experience and protocols; it can delegate the actual credential check to an identity store (e.g. Okta reaching back to AD).




                  
                  MFA is not "three factors" 
                  
                

MFA means two or more factor categories (knowledge, possession, inherence). 2FA is simply the two-factor case.


Service user vs context user






























Service user (named principal)Context user (per-user / per-user principal)HowOne integration user authenticates every callEach end user authenticates individually to the target systemProsSimple; one credential to rotate; easy to scaleHonest audit trail; target enforces that user’s permissions; least privilegeConsEveryone gets the integration user’s access; weak audit; breaks least privilegeMore complex; needs token storage/refresh per user; user must exist in both systemsWhen to useBack-end batch/system integration, no user contextUser-facing callouts where sharing/FLS must reflect the real user
See Named Credentials — a Named Credential with Named Principal vs Per User identity type is this exact choice in practice.
Standards and protocols


                  
                  Board rule 
                  
                

Use standard protocols (SAML, OAuth 2.0, OIDC). Do not invent custom authentication schemes in a board solution.










































ProtocolDoesFormatUse forAvoid forSAML 2.0Authentication (and attribute exchange)XML assertion, signed (XML-DSig)Browser-based enterprise SSOMobile apps, JavaScript clients, APIsOAuth 2.0Authorization — delegated access to a resourceAccess/refresh tokensAPI access on a user’s behalf, server-to-serverAuthentication on its own (it proves access was granted, not who the user is)OpenID ConnectAuthentication layered on OAuth 2.0JSON, ID token (JWT)Social sign-on, modern SSO, mobile/SPA—KerberosIntranet SSOTicketsInternal Windows networkAnything leaving the corporate network
Trust in SAML is established by certificates: the IdP signs the assertion with its private key; the SP verifies with the IdP’s public certificate uploaded in advance. See my-domain-and-login-controls for certificate management.
Token types





















































TokenUsed inPurposeNotesAccess tokenOAuth, OIDCPresented to the resource server to call APIsShort-lived; Salesforce session ID behind itRefresh tokenOAuth, OIDCObtain new access tokens without re-loginLong-lived (policy-controlled); why you log into mobile apps once. Store securelyID tokenOIDC onlyProves who the user is; signed JWT with claimsValidate signature, iss, aud, expAuthorization codeWeb server flow (and PKCE)One-time code exchanged for tokensShort-lived; travels via the browser, tokens do notSAML assertionSAMLSigned XML statement of identity + attributes + validity windowAlso usable in the SAML Bearer flowJWTJWT Bearer, ID token, asset tokenCompact signed (JWS) or encrypted (JWE) claims: header · payload · signatureMost are signed, not encryptedSession IDBrowserIdentifies a logged-in browser sessionCookie; protect with HttpOnly, IP lock — see session-settings
OAuth role vocabulary: client (the app asking), resource owner (the user), authorization server, resource server, client ID / secret (called consumer key / secret in Salesforce). The secret must never reach a browser or device the user controls.
Related

iam — one-page cheat sheet and decision table
OAuth 2.0 Flows — per-flow comparison and sequence steps
iam-solution-design-and-scenarios — putting it together for the board

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: IAM Solution Design and Board Scenarios
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
How to turn the building blocks into a defensible board answer. Read after iam-concepts-and-terminology.
Decision flow

Who authenticates? Employee · partner · customer · system/integration · device.
Where do identities live? Corporate IdP/AD · HR system · none (self-registration) · third-party (social).
What client? Browser · mobile app · SPA · server · CLI/IoT.
How strong? MFA at IdP · Salesforce MFA · step-up for sensitive data.
How do users arrive and leave? JIT · SCIM · middleware · self-registration; freeze + deactivate + revoke.
What breaks operationally? Certificate expiry, IdP outage, MFA lost-device, API caller IP change.

Pattern table
















































































ScenarioRecommended approachDetailEmployees, corporate IdP, browserSAML SP-initiated SSO with Federation ID; MFA at the IdPsaml-ssoEmployees, starting from an IdP portalAdd IdP-initiated on the same SAML configsaml-ssoSeveral IdPs (acquisition, contractors)Multiple SAML configs + Login Discovery / per-IdP buttonssaml-ssoMultiple Salesforce orgs / sites, one loginHub-and-spoke: one org as IdP, others SPssaml-ssoPartners with their own IdPFederate partner IdP to Experience Cloud site (SAML/OIDC); Partner Community licencecustomer-identity-and-headless-identityB2C self-registration, social loginExperience Cloud + External Identity or Customer Community licence + auth providers + registration handleropenid-connect-and-auth-providersFully custom mobile/SPA loginHeadless Identity or Authorization Code + PKCEcustomer-identity-and-headless-identityServer-to-server, no userJWT Bearer (cert-based), integration user, pre-authorisedoauth-tokens-and-external-client-appsM2M where certs are impracticalClient Credentials with a run-as integration useroauth-tokens-and-external-client-appsIntegration needs per-user permissionsContext user: Per-User Named Credential / OAuth auth code per useriam-concepts-and-terminologyCentral IdP and many microservicesOAuth Token Exchangeoauth-tokens-and-external-client-appsMFA step-up on sensitive dataHigh Assurance session + session-based permission setmfa-and-step-up-authenticationLegacy directory, no SAML/OIDCDelegated authentication — last resortsaml-ssoAutomated joiner/leaverIdP SCIM connector or MuleSoft + Federation IDuser-provisioning-and-lifecycle
Worked scenarios
1. Global employer, Okta, 40k employees, 3 Salesforce orgs

Situation: Employees use Okta; sales, service and a regional org. They want one login and to be removed from all orgs on exit. Regulators want MFA.
Solution: Okta is the enterprise IdP (SAML SP-initiated + IdP-initiated tile) to every org; Federation ID = employee number. MFA in Okta (phishing-resistant for admins) and AuthnContextClassRef mapped to High Assurance. Okta SCIM connector provisions and deactivates users and assigns permission set groups from Okta groups. My Domain per org; password form removed from login pages; break-glass admins with Salesforce MFA.
Why not Salesforce-as-IdP hub? Okta already covers the whole application estate; making an org the IdP duplicates identity governance.
Watch for: certificate rotation per org, group-to-permission drift, sandboxes needing separate SAML configs.

2. Retailer, 5 million consumers, mobile app + web

Situation: Consumers register, log in with Apple/Google or email OTP, manage preferences and consent. Brand wants a fully custom mobile login.
Solution: Experience Cloud site + External Identity licences; self-registration through a configurable handler creating Contact + shared account model; Apple/Google as auth providers; passwordless email/SMS code. Mobile app uses Headless Identity + PKCE; web uses hosted login with Login Discovery. Consent captured via login flow (privacy-and-consent-management).
Trade-offs: Headless gives UX control but you own bot protection, password reset hardening and token storage. Hosted pages are cheaper to run.
Watch for: account model and ownership skew at 5M contacts; API/login volume limits; email verification before account linking.

3. Nightly integration from ERP and CI/CD deployments

Situation: On-prem ERP loads orders; a Jenkins pipeline deploys metadata.
Solution: External client app per client, JWT Bearer with a certificate per environment, admin-pre-authorised integration user with a minimal permission set; IP relaxation only if egress IP is not stable; secrets/keys in a vault. Certificate expiry alert 60 days ahead.
Why not username-password: credentials in transit, blocked by default on newer orgs, bypasses interactive MFA.
Watch for: the integration user is a service user; if the ERP must act with real user permissions use per-user OAuth instead.

4. Sensitive financial data inside the CRM

Situation: Relationship managers can read all accounts but only view tax IDs and export client lists when strongly authenticated.
Solution: Tax ID encrypted with Platform Encryption (cryptography); permission to view it granted by a session-activation-required permission set; High Assurance via MFA (IdP AuthnContextClassRef or Salesforce Authenticator step-up); Transaction Security policy to block bulk export without step-up.
Trade-offs: extra friction vs least privilege; keep the step-up window short.

5. Partner portal with partners’ own IdPs

Situation: 200 partners; each has its own corporate IdP; partner users need leads/opps.
Solution: Experience Cloud with Partner Community licences; SAML (or OIDC) per partner IdP with Federation ID; JIT with a custom handler mapping partner org attributes to Account/Contact and permission set; partner admins manage their users via delegated administration; deprovisioning via partner IdP + periodic reconciliation.
Alternative: a shared customer-identity IdP that brokers all partner IdPs, if partner count grows large.

Anticipated examiner questions

















































QuestionStrong answerWhat happens when a user’s email changes?Match on Federation ID, not email/usernameHow does Salesforce know the IdP performed MFA?AuthnContextClassRef / session level, or Salesforce step-upHow are leavers removed?Provisioning (SCIM/middleware) → freeze → deactivate → revoke tokens; JIT does not deprovisionWhy not delegated authentication?Password reaches Salesforce and a custom endpoint; availability risk; SAML is standardWhy JWT Bearer over username-password?Cert-based, no password in transit, pre-authorised, not blocked by defaultWhat if the IdP is down?Break-glass admin path with Salesforce MFA; monitor and runbook; availability SLA in the IdP selectionWhat if a certificate expires?SSO/JWT/mTLS fail; certificate register, alerts, overlap rotationIdP-initiated vs SP-initiated?SP-initiated for deep links and request correlation; IdP-initiated for portal tilesSAML or OIDC?SAML for enterprise browser SSO; OIDC for consumer/social/mobileHow do you secure a mobile app login?Auth Code + PKCE or Headless APIs; refresh tokens in secure storage; no implicit flow


                  
                  Board defence checklist 
                  
                

For every IAM recommendation state: (1) licence type, (2) My Domain and login-page change, (3) MFA strategy, (4) provisioning and deprovisioning path, (5) the matching key (Federation ID), (6) certificate/token expiry and the break-glass plan. Examiners test the operational story, not the happy path.


Related

my-domain-and-login-controls — login restrictions and certificates
Integration Patterns (Official Reference) — where authentication fits in integration design

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: Identity & Access Management
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
One-page cheat sheet for the domain. Deep dives:













































TopicNoteVocabulary, protocols, tokens, service vs context useriam-concepts-and-terminologySAML flows, configuration, Salesforce as IdP, delegated authsaml-ssoOIDC, social sign-on, auth providers, registration handlersopenid-connect-and-auth-providersOAuth clients, External Client Apps, flow selectionoauth-tokens-and-external-client-appsMFA, High Assurance, session-based permission sets, login flowsmfa-and-step-up-authenticationJIT, SCIM, joiner/mover/leaveruser-provisioning-and-lifecycleCustomer/partner identity, licences, Headless Identitycustomer-identity-and-headless-identityMy Domain, certificates, IP/login restrictionsmy-domain-and-login-controlsPattern table, worked scenarios, examiner Q&Aiam-solution-design-and-scenarios


                  
                  Platform change 
                  
                

Connected App creation is restricted from Spring ‘26 — use External Client Apps for new OAuth/SAML apps. See oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps.


Core Concepts

Identity Provider (IdP) — the system that authenticates the user and asserts identity (e.g. Okta, Azure AD, ADFS)
Service Provider (SP) — the system that consumes the assertion and grants access (e.g. Salesforce)
Salesforce can act as both IdP and SP — as SP for employee/partner SSO, as IdP for connected apps or other systems


SAML SSO
SAML 2.0 is the dominant enterprise SSO protocol; XML-based assertions carry user identity and attributes.
IdP-Initiated Flow

User logs into IdP portal (already authenticated)
IdP generates a SAML Assertion and POSTs it to Salesforce ACS (Assertion Consumer Service) URL
Salesforce validates the assertion, maps to a user record, creates a session


When to use: Employees already SSO’d into a corporate portal (Okta, AD FS); user starts in the IdP
Risk: No SP context in the assertion — any valid assertion can replay into Salesforce

SP-Initiated Flow

User accesses a Salesforce URL; not authenticated
Salesforce redirects to IdP with an AuthnRequest
IdP authenticates user, returns SAML Response to Salesforce ACS URL
Salesforce validates, maps user, creates session


When to use: User lands directly on a Salesforce URL; most secure for deep-link scenarios

SAML Configuration in Salesforce

Setup → Single Sign-On Settings → enable SAML
Upload IdP certificate; configure Issuer, Entity ID, ACS URL
My Domain is a prerequisite — provides org-specific login URL needed as ACS endpoint
User matching: by Federation ID, username, or email (Salesforce username = SAML NameID by default)



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Examiners often ask: If a user’s email changes, what breaks? → If NameID is mapped to username/email, SSO breaks. Use Federation ID (persistent, separate from email) to decouple identity from email.



OpenID Connect (OIDC) and Social Sign-On

OIDC is OAuth 2.0 + an ID Token (JSON/JWT) that carries user identity claims
Used for Social Sign-On (Google, Facebook, Apple) and modern employee SSO
Salesforce supports OIDC as both SP (consuming tokens from an external IdP) and IdP (issuing tokens)




































SAMLOIDCFormatXML assertionJSON ID token (JWT)Protocol baseSAML 2.0OAuth 2.0Primary useEnterprise employee SSOConsumer / B2C / mobile SSODiscoveryStatic metadata XML/.well-known/openid-configurationBest forLegacy enterprise IdPs (ADFS)Modern IdPs, social login, mobile apps
Configuring Social Sign-On

Setup → Auth. Providers → create provider (Google, Facebook, custom OIDC)
Generates a Callback URL to register with the third-party IdP
Registration handler Apex class maps the external identity to a Salesforce user (create or match)


My Domain

Org-specific subdomain: mycompany.my.salesforce.com
Required for: SSO configuration, Lightning components in iframes, Connected Apps, Einstein features
Login Policy: can restrict login to SSO only (block username/password) — useful post-SSO cutover
Prevent iframe login attacks: My Domain login page enforces same-origin restrictions



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

My Domain is a prerequisite before deploying SSO. Failing to set it up is a common migration gap.



MFA / 2FA
Salesforce requires MFA for all users logging in via UI (effective Feb 2022, contractually enforced).
Verification Methods





























MethodNotesSalesforce AuthenticatorPush notification app; trusted networks / trusted devicesTOTP app (e.g. Google Authenticator)Time-based one-time passwordBuilt-in authenticatorPlatform biometrics (Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello)Security key (FIDO2/WebAuthn)Hardware token; phishing-resistantSMS/email OTPNot recommended by Salesforce for high-assurance
MFA Enforcement Options

UI login: permission set or profile → MFA enforcement
API: API-only users exempt from MFA UI prompt; JWT Bearer / Client Credentials flows are not subject to interactive MFA
SSO: Salesforce can delegate MFA verification to the IdP via High Assurance session level

High Assurance Sessions

A session level assigned when the IdP asserts MFA was satisfied (via SAML AuthnContextClassRef = PasswordProtectedTransport or custom)
Session-based permission sets can be gated on High Assurance — grants elevated access only after MFA step-up
Use to gate sensitive operations (e.g. view encrypted fields, export data)



                  
                  CTA exam trap 
                  
                

“How does Salesforce know the external IdP performed MFA?” → The IdP must include the correct AuthnContextClassRef value in the SAML assertion, OR the session must be promoted to High Assurance by re-authenticating via Salesforce Authenticator.



Connected Apps
A Connected App is the configuration object for any OAuth or SSO integration.
Key Settings





























SettingPurposeOAuth ScopesDefine what the token can access (api, refresh_token, etc.)Callback URLWhere Salesforce redirects after auth (must match exactly)IP RelaxationControls whether IP restrictions are enforced for this appRefresh Token PolicyWhen refresh tokens expire (idle timeout, fixed expiry, or never)Admin-Approved Users OnlyRestricts the app to specific profiles/permission sets
IP Relaxation Options

Enforce IP restrictions — respects org-level trusted IP ranges
Relax IP restrictions with second factor — bypasses IP restriction if MFA satisfied
Relax IP restrictions — bypasses entirely (use for server-to-server integrations with JWT Bearer)



                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

Username-Password OAuth flow is blocked if IP is not in trusted range unless IP relaxation is set. Examiners test this when an integration suddenly fails after a network change.



OAuth 2.0 Flows
See also OAuth 2.0 Flows for the full comparison table.













































FlowUse CaseUser InteractionWeb Server (Auth Code)Web apps with server-side secret storageBrowser redirectWeb Server + PKCESPAs, mobile — no secret storedBrowser redirect, no secretJWT BearerServer-to-server, CI/CD, integrationsNone (pre-approved)Client CredentialsDaemon / machine-to-machineNoneDevice FlowIoT, CLI toolsCode displayed on deviceUsername-PasswordLegacy integrations (avoid)Credentials in requestSAML BearerWhen a SAML assertion is already held (federated users making API calls)None
JWT Bearer Flow — CTA favourite

Client creates a JWT signed with a private key
Sends JWT to login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token
Salesforce validates signature against the Connected App’s uploaded certificate
Returns access token (no user interaction, no refresh token)


Requires: pre-authorise the user in the Connected App (admin-approved or direct URL approval)
Best for: integration users, CI/CD pipelines, automated processes


Delegated Authentication

Pre-SAML Salesforce-specific mechanism; Salesforce calls a customer-hosted web service to validate credentials
Salesforce sends username + password to the customer endpoint; endpoint returns success/failure
When you’d still see it: legacy on-prem AD integration before SAML was available; some older orgs still running it
Trade-off: customer must host and maintain the endpoint; single point of failure; password transmitted to SF































Delegated AuthSAML SSOProtocolCustom SOAP callSAML 2.0Password visibilitySF sends password to customer endpointPassword never leaves IdPComplexitySimple endpoint to buildIdP configuration requiredRecommendedNo — legacy onlyYes

Salesforce Identity Licenses






























LicenseAudienceKey FeaturesSalesforce (full)Internal employeesFull CRM + identityIdentity (add-on)Employees needing SSO/MFA onlyNo CRM objects; SSO, MFA, Connected AppsExternal IdentityHigh-volume B2C / identity-only external usersSelf-registration, social login, passwordless; lowest cost external user; limited object accessCustomer / Partner Community (+ Login variants)Customers and partners needing portal CRM accessSharing sets / sharing rules, reports (Plus), Leads/Opps (Partner)
“Customer Identity” is the capability set (CIAM) delivered through Experience Cloud and these external licences, not a separate licence in this table.


                  
                  CTA exam point 
                  
                

For “customers log in to a branded portal, register themselves and use social login” at large scale, External Identity is the cost-effective licence; step up to Customer Community Plus only if users need reports or richer sharing. See customer-identity-and-headless-identity.



Certificates and Key Management

Setup → Certificate and Key Management
Self-signed certificate: quick, Salesforce-managed; not trusted by most external systems
CA-signed (keystore) certificate: signed by a trusted CA; required for inbound HTTPS, mTLS, and many IdP integrations
Used for: SAML IdP certificate upload, JWT Bearer signing, mTLS outbound (Named Credentials), mTLS inbound



                  
                  Certificate expiry risk 
                  
                

Expired certificate breaks SSO (SAML signature validation fails), JWT Bearer flows, and Named Credential mTLS. Put certificate renewal dates in a governance calendar.



Session Security

























SettingPurposeSession TimeoutIdle timeout before re-authentication (15 min–8 hrs)Session Security LevelStandard vs High Assurance — gates elevated actionsIP LockingBind session to the IP it was created onConcurrent Session LimitMax simultaneous sessions per user
Session-Based Permission Sets

Assign a permission set that is inactive by default
Activated at runtime when session level is promoted to High Assurance (MFA step-up)
Insert a record into SessionPermSetActivation (session ID + permission set ID) to activate programmatically; or use a Flow on a Lightning app page — no code required
The PermissionSet SOAP API object has HasActivationRequired Boolean field
Deactivates when the session ends — must be re-activated on next login
Permission Set Groups can also have Session Activation Required — select during group creation
Pattern: lock sensitive data behind step-up auth — user does MFA → session promoted → permission set activates → access granted


Headless Identity
For custom-branded login UIs (mobile apps, SPAs) that don’t use Salesforce’s hosted login page.

Implement OAuth 2.0 Web Server + PKCE or JWT Bearer on the client side
Experience Cloud supports Headless Registration and Login APIs — call via REST to register/login without Salesforce UI
Key flows: passwordless (email/SMS OTP), TOTP, social login via OIDC — all callable programmatically
When to use: fully custom mobile app or SPA where the Salesforce login page UX is not acceptable


Network-Based Security

Login Hours (per profile) — restrict hours when users can log in; to prohibit a day, set Start = 12 AM and End = End of Day
Trusted IP Ranges — org-wide (Setup → Network Access) and per-profile; users within a trusted range skip the identity verification (device activation) challenge
Profile IP Restrictions — when “Enforce login IP ranges on every request” is enabled in Session Settings, requests outside the range are blocked mid-session, not just at login



                  
                  Note
                  
                

Users are NOT asked for a verification code the first time they log in to Salesforce.



Device Activation
When a user logs in from an unrecognised browser or application, Salesforce prompts for identity verification. Priority order of methods:

Push notification / location-based (Salesforce Authenticator connected to the account)
U2F security key registered with the account
TOTP verification code from a mobile authenticator app
SMS OTP to verified mobile number
Email OTP to registered email address


Custom Login Flows
Allow you to build post-authentication processes (using Flow Builder or Visualforce) and associate them with profiles.
Benefits

Collect / update user data at login
Enforce strong authentication (hardware, SMS, biometric, TOTP)
Geo-fencing or external identity service check
Limit concurrent sessions
Run confirmation processes (secret question, ToS acceptance)
Create granular policies (e.g. notify on off-hours login)

Setup

Create a Flow or Visualforce page for the login logic
Designate it as a login flow; associate with profiles in Setup → Login Flows
Applies on every login from: Salesforce UI, communities, Salesforce app, Salesforce for Outlook
Call Auth.SessionManagement.finishLoginFlow() to complete the flow and redirect to Home, or finishLoginFlow(startURL) for a specific URL

Limitations

Can’t apply to API logins or when sessions are passed via frontdoor.jsp from a non-UI context
Supports all authentication methods: username/password, delegated auth, SAML SSO, social sign-on


Password Policies

Set history, length, complexity, and lockout policy per profile
Passwords cannot exceed 16,000 bytes
Logins limited to 3,600 per hour per user (orgs created after Summer ‘08)
Admin can expire all passwords on demand: Setup → Expire All Passwords


CTA Decision Framework — Which IAM Pattern When

















































ScenarioRecommended ApproachInternal employees with corporate AD/OIDC IdPSAML SP-initiated SSO via IdP (Okta, Azure AD, ADFS)Employees starting from Salesforce URLSAML SP-initiated (AuthnRequest sent to IdP)B2C customers self-registeringCustomer Identity licence + OIDC/social login + self-registration handlerPartner portal with existing IdPSAML SSO + Partner Community licenceServer-to-server integration (no user)JWT Bearer (no user interaction, pre-authorised)Automation/CI pipelineJWT Bearer or Client CredentialsLegacy on-prem AD, no SAML supportDelegated Authentication (last resort)Mobile app with custom login UIHeadless Identity + PKCE web server flowMFA step-up for sensitive dataHigh Assurance session + session-based permission setExternal users need SSO to a communitySAML or OIDC configured on Experience Cloud site


                  
                  Board defence tip 
                  
                

Always pair your IAM recommendation with: (1) the licence type, (2) the My Domain requirement, (3) the MFA strategy, and (4) what happens at certificate/token expiry. Examiners test the operational story, not just the happy path.

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: MFA and Step-Up Authentication
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
How Salesforce verifies how strongly a user authenticated, and how you raise that bar for sensitive actions. Complements session-settings (timeouts, IP lock) and saml-sso.
MFA is a contractual requirement
Salesforce requires customers to enable MFA for all users accessing the UI of Salesforce products. It can be satisfied by:

Salesforce-native MFA on direct (username/password) logins, or
MFA at the IdP for SSO users — SSO with MFA enforced upstream satisfies the requirement, so you do not make SSO users do it twice.

Relevant permissions: Multi-Factor Authentication for User Interface Logins (UI) and for API Logins. Interactive MFA does not apply to non-interactive flows such as JWT Bearer or Client Credentials; those rely on certificates/secrets and IP controls (oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps).
Verification methods



































MethodCounts toward MFA?NotesSalesforce AuthenticatorYesPush approval, location-based automation, trusted locationsTOTP authenticator app (Google/Microsoft Authenticator, Authy)YesTime-based 6-digit codeSecurity key (WebAuthn / U2F, e.g. YubiKey)YesPhishing-resistant; strongestBuilt-in authenticator (Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello)YesPlatform biometrics via WebAuthnSMS / email / voice codeNoUsable for identity verification (device activation, password reset), not as the MFA factor


                  
                  Common trap 
                  
                

SMS and email codes verify identity on an unrecognised device but are not accepted as the MFA factor. Do not propose them as the compliance answer.


Device activation (identity verification)
When a user logs in from an unrecognised browser or device, or an IP outside the trusted ranges, Salesforce challenges them to verify identity. This is distinct from MFA. Methods are offered in priority order: Salesforce Authenticator push → security key → TOTP → SMS → email.

Logins from trusted IP ranges (org Network Access or profile login IP ranges) skip the activation challenge.
First login is not challenged by a code in the normal case; the challenge is for new browsers/devices afterwards.

Session security levels and High Assurance
Each session has a security level:

















LevelHow reachedStandardUsername/password, SSO without MFA context, social loginHigh AssuranceLogin that included MFA, or step-up verification during the session
How the level is raised:

Salesforce MFA at login or step-up → High Assurance.
SSO with MFA at the IdP: the SAML assertion must carry the right AuthnContextClassRef (a value that maps to a session level in Setup → Login Settings / SSO settings) so Salesforce knows MFA was performed.
Step-up on demand: a user or connected app requests High Assurance; Salesforce prompts for MFA.



                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

“How does Salesforce know the external IdP performed MFA?” → The IdP asserts it in the SAML AuthnContextClassRef (mapped to a session level), or the session is promoted to High Assurance by re-verifying with a Salesforce MFA method.


Where High Assurance is enforced

Profile / permission-based: Session security level required at login in profile session settings.
Connected / External Client App policy: Require high assurance session (or require MFA).
Session-based permission sets (below).
Transaction Security policies (Shield / Event Monitoring) can trigger step-up on events like report export or API anomalies.

Session-based permission sets
A way to grant sensitive access only while strongly authenticated.

Permission set (or permission set group) flagged Session Activation Required. Inactive by default.
Activated at runtime by creating a SessionPermSetActivation record (session + permission set) — via Flow on a Lightning page, Apex, or automatically when the session reaches High Assurance.
Deactivates when the session ends.

Pattern: user opens sensitive data → prompted for MFA → session promoted → permission set activates → access granted. Use to protect encrypted-field access, data export, approval of payments. See Session-Based Permission Sets and Permission Set Groups for the permission side, and cryptography for Shield.
Custom login flows
Run a Flow (or Visualforce) after authentication and before the user lands in the app. Assign by profile in Setup → Login Flows.

























Use forNotesCollect missing data / progressive profilingFields on User/ContactTerms-of-service or consent captureTies to privacy-and-consent-managementExtra verification (TOTP, security question, external risk call)Strong auth beyond platform defaultsGeo-fencing, off-hours alerts, concurrent session limitsCombine with Apex/Flow checks
Details:

Applies to UI logins across username/password, delegated, SAML, and social — including Experience Cloud and the mobile app.
Does not apply to API logins or frontdoor.jsp sessions from non-UI contexts.
Call Auth.SessionManagement.finishLoginFlow() (or finishLoginFlow(startUrl)) to end the flow and continue.
If the flow doesn’t finish, the user is not logged in.

Trade-offs









































OptionProsConsWhen to useMFA at the IdPOne experience, central policy, reuse existing factorsSalesforce must be told via AuthnContextClassRef; no per-Salesforce step-up unless re-promptedEnterprise SSOSalesforce-native MFAWorks for direct logins and step-upSeparate enrolmentNon-SSO users, break-glass admins, step-upSecurity keys (WebAuthn)Phishing-resistantHardware logisticsAdmins, privileged usersSession-based permission setsLeast privilege with time-bound accessExtra configuration; users must step upSensitive data tiersLogin flowsCustom logic at loginUI-only; extends login latencyConsent, progressive profiling
Related

iam-solution-design-and-scenarios — “MFA step-up for sensitive data” pattern
my-domain-and-login-controls — IP ranges, login hours, password policy

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: My Domain, Certificates and Login Controls
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
The org-level plumbing that every SSO / OAuth design depends on: the login URL, the certificates that carry trust, and the policies that gate who can log in from where.
My Domain

Your org-specific hostname, for example mycompany.my.salesforce.com (and mycompany.sandbox.my.salesforce.com for sandboxes).
Prerequisite for SSO: it provides the SP login URL and ACS endpoint, and is how SP-initiated flows find the org (saml-sso).
Also required for: Lightning Components in many contexts, connected / external client apps, auth providers on the login page, Login Discovery, and identity-related branding.
Login page controls (Setup → My Domain → Authentication Configuration):

Show or hide the username/password form.
Add buttons for each SAML IdP and auth provider.
Enable Login Discovery.


Prevent login from login.salesforce.com (and the generic URL) after cutover so users cannot bypass SSO via the old entry point.



                  
                  SSO cutover checklist 
                  
                

Deploy My Domain → configure SAML/auth provider → set Federation IDs → test with a pilot group → remove password form from login page → disable direct login by profile → keep a break-glass admin with MFA and a locked-down path.


Certificate and key management
Setup → Certificate and Key Management.






























TypeUseNotesSelf-signedQuick setup; SAML request signing; Salesforce-as-IdP; JWT signingNot trusted by external CAs; fine when the counterparty uploads the cert directlyCA-signedInbound/outbound TLS, mTLS, many partner integrationsRequires CSR → CA → importImported keystore (JKS)Move an existing key pair into SalesforceNeeded for some corporate PKICustomer-managed BYOK keysPlatform EncryptionSee cryptography
Used for: SAML IdP signing and request signing, JWT Bearer private-key counterpart, mutual TLS (inbound and outbound via Named Credentials), and external client app OAuth certificates.


                  
                  Expiry is an outage 
                  
                

An expired certificate breaks SSO (signature validation fails), JWT Bearer integrations and Named Credential mTLS. Keep a certificate register with owner, expiry and rotation steps; use overlapping certificates where the protocol allows. Related: Mutual TLS (2-Way SSL), Named Credentials.


Login restrictions













































ControlScopeWhat it doesLogin hoursProfileAllowed hours. To block a day set start = 12:00 AM and end = End of Day (same moment)Login IP rangesProfileOnly these IPs may log in with that profile; outside → blockedTrusted IP rangesOrg (Network Access)Logins from these IPs skip the identity-verification (device activation) challenge; do not by themselves block othersEnforce login IP ranges on every requestSession settingsApplies profile IP ranges to every request, not just at loginLock sessions to IP / domain, HttpOnly, secure cookiesSession settingsAnti-hijack; full detail in session-settingsSession timeoutOrg / profileIdle timeout, warning popupConcurrent session limitVia login flow / ApexLimit parallel sessions


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Org-level Trusted IP ranges relax verification; profile Login IP ranges restrict access. Examiners like to see you distinguish them. Note that OAuth flows that depend on the user’s profile (e.g. username-password) are also bound by these ranges unless the app uses IP relaxation (oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps).


Password policies

Configured org-wide (Setup → Password Policies) and overridden per profile: expiry, history, minimum length, complexity, lockout threshold/duration, “don’t allow password containing username”.
Passwords are limited to 16,000 bytes; maximum 3,600 logins per hour per user in orgs created after Summer ‘08 (existing note: iam).
Expire all passwords on demand after an incident.
Prefer passwordless/SSO/MFA to password complexity rules; SSO-only orgs should still protect the break-glass accounts.
Forgot-password flows for external users: branded pages, OTP/email links — customer-identity-and-headless-identity.

Monitoring and audit

Login History (6 months), Login Forensics (Shield/Event Monitoring), Setup Audit Trail, Login Event and Login As logging.
Event Monitoring / Transaction Security to alert on anomalous logins, impossible travel, mass exports, and trigger step-up (mfa-and-step-up-authentication).
Alert on certificate expiry, failed SAML assertions (SAML Validation Tool in Setup helps debug) and unusual connected-app usage.

Related

session-settings — session timeout and cookie settings
Permissions & Sharing overview — authorisation after login
