CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: IAM Terms
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
This section will cover all of the important IAM terms that you should be familiar with for the CTA Board.
What is IAM?
IAM or Identity and Access Management is the process of defining the tools, processes, monitoring and governance to leverage in order to grant internal and external users access to a system. For external users IAM is sometimes referenced as CIAM (Customer Identity and Access Management).

The key elements of an IAM Solution

An Identity Repository - A place or system that keeps the personal details of each user. (Something like an LDAP accessible service or database like AD)
A Management Toolbox - To manage, edit, add, and delete the data in the identity repo. (Something like Okta)
A Monitoring Platform - A continuous monitoring solution to log user activities and storing it in an audit log (Something like Salesforce Shield Event Monitoring.
A Policy Enforcer - To regulate and enforce the users access in the system.


Key IAM Terms
Identity - This is pretty straightforward. Identity if the unique identifier you use to identify a user in your system. Typically this is some kind of unique key like an employee id, a user name or an email. The users identity should determine who they are in the system and the rights they have as a user in the system.
Authentication - Authentication is the act of verifying a user is who they say they are. This is normally done by having the user enter a password but it could include things like having the user use an id card, fingerprint scan, facial recognition scan, etc.
Authorization -  Authorization is what happens after a user has been authenticated. It is the act of determining what rights a user has in a given system (Can they access Opportunities, Cases, fields on specific objects, etc). It is critical to ensure you design authorization rights with the principle of least privilege in mind, not just for the CTA Board, but in general.
Identity Store - This is a database or system that is used to hold information about the users that a system is using. This information could be emails, name, numbers, etc as well as the information necessary to authenticate a user. This is typically something like Microsoft Active Directory.
Identity Provider (IdP) - The system that manages the identities for users. IdP’s normally allow you to create, update and maintain identity info for users. It provides authentication services for multiple applications. The primary difference between IdP’s and Identity Stores is that IdP’s do not need to maintain the data used for authentication (passwords, etc). They can connect to an identity store and have it manage that instead. The IdP then just becomes a layer on top of the Identity Store that allows you to standardize the authentication processes and user experience for authentication (Think loggin in everywhere with Okta, but Okta reaches back to Microsoft AD to authenticate a users identity). It’s worth noting that Salesforce can be your IdP for other systems (though it is limited), it can connect to a Microsoft AD Identity store using Identity Connect or your could connect to an LDAP accessible directory service or database using Mulesoft as described here or a more custom solution like Salesforce2Ldap (for the CTA always pick Mulesoft options if asked).
Service Provider (SP) - Service providers are the platforms that actually provide the services/functionality a user is typically using an IdP to login to. So for instance if a user was using Okta to login (IdP) to Salesforce, Salesforce would be the Service Provider (SP). Service Providers have their own user databases typically that determines user permissions (or authorizations) to perform specific operations in the system. The link from the users IdP credentials and the SP credentials is normally provided by Single Sign On (SSO) which we go over below.
Single Sign On (SSO) - Single Sign On is where a user is allowed to authenticate once to access multiple applications. This allows users to be more productive since they have to login less, it also provides a centralized place/tool to monitor user authentication activities and increases security and compliance (login policies, login restrictions, etc). In an SSO setup users are replicated in both the IdP and the SP. The IdP will the full list of a companies users and their authentication mechanisms (passwords, cards, etc) while the SP would just maintain a sub-list of the users allowed to actually work in the SP’s system. To identify the user in the SP from the IdP there needs to be a unique id to link them. This is typically referred to at the federation identifier (there is a field on the user object in Salesforce for this).
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) - Multi-Factor authentication is the process that forces a user to verify their identity in three or more ways. For example, using a password to login (something you know) and then being asked to authenticate using a password sent via text to your mobile phone (something you have) and then having something scan your fingerprint (something you possess). A lighter weight version of MFA is 2FA (two factor authentication). This is a bit simpler, where you have a user authenticate using a password and then send them a one time code via text or email to complete the login. MFA is typically managed by your Identity Provider (IdP).
User Provisioning and Deprovisioning - Pretty simple, this is the act of adding or removing a user from an identity store/repo.
Role-Based Access (RBA) - Role based access effectively controls a users access to different functionalities in different systems. This is normally managed by an IdP or Identity Store. These systems normally have something called Role Based Access Control (RBAC) or Group Memberships. You apply these roles to your users (for example Salesforce - Sales User) and when a user is provisioned in the Service Provider (by a middleware connector or pre-built mechanism) by the IdP they are given a role in the SP that mirrors their role (or group) in the IdP.
Identity as a Service (IDaaS) - These are products like Okta that offer identity products in a Software as a service manner.
LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) - LDAP is a protocol that was designed to provide a standardized mechanism in which to interact data stored in a hierarchical data structure. It is the communication language used to communicate with other directory services servers.
Service User and Context User Authentication - Service user is a single integration user that is used to authenticate every user reaching out to the system in the same way. This is detrimental to the principle of least privilege. Context user is authenticating each user individually with the other system. This methodology allows for a more fine tuned approach to giving the user only the access/privileges they should have.

Common IAM Standards/Protocols
What are IAM Standards/Protocols - The various way data is exchanged between an identity provider and service provider. These protocols are things like SAML, OAuth and OpenID Connect. Using one of these standards to exchange data not only saves time when developing a solution but ensures your authentication mechanisms are secure, scalable and compliant. DO NOT DEVIATE FROM THESE STANDARDS AT A CTA BOARD!
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) -  SAML is an XML based protocol that can be used for both authorization and authentication purposes. SAML Assertions are signed using XML Signature Wrapping which is a form of digital signature. Verifying a this digital signature requires access to a public key (typically a digital certificate). This digital certificate establishes trust between the IdP and SP. The IdP normally generates this certificate and it gets uploaded to the SP to be used to verify SAML assertions sent by the IdP. SAML is most often used for SSO and, ideally, should not be used for mobile phones, javascript and API’s.
Open Authorization (OAuth) - OAuth was created and is used for access delegation (secure delegated access) between a client (basically any connecting application) and a resource server (server being connected to to view or alter data) on behalf of a user. This allows a user to connect to another server without needing to authenticate with that server. Instead a token is used that is issued by an IdP that informs the resource server what the connecting client application is allowed to do.
OpenID Connect - OpenID Connect is based on OAuth 2.0 but is designed for a different purpose. It adds additional functionality on top of OAuth, the most important addition is the additional ID token (This Id is a JWT) that gets generated that contains information about the user and information about the connecting client server. There can also be custom attributes in this ID token. The ID Token can help verify the identity of the individual the token was issued to. This ID Token is digitally signed by its issuing IdP making it easy to validate and determine whether it is legitimate. OpenID Connect is most commonly leveraged for signing in using credentials from a social media platform like Facebook, Twitter, etc. OpenID Connect is leveraged by Salesforce’s Social Sign On. That being said it can also be leveraged for SSO purposes in general but it is unlikely to be used in that way for the CTA Board.
Kerberos - Kerberos is an authentication protocol that allows you to access services across a network using a ticket distribution center. This is effectively an inside the corporate network SSO protocol.  When a user wants to access a service, behind the scenes they connect to the ticket distribution center that authenticates the user and sends them back a ticket granting ticket (TGT). That TGT then gets sent to the Ticket Granting Server (TGS) which decrypts the TGT and sends back a Service Ticket. The service ticket then gets sent to the Service to authenticate the user. The Service server then informs the user that they were successfully identified.

Token Types
Access Tokens - This is a token used in OAuth and OpenId Connect. This is the token sent at the end of the authentication and is used by the requesting client server to get access to resources on the resource server. A copy of this token is stored on the resource server for the longevity of the tokens existence, which is how it is verified.
Refresh Tokens - This is also a token type for OAuth and OpenId Connect. Refresh tokens are issued for clients in specific use cases. The refresh token normally lasts longer than an access token and can sometimes be set to never expire. The refresh token should be stored by the client server and used to get new token whenever needed. Most mobile phone applications utilize refresh tokens to login/connect to the resource server. That’s why you often only login once on mobile apps. Refresh tokens don’t really replace access tokens, they are just an additional token to retrieve a new access token when the old one has expired. They prevent users from needing to login over and over.
ID Token - This is a token only used by OpenId Connect. The ID Token is sent by the client to the resource server to actually verify the identity of the individual user sending the request for access.
JWT (JSON Web Token) - JWT is a standard to format data that can be used to assert the identity of a party to other parties. JWT’s can either be signed tokens called JWS’s (JSON Web Signature) or encrypted tokens called JWE’s(JSON Web Encryption). The most common variety are JWS’s, most JWT’s are signed. JWT’s consist of three main parts after being decoded: a header, a payload and a signature. More info on this in the linked video and page 118 of the Becoming a CTA Book.
Session Token (Session Id) - A session token is a unique string (that is normally hashed) that represents a login session for a user. Session tokens are normally stored in the browser cache and destroyed when a user logs out.
Authorization Code - This token type is only used in one OAuth and OpenId Connect flow (the web-server flow). It is created by the auth server and returned (via the browser) back to the client application. The client then sends this back to the auth server in exchange for an access and potentially a refresh token as well.
SAML Assertion - SAML assertions (like JWT) can be used to authenticate an individual user to a resource server. They contain user identity info, issue time and expiration time.

The Key Authentication Flows for Each Standard
SAML Flows - SAML has three main flows. IdP-Initiated, SP-Initiated and SAML Bearer assertion flow.
SAML IdP-Initiated Flow - This flow is typically used when an organization has an IdP with a home page/application page for their employees to access all applications (service providers).
The steps in this flow are as follows:

The user visits the IdP login/home page.
The home page will check whether the user is authenticated by checking if there is a stored cookie for the IdP domain with a valid session token. If there is no session token the user will see a login page.
The user logs in using their username, password and whatever MFA junk they need to do. They are then redirected to the IdP home page.
The user sees a list of links on the home page to difference service providers, they then click one of those links.
The IdP generates a SAML assertion signed with the IdP’s private key/cert.
The assertion is sent via the browser to the SP.
The SP receives the SAML assertion validates it using the IdPs public key/cert. The user is authenticated and a session token for the specific service provider is created and saved in a browser cookie. The user is redirected to the SP Home page.



SAML SP-Initiated Flow - This flow is typically used when an organization has a login link for the IdP on the SP’s home page, when a user uses a bookmark to traverse to the SP’s homepage, tries to access the SP from a direct link in an email, etc, etc. Basically when the user tries to traverse to the homepage of an SP without going through the IdP first.
The steps in this flow are as follows:

The user visits the homepage of the SP directly.
The SP checks for an existing and valid session token stored in a cookie associated with the SP’s domain.
If there is no valid cookie for the SP, the user is redirected to the IdP via the browser with a SAML assertion request. The target url (SP url) is passed in a parameter called RelayState. The RelayState helps redirect the user to the proper place after logging in with the IdP.
User redirected to the IdP with RelayState param.
The IdP checks for an existing and valid session token stored in a cookie associated with the IdP’s domain.
If there is no cookie, the user is asked to login with the IdP.
After the user logs in successfully a SAML assertion will be created and signed with the IdP private key/cert.
A SAML assertion is sent to the SP via the browser along with RelayState.
The SP receives the assertion and validates it using the IdP’s public key/cert. The user is authenticated and a session token for the SP is stored in a cookie in the browser. The user is then redirected to the page on the SP specified in the RelayState param.



OAuth 2.0 and OpenId Connect Flows
Since OpenId Connect has been built as a layer on top of OAuth most of the flows are shared between them (though there are some differences). There are 7 different flows to memorize for these two protocols, we’ll go over each of them and some key terms below.
Key Terms:
Client Application - An application that is trying to access resources on a resource server. Basically, the application making a request for data on another server.
Authorization Server - The auth server grants the right authorization to the logged in user. Essentially this is the server that grants the rights to access data on the resource server.
Resource Server - This is the server with the data/resources that the client application would like to access on behalf of the user.
Client Id/Consumer Id - A unique id given for the client application to utilize. The auth server generates this value for a specific client app after registering it with the auth server (think connected apps in Salesforce).
Client Secret/Consumer Secret - This key is a confidential unique key that the client app should never expose to the user or any external entities aside from the auth server. The auth server generates this secret when the client application is registered with the auth server (again think connected apps).

Web Server Flow (Auth-Code Flow) - This flow is typically used when a website is trying to access resources from a resource server on behalf of the user. There is one requirement to use this flow, the client server making the connected to the resource server needs a secure way to store the client secret value. The client secret should only ever be used when communicating directly with the auth server. If there is no way to secure the client secret, then this flow shouldn’t be used. This flow will eventually grant the client an access token (and potentially a refresh token) to access data on its servers.
The steps for the Web Server Flow are as follows (More detail on page 129 of Becoming a CTA Book):

The user visits the client application (basically they visit a website) that they have already logged in to. At some point the user travels to a page that needs to access data from a resources server to display data to the user.
The client application checks for an existing and valid access token or refresh token for the current user and the resource server it needs to access.
If no access or refresh token is found by the client application, the client app starts the authorization process by sending an OAuth Request. The client app redirects via the browser to the target authorization endpoint and passes it some parameters.
The authorization request built in step three is sent to the authorization server.
The auth server checks for an existing and valid session token stored in a cookie associated with its domain.
If no session token is found the user is presented with a login screen served by the auth server. Once the user logs in the user will be presented with a screen asking for approval to allow the client app to access specific data (the scopes you would pass as parameters in step 3) on the resource server.
If the user accepts the client app accessing data in step 6, the user is authenticated and an authorization code is generated.
The auth code is sent to the client app via the browser to the redirect_uri (another parameter you would specify in step 3).
The client app sends this auth code to the authorization server to generate an access token.
The auth server receives the POST request the client app sent with the auth code and issues the access token the client app needs.
The client app receives the access token and uses it to request the resources it needs from the resource server.
The resources server responds by sending back the requested resource.



Refresh Token Flow -
The Refresh Token flow is used to get a new access token using a refresh token.
Steps for the Refresh Token Flow (more detail on page 133 of the Becoming a CTA Book):

The user visits the client application (for example a website a user visits). The app tries to access data on behalf of the user from the resource server.
The client app checks for a valid access token for the resource server that corresponds to the user. It finds one but it’s expired, however the client app is unaware it’s expired.
The client app uses the expired access token to request the resource from the resource server.
The resource server returns a response indicating the request isn’t authorized due to the expired token.
The client app uses the refresh token to get a new access token from the authorization server.
The authorization server receives the post request, issues an access token and returns it to the client app.
The client app receives the access token and uses this new token to request resources from the resource server.
The resource server responds and sends back the requested resource.



User Agent Flow (Implicit Flow) -
This flow is less secure than the web server flow and is primarily used for client apps that are unable to provide secure storage for the client secret value. Javascript single page apps and mobile applications are good examples of when this flow is often used.
Steps for the User Agent Flow (more detail on page 134 of the Becoming a CTA Book):

The user starts the application.
The application checks for a valid access token or refresh token. If none are found, the app starts the OAuth/OpenId connect user agent flow. This is similar to the web server flow but the response type passed is token.
The request is sent to the authorization server.
The auth server checks for an existing and valid session token stored in a cookie associated with the servers domain.
The user is presented with a login screen served by the auth server. They enter their username and password to authenticate. They are then presented with a screen asking for approval to allow the app to access specific scopes (resources) on the resource server.
The user is authenticated and an access token is granted. A refresh token and ID token can also be generated depending on the scopes used.
(Steps 7-10 are optional recommended steps if an ID token is retrieved) The client app validates the ID Token by verifying its digital signature.
The client app can use the information in  the ID token to request the full profile details of the logged in user.
Profile details are returned.
The client app uses the access token to request the resources from the resource server.
The resource server sends back the requested resource.



JWT Bearer Flow - The JWT flow is most often used when you want to authorize a client app to a resource server without requiring the user to login. The digital signature in the JWT token will be used to authenticate the client app to the resource server. Since there it is not required the user actually login with this flow, the user will have needed to authorize this app by logging in at a different stage in the client app or be authorized by an admin to be able to execute this flow. A good example of admin authorized users for authentication flows in SF is when you setup a connected app, there is a setting you can adjust called “Admin approved users are pre-authorized”. The users filled out in that section of the connected app are “admin authorized users” that can run the authentication flow. This flow is often used for automated background processes, scheduled jobs, etc.
Steps for the JWT Bearer Flow (more detail on page 137 of the Becoming a CTA Book):

The client app checks for a valid access token.
The client app generates a JWT and signs is using its private key/certificate and then sends this to the auth server to request an access token.
The auth server receives the JWT and validates its signature using the public key/cert of the client app.
The access token is returned to the client app.
The client app uses the access token to request the resource from the resource server.
The resource server returns the requested resource.



The Device Flow - The device flow is normally used for devices that have limited input and display capabilities like TV’s and appliances.
The Asset Token Flow - This flow is normally used for IoT (Internet of Things) devices
The Username-Password Flow -

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: OAuth, Tokens and External Client Apps
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
The identity-side view of OAuth: how to register clients, control them, and choose and constrain flows. For the per-flow sequence steps and scope list see OAuth 2.0 Flows (Integration). For the older detailed walkthrough see oauth-saml-flows-and-iam.
Connected Apps vs External Client Apps
Every OAuth flow except the SAML Assertion flow needs a registered app (OAuth Authorization Flows).


                  
                  Platform change — know this for the board 
                  
                

Connected App creation was restricted as of Spring ‘26. Existing connected apps keep working; Salesforce recommends External Client Apps (ECAs) for new work, and you must contact Support to keep creating connected apps (Connected Apps).










































Connected AppExternal Client AppStatusLegacy; creation restricted from Spring ‘26Recommended for new appsSettings modelSingle definitionDeveloper settings (packaged) split from admin policies (local to each org)OAuth secretsIn the appSplit into a global OAuth settings file (secrets, never packaged) and a local settings filePackagingPackageable in managed packagesdistributionState = local or packageable (1GP / 2GP managed)Metadata APIConnectedAppExternalClientApplication, ExtlClntAppOauthSettings, etc.Sandbox refreshCopiedLocal ECAs are not copied on sandbox clone/refresh; only packaged ones (External Client Apps)
Separation of duties is the design point: developers define what the app can do; subscriber-org admins set who can use it and under which policies, and cannot edit developer settings.
Policies to set on every client









































PolicyOptions / effectOAuth scopesLeast privilege: api, refresh_token/offline_access, openid, web, full (avoid)Callback URLExact match; HTTPSPermitted usersAll users may self-authorize vs Admin-approved users are pre-authorized (required for JWT Bearer, Client Credentials)IP relaxationEnforce IP restrictions / relax with second factor / relax (server-to-server only)Refresh token policyValid until revoked · immediately expire · expire if not used for N · expire after NSession / MFARequire high assurance session; require MFA at loginRequire PKCEFor code flow with public clientsRequire secret for web server / refresh flowsEnforce for confidential clients

Default is five authorizations per client per user; the oldest unused token is revoked when exceeded.
Revoke tokens explicitly (user: Settings → Connected Apps OAuth Usage; admin: OAuth Connections Usage, or revoke via the app’s policies). Do not assume a password reset ends every issued token — design and test your offboarding path.

Choosing and restricting flows




























































ScenarioFlowWhyWeb app with a secure back end, user contextWeb Server (Authorization Code)Secret stays on the server; supports MFASPA / mobile appAuthorization Code + PKCENo secret to store; replaces user-agent/implicitServer-to-server, no user, strongest assuranceJWT BearerCertificate-signed; pre-approved; no secret transmittedMachine-to-machine, can’t manage certsClient CredentialsShared secret; runs as designated integration userCLI / TV / IoT with little inputDeviceUser approves on another deviceIoT devices to be linked to CRM dataAsset TokenDevice-identity JWTCentral IdP fronts many apps / microservicesToken ExchangeSwap an external IdP token for a Salesforce tokenHybrid mobile app needing web sessionHybrid app flowsLinks tokens to the web sessionCustom login UI for external usersAuthorization Code and Credentials (Headless)See customer-identity-and-headless-identityAlready holds IdP SAML assertionSAML Bearer / SAML Assertionsaml-sso


                  
                  Block the weak flows 
                  
                

The user-agent (implicit) and username-password flows pass credentials or tokens through insecure channels and are “considered insecure and not recommended”. Salesforce says to block them; orgs created from Summer ‘23 have username-password blocked by default. You can also block flows that don’t use PKCE. Username-password also bypasses interactive MFA. (OAuth Authorization Flows)




                  
                  Why integrations break after a network change 
                  
                

With “Enforce IP restrictions”, a flow that depends on a user’s profile IP ranges (e.g. username-password) fails once the caller’s egress IP changes. Fix with the correct IP relaxation policy or a certificate-based flow — not by widening trusted IP ranges.


Token lifecycle

Access token — short-lived; tied to a session. Session timeout from the user’s profile/org applies (see session-settings).
Refresh token — exchanges for new access tokens (Refresh Token flow). Governed by the app’s refresh-token policy.
JWT Bearer — no refresh token; the client mints a new signed JWT each time (aud, iss = consumer key, sub = username, exp ≤ 3 minutes).
Revocation — /services/oauth2/revoke; admin revoke; freezing or deactivating a user ends access.
Introspection — /services/oauth2/introspect lets a resource server verify a token.

Securing credentials

Store client secrets and private keys in a secrets manager or a Named Credential / External Credential, never in code (Named Credentials).
Prefer certificate-based flows; rotate certificates before expiry (my-domain-and-login-controls).
Use a dedicated integration user with a minimal permission set for JWT Bearer / Client Credentials.
For stronger transport trust add mutual TLS (Mutual TLS (2-Way SSL)).

Related

openid-connect-and-auth-providers — OIDC scopes and ID tokens
iam-solution-design-and-scenarios

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: OpenID Connect and Authentication Providers
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer on OAuth 2.0. On top of the access token it issues an ID token — a signed JWT carrying claims about the authenticated user (sub, iss, aud, exp, plus profile/email claims). It is the protocol behind social sign-on and most modern IdPs. Terms: iam-concepts-and-terminology.
SAML vs OIDC








































SAML 2.0OIDCBuilt onOwn XML protocolOAuth 2.0Identity artifactSigned XML assertionSigned JWT ID tokenDiscoveryMetadata XML exchange/.well-known/openid-configuration + JWKSFitsBrowser enterprise SSOSocial login, SPA, mobile, API-centric appsTypical IdPADFS, legacy enterpriseGoogle, Apple, Entra ID, Okta, Auth0Board defaultEmployee / partner SSO (saml-sso)Customer / social login


                  
                  Board default 
                  
                

Employees and partners on an enterprise IdP → SAML. Customers and social identities → OIDC via an Authentication Provider. OIDC can do enterprise SSO, but expect SAML to be the expected answer unless the scenario says otherwise.


Authentication Providers (Salesforce as relying party)
An Auth. Provider lets users log in to a Salesforce org or Experience Cloud site with credentials from a third party, and can also give Salesforce an access token to that party’s APIs. Types (Authentication Provider SSO with Salesforce as the Relying Party):

Predefined providers (Google, Facebook, LinkedIn, Apple, Microsoft, and others)
Salesforce-managed providers
OpenID Connect provider (any OIDC-compliant IdP; supply authorize / token / user-info endpoints)
Custom provider (Apex Auth.AuthProviderPluginClass for non-standard OAuth 2.0)

Setup → Auth. Providers. Salesforce generates a Callback URL you register with the third party. Then add the provider as a button on the My Domain login page or the Experience Cloud login page.
Registration handler
The Apex class implementing Auth.RegistrationHandler decides what happens after a successful external login:

















MethodDoescreateUser(portalId, userData)Create (JIT) or link a Salesforce user from the claims. Also creates Account/Contact for external usersupdateUser(userId, portalId, userData)Sync changed claims (name, email) on subsequent logins
Design points:

Decide the match key (email is convenient but risky — an attacker-controlled IdP with an unverified email could take over an account; prefer the verified sub/Federation ID or require verified email).
Decide whether to link a social identity to an existing user or create new, and require re-authentication before linking.
Set the default profile / permission sets / account assignment in code.

Single Logout and token use

Provider tokens can be retrieved with Auth.AuthToken to call the third party’s API (e.g. Google Drive) as the user.
Users can have multiple linked third-party identities (Settings → Third-Party Account Links).

Salesforce as an OpenID Connect provider
An org or Experience Cloud site can act as an OIDC IdP for your own apps.

Register the app as a connected / external client app with the openid (and profile, email) scopes.
Endpoints: authorize, token, UserInfo, JWKS, introspection, and a discovery document.
Related features: Dynamic client registration (clients register themselves with an initial access token) and token introspection so an API gateway can check token state (OAuth Authorization Flows).
OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange lets an app swap a token from an external IdP for a Salesforce token when a central IdP fronts many apps and microservices.

Login Discovery
For multi-IdP or consumer scenarios, Login Discovery asks for an identifier first (email, phone, username), then routes the user to the right method: password, passwordless code, an SSO provider, or an auth provider. Pairs well with M&A estates where users belong to different IdPs. See customer-identity-and-headless-identity.
Trade-offs



































OptionProsConsWhen to useSocial auth provider (Google, Apple, Facebook)Low friction, no password to manage, high conversionLimited assurance; email verification and account-linking risk; dependence on third partyB2C self-registrationEnterprise OIDC provider (Entra ID / Okta)Modern, JSON/JWT, good for SPA/mobileSAML still more common for employee SSOWhen IdP prefers OIDCCustom auth provider pluginSupports non-standard OAuthMaintenance, security reviewLast resortSalesforce as OIDC IdPReuse CRM identities for custom appsNot a full IDaaSApps on the Salesforce user base

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: SAML SSO
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
SAML 2.0 is the default answer for browser-based employee and partner SSO to Salesforce. The IdP authenticates the user and sends a signed XML assertion; Salesforce (the SP) validates it against the IdP’s certificate and creates a session. Terms: iam-concepts-and-terminology.


                  
                  Note
                  
                

SAML suits browser SSO. It is a poor fit for mobile apps, JavaScript clients and APIs — use OAuth/OIDC there (oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps).


Login flows
IdP-initiated

User signs in to the IdP portal / app launcher.
User clicks the Salesforce tile.
IdP builds a signed assertion and posts it via the browser to Salesforce’s ACS (Assertion Consumer Service) URL.
Salesforce validates signature, issuer, audience and validity window, matches the user, creates a session.



Use when: the organisation already has an IdP home page / portal that employees start from.
Weakness: no preceding request, so there is nothing to correlate the response to (no InResponseTo). It is more exposed to unsolicited-response and login-CSRF style attacks; deep links to a specific Salesforce page need extra work.

SP-initiated

User opens a Salesforce URL (bookmark, email link, deep link) with no session.
Salesforce redirects the browser to the IdP with a SAML AuthnRequest and a RelayState (the original target URL).
IdP authenticates the user (or reuses its own session).
IdP returns the assertion + RelayState to the ACS URL.
Salesforce validates, creates the session and sends the user to the RelayState target.



Use when: users land on Salesforce directly. Preserves deep links; response can be tied to a request.
Salesforce supports both on the same configuration; SP-initiated needs the IdP login URL and requires My Domain.

SAML Bearer vs SAML Assertion (API access)




















FlowWhat it doesNeeds connected / external client app?OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer AssertionClient presents a signed SAML assertion to the token endpoint and gets an OAuth access tokenYesSAML Assertion flowFederate to the API the same way as web SSO, no OAuth appNo
(OAuth Authorization Flows). Use when an app already holds an IdP-issued assertion for the user and must call Salesforce APIs as that user.
Configuring Salesforce as the Service Provider
Setup → Single Sign-On Settings. Key fields:













































SettingMeaningIssuer / Entity IDWho the IdP says it is; must match the assertion’s IssuerIdP certificatePublic cert used to verify signatures; expiry breaks SSOSAML Identity TypeWhat identifies the user: Salesforce username, Federation ID, or User IDIdentity LocationNameID element or a named AttributeACS / Login URLUse the My Domain URL (Experience Cloud sites: include /login)Request bindingHTTP Redirect or HTTP POST for SP-initiatedRequest signing certificateSign AuthnRequests if the IdP requires itUser provisioningNone, Standard JIT, or Custom (Apex Auth.SamlJitHandler) — see user-provisioning-and-lifecycleSingle LogoutOptional, if the IdP supports it

Multiple SAML configurations can coexist (e.g. after an acquisition, or employees vs contractors). Combine with Login Discovery or per-IdP buttons on the My Domain login page to route users.
Expose SSO on Experience Cloud sites by using the site’s login URL in the assertion (SAML for Experience Cloud Sites).



                  
                  Exam trap: email change breaks SSO 
                  
                

If the assertion subject is mapped to username or email and that value changes, matching fails. Use a Federation ID (immutable employee ID or GUID) so identity is decoupled from mutable attributes. Federation ID matching is case-sensitive and must be unique.




                  
                  Certificate expiry 
                  
                

The IdP signing certificate uploaded to Salesforce, and Salesforce’s own certificates for IdP/request signing, all expire. Track them in a governance calendar and rotate with overlap. See my-domain-and-login-controls.


Salesforce as the Identity Provider
Salesforce can issue assertions to other SPs (other orgs, Experience Cloud sites, third-party SaaS apps).

Setup → Identity Provider → enable; pick a signing certificate (self-signed is auto-created).
Download the certificate and metadata (or copy the metadata discovery URL).
Add each target app as a SAML connected app / external client app in the IdP org (entity ID, ACS URL, subject type).
Control who can reach the app with profiles / permission sets assigned to it.

Hub-and-spoke multi-org SSO: one org or Experience Cloud site is the authentication hub (IdP); other orgs/sites are the spokes (SPs). Users log in once and move between them (Configure SAML SSO Between Salesforce Orgs or Experience Cloud Sites).


                  
                  CTA note 
                  
                

Salesforce-as-IdP is fine for a hub of Salesforce orgs/sites or a handful of apps. If the enterprise already runs a corporate IdP (Okta, Entra ID), federate Salesforce to that IdP instead of making Salesforce the enterprise-wide IdP — its provisioning, adaptive MFA and app catalogue breadth are limited.


Delegated Authentication (legacy)
Salesforce calls a customer-hosted SOAP web service with the username, password and source IP; the service returns true/false. Needs the Is Single Sign-On Enabled permission on the profile and the endpoint configured.






























Delegated authSAML SSOPassword handlingSalesforce receives the password and forwards itPassword never reaches SalesforceAvailabilityCustomer endpoint is a single point of failure, must be reachable from SalesforceIdP availability, but standard and redundantPhishing resistanceWeakBetter (IdP can enforce MFA / phishing-resistant factors)VerdictLast resort for IdPs with no SAML/OIDC supportDefault
Trade-offs



































OptionProsConsWhen to useSAML SP-initiatedDeep links, request correlationNeeds My Domain and IdP login URLDefault for employeesSAML IdP-initiatedSimple portal UXWeaker CSRF/replay posture, no deep linkExisting corporate app launcherDelegated authWorks with legacy directoryPassword transits Salesforce; custom endpointOnly when no SAML/OIDC possibleSalesforce as IdPFast for Salesforce-only estatesLimited vs enterprise IdPHub-and-spoke of orgs / sites

CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.title: User Provisioning and Lifecycle
CTA-Notes/Security/Identity--and--Access.content:
SSO answers “who is this user right now?“. Provisioning answers “does a Salesforce user exist, with the right access, and does it go away when they leave?” Boards frequently test the leaver path — SSO does not remove users.
Joiner – Mover – Leaver

























StageNeedsMechanismJoinerUser record, profile, permission sets, licence, federation IDJIT, SCIM / IdP connector, middleware, manualMoverRole / permission change when job changesRe-sync from IdP group → permission set groupLeaverAccess removed immediately, licence reclaimedFreeze → deactivate; revoke tokens
Provisioning options




































































OptionHow it worksHandles update?Handles deprovision?NotesManual / Data LoaderAdmin creates usersManualManualSmall orgs onlySAML JIT (Standard)Salesforce creates/updates the user from assertion attributes at loginYes (on login)NoAssertion must supply required fields (e.g. User.ProfileId, Username, Email)SAML JIT (Custom)Apex Auth.SamlJitHandler (createUser, updateUser)Yes (on login)NoMap groups → profile / permission sets; create Contact/Account for external usersAuth provider JITAuth.RegistrationHandler after OIDC/social loginYesNoSee openid-connect-and-auth-providersSCIM / IdP connectorIdP pushes create/update/disable ahead of login via the Salesforce API (Okta, Entra ID connectors use Salesforce’s provisioning APIs, including a SCIM API)Yes (proactive)YesPreferred for enterprises with an IdPIdentity ConnectSalesforce tool that syncs Microsoft AD users to Salesforce user records; deprovision revokes the session (Identity Connect docs)YesYesAD-centric; check current availability and roadmap before recommendingMuleSoft / middlewareIntegration reads LDAP/HR system and writes to SalesforceYesYesBoard preference when integration spans HR/LDAP + SalesforceHR system as source (Workday, SuccessFactors)HR event → IdP → SalesforceYesYesAuthoritative joiners/leavers


                  
                  Key limit of JIT 
                  
                

JIT creates and updates only when the user logs in. A leaver who never logs in again keeps an active, licensed user. Pair JIT with a deprovisioning mechanism (SCIM, middleware, or a scheduled reconciliation).




                  
                  Board default 
                  
                

Enterprise IdP with HR source of truth → IdP-driven provisioning (SCIM/connector) with Federation ID as the key. No suitable connector or a custom HR/LDAP feed → MuleSoft. Small/simple → JIT plus a leaver process.


Identity key strategy

Pick one immutable key per person and store it as Federation ID (employee number or IdP GUID). Do not key on email or username.
Federation ID is unique, case-sensitive, and fixed for the life of the identity.
Align the SAML Identity Type or OIDC claim mapping (saml-sso) with that key.

Access assignment (RBAC)

Map IdP groups to Salesforce permission set groups (not profiles) so a move changes access cleanly. See Permissions & Sharing overview.
JIT handler pattern: read group claims → assign permission set groups; remove those no longer asserted on updateUser.
Use a minimal profile + permission sets; avoid per-user entitlements.
Licence mapping: ensure the handler picks the right user licence; failing here is a common cause of JIT errors.

Leaver handling

Freeze the user (UserLogin.IsFrozen = true) — immediately blocks login; use when you cannot yet deactivate (user is in a default workflow user, assignment rule, etc.).
Deactivate (User.IsActive = false) — frees the licence.
Revoke OAuth tokens/sessions as part of offboarding (oauth-tokens-and-external-client-apps).
Reassign owned records, scheduled jobs, approvals before deactivation.
Keep an audit trail: Login History, Setup Audit Trail, Event Monitoring.



                  
                  Exam trap 
                  
                

“Disabling the user in the IdP” blocks new SSO logins but may leave existing sessions, refresh tokens and API access alive until timeout. State how you will terminate them.


Salesforce as the source of identities

User Provisioning for Connected Apps (Salesforce Identity) provisions Salesforce users to external apps such as Google Workspace, so Salesforce can drive joiner/mover/leaver for downstream SaaS.
Hub pattern: Salesforce Identity as IdP + provisioning engine for a modest app set; use a dedicated IDaaS when the app estate is large.

External users
External (customer/partner) provisioning is usually self-registration or invitation, not admin-driven:

Self-registration handler (Auth.ConfigurableSelfRegHandler) creates Contact + User.
Partner users often provisioned by a partner admin (“delegated external user administration”).
See customer-identity-and-headless-identity for licences and scale.

CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.title: Cryptography
CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.content:
Cryptography Key Terminology
Key/Encryption Key - An encryption key is an input parameter that controls the output of a cryptographic algorithm to encrypt data. The key is also required to decipher the data. An example of how this works is the following. If our key was to, “write our words using the letter following the original letter in the alphabet” we would end up with something the words “Hi There” equating to  “Ij Uifsf”. If we use our key of alphabet character + 1 to decrypt it we can easily figure out that Ij Uifsf = Hi There, but without it, it would be impossible to understand.
Key Management - This is literally the process of managing our cryptographic keys. It involves generating, exchanging, storing, using, replacing and destroying keys. It’s important to know that Salesforce Shield supports bring your own key (BYOK), which allows a customer to have full control over the encryption keys in their org instead or relying on Salesforce’s cloud generated keys. Documentation on Salesforce Key Management
Initialization Vector - The initial value used during the cipher process to encrypt data. This value is somewhat random and it is important because without it you cannot decrypt your first block of cipher text. You can still decrypt subsequent blocks but without the initialization vector it becomes impossible to decrypt the first block of your encrypted data. More info on decrypting using the initialization vector here. It’s important to note that Initialization Vectors are not meant to be kept secret. They need to be known to be able to decrypt the first block of cipher text.
Salt - The salt is a piece of pseudorandom data that is added to the input data. A salt is primarily used with one-way hashing algorithms. A good example of a salt being used is a system taking a password and adding a salt value to it before hashing the combined text. This makes it more difficult for an attacker to guess the length of the password or whatever value you were encrypting. Since the salt is random each time it’s used, there each output would look different so no one could easily guess the portion of the encrypted value that was a salt. Salts are also not meant to be kept secret, they are usually stored in a database somewhere.
Certificate - A certificate is an electronic document that contains an encryption key called the public key in addition to data like the issuer, the purpose of the cert and more. The cert is used to prove the authenticity of an entity (such as a server) that owns the private key of the certs public key. A good example of this is how secure https websites work. They register with a certificate authority who digitally signs and produces a cert for the site to store. Now, when a user traverses to the site it presents that cert with the CA’s digital signature on it to prove the sites identity. This allows the browser to verify the site is legitimate to prevent man in the middle attacks.
Block Cipher - The name given to crypto algorithms that operate on fixed length groups of bits (blocks).

Symmetric Cryptology Algorithms
These are the algorithms that rely on a symmetric key (or the same key) for encrypting and decrypting cipher text. Storing the key in a safe place is absolutely critical for these algorithms. Since you must share the key between the sender of the encrypted data and the receiver of the encrypted data it presents an opportunity for malicious individuals to intercept the key in transit, there are however ways to deal with this issue. The two main types of symmetric crypto algorithms are stream ciphers and block ciphers. Some of the most popular symmetric crypto algorithms are DES and AES. AES is supported by the Salesforce Crypto class.

Hashing Algorithms
Hashing algorithms exist to solve the problem of how to ensure the message I’ve received hasn’t been tampered with. Hashing algorithms create a digest out of plain text that cannot be reversed back into plaintext. Hashing Algorithms typically do not need or use a key as their purpose is simply to ensure the integrity of the original plaintext. Hash algorithms are used in digital signatures, MAC algorithms, generating encryption keys, creating index data, detecting duplicate data and creating message checksums. Some popular hashing algorithms include MD5 and SHA. Both MD5 and SHA are supported by the Salesforce Crypto class although MD5 has many weaknesses and should not be used.


MAC Algorithms
MAC Algorithms are similar to Hashing Algorithms in that they both generate a one-way digest of plain text but MAC algorithms are primarily created to verify the authenticity of the sender of the message as well as the authenticity of the message. To do this MAC algorithms use a key. This key must be known by both the sender and the receiver of the message. One popular MAC Algorithms is the HMAC algorithm and its variants, all of which are supported by
the Salesforce Crypto class.


Asymmetric Cryptography Algorithms
Asymmetric crypto algorithms are also often called public key crypto algorithms. These algorithms use two different keys to verify authenticity between communicating entities. The first key is referred to as the private key, which must be kept secret and the second is referred to as the public key which is ok to be shared. In these algorithms the outbound message is encrypted using the public key but it can only be decrypted by the private key. Asymmetric algorithms are typically used in two different scenarios (though there are many others). They are Message Confidentiality and Digital Signatures. RSA-SHA is the most popular asymmetric crypto algorithm and it’s supported by the Salesforce Crypto class.

How TLS (Transport Layer Security) Works
TLS is a crypto protocol that has superseded the SSL (Secure Socket Layer Protocol). It is designed to secure communication between two applications over a network. When communication is secured by TLS the communication between two parties (typically a client and a server) has one or more of the following properties:


A private connection: A symmetric encryption algorithm is used to encrypt all data transmitted between the two entities. The key that’s used for this is unique per session and is generated as part of a handshake process.


Authentic Identity: The identity of the two parties can be verified using an asymmetric algorithm that utilizes CA signed certs.


Reliable: Each message exchanged by the parties will include a MAC value to ensure that the message hasn’t been modified.


An in depth example of TLS communication starts on page 91 of the Becoming a CTA book.

How Two-way TLS Works
Two-way TLS (sometimes referred to as two-way SSL) is similar to one way TLS with one main difference. In one-way TLS the client validates the servers cert to confirm the servers identity, but the server has no way to identify the client. In many cases the server verifying a client is not super important, but sometimes it is necessary for the server to verify this when it should only be serving data to specific clients. This scenario is when two way TLS is utilized.
How to setup two way TLS in Salesforce
How to configure your client to use two way TLS in Salesforce

CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.title: Privacy and Consent Management
CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.content:
Why Care About Consent and What Info To Capture for Consent
We care about consent because we must abide by federal regulations (such as GDPR) around the world that give customers control over how their data is handled by businesses (and just because it’s the right thing to do).
The information we need to capture for consent management is:

The Individual (contact, lead, user etc)
The Data Use Purpose (Why we need the data we are capturing)
The Contact Point Type (Email, Address, Phone, etc)
The Capture Source (where we captured the data)
Effective From & Expiration (How long we would store that data)


Core Salesforce Privacy and Consent Management
The Consent Management Objects



Individual - A way to provide a single view/golden record to link together all Contact, Person Account, Lead, User, and Employee records that represent someone in your system. The individual object is then linked to other consent mgmt objects to determine what points of contact they have approved for you to communicate with them. It also stores information about an individuals global consent choices for various communication and tracking options (opting in to geolocation tracking, email marketing, etc).


Contact Point Objects (Contact Point Email, Contact Point Phone, Contact Point Address) -  These objects represent the many different points of contact for an individual, for example, if a user has 20 email addresses, 3 physical addresses, and 6 phone numbers, you would represent each of these as an individual contact point record.


Contact Point Consent - This object is tied to your contact point objects and determines their individual consent statuses for various communication types.


Contact Point Type Consent - This is used to log the types of contact methods that an individual has stated its ok for your business to contact them with (ex: Email, Phone, Mail, etc).


Brand - Brand allows you to distinguish a customers contact point consent decisions on a brand by brand basis.


Data Use Purpose - In many cases you are legally required to disclose how you are using an individuals information. This object allows you to create records for those purposes and reuse those purposes across different contact point consent and contact point consent type records


Data Use Legal Basis - This allows you to log the legal information regarding your data use purposes.



The Levels of Consent


Global Consent - This consent is managed by the individual object. If a user opts out of email on their individual object, all email communication should be turned off for that user.


Engagement Channel Consent - This consent level is managed by the ContactPointTypeConsent object. This can be used to turn off communication for all Contact Points that match this contact point type.


Contact Point Consent - This consent level is managed by the ContactPointConsent object and allows you to have your users opt out on a contact point by contact point basis. So they could opt out just a single email from email communications instead of all of their emails.


Brand Consent - This consent level allows you to get even more granular and have contacts opt out their contact points on a brand by brand basis instead of for your entire company at once.



Consent Capture Managed App
There is a free Salesforce Labs Consent Management App called Consent Capture that can be found here. It will allow you to place an easy to use (and customizable), prebuilt flow to capture consent related information.

Consent API
The Salesforce Consent API gives you the ability to track consent information across all objects that relate to consent management (Lead, Contact, Person Account, User, Individual, Contact Point, Contact Point Consent, Contact point type consent, Authorization form consent) in a single call. It can also be used to find duplicate users, contacts, leads, individuals, etc to allow you to easily link all these records to a parent Individual object. You can even find information for multiple emails or records in a single call.
The Consent API cannot locate records that have the email address protected by shield platform encryption.
More information on the Consent API here: Consent API Info

Consent Event Stream
There is a special Consent Message Handler on the Salesforce Streaming API that wraps all consent objects into a single event (Lead, Contact, Person Account, User, Individual, Contact Point, Contact Point Consent, Contact point type consent, Authorization form consent).
Consent Management Overview Video

Marketing Cloud Privacy and Consent Management
This video goes over how to sync consent data from Core SF to MC:
Video Guide on How to Sync Consent Info from Core SF to MC
Alternatively, if there is no need to sync or capture consent management info within core Salesforce, you could simply leverage the preferences center within Marketing Cloud to capture any necessary contact communication preferences for your Marketing Cloud contacts (or build a custom preferences center utilizing cloud pages).

CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.title: Session Settings
CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.content:
SF Session Settings
Session settings primarily revolve around user session timeouts and the security around them. Below you’ll find a list of each, what they are and when to use them.

Session Timeout
Timeout Value: This sets the amount of time a user can be inactive in an open session before their session ends/is terminated. SF polls user activity to make this determination every 5 minutes.
Disable Session Timeout Warning: Disables the popup that will show to users 30 seconds prior to their session ending.
Force logout on session timeout: This causes the browser to logout of SF and return to the SF login page when your SF session ends, forcing the user to login again.

Session Settings
Lock sessions to the IP address from which they originated: This is used to lock a session for a user to the original ip address their session originated from. It’s helpful in preventing session hijacking, however it can cause problems if the user logs in via a variety of browsers, mobile, or other devices at the same time.
Lock sessions to the domain in which they were first used: This means that if a user logins to Salesforce, their session is only valid for the SF domain they originally logged into and their session would not be valid on another domain (an experience cloud site perhaps). This helps to prevent the unauthorized use of a session id.
Allow employees to log in directly to an Experience Cloud site: This setting allows internal employees to use the same credentials that they use to login to SF to login to experience cloud sites they are a member of instead of needing separate sets of login credentials.
Force relogin after Login-As-User: This setting forces admins that login as a user to be logged out after logging out as that user. Suggested to be enabled to better track user activity (but it’s really irritating in practice lol)
Require HttpOnly attribute: Restricts access to session id cookie by making it non-accessible to javascript. This can potentially break managed packages and breaks the SF AJAX toolkit in some places so be careful.
Use POST requests for cross-domain sessions: This ensures that session information is stored in the body of a request which keeps session info more secure. However this can cause images to fail to load in some situations.
Enforce login IP ranges on every request: For all users that have IP restrictions, this ensures that the IP restrictions are upheld on every page request to the server, not just when they login to the org.
Enable caching and autocomplete on login page: If a user selects the “remember me” checkbox with this setting enabled it will remember the users username and pre-fill it out next time they try to login to SF.

CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.title: Shield Platform Encryption
CTA-Notes/Security/Other-Security-Capabi.content:
See also iam for Crypto class and sensitive data storage patterns.
How It Works

Encrypts data at rest using AES-256 (HSM-based key derivation)
Key = derived from master secret (Salesforce-managed, rotated 3x/year) + tenant secret (customer-managed)
Tenant secret is unique per org; can generate in Salesforce or bring your own (BYOK)
Cache-Only Key Service: store key outside Salesforce; fetched on demand; revokable instantly

Probabilistic vs Deterministic Encryption



































ProbabilisticDeterministicCiphertextDifferent every timeSame for same inputFiltering/SOQL WHERENot supportedSupportedORDER BYNot supportedNot supportedGROUP BYNot supportedNot supportedUse caseMaximum security, no filtering neededFields used in reports, list view filters
Key Trade-offs and Limitations

Encrypted fields can’t be used in criteria-based sharing rules
Probabilistic encrypted fields can’t be used in SOQL WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, MAX/MIN/COUNT_DISTINCT
Can’t sort list views by encrypted fields
Flows: can’t reference encrypted fields in filter/sort contexts; paused flow interviews may save data unencrypted
Custom fields: can’t be Unique or External ID with probabilistic encryption; can’t use in account contact relations
Can’t use with Custom Metadata Types
File encryption is all-or-nothing (can’t be enabled per file)
When you encrypt a field, existing values are NOT immediately encrypted — must sync via Encryption Statistics page
Classic encryption: 128-bit AES, only custom text fields, limited to 175 chars, not searchable, no FLS override

Best Practices

Encrypt only what is necessary
Create a key backup/archive strategy early
Test AppExchange apps before deploying with encryption
Only grant Manage Encryption Keys to authorized users
Communicate encryption impacts to users

Official References

Salesforce Help: Strengthen Your Data’s Security with Shield Platform Encryption
Architect: Data Protection Patterns (Well-Architected)

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 1. Organization-Wide Defaults
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD)

Sets the default level of access users have to each other’s records
Only way to restrict access to a record
Changes require a full sharing recalculation — can take a very long time on large orgs
Options (per object): Private, Public Read Only, Public Read/Write (and Controlled by Parent for detail objects)
For custom objects only: Grant Access Using Hierarchies — if unchecked, managers do NOT inherit access through the role hierarchy (overrides normal hierarchy rollup)
As of Spring ‘22: OWD for Products is configurable; sharing rules and manual sharing are NOT supported for Products



                  
                  Performance risk 
                  
                

Changing OWD in a large org can cause very long recalculations. Plan for a maintenance window and test in a sandbox first.


Recent changes

OWD for Products configurable (Private restricts amendment/renewal flows)

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 2. Role Hierarchy
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Role Hierarchy

Managers inherit the same access as their subordinates for standard objects (and custom objects unless Grant Access Using Hierarchies is off)
Access applies to records owned by subordinates and records shared with them
Peers within the same role do not automatically see each other’s records

Limits





























LimitValueMax roles (legacy)500 (increasable)Max roles (orgs from Spring ‘21+)5,000Non-portal roles best practice≤ 25,000Portal roles best practice≤ 100,000Max hierarchy depth (best practice)10 levels
Best Practices

Structure by manager scope top-down (CEO → SVP → VP → Manager → Rep)
Overlays (cross-org visibility): put in their own branch; use sharing rules or territory to provide cross-branch access
When territory management is enabled: flatten the role hierarchy as much as possible to avoid double complexity

Recent changes

Secure Roles Behavior: “Roles and Subordinates” sharing group renamed to “Roles and Internal Subordinates” — prevents external site users gaining unintended access; update code/flows referencing old name before the change enforces

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 3. Public Groups
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Public Groups
A public group can contain: Users, Customer Portal Users, Partner Users, Roles, Roles + Internal Subordinates, Roles + Internal and Portal Subordinates, Portal Roles, Portal Roles + Subordinates, Territories, Territories + Subordinates, other public groups (nesting — max 5 levels deep)

Group membership alone does NOT provide record access — must be the target of a sharing rule or manual share
Best practice: ≤ 100,000 public groups per org

Use Cases

Create an arbitrary cross-branch grouping and share records to it
Groups can protect shared data from rolling up the role hierarchy above the group (when used as the target rather than source of a sharing rule and the group does not include “Roles and Subordinates”)

Sharing Rules
Limits

Ownership-Based Sharing Rules

Based solely on the record owner (not record fields)
Don’t apply to private contacts
Use cases: role-based overlays, providing access across branches, peers in the same role

Criteria-Based Sharing Rules

Based on field values of the record
Use cases: share when field equals a value (e.g. Region = APAC), dynamic access based on record state

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 5. Account, Opportunity & Case Teams
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Account, Opportunity & Case Teams

Account Team, Opportunity Team, Case Team — one team per record
Team members receive configurable access: Account Access, Opportunity Access, Case Access, Contact Access
Creating a team member creates two records: a team record + an associated share record — both must be managed programmatically
Only owners, users above in hierarchy, and admins can add team members
You can’t create custom fields, validation rules, or triggers on Team objects

Use Cases

Multiple owners / shared account management
If teams are managed by an external system → integrate to sync membership via API

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 6. Territory Management (Hierarchy & ETM)
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Territory Management (Hierarchy & ETM)

A second hierarchy (in addition to role hierarchy) — single-dimensional, structured by any business dimension
Applies to: Account, Opportunity, and master/detail children of those objects
When enabled: you manage both hierarchies — sharing is more complex
Best practice: keep territory hierarchy to ≤ 10 levels; flatten role hierarchy
Limit: 500 territories per org (increasable)
Using both role hierarchy and territory hierarchy identically causes unnecessary sharing activity

Enterprise Territory Management Features





























ConceptDescriptionTerritory TypeCategorises territories; used for organising only — not shown in hierarchyTerritory Type PriorityNumeric scheme to help choose the right typeTerritory ModelComplete territory management system; only one can be Active at a timeTerritory HierarchyStructure within a model; shows account/user assignmentsTerritory Model StatePlanning, Active, Archived; can’t reactivate Archived

Territory model limits: 4 models (Unlimited/Performance/Developer), 2 models (Enterprise); up to 1,000 territories per model (increasable to 99,999)
Account territory sharing rules become available only after Territory Management is enabled
Filter-based Opportunity Territory Assignment: Apex class assigns territories to opportunities based on account territory assignments



                  
                  CTA decision point 
                  
                

Use Enterprise Territory Management when: (1) multiple teams need read/read-write to the same accounts, (2) an additional hierarchy different from role hierarchy is needed, or (3) a single user must hold multiple levels in the hierarchy (GAM scenario).

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 7. Manual Sharing
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Manual Sharing

Record owner (or admin, or user above in hierarchy) can grant read/edit to individual users, groups, or roles
Removed when record owner changes or when the sharing no longer grants additional access
Only manual share row cause records (not Apex sharing reasons) can be created on standard objects
Manual shares with RowCause="Manual" are deleted on owner transfer; Apex sharing reason records survive owner transfer

Use when no declarative mechanism meets requirements, or an external system of truth drives access
Available only for custom objects (Apex sharing reasons)

No other method meets requirements
External system of truth will drive access via integration
Poor performance with native sharing at very large data volumes
Team-like functionality needed on custom objects

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 9. Implicit Sharing

Implicit Sharing
Implicit sharing is automatic — cannot be turned on or off.
Parent Implicit Sharing

If a user has access to a child record (opportunity, case, contact), they get Read Only access to the parent account

If a user owns or has access to an account, they have access to the account’s associated child records

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 21. Record-Level Access Architecture
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Record-Level Access Architecture
When a user accesses any record/list view/report, Salesforce queries pre-calculated sharing data rather than recalculating in real time.
The Four Access Grant Types

























TypeDescriptionExplicitRecord shared directly to a user/group via ownership, sharing rule, assignment rule, team membership, or manual shareGroup MembershipUser inherits access because they are a member of a group that has an explicit grantInheritedUser/group inherits access through a role or territory hierarchy (manager inherits from subordinate)ImplicitNon-configurable built-in sharing (parent-child on Account)
Database Tables

Object Record Table — stores records and indicates owner (user, group, or queue)
Object Sharing Table (__Share) — stores explicit and implicit grants; exists unless object is a detail in MD relationship OR both OWDs are Public Read/Write or Controlled by Parent OR object type doesn’t support sharing tables
Group Maintenance Tables — membership data for every group; system-defined groups exist for every role hierarchy node:

Role group — direct members = users in that role; managers are indirect members
RolesAndSubordinates group — shares record with role and all subordinates
RoleAndInternalSubordinates group — same as above but excludes portal users

Sharing Recalculation
Changes that trigger recalculation: OWD change, sharing rule create/edit/delete, user role change, role move, group membership change, territory change, portal account owner change.
Tools for Large-Scale Realignments





















ToolPurposeGranular LockingAllow concurrent group maintenance in disjoint branchesParallel Sharing Rule RecalculationSplits large recalculation into parallel async jobs; resilient to server restartsDeferred Sharing Maintenance”Turns off” sharing processing during bulk changes; full recalculation runs at end of maintenance window
Performance Best Practices

Process hierarchy changes bottom-up (leaf nodes first, then upward) to avoid duplicate work
Limit records per owner to < 10,000
Remove redundant sharing (sharing rules that duplicate hierarchy access)
Schedule large group membership operations off-peak
Implement retry logic for group membership lock exceptions
Tune batch sizes for max throughput using Bulk API

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: 23. Data Skew (Ownership & Parent-Child)
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
Data Skew (Ownership & Parent-Child)
Ownership Data Skew

Single user owns > 10,000 records of an object → ownership data skew
Moving such a user in the hierarchy causes long-running transactions
Fix: distribute ownership; if a high-volume owner must have a role, place them at the top of the hierarchy in their own branch and never move them; don’t add them to public groups used as sharing rule sources

Parent-Child Data Skew



10,000 child records under one parent account → data skew


Causes locking when any child record loses access (Salesforce must scan all other children)
Fix: limit accounts to < 10,000 children; consider Public Read/Write OWD to avoid implicit share calculations; batch redistributions during off-peak hours

CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.title: Data Security
CTA-Notes/Security/Permissions--and--Sha.content:
This section covers data encryption, data masking, data restoration and data destruction.

Data Encryption
Data encryption can be done at rest or in transit. It’s goal is to mask the data to avoid data leaks, breaches, etc.
Encryption in Transit
Encryption in transit is normally achieved by encrypting a message before it is transmitted and decrypting it at its destination. This is done to prevent attackers from intercepting the data in transit (man in the middle attacks). This is normally dealt with by using a secure HTTPS channel
Encryption at Rest
Encryption at rest is the act of storing data that is encrypted, which makes it impossible to read or display the data without having an encryption key to decrypt it. This protects the system from attackers who gain access to the database where the data is stored.
The difference between Encryption and Masking
Encryption is the act of essentially scrambling data in the database itself, the only way to unscramble that data is with a complex key. Masking on the other hand is the act of hiding data from the eyes of an end users (for instance only seeing the last four digits of a credit card), but it does not include encrypting the data in the database, just at the time of viewing.
More info here: Encryption vs Masking

Salesforce Encryption Options
If you must use one of these for your solution it should be present on your system landscape diagram.
Salesforce Classic Encryption
This is the free data encryption option that comes with Salesforce OOTB. It only allows for 128 bit AES. It is very limited in comparison to Shield encryption (more below). It does however support masking, whereas Shield currently does not. It cannot encrypt standard fields.
Salesforce Shield Platform Encryption
Shield is a more robust encryption solution (as opposed to OOTB encryption) that allows you to provide encryption at rest for the data in your Salesforce environment. This encryption can be done to files, records and search index files.

More Info on Encryption Options
More info on the differences between Shield and Classic encryption
There are tons of tradeoffs when encrypting data in Salesforce. Make sure to know what you’re going to lose by encrypting your fields (classic tradeoffs are listed in the classic link above):
Shield Tradeoffs

Data Restoration
In your data governance strategy you should provide a data restoration (backup and restore) strategy. This could be done using an ETL (extract transfer load) custom solution, but it’s preferable to use a product such as OwnBackup, Druva or Flosum’s addon for backup and recovery.
